children.title: Trajectory Regularities
children.top_down_role: Classical, weak, mild, bounded-variation, and measure-driven trajectory settings.

assumptions_latex: \(I=[0,T]\) and trajectories take values in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(A\) generates a strongly continuous semigroup \(S\) when the mild formulation is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected regularity determines whether the dynamics holds pointwise, almost everywhere, in integral form, or as a measure identity.

notation.meaning: strongly continuous semigroup generated by A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional trajectories, with a semigroup formulation included for mild solutions.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.1 Differential Inclusions and Their Discrete Approximations p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trajectory \(x:I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is classical if \(x\in C^1(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\); weak or absolutely continuous if \(x\in W^{1,1}(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\) and its differential relation holds almost everywhere; mild for \(\dot x=Ax+f\) if \(x(t)=S(t)x(0)+\int_0^tS(t-s)f(s)\,ds\); of bounded variation if \(x\in BV(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\); and measure-driven if its distributional derivative \(Dx\) is a finite vector measure satisfying the prescribed measure differential relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical, weak, mild, bounded-variation, and measure-driven trajectories differ by regularity and by the pointwise, integral, or measure interpretation of their dynamics.
knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory Regularities

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1.1 Differential Inclusions and Their Discrete Approximations p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record combines finite-dimensional classical, Sobolev, BV, and measure-driven trajectories with a semigroup mild formulation, but the cited differential-inclusion section does not specifically support all of these distinct settings. The mild formula also leaves the domain of the generator and the integrability of f unstated. A source covering this full taxonomy, or separate sources for the semigroup and BV/measure formulations, is required before the mathematical version can be fixed reliably.

children.title: Dynamic Set-Valued Data
children.top_down_role: Measurability, semicontinuity, compactness, convexity, and state regularity of evolving multifunctions.

assumptions_latex: \(I=[0,T]\), and \(F:I\times\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) has nonempty values.
The Lebesgue sigma-algebra is used on \(I\), and Borel sigma-algebras are used on Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These conditions specify a standard finite-dimensional regularity package for dynamic multifunctions.

notation.meaning: closed unit ball in the codomain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonautonomous multifunctions with explicitly defined time measurability and an integrable growth bound.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.3 Elementary set-valued analysis p. 138
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dynamic set-valued data satisfy the stated regularity package if: for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and every open set \(O\subset\mathbb{R}^m\), the set \(\{t\in I:F(t,x)\cap O\neq\varnothing\}\) is Lebesgue measurable; for almost every \(t\in I\), the map \(x\mapsto F(t,x)\) is outer semicontinuous and compact-valued; and there exist \(a\in L^1(I;[0,\infty))\) and \(b\geq0\) such that \(F(t,x)\subseteq (a(t)+b\lVert x\rVert)\mathbb{B}\) for almost every \(t\in I\) and every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). In the convex-valued variant, \(F(t,x)\) is also convex for almost every \(t\in I\) and every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularity package consists of measurable dependence on time, outer-semicontinuous compact-valued dependence on state, a nonnegative integrable growth bound, and, in the convex variant, convex values.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Set-Valued Data

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.3 Elementary set-valued analysis p. 138

children.title: Dynamic Tangent-Normal Duality
children.top_down_role: Tangent, normal, projection, and prox-regular geometry used to encode feasible velocities and reactions.

children.title: Dynamic Tangent Geometry
children.top_down_role: Time-dependent tangent constructions used to organize feasible velocities.

assumptions_latex: \(C:I\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) has closed graph.
\((t,x)\in\operatorname{gph}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A velocity \(v\) is dynamically tangent to \(C\) at \((t,x)\) exactly when \((1,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}C}(t,x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based contingent geometry for a finite-dimensional moving set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dynamic contingent tangent set of \(C\) at \((t,x)\) is \[\mathcal{T}_C(t,x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(1,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}C}(t,x)\}.\] Equivalently, \(v\in\mathcal{T}_C(t,x)\) when there exist \(h_k\downarrow0\), \(v_k\to v\), and points \(x_k\in C(t+h_k)\) such that \(x_k=x+h_kv_k\). This cone records first-order state velocities compatible with forward motion of time and the moving constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic tangent velocities are precisely state components of graph-tangent directions whose time component equals one.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Tangent Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-tangent construction fits the leaf and the definition role, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied. The sequential characterization also needs an explicit restriction ensuring t+h_k belongs to I, particularly at the terminal endpoint. Source support is required before choosing the appropriate endpoint convention.

children.title: Dynamic Normal Geometry
children.top_down_role: Time-dependent normal constructions used to organize constraint reactions.

assumptions_latex: \(C:I\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) has locally closed graph.
\((t,x)\in\operatorname{gph}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dynamic normals are the time-state covectors in the limiting normal cone to the graph of the moving set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting normal geometry of the space-time graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dynamic limiting normal cone of \(C\) at \((t,x)\) is \[\mathcal{N}_C(t,x):=N_{\operatorname{gph}C}(t,x)\subset\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n.\] Thus \((\tau,\xi)\in\mathcal{N}_C(t,x)\) precisely when there are \((t_k,x_k)\to(t,x)\) with \(x_k\in C(t_k)\) and \((\tau_k,\xi_k)\to(\tau,\xi)\), where \((\tau_k,\xi_k)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}C}(t_k,x_k)\). The component \(\tau\) captures temporal sensitivity and \(\xi\) captures the state-normal reaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic normal is a limiting normal covector to the space-time graph, with separate temporal and state components.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Normal Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limiting-normal definition is mathematically standard and fits Dynamic Normal Geometry, but the record supplies no citation. An authoritative locator for limiting normals to locally closed graphs is required.

children.title: Tangent–Normal Duality
children.top_down_role: Geometric correspondences linking feasible motion with reaction directions.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a nonempty index set, \(C:I\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(C(t)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(t\in I\).
Fix \(t\in I\) and \(x\in C(t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex normal cone and contingent tangent cone to the time slice are mutually negative polar.

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to the time slice
contingent tangent cone to the time slice

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slice-wise convex polar duality; this is not a claim about the full space-time graph cones.

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define its negative polar by \(K^\circ:=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle\xi,v\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }v\in K\}\). Define the convex normal cone by \(N_{C(t)}(x):=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle\xi,w-x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }w\in C(t)\}\). Then \[N_{C(t)}(x)=T_{C(t)}(x)^\circ\quad\text{and}\quad T_{C(t)}(x)=N_{C(t)}(x)^\circ.\] Consequently, \(v\in T_{C(t)}(x)\) if and only if \(\langle\xi,v\rangle\leq0\) for every \(\xi\in N_{C(t)}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every closed convex time slice, its convex normal cone and contingent tangent cone are mutually negative polar, so tangent velocities pair nonpositively with every normal vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangent–Normal Duality

source_witnesses.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Projection Geometry for Moving Sets
children.top_down_role: Projection structures associated with evolving feasible regions.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a nonempty index set, \(C:I\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(C(t)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(t\in I\).
Fix \(t\in I\) and \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection onto the time slice is unique, and its residual belongs to the convex normal cone at the projected point.

notation.meaning: Euclidean metric projection onto the time slice
convex normal cone to the time slice

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Euclidean projection geometry for closed convex slices of a moving set.

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a unique point \(y=P_{C(t)}(z)\). For \(y\in C(t)\), the following conditions are equivalent: \[y=P_{C(t)}(z),\qquad \langle z-y,w-y\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }w\in C(t),\qquad z-y\in N_{C(t)}(y).\] Thus projection can be applied separately to each time slice, and the projection residual is a normal vector to the current slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto each nonempty closed convex time slice is unique and is characterized by the projection residual belonging to the convex normal cone at the projected point.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Geometry for Moving Sets

source_witnesses.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Dynamic Prox-Regularity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes where regular projection or normal behavior deteriorates.

assumptions_latex: The moving set is constant: \(C(t)=\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) for every \(t\), with \(n\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At the reach boundary, metric projection can lose uniqueness even though the set is smooth and uniformly prox-regular below that radius.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp projection-uniqueness boundary illustrated by the unit sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unit sphere \(C(t)=\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\) has reach \(1\), so every point \(z\) satisfying \(0<\operatorname{dist}(z,C(t))<1\) has a unique nearest point. At the center, however, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,C(t))=1\) and \[P_{C(t)}(0)=\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.\] Thus uniqueness guaranteed inside the prox-regularity tube need not extend to its boundary. Any dynamic argument requiring a single-valued projection must keep the state strictly within the asserted uniform prox-regularity radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection uniqueness may fail exactly at the prox-regularity radius: every point of the unit sphere projects the center at distance one.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Prox-Regularity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sphere example is a correct failure-boundary phenomenon and the selected content kind is exact, but no source is supplied for the reach-one assertion or its interpretation as a sharp prox-regularity boundary. An inspectable source locator is required.

children.title: Dynamic Variational Convergence
children.top_down_role: Graphical, Mosco, epigraphical, moving-set, and trajectory convergence interfaces.

assumptions_latex: \(C_k,C:I\rightrightarrows H\), where \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
All stated convergence conditions are imposed for almost every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dynamic Mosco convergence combines weak sequential stability of feasible limits with strong recoverability of every limiting feasible state.

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Hilbert space
strong convergence in the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise-almost-everywhere Mosco convergence of Hilbert-space moving sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \(C_k\) converges dynamically in the Mosco sense to \(C\) when, for almost every \(t\), both conditions hold: if \(x_{k_j}\in C_{k_j}(t)\) and \(x_{k_j}\rightharpoonup x\), then \(x\in C(t)\); and for every \(x\in C(t)\), there exist \(x_k\in C_k(t)\) with \(x_k\to x\). The first condition is the weak outer-limit inequality, while the second is strong recovery. Additional temporal estimates are required to infer convergence of trajectories selected from these sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic Mosco convergence requires weak closure of feasible limits and strong recovery of every feasible state at almost every time.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Variational Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two pointwise conditions are the standard Mosco conditions for each fixed time, and the record carefully avoids claiming trajectory convergence without temporal estimates. However, no source supports the almost-everywhere dynamic formulation or the terminology used for it, so an authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Explicit Velocity Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Evolution governed by directly specified admissible-velocity maps.

assumptions_latex: \(I=[0,T]\), \(F:I\times\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) has nonempty values, and \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solution is an absolutely continuous curve whose derivative belongs to the specified admissible-velocity set almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard nonautonomous explicit differential inclusion in Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.1 Differential Inclusions and Their Discrete Approximations p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The explicit velocity inclusion with initial state \(x_0\) is \[\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in I,\qquad x(0)=x_0.\] A solution is a trajectory \(x\in AC(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\) satisfying these relations. Equivalently, there exists \(v\in L^1(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\) such that \(v(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) for almost every \(t\in I\) and \(x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t v(s)\,ds\) for every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit velocity inclusion directly constrains the almost-everywhere derivative of an absolutely continuous trajectory through an admissible-velocity multifunction.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Velocity Inclusions

children.title: Implicit Velocity Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Evolution formulations in which admissible velocities are specified through implicit relations.

assumptions_latex: \(I=[0,T]\), \(G:I\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admissible velocities are defined implicitly as those for which the residual multifunction contains the zero vector.

notation.meaning: set-valued residual defining the velocity constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-form implicit velocity inclusion in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Optimization of Differential-Algebraic Inclusions with Delays p. 336
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((t,x)\in I\times\mathbb{R}^n\), define \[V(t,x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:0_{\mathbb{R}^m}\in G(t,x,v)\}.\] The implicit velocity inclusion with initial state \(x_0\) requires \(x\in AC(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\) and \[0_{\mathbb{R}^m}\in G(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in I,\qquad x(0)=x_0.\] Equivalently, \(\dot x(t)\in V(t,x(t))\) for almost every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit velocity inclusion defines admissible derivatives as the velocities for which a state-and-velocity residual multifunction contains the zero vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Velocity Inclusions

children.title: Differential-Algebraic Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Set-valued evolution constrained by simultaneous algebraic relations.

assumptions_latex: \(I=[0,T]\), \(F:I\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^q\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\), \(G:I\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^q\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A differential-algebraic inclusion couples an absolutely continuous differential state with a measurable auxiliary state satisfying an instantaneous algebraic inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order finite-dimensional differential-algebraic inclusion without delays.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Optimization of Differential-Algebraic Inclusions with Delays p. 336
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

source_refs.locator: 7.1.1 Discrete Approximations of Differential-Algebraic Inclusions p. 338
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A differential-algebraic inclusion seeks \(x\in AC(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\) and a measurable map \(y:I\to\mathbb{R}^q\) such that \[\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t),y(t))\quad\text{and}\quad 0_{\mathbb{R}^m}\in G(t,x(t),y(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in I,\] together with \(x(0)=x_0\). The first inclusion governs the differential state, while the second constrains the instantaneous pair \((x(t),y(t))\) without prescribing a derivative of \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differential-algebraic inclusion combines the differential evolution of an absolutely continuous state with an instantaneous set-valued algebraic constraint on a measurable auxiliary state.
knowledge_statements.title: Differential-Algebraic Inclusions

children.title: State–Velocity Constraint Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interfaces between evolving states, admissible velocities, and constraint variables.

assumptions_latex: \(K:I\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\) is a state-velocity constraint multifunction.
\(F:I\times\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is an admissible-velocity map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The actual derivative must belong simultaneously to the dynamic velocity set and the velocity fiber allowed by the coupled constraint.

notation.meaning: state-velocity constraint set at time t
velocity fiber of K at state x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coupling through a time-dependent constraint on state-velocity pairs.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Optimization of Differential-Algebraic Inclusions with Delays p. 336
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \((t,x)\), define the feasible velocity fiber \[K_t(x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(x,v)\in K(t)\}.\] A trajectory \(x\in AC(I;\mathbb{R}^n)\) satisfies the coupled state-velocity constraint when \[\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\cap K_t(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in I.\] Equivalently, both \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) and \((x(t),\dot x(t))\in K(t)\) must hold almost everywhere; feasibility requires their intersection to be nonempty along the trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State-velocity coupling requires each derivative to satisfy both the dynamic inclusion and a joint constraint on the current state and velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: State–Velocity Constraint Coupling

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Optimization of Differential-Algebraic Inclusions with Delays p. 336
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

A specific source locator for joint state-velocity constraints is required before selecting the corrected formulation.

children.title: Constraint Consistency Regimes
children.top_down_role: Initial and evolving configurations compatible with the algebraic constraint structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Consistency Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and trajectory consistency for an implicit differential-algebraic inclusion; neither condition alone asserts local extendability or continuation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(t\in[0,T]\), define
\[V(t,x,z):=\{v\in X:0_Y\in\Phi(t,x,z,v)\},\qquad \mathcal C(t):=\{(x,z)\in X\times Z:0_W\in\Psi(t,x,z),\ V(t,x,z)\neq\varnothing\}.\]
An initial datum \((t_0,x_0,z_0)\) is called pointwise consistent when \((x_0,z_0)\in\mathcal C(t_0)\). An absolutely continuous pair \((x,z):I\to X\times Z\) is called trajectory-consistent when
\[(x(t),z(t))\in\mathcal C(t),\qquad \dot x(t)\in V(t,x(t),z(t))\]
for almost every \(t\in I\). These definitions express instantaneous algebraic and velocity feasibility but do not by themselves guarantee a locally feasible trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise consistency means that the algebraic inclusion holds and at least one velocity is admissible. Trajectory consistency requires algebraic feasibility and the actual velocity inclusion almost everywhere, without asserting existence or continuation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\), \(Z\), \(Y\), and \(W\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces, with zero elements \(0_Y\) and \(0_W\).
\(\Phi:[0,T]\times X\times Z\times X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(\Psi:[0,T]\times X\times Z\rightrightarrows W\) are multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership \((x_0,z_0)\in\mathcal C(t_0)\) defines pointwise algebraic and velocity feasibility at \(t_0\), but does not alone imply local trajectory existence.

notation.meaning: Pointwise consistent state–algebraic pairs at time t
Admissible velocities at a state–algebraic pair

\(F:I\times X\rightrightarrows X\) has nonempty values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A solution of the nonautonomous differential inclusion with initial state \(x_0\in X\) is a curve \(x\in AC(I;X)\) satisfying
\[x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad \dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in I.\]
The inclusion is nonautonomous because the admissible-velocity set depends explicitly on \(t\). Any endpoint or state constraint is additional data and is not part of this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonautonomous inclusion is solved by an absolutely continuous curve whose derivative belongs almost everywhere to a velocity set depending explicitly on time and state.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonautonomous Differential Inclusions

children.title: Hereditary Inclusion Family
children.top_down_role: Set-valued evolution depending on trajectory history.

children.title: Discrete-Delay Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Set-valued evolution driven by finitely lagged trajectory values.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Delay Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retarded inclusion with finitely many exogenous, time-dependent delays and a continuous prescribed history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A discrete-delay inclusion trajectory is a function \(x\in C([-r,T];X)\) whose restriction to \([0,T]\) is absolutely continuous and which satisfies
\[x(s)=\varphi(s)\quad\text{for }s\in[-r,0],\qquad \dot x(t)\in F\bigl(t,x(t),x(t-\tau_1(t)),\ldots,x(t-\tau_m(t))\bigr)\]
for almost every \(t\in[0,T]\). The bounds \(0\leq\tau_j(t)\leq r\) ensure that each delayed time belongs to \([-r,T]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The current velocity belongs almost everywhere to a multifunction evaluated at the current state and finitely many delayed states, with negative-time values supplied by the prescribed history.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space, \(r>0\), and \(\varphi\in C([-r,0];X)\) is prescribed.
\(m\in\mathbb N\), and \(\tau_j:[0,T]\to[0,r]\) is measurable for each \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
\(F:[0,T]\times X^{m+1}\rightrightarrows X\) is a velocity multifunction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The history condition and delayed almost-everywhere inclusion define a discrete-delay trajectory.

children.title: Distributed-Memory Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Evolution governed by aggregated trajectory history over a time interval.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(r>0\), and \(x\in C([-r,T];X)\) has prescribed history on \([-r,0]\).
For each \(t\), \(K(t,\cdot)\) is integrable on \([-r,0]\), and \(g:X\to E\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusion is hereditary because its admissible velocity depends on the distributed history statistic \(M_x(t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-memory convolution-type statistic; more general history-space functionals are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the distributed memory statistic, whenever the Bochner integral exists, by
\[M_x(t):=\int_{-r}^{0}K(t,\theta)g(x(t+\theta))\,d\theta.\]
A distributed-memory inclusion trajectory is a curve whose restriction to \([0,T]\) is absolutely continuous and which satisfies
\[\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t),M_x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].\]
Unlike a discrete-delay inclusion, the velocity depends on a continuum of past states through the weighted statistic \(M_x(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed-memory inclusion makes the current velocity depend on an integral statistic of a continuum of past states rather than finitely many delayed samples.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed-Memory Inclusions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No inspectable source is supplied, and the spaces and mapping properties needed to define the Bochner-integral memory operator are underspecified. The mathematical version cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: State-Dependent Delay Inclusions
children.top_down_role: History-dependent dynamics whose effective lag varies with the evolving state.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(r>0\), and \(x\in C([-r,T];X)\) has prescribed history.
The delay functional \(\tau:[0,T]\times C([-r,0];X)\to[0,r]\) is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed relation defines a retarded state-dependent delay inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retarded state-dependent delay using the full recent history as the delay functional's argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t\in[0,T]\), let the history segment \(x_t\in C([-r,0];X)\) be defined by \(x_t(\theta)=x(t+\theta)\). A state-dependent delay inclusion trajectory is continuous on \([-r,T]\), absolutely continuous on \([0,T]\), and satisfies
\[\dot x(t)\in F\bigl(t,x(t),x(t-\tau(t,x_t))\bigr)\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].\]
The range condition \(0\le\tau(t,x_t)\le r\) makes the delayed evaluation well-defined from the recent history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The delay is itself determined by the current history segment, so both the sampling time and the delayed state vary with the evolving trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: State-Dependent Delay Inclusions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard state-dependent-delay form fits the leaf, but no source is supplied and the velocity multifunction's domain and codomain are unspecified.

children.title: Memory-State Representations
children.top_down_role: Extended-state formulations that encode trajectory history as an evolving component.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(r>0\), and \(x\in C([-r,T];X)\).
The history space is \(\mathcal H=C([-r,0];X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hereditary equation is represented as a current-state/history-state evolution subject to the compatibility condition \(h(t)(0)=x(t)\).

notation.meaning: Left-translation generator on the history variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-delay history lifting; the transport equation is understood in the mild sense unless additional regularity holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(h(t):=x_t\in\mathcal H\), where \(h(t)(\theta)=x(t+\theta)\). Then a hereditary inclusion
\[\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t),x_t)\]
is represented on \(X\times\mathcal H\) by
\[\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t),h(t)),\qquad \partial_t h(t,\theta)=\partial_\theta h(t,\theta),\qquad h(t,0)=x(t).\]
Equivalently, the history component follows left translation generated by \(A h=h'\), with its boundary value coupled to the current state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A delay equation can be lifted to a current-state plus history-state system, where the history evolves by translation and its boundary equals the current state.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory-State Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but no source supports the history-space lifting. For merely continuous histories, the displayed transport PDE requires a precise mild or generator-domain interpretation that is not stated in the formula.

children.title: Euler–Polygonal Constructions
children.top_down_role: Time-discrete compactness constructions for inclusion trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) has nonempty compact values and an integrable growth bound.
A partition \(0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T\) and initial state \(x_0\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an absolutely continuous polygonal curve satisfying \(\dot x_h(t)=v_k\) on each open mesh interval.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit Euler construction with frozen left-endpoint velocities and piecewise-affine interpolation.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.1 Differential Inclusions and Their Discrete Approximations p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_0^h=x_0\). For \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\), choose
\[v_k\in F(t_k,x_k^h),\qquad x_{k+1}^h=x_k^h+h_kv_k.\]
Define the Euler polygon by
\[x_h(t):=x_k^h+(t-t_k)v_k\quad\text{for }t\in[t_k,t_{k+1}].\]
Stop after \(k=N-1\) and output \(x_h\). For a refining sequence of partitions, compactness estimates may be applied to convergent subsequences; such convergence is not asserted by the construction alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an admissible velocity at each left mesh point, take an explicit Euler step, and interpolate the resulting states by affine segments.
knowledge_statements.title: Euler–Polygonal Constructions

children.title: Selection-Fixed-Point Construction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Existence routes using selections and trajectory-space fixed points.

children.title: Measurable-Selection Constructions
children.top_down_role: Existence constructions based on measurable representatives of set-valued dynamics.

assumptions_latex: \((S,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a complete finite measure space and \(Y\) is Polish.
\(G:S\rightrightarrows Y\) has nonempty closed values and measurable graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a measurable selector \(g:S\to Y\) satisfying \(g(s)\in G(s)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(s\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-valued measurable selection in a Polish range, stated in the almost-everywhere form used for velocity choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((S,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a complete finite measure space and let \(Y\) be a Polish space. Suppose \(G:S\rightrightarrows Y\) has nonempty closed values and
\[\operatorname{gph}G:=\{(s,y)\in S\times Y:y\in G(s)\}\]
is measurable in \(\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\). Then there exists a \(\Sigma\)-measurable function \(g:S\to Y\) such that \(g(s)\in G(s)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(s\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-valued multifunction with measurable graph and Polish range admits a measurable pointwise choice, up to a null set.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable-Selection Constructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is correctly classified as a theorem, but no citation is supplied. The exact measurable-graph selection theorem and its measure-space completeness hypotheses require authoritative support.

children.title: Continuous-Selection Constructions
children.top_down_role: Existence routes using continuous representatives under suitable selection structure.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is paracompact and \(Y\) is a Banach space.
\(G:S\rightrightarrows Y\) is lower semicontinuous with nonempty closed convex values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a continuous selector \(g:S\to Y\) with \(g(s)\in G(s)\) for every \(s\in S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Michael-type continuous selection theorem for closed convex values in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a paracompact topological space and \(Y\) a Banach space. If \(G:S\rightrightarrows Y\) is lower semicontinuous and every \(G(s)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then there exists a continuous map \(g:S\to Y\) such that
\[g(s)\in G(s)\quad\text{for every }s\in S.\]
Thus the multifunction admits a globally continuous single-valued selection under the stated topological and convexity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous multifunction from a paracompact space into a Banach space has a continuous selector when all values are nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Selection Constructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Michael-type theorem is standard and correctly classified, but the record supplies no inspectable citation with a theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Trajectory-Space Fixed Points
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point frameworks posed on spaces of candidate trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory-Space Fixed Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral fixed-point formulation; a separate fixed-point theorem supplies existence after its compactness and continuity hypotheses are verified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(y\in K\), define
\[\Gamma(y):=\left\{x\in K:\exists v\in L^1([0,T];X),\ v(t)\in F(t,y(t))\ \text{for a.e. }t,\ x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t v(s)\,ds\ \text{for every }t\in[0,T]\right\}.\]
If \(x\in\Gamma(x)\), then \(x\) is absolutely continuous, \(x(0)=x_0\), and
\[\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].\]
Thus every fixed point of \(\Gamma\) is a trajectory of the differential inclusion; this implication does not itself assert that a fixed point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Freeze a candidate trajectory in the velocity multifunction, integrate an admissible velocity selection, and seek a trajectory reproduced by the resulting integral multifunction. Any such fixed point solves the inclusion, although its existence requires a separate fixed-point theorem.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space, \(x_0\in X\), and \(K\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of \(C([0,T];X)\).
\(F:[0,T]\times X\rightrightarrows X\) is a multifunction for which every \(y\in K\) admits some \(v\in L^1([0,T];X)\) satisfying \(v(t)\in F(t,y(t))\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fixed point \(x\in K\) satisfying \(x\in\Gamma(x)\) is an absolutely continuous solution of \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) with \(x(0)=x_0\).

children.title: Selection–Fixed-Point Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing how selected velocities support a fixed-point construction.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset C([0,T];X)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
For every \(y\in K\), the selection set \(S_F(y):=\{v\in L^1:v(t)\in F(t,y(t))\text{ a.e.}\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three displayed requirements make the selection-based integral operator compatible with a trajectory-space fixed-point argument.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate separating selection existence, invariance, and fixed-point regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[\Gamma(y):=\left\{x_0+\int_0^{\cdot}v(s)\,ds:v\in S_F(y)\right\}.\]
A selection–fixed-point construction is compatible on \(K\) when
\[S_F(y)\neq\varnothing\ \text{for every }y\in K,\qquad \Gamma(K)\subset K,\]
and \(\Gamma:K\rightrightarrows K\) has the closedness or semicontinuity together with compactness properties required by the chosen fixed-point theorem. The first condition permits velocity selection, the second preserves the trajectory domain, and the third permits extraction of a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selection and fixed-point steps are compatible when selections exist, their integrated trajectories remain admissible, and the resulting operator satisfies the chosen fixed-point theorem's regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection–Fixed-Point Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, but the phrase 'properties required by the chosen fixed-point theorem' does not identify a precise theorem or explicit hypotheses. No source is supplied to determine the intended compatibility criterion.

children.title: Nonconvex Existence Theory
children.top_down_role: Existence mechanisms for nonconvex-valued and mixed-regularity multifunctions.

assumptions_latex: \(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) has nonempty compact, not necessarily convex, values.
For each \(x\), \(t\mapsto F(t,x)\) is measurable, and for almost every \(t\), \(d_H(F(t,x),F(t,y))\le k(t)\lVert x-y\rVert\).
There are \(a,b,k\in L^1(0,T)\) such that \(\sup_{v\in F(t,x)}\lVert v\rVert\le a(t)+b(t)\lVert x\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), there exists \(x\in AC([0,T];\mathbb R^n)\) with \(x(0)=x_0\) and \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Hausdorff-Lipschitz existence theorem retaining compact nonconvex velocity sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) satisfy the stated measurability, compact-valuedness, Hausdorff-Lipschitz, and integrable growth hypotheses. Then, for each \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), the Cauchy problem
\[x(0)=x_0,
\qquad \dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T]
\]
has at least one solution \(x\in AC([0,T];\mathbb R^n)\). Convexity of the values \(F(t,x)\) is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measurability, compact values, integrable growth, and Hausdorff-Lipschitz state dependence ensure a trajectory exists even when the velocity sets are nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Existence Theory

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and finite-dimensional nonconvex scope fit the leaf, but this existence result has no authoritative citation. Its exact measurability, common-null-set, Hausdorff-Lipschitz, and growth hypotheses require source verification.

children.title: Global-Continuation Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Continuation alternatives and obstructions to global trajectories.

children.title: Local Trajectory Extension
children.top_down_role: Extension of solution arcs beyond their current time intervals.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and \(F:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact convex values and is locally bounded.
\(x:[0,T)\to D\) is absolutely continuous on compact subintervals and satisfies \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) for almost every \(t<T\).
For some \(t_0<T\), the tail \(x([t_0,T))\) lies in a compact set \(K\subset D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and an absolutely continuous \(\widetilde x:[0,T+\varepsilon]\to D\) such that \(\widetilde x(t)=x(t)\) for \(0\le t<T\) and \(\dot{\widetilde x}(t)\in F(\widetilde x(t))\) for almost every \(t\in[0,T+\varepsilon]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional autonomous differential inclusions with compact convex velocity values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let \(F:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be upper semicontinuous, locally bounded, and nonempty compact convex valued. Suppose \(x:[0,T)\to D\) is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) almost everywhere. If a terminal tail of \(x\) is contained in some compact set \(K\subset D\), then \(x(t)\) has a limit \(x_T\in K\) as \(t\uparrow T\), and local existence from \(x_T\) yields an extension \(\widetilde x\) to \([0,T+\varepsilon]\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-time trajectory whose terminal tail remains in a compact subset of the domain can be continued beyond its endpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Trajectory Extension

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Local Trajectory Extension, but it must explicitly assume a finite terminal time T. The final clause sketches a proof, and no inspectable source is cited for the continuation hypotheses or conclusion.

children.title: Maximal Trajectories
children.top_down_role: Trajectory families organized by nonextendability.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and \(F:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(x:[0,T)\to D\) is a trajectory of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\), where \(0<T\le\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trajectory \(x\) is maximal precisely when no \(T'>T\) and no trajectory \(y:[0,T')\to D\) satisfy \(y(t)=x(t)\) for every \(t<T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximality is ordered by extension while preserving the initial time and trajectory history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trajectory \(x:[0,T)\to D\) of the differential inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) is maximal if it has no proper trajectory extension: there do not exist \(T'>T\) and a trajectory \(y:[0,T')\to D\) satisfying the same inclusion such that \(y(t)=x(t)\) for all \(t\in[0,T)\). Maximality concerns extension of the parametrized trajectory, not maximality of its image as a subset of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trajectory is maximal when no solution on a strictly longer interval agrees with it throughout its existing interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Trajectories

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the terminal container and correctly distinguish extension maximality from maximality of the image. An inspectable definition-level source or an explicit standard-field rationale is still required.

children.title: Global Continuation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings supporting trajectories over the full prescribed horizon.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact convex values.
There exist \(a,b\ge0\) such that \(\sup_{v\in F(x)}\lVert v\rVert\le a+b\lVert x\rVert\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every maximal trajectory \(x:[0,T)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) has \(T=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard linear-growth regime excluding finite-time blow-up on the full state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact convex values. Assume that constants \(a,b\ge0\) satisfy \(\sup_{v\in F(x)}\lVert v\rVert\le a+b\lVert x\rVert\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then every maximal solution \(x:[0,T)\to\mathbb{R}^n\) of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) is global, meaning \(T=\infty\). Indeed, the growth bound prevents \(\lVert x(t)\rVert\) from becoming unbounded on a finite interval, leaving no finite-time continuation obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the full state space, compact convex dynamics with a linear velocity-growth bound admit no finite terminal time for maximal trajectories.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Continuation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear-growth global-continuation theorem is mathematically standard and fits the container, but no source supports the precise hypotheses. The sentence beginning with the growth-bound explanation is proof text and should be removed once a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Finite-Time State Escape
children.top_down_role: Loss of continuation through unbounded or noncompact state behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and \(F:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies the local existence hypotheses.
\(x:[0,T)\to D\) is maximal with \(T<\infty\).
There exists a compact set \(K\subset D\) containing \(x([0,T))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These assumptions are incompatible; equivalently, for every compact \(K\subset D\) and every \(t_0<T\), there exists \(t\in[t_0,T)\) with \(x(t)\notin K\).

notation.meaning: Maximal trajectory and finite terminal time
Arbitrary compact subset of the domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-time failure characterized as escape from every compact subset of the state domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the local extension theorem holds for \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) on an open set \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(x:[0,T)\to D\) is maximal and \(T<\infty\), then its terminal tail cannot remain in any compact subset of \(D\). Thus, for every compact \(K\subset D\) and every \(t_0<T\), some \(t\in[t_0,T)\) satisfies \(x(t)\notin K\). When \(D=\mathbb{R}^n\), this implies \(\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\lVert x(t)\rVert=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal solution ending at finite time must leave every compact subset of its domain; on the full space, its state becomes unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Time State Escape

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary claim fits the leaf, but the assumptions posit one compact set containing the whole trajectory while the conclusion states the stronger quantified escape characterization. The intended result should instead directly assume maximality and finite T, then quantify over every compact subset and terminal tail. No continuation source is supplied.

children.title: Domain-Exit Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Termination caused by departure from the admissible state domain.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and \(F:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies the local extension hypotheses.
\(x:[0,T)\to D\) is maximal, \(T<\infty\), and \(x(t)\to x_T\in\mathbb{R}^n\) as \(t\uparrow T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One necessarily has \(x_T\in\partial D\); if \(x_T\in D\), local extension would contradict maximality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded finite-time termination caused by approach to the boundary of a proper open domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and suppose the usual local existence and extension hypotheses hold for \(F:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\). If a maximal trajectory \(x:[0,T)\to D\) has \(T<\infty\) and converges to a finite point \(x_T\) as \(t\uparrow T\), then \(x_T\in\partial D\). In particular, convergence to a point of \(D\) is not an obstruction, because local existence from that point extends the trajectory. Hence bounded finite-time failure can arise from domain exit even without norm blow-up.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a bounded maximal trajectory ends in finite time and has a terminal limit, that limit must lie on the domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Exit Obstructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary-limit property fits Domain-Exit Obstructions and is correct under a valid local extension theorem, but that theorem is only referenced generically and has no source. The local-extension explanation is proof text rather than statement content.

children.top_down_role: Convexification, fine-scale approximation, and the boundary between original and relaxed dynamics.

children.title: Convexified Inclusion Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Trajectory families generated by convexified velocity fields.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a measurable-control set, and \(f:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\times U\to\mathbb{R}^n\) has measurable time dependence and sufficient state regularity for trajectories.
For each \((t,x)\), define \(F(t,x)=\{f(t,x,u):u\in U\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed trajectories are exactly the absolutely continuous maps satisfying \(\dot x(t)\in\overline{\operatorname{co}}F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere, equivalently \(\dot x(t)=\int_U f(t,x(t),u)\,\mu_t(du)\) for a measurable family \((\mu_t)\) of probability measures when the barycentric representation applies.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexification, including its relaxed-control barycentric representation.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given ordinary velocities \(F(t,x)=\{f(t,x,u):u\in U\}\), the convexified inclusion is \(\dot x(t)\in\overline{\operatorname{co}}F(t,x(t))\) for almost every \(t\in[0,T]\). A relaxed control is a measurable family of probability measures \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}\) on \(U\), and its trajectory satisfies \(\dot x(t)=\int_U f(t,x(t),u)\,\mu_t(du)\) almost everywhere. Under the standard compactness and measurability assumptions, these barycentric velocities constitute the closed convex hull of the original velocities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexified trajectories use velocities in the closed convex hull of ordinary velocities, equivalently barycenters generated by probability-valued controls.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexified Inclusion Dynamics

children.title: Chattering Approximation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Fine-scale approximation connecting relaxed and original trajectories.

children.title: Chattering Controls
children.top_down_role: Rapidly switching realizations used to represent relaxed behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(v_i:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda_i:[0,T]\to[0,1]\) are measurable for \(1\le i\le m\), with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i(t)=1\) almost everywhere.
A partition is chosen finely enough that time averages of the selected modes approximate the weights \(\lambda_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist piecewise-constant selectors \(\sigma_k:[0,T]\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that \(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\lVert\int_0^t\left(v_{\sigma_k(s)}(s)-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i(s)v_i(s)\right)ds\right\rVert\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-mode time sharing that approximates an integrable convex combination in cumulative norm.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For measurable modes \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) and weights \(\lambda_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), subdivide \([0,T]\) into cells and, within each cell, activate mode \(i\) for the fraction prescribed by the cell average of \(\lambda_i\). Refining the partition produces piecewise-constant selectors \(\sigma_k\) satisfying \(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\lVert\int_0^t(v_{\sigma_k(s)}(s)-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i(s)v_i(s))ds\right\rVert\to0\). The output at level \(k\) is the switching control \(\sigma_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rapid time sharing among finitely many modes makes their cumulative velocity converge uniformly to the prescribed convex combination.
knowledge_statements.title: Chattering Controls

children.title: Original-Trajectory Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation of relaxed motions by trajectories of the unconvexified dynamics.

assumptions_latex: \(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) has nonempty compact values, measurable time dependence, and an integrable local bound.
On a neighborhood of the relaxed trajectory, \(F(t,\cdot)\) is Lipschitz in Hausdorff distance with an integrable modulus.
\(z\) satisfies \(\dot z(t)\in\overline{\operatorname{co}}F(t,z(t))\) almost everywhere and \(z(0)=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a trajectory \(x\) of \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) with \(x(0)=x_0\) and \(\lVert x-z\rVert_\infty<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filippov-Ważewski approximation on a fixed compact time interval with the initial point preserved.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) have nonempty compact values, measurable time dependence, an integrable local bound, and an integrable Hausdorff-Lipschitz modulus in the state variable near a relaxed trajectory \(z\). If \(\dot z(t)\in\overline{\operatorname{co}}F(t,z(t))\) almost everywhere and \(z(0)=x_0\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists an original trajectory \(x\) satisfying \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere, \(x(0)=x_0\), and \(\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\lVert x(t)-z(t)\rVert<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relaxed trajectory can be uniformly approximated on a finite interval by original trajectories having the same initial state.
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Trajectory Approximation

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168

children.title: Endpoint-Preserving Approximation
children.top_down_role: Trajectory approximation organized around preservation of terminal behavior.

assumptions_latex: The hypotheses for uniform original-trajectory approximation hold for a relaxed trajectory \(z:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^n\).

There are neighborhoods \(V\) of \(z(T)\), constants \(c,\rho>0\), and admissible endpoint corrections satisfying \(\lVert y-z(T)\rVert\le c\lVert x(T)-z(T)\rVert\) and reaching \(y=z(T)\) whenever \(x(T)\in V\) and \(\lVert x-z\rVert_\infty<\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), an original trajectory \(x_\varepsilon\) exists with \(x_\varepsilon(0)=z(0)\), \(x_\varepsilon(T)=z(T)\), and \(\lVert x_\varepsilon-z\rVert_\infty<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient endpoint-correction condition; basic relaxation alone preserves only the initial endpoint exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Uniform relaxation becomes endpoint preserving if nearby terminal errors admit an admissible correction whose trajectory perturbation is controlled by that error. Concretely, suppose each sufficiently close original approximant \(x\) can be modified, without changing \(x(0)=z(0)\), to an original trajectory \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(\widehat x(T)=z(T)\) and \(\lVert\widehat x-z\rVert_\infty\le c\lVert x-z\rVert_\infty\) for a constant \(c\) independent of \(x\). Then for every \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing the preliminary approximation sufficiently close yields \(x_\varepsilon(0)=z(0)\), \(x_\varepsilon(T)=z(T)\), and \(\lVert x_\varepsilon-z\rVert_\infty<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact terminal matching requires a separate controllable endpoint-correction property; under it, uniform relaxed approximants can preserve both endpoints.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint-Preserving Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate because exact terminal matching is not supplied by basic relaxation. However, the assumptions introduce an undefined endpoint y and do not formally specify the admissible correction operation used in the statement. A source is needed to state a noncircular endpoint-correction hypothesis and its precise conclusion.

children.title: Uniform Trajectory Topologies
children.top_down_role: Uniform modes used to compare relaxed and original trajectories.

assumptions_latex: For \(x,y\in X\), define \(d_\infty(x,y)=\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\lVert x(t)-y(t)\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A sequence \((x_k)\subset X\) converges to \(x\in X\) in the uniform trajectory topology exactly when \(d_\infty(x_k,x)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong uniform topology on continuous trajectories over a common compact time interval.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=C([0,T];\mathbb{R}^n)\), the uniform trajectory topology is induced by \(d_\infty(x,y)=\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\lVert x(t)-y(t)\rVert\). Thus \(x_k\to x\) uniformly exactly when \(\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\lVert x_k(t)-x(t)\rVert\to0\). This topology controls every time point simultaneously and, in particular, implies convergence of both endpoints: \(x_k(0)\to x(0)\) and \(x_k(T)\to x(T)\). It does not by itself imply convergence of derivatives or exact equality of endpoints at finite \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform trajectory convergence means that the maximum state error over the entire common time interval tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Trajectory Topologies

children.title: Switching-Rate Limitations
children.top_down_role: Restrictions arising when arbitrarily fine switching is unavailable.

assumptions_latex: Consider the scalar modes \(F=\{-1,1\}\) on \([0,1]\), whose convexification contains the relaxed velocity \(0\).
An original control \(u:[0,1]\to\{-1,1\}\) is piecewise constant with at most \(N\) switches, and \(x(t)=\int_0^t u(s)\,ds\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(\lVert x\rVert_\infty\ge 1/(2(N+1))\); hence uniform approximation of the relaxed zero trajectory with error \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) requires \(N\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A binary-mode example showing that arbitrarily accurate relaxation may require unbounded switching frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scalar inclusion with original velocities \(F=\{-1,1\}\), the convexified system admits the stationary relaxed trajectory \(z(t)=0\). Let \(u:[0,1]\to\{-1,1\}\) be piecewise constant with at most \(N\) switches and let \(x(t)=\int_0^t u(s)\,ds\). The control has at most \(N+1\) constant-sign intervals, one of length at least \(1/(N+1)\). Across that interval, \(x\) changes by at least \(1/(N+1)\), so \(\sup_{t\in[0,1]}|x(t)|\ge1/(2(N+1))\). Therefore bounded switching counts cannot yield arbitrarily accurate uniform relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For binary velocities, any fixed switch limit leaves a positive uniform error when approximating the stationary convexified trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Switching-Rate Limitations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary-mode lower bound is mathematically plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source is provided for the quantitative constant. The interval-length derivation is proof text and must be omitted from a sourced knowledge statement.

children.title: Relaxation Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of reachable behavior and optimization values under relaxation.

assumptions_latex: Original trajectories are dense in relaxed trajectories under \(d_\infty\) on the fixed feasible initial-state class.

The endpoint constraint set \(S\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and compatible with approximation, and the cost \(J(x)=\varphi(x(0),x(T))+\int_0^T L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))dt\) is continuous along the chosen approximating sequences.
Every original trajectory is also feasible for the convexified dynamics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed and original infima agree, \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{rel}}}J(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{orig}}}J(x)\), and every relaxed minimizer can be approximated by original feasible trajectories whose costs converge to its cost.

notation.meaning: Original and relaxed feasible trajectory classes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: No relaxation gap under feasible trajectory density and cost continuity.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X_{\mathrm{orig}}\subset\mathcal X_{\mathrm{rel}}\) be the original and convexified feasible trajectory classes for a fixed initial condition and compatible endpoint constraints. If every \(z\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{rel}}\) admits \(x_k\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{orig}}\) with \(d_\infty(x_k,z)\to0\) and \(J(x_k)\to J(z)\), then \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{orig}}}J(x)=\inf_{z\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{rel}}}J(z)\). Moreover, every relaxed minimizer is the uniform limit of an original feasible minimizing sequence. Thus convexification preserves the optimal value under trajectory density, endpoint compatibility, and cost stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When feasible original trajectories densely approximate relaxed ones and costs converge, convexification preserves the optimal value and relaxed minimizers are limits of original minimizing sequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Stability

children.title: Trajectory Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Discrepancies between relaxed motions and closures of original trajectory families.

assumptions_latex: \(T>0\) and trajectories belong to \(C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\) with the uniform norm.
\(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) has nonempty values, and original and convexified inclusions use the same initial condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\bar x,\mathcal S_F)>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform-topology nonapproximation for a fixed initial condition.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S_F\) contain the absolutely continuous trajectories satisfying \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere and \(x(0)=x_0\), and let \(\mathcal S_{\operatorname{co}F}\) be defined by replacing \(F\) with its closed convex hull. A trajectory relaxation gap occurs at \(\bar x\in\mathcal S_{\operatorname{co}F}\) when \[\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\bar x,\mathcal S_F):=\inf_{x\in\mathcal S_F}\max_{t\in[0,T]}\lVert \bar x(t)-x(t)\rVert>0.\] Equivalently, \(\bar x\notin\overline{\mathcal S_F}^{\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trajectory gap exists when a convexified solution remains a positive uniform distance from every original solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory Relaxation Gaps

children.top_down_role: Differences between terminal states reachable in relaxed and original dynamics.

assumptions_latex: \(T>0\), and original and convexified trajectories have the same initial condition.
Endpoint sets are taken from absolutely continuous solutions existing on \([0,T]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,E_F)>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap measured only at the terminal time.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(E_F:=\{x(T):x\in\mathcal S_F\}\) and \(E_{\operatorname{co}F}:=\{x(T):x\in\mathcal S_{\operatorname{co}F}\}\). An endpoint relaxation gap occurs at \(\bar y\in E_{\operatorname{co}F}\) when \[\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,E_F):=\inf_{y\in E_F}\lVert\bar y-y\rVert>0.\] Thus the relaxed endpoint cannot be approximated by endpoints of original trajectories, even though approximation of the entire relaxed trajectory is not required in this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An endpoint gap occurs when a convexified reachable endpoint is separated from all endpoints reachable by the original inclusion.

children.title: Value Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Discrepancies between optimization values over relaxed and original trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(J:C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is the same objective for both problems.
The original and convexified feasible trajectory sets are \(\mathcal S_F\) and \(\mathcal S_{\operatorname{co}F}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_F>v_{m rel}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention with extended-real objective values.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.2 Bolza Problem for Differential Inclusions and Relaxation Stability p. 168
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \[v_F:=\inf_{x\in\mathcal S_F}J(x),\qquad v_{\rm rel}:=\inf_{x\in\mathcal S_{\operatorname{co}F}}J(x),\] with \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\). Since \(\mathcal S_F\subseteq\mathcal S_{\operatorname{co}F}\), one has \(v_{\rm rel}\le v_F\). A value relaxation gap is the strict inequality \[v_F>v_{\rm rel}.\] Its magnitude is \(v_F-v_{\rm rel}\) when both values are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value gap is the strict improvement in the infimum produced by replacing the original dynamics with their convexification.

At some \(z\in K\), \(0\in\overline{\operatorname{co}}F(z)\) but \(F(z)\cap T_K(z)=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Induced Gap Formation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary one-dimensional state-constraint counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T>0\), \(K=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\), and \(x(0)=0\), with the state constraint \(x(t)\in K\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\). For the original inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in\{-1,1\}\) almost everywhere, the constrained feasible set is empty. For the relaxed inclusion \[\dot x(t)\in\operatorname{co}\{-1,1\}=[-1,1]\] almost everywhere, the constant trajectory \(x(t)=0\) is feasible. Thus convexification creates a constrained trajectory that cannot be approximated by original trajectories while preserving the constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With velocity set minus or plus one and the state constrained to zero, the original inclusion has no feasible trajectory, whereas the convexified inclusion admits the constant zero trajectory.
assumptions_latex: \(T>0\), \(K=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\), \(x(0)=0\), and \(x(t)\in K\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\).
