children.title: Solution-Set Compactness-Closure Theory
children.top_down_role: Compactness and closure properties of trajectory families.

children.title: Trajectory-Family Compactness
children.top_down_role: Relative and sequential compactness regimes for families of solution trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) has nonempty compact convex values, is measurable in time, and upper semicontinuous in state almost everywhere.
Every solution satisfies \(\lVert\dot x(t)\rVert\le m(t)\) almost everywhere for a common \(m\in L^1(0,T)\).
Initial states range over a compact set, and all trajectories are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trajectory family is compact in \(C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\) with the uniform norm.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Arzela-Ascoli plus closedness of convex differential inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness under a common integrable velocity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\) be the set of absolutely continuous solutions of \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere whose initial states lie in a fixed compact set. The common bound gives \[\lVert x(t)-x(s)\rVert\le\int_s^t m(r)\,dr\qquad(0\le s\le t\le T),\] so \(\mathcal S\) is equicontinuous. Uniform boundedness and finite dimensionality give relative compactness by Arzelà–Ascoli; upper semicontinuity, convex compact values, and the stated measurability ensure that uniform limits remain solutions. Consequently, \(\mathcal S\) is compact in the uniform topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform boundedness, a common integrable velocity bound, and closed convex dynamics make the trajectory family uniformly compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory-Family Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Relative compactness follows from the stated bounds, but compactness also requires a sourced closedness theorem with exact hypotheses on the multifunction. No citation is supplied, and the statement contains proof text.

children.title: Solution-Set Closedness
children.top_down_role: Closure behavior of solution families under trajectory limits.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is measurable in time, upper semicontinuous in state almost everywhere, and has nonempty closed convex values.
\(x_n\) solve \(\dot x_n(t)\in F(t,x_n(t))\), converge uniformly to \(x\), and their derivatives are uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is absolutely continuous and satisfies \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak compactness of velocities and closed convex values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential closedness in the uniform trajectory topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(x_n(0)\to x(0)\), \(x_n\to x\) uniformly, and \(\{\dot x_n\}\) is uniformly integrable in \(L^1(0,T;\mathbb R^d)\). Then a subsequence of the velocities converges weakly in \(L^1\) to some \(v\), and \[x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t v(s)\,ds.\] Under the stated measurability and upper-semicontinuity hypotheses, closed convexity of \(F(t,x)
\) yields \(v(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere. Hence \(x\) is a solution and the solution set is sequentially closed in \(C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform limit of solutions remains a solution when velocities are uniformly integrable and the multifunction has closed convex values.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Closedness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-velocity limit passage is nontrivial and may require stronger integrable boundedness or graph hypotheses than stated. An authoritative theorem with an exact locator is required.

children.title: Compactness Topologies
children.top_down_role: Trajectory topologies supporting compactness or closure analysis.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset AC([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\) is uniformly bounded.
The derivatives \(\{\dot x:x\in X\}\) are uniformly integrable in \(L^1(0,T;\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform trajectory convergence pairs naturally with weak \(L^1\) convergence of velocities.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Arzela-Ascoli and Dunford-Pettis compactness framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled trajectory–velocity topology used for compactness and limit passage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), use the graph representation \[x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t\dot x(s)\,ds.\] Uniform integrability makes the derivative family relatively weakly compact in \(L^1(0,T;\mathbb R^d)\), while the integral estimate gives equicontinuity of trajectories. Thus subsequences are naturally extracted so that \[x_n\to x\ \text{in }C([0,T];\mathbb R^d),\qquad \dot x_n\rightharpoonup v\ \text{in }L^1(0,T;\mathbb R^d),\] with \(x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t v(s)\,ds\). This coupled topology separates compactness from identification of the limiting inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trajectory compactness uses uniform convergence, while velocities are commonly compact only in the weak L1 topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Topologies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coupled uniform/weak-L1 compactness framework is standard, but the record asserts Dunford–Pettis compactness and limit representation without a cited source and includes derivational text.

children.title: Limit-Trajectory Identification
children.top_down_role: Recognition of limiting curves as solutions of the governing inclusion.

assumptions_latex: \(x_n\to x\) uniformly and \(\dot x_n\rightharpoonup v\) weakly in \(L^1\).
\(x_n(0)\to x_0\), and each \(x_n\) satisfies \(\dot x_n(t)\in F(t,x_n(t))\) almost everywhere.
\(F\) is measurable in time, upper semicontinuous in state almost everywhere, and has closed convex values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t v(s)\,ds\) and \(v(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak derivative limit and closed-convex graph passage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification after uniform trajectory and weak velocity convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weak convergence of the derivatives and convergence of initial values imply \[x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t v(s)\,ds\qquad(0\le t\le T).\] Hence \(x\) is absolutely continuous and \(\dot x=v\) almost everywhere. Because \(x_n(t)\to x(t)\), upper semicontinuity controls outer limits of \(F(t,x_n(t))\); closed convexity permits passage from weak or convexified velocity limits to membership. Therefore \[\dot x(t)=v(t)\in F(t,x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t,\] identifying the compactness limit as a trajectory of the same inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform trajectory convergence and weak velocity convergence identify a limit solution when the dynamics have closed convex values.
knowledge_statements.title: Limit-Trajectory Identification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Weak convergence of selected velocities does not justify pointwise membership merely by an informal appeal to upper semicontinuity and convexity. The exact closed-graph or convergence theorem and all required domination hypotheses must be sourced.

children.title: Compactness-Loss Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where trajectory families cease to possess convergent subsequences.

assumptions_latex: Trajectories are considered in \(C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\) with the uniform topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compactness may fail through loss of uniform boundedness or loss of equicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arzelà–Ascoli failure modes illustrated by solution families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t)):=\mathbb R\), every absolutely continuous scalar path is a solution. The family \(x_n(t)=n\) has no uniformly convergent subsequence because \(\lVert x_n\rVert_\infty=n\), exhibiting loss of boundedness. The bounded family \(y_n(t)=\sin(nt)\) has no uniformly convergent subsequence because it is not equicontinuous, exhibiting loss of a common velocity modulus. These are precisely the two Arzelà–Ascoli compactness boundaries in finite-dimensional uniform trajectory space: pointwise relative compactness and equicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trajectory compactness fails when solutions escape every uniform bound or oscillate without a common continuity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness-Loss Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two examples correctly illustrate loss of boundedness and equicontinuity, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The record nevertheless lacks the required differential-inclusion or Arzelà–Ascoli source and contains explanatory proof text.

children.title: Solution-Set Connectivity-Selection Theory
children.top_down_role: Topological organization and continuous selection of nonunique trajectories.

children.title: Connected Solution Sets
children.top_down_role: Connectedness structure within families of nonunique trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S(x_0)\) is the set of solutions on \([0,T]\) with fixed initial state \(x_0\).
Connectivity is taken in the uniform topology of \(C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S(x_0)\) cannot be partitioned into two disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: topological definition specialized to solution sets
source connecting this definition to differential-inclusion theory required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological connectedness of the fixed-initial-state solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution set \(\mathcal S(x_0)\subset C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\) is connected when there do not exist nonempty sets \(U,V\), open in the relative uniform topology, such that \[\mathcal S(x_0)=U\cup V,
\qquad U\cap V=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, every continuous map \(q:\mathcal S(x_0)\to\{0,1\}\), where \(\{0,1\}\) has the discrete topology, is constant. This definition concerns connectivity of the entire trajectory set, not merely connectivity of its endpoint image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution set is connected when it admits no separation into two nonempty uniformly open trajectory families.
knowledge_statements.title: Connected Solution Sets

children.title: Path-Connected Solution Families
children.top_down_role: Trajectory families linked through continuous paths in solution space.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a nonempty subfamily of solutions in \(C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\).
Continuity of paths through \(\mathcal P\) is measured with the uniform norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every pair of trajectories in \(\mathcal P\) is joined by a continuous path consisting entirely of solutions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: path-connectedness specialized to trajectory families
source connecting this definition to solution-selection theory required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-connectedness in the uniform topology, stronger than connectedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A solution family \(\mathcal P\) is path-connected when, for every \(x_0,x_1\in\mathcal P\), there exists a map \(\Gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal P\) such that \[\Gamma(0)=x_0,
\qquad \Gamma(1)=x_1,
\qquad \lim_{s\to r}\lVert\Gamma(s)-\Gamma(r)\rVert_\infty=0\quad(r\in[0,1]).\] Thus each intermediate \(\Gamma(s)\) remains a solution satisfying the defining initial, dynamical, and constraint conditions of \(\mathcal P\). Every path-connected solution family is connected, but the converse need not hold in a general trajectory space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution family is path-connected when any two trajectories can be joined continuously through trajectories that remain solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Path-Connected Solution Families

children.title: Continuous Solution Selections
children.top_down_role: Continuous choices of trajectories across initial data or parameter values.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(s\) continuously chooses one solution for every parameter.

notation.meaning: Set of solutions corresponding to a parameter

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for parameterized differential inclusions on a fixed finite time interval.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a topological space, let \(X=C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\) carry the uniform norm, and let \(\mathcal S:P\rightrightarrows X\) assign to each parameter the nonempty set of absolutely continuous solutions of a specified differential inclusion. A continuous solution selection is a continuous map \(s:P\to X\) satisfying \(s(p)\in\mathcal S(p)\) for every \(p\in P\). Continuity therefore means that \(p_n\to p\) implies \(\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|s(p_n)(t)-s(p)(t)\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous solution selection assigns one trajectory to each parameter so that uniformly small parameter changes produce uniformly small trajectory changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Solution Selections

children.title: Selection-Compatible Components
children.top_down_role: Components of solution families that support coherent trajectory choices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The component \(K\) is selection-compatible precisely when some continuous local solution branch passes through it.

notation.meaning: Parameterized solution map into the trajectory space
A connected component of the reference solution set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local compatibility of one connected component with continuous trajectory selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a topological space, let \(X=C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\), and let \(\mathcal S:P\rightrightarrows X\) be a nonempty-valued solution map. For \(p_0\in P\), a connected component \(K\) of \(\mathcal S(p_0)\) is selection-compatible at \(p_0\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(p_0\) and a continuous map \(s:U\to X\) such that \(s(p)in\mathcal S(p)\) for every \(p\in U\) and \(s(p_0)\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution component is selection-compatible when a continuous local family of solutions can be chosen through that component.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Compatible Components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed local definition is plausible, but the exact term and its component-based formulation have no cited source. In addition, the membership condition contains the malformed text \(s(p)in\mathcal S(p)\). A dedicated source is required before choosing a definitive mathematical formulation.

children.title: Selection Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Topological or branching structures preventing continuous trajectory choices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multifunction \(R\) has no continuous single-valued selection on \(S^1\).

notation.meaning: Unit circle in the complex plane

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical topological obstruction illustrating failure of global continuous solution selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}\) and define \(R:S^1\rightrightarrows S^1\) by \(R(z)=\{w\in S^1:w^2=z\}\). Every value consists of two points, and local continuous selections exist on sufficiently short arcs. Nevertheless, no continuous map \(r:S^1\to S^1\) satisfies \(r(z)\in R(z)\) for all \(z\in S^1\), because such a map would be a continuous right inverse of the degree-two covering \(w\mapsto w^2\). Thus connected parameter topology can obstruct a global solution selection even when all values are finite and locally selectable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two square roots of a point on the circle can be selected continuously on arcs but not continuously around the entire circle.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection Obstructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The square-root multifunction is a mathematically appropriate counterexample for the selection-obstruction leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied for the covering-space obstruction.

children.title: Forward Trajectory Branching
children.top_down_role: Divergence of multiple future trajectories from common data.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Forward branching occurs exactly when two solutions share the same initial state but are not identical on the forward interval.

notation.meaning: Set of solutions from the initial state

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the differential inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) almost everywhere on \([t_0,T]\), a state \(x_0\) exhibits forward trajectory branching if there exist distinct absolutely continuous solutions \(x_1,x_2\in\mathcal S(x_0)\) satisfying \(x_1(t_0)=x_2(t_0)=x_0\) and \(x_1(t)\ne x_2(t)\) for at least one \(t>t_0\). Equivalently, the forward solution set \(\mathcal S(x_0)\) is not a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward branching means that one initial state admits at least two different future solution trajectories.

children.title: Velocity-Induced Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity generated by competing admissible velocity choices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct realizable initial velocities certify local forward nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient certificate; distinct elements of the velocity set alone need not suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) from \((t_0,x_0)\). A velocity-induced nonuniqueness certificate consists of \(v_1,v_2	rong\in F(t_0,x_0)\) with \(v_1\ne v_2\) and two solutions \(x_1,x_2\) defined on \([t_0,t_0+\delta]\) such that \(x_i(t_0)=x_0\) and \(x_i(t_0+h)=x_0+h v_i+o(h)\) as \(h\downarrow0\), for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). The distinct first-order expansions imply \(x_1\ne x_2\) on every sufficiently short forward interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct velocities that are actually realized to first order by solutions certify local nonuniqueness; mere membership in the velocity set does not.
knowledge_statements.title: Velocity-Induced Nonuniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between arbitrary velocities and velocities realized by first-order solution expansions is mathematically important, and certificate is an appropriate content kind. However, no source supports the realizability formulation, and the statement contains the malformed command sequence \(v_1,v_2\trong\in F(t_0,x_0)\).

children.top_down_role: Regions of state space where distinct trajectory branches emerge.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\), define \(\mathcal S_{\tau}(z)\) as the set of absolutely continuous solutions on \([\tau,T]\) satisfying \(x(\tau)=z\). The time-state pair \((\tau,z)\) is a state-dependent branch point if \(\mathcal S_{\tau}(z)\) contains two distinct trajectories. A trajectory \(x\) encounters this branch point when \(x(\tau)=z\); its future is then nonunique even if its history on the interval preceding \(\tau\) was uniquely determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state-dependent branch point is a time-state pair from which at least two different forward continuations are possible.
knowledge_statements.title: State-Dependent Branch Points

children.title: Delayed Branching
children.top_down_role: Trajectories that coincide initially before separating at later times.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Delayed branching is witnessed by a positive common prefix followed by unequal continuations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching after two solutions share a nontrivial initial trajectory segment.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two solutions \(x_1,x_2\) of the same differential inclusion exhibit delayed branching at time \(\tau\in(t_0,T)\) if \(x_1(t)=x_2(t)\) for every \(t\in[t_0,\tau]\), while \(x_1(t)\ne x_2(t)\) for at least one \(t\in(\tau,T]\). The common point \((\tau,x_1(\tau))\) is therefore a branch point, but nonuniqueness is invisible on the nontrivial prefix \([t_0,\tau]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delayed branching occurs when two solutions coincide for a positive time and separate only after reaching a later branch point.
knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Branching

children.title: Uniqueness-Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where branching is excluded or collapses.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\) defines the autonomous inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
On an open neighborhood \(U\) of the initial state, \(F(x)=\{f(x)\}\) and \(f:U\to X\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x_0\in U\), there is a time \(\tau>0\) such that the inclusion has exactly one absolutely continuous solution \(x:[0,\tau]\to U\) with \(x(0)=x_0\). Thus trajectory branching is excluded while the reachable states remain in \(U\). More generally, any regime reducing the active velocity set to a locally Lipschitz single-valued field recovers local uniqueness.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Picard-Lindelof uniqueness applied after local singleton reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient local regime for recovering uniqueness, not a characterization of every uniqueness mechanism.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) on \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\). A local uniqueness-recovery regime at \(x_0\) is obtained when there exists an open neighborhood \(U\ni x_0\) and a locally Lipschitz map \(f:U\to X\) such that \(F(x)=\{f(x)\}\) for every \(x\in U\). Then the initial-value problem has a unique local solution through each point of \(U\), up to its first exit from \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching disappears locally when the active set-valued dynamics reduce to a locally Lipschitz vector field; each initial state then has one trajectory until it leaves that regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness-Recovery Regimes

children.title: Lyapunov Theory for Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Lyapunov families for stability, invariance, and descent.

knowledge_statements.title: Lyapunov Theory for Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Lyapunov decrease along every admissible velocity in finite dimensions; weak and solution-dependent variants are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\) have nonempty values, and consider \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\). A locally Lipschitz function \(V:X\to[0,\infty)\) is a strong Lyapunov function for a closed set \(S\subset X\), with dissipation \(W:X\to[0,\infty)\), when \(V^{-1}(0)=S\) and \[\sup_{v\in F(x)}V^{\circ}(x;v)\le -W(x)\] at every state \(x\) under consideration, where \(V^{\circ}\) is the Clarke generalized directional derivative. Then \(V(x(t))\) is nonincreasing along every absolutely continuous solution, with descent wherever \(W(x(t))>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Euclidean space, a strong Lyapunov function decreases along every admissible trajectory when its Clarke directional derivative is bounded above by a nonpositive dissipation rate for every admissible velocity.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\) has nonempty values and admits absolutely continuous solutions of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
\(V:X\to[0,\infty)\) is locally Lipschitz, \(S\subset X\) is closed, and \(W:X\to[0,\infty)\).
\(V^{\circ}(x;v)\) denotes the Clarke generalized directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(V^{-1}(0)=S\) and \(\sup_{v\in F(x)}V^{\circ}(x;v)\le -W(x)\), then \(V(x(t))\) is nonincreasing along every absolutely continuous solution. Positive \(W(x(t))\) yields descent along the trajectory; invariance and asymptotic conclusions require additional continuation and compactness hypotheses.

children.title: Equilibrium-Set Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A basic closedness property; no manifold, stratification, or dimension claim is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a metrizable topological vector space, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\), and define \(E:=\{x\in X:0\in F(x)\}\). If \(\operatorname{gph}F:=\{(x,v)\in X\times X:v\in F(x)\}\) is closed in \(X\times X\), then \(E\) is closed in \(X\). Equivalently, if \(x_k\in E\) and \(x_k\to x\), then \((x_k,0)\to(x,0)\), so \(0\in F(x)\) and \(x\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed-graph velocity map on a metrizable topological vector space, the equilibrium set is closed, so every convergent sequence of equilibria has an equilibrium limit.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metrizable topological vector space and \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\) has closed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equilibrium set \(E=\{x\in X:0\in F(x)\}\) is closed. Consequently, every sequence \((x_k)\subset E\) converging to \(x\in X\) has \(x\in E\).

children.title: Stationarity-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Transitions where states cease to support stationary trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity-Loss Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological loss of the zero-velocity condition, without asserting bifurcation or parameter sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and define \(E:=\{x\in X:0\in F(x)\}\). The stationarity-loss boundary is \[\partial E:=\overline{E}\cap\overline{X\setminus E}.\] A point \(x_*\in X\) lies in \(\partial E\) exactly when every neighborhood of \(x_*\) contains some \(x\in E\) and some \(y\in X\setminus E\), equivalently states satisfying \(0\in F(x)\) and \(0\notin F(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationarity-loss boundary, every neighborhood contains both states allowing zero velocity and states that do not.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(E=\{x\in X:0\in F(x)\}\) is the stationary set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stationarity-loss boundary is \(\partial E=\overline{E}\cap\overline{X\setminus E}\). Every neighborhood of each \(x_*\in\partial E\) contains both a stationary state and a nonstationary state.

notation.meaning: topological boundary of the stationary set

children.title: Periodic Trajectories
children.top_down_role: Trajectory families exhibiting exact temporal repetition.

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodicity of a selected solution, not periodicity of every solution from the same initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An absolutely continuous solution \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\) of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) is periodic if there exists \(T>0\) such that \(x(t+T)=x(t)\) for every \(t\in[0,\infty)\). Any such \(T\) is a period. A periodic trajectory is nonconstant when its image contains more than one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected inclusion trajectory is periodic when it repeats after a fixed positive time. This does not require all trajectories from its initial state to repeat.
assumptions_latex: \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\) is an absolutely continuous solution of the autonomous inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trajectory is periodic when some \(T>0\) satisfies \(x(t+T)=x(t)\) for every \(t\in[0,\infty)\).

children.title: Recurrent Trajectories
children.top_down_role: Nonunique motions returning repeatedly near prior states.

knowledge_statements.title: Recurrent Trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive recurrence of one complete trajectory at its initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\) be a complete trajectory. Define \[\omega(x):=\{y\in X:\text{ there exists a sequence }t_k\to\infty\text{ such that }x(t_k)\to y\}.\] The trajectory is recurrent at its initial state if \(x(0)\in\omega(x)\), equivalently if there exists a sequence \(t_k\to\infty\) such that \(d(x(t_k),x(0))\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trajectory is recurrent at its initial state when it returns arbitrarily close to that state along a sequence of times tending to infinity.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\) is a complete trajectory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trajectory is recurrent at its initial state exactly when \(x(0)\in\omega(x)\), equivalently when there exists \(t_k\to\infty\) with \(d(x(t_k),x(0))\to0\). Periodicity implies recurrence, but recurrence need not imply an exact positive period.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard point-recurrence definition through the omega-limit set

children.title: Return-Time Structure
children.top_down_role: Organization of recurrence through repeated visits to phase-space regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Return-Time Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Return times of a selected trajectory to metric neighborhoods of a nonempty target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\), and let \(A\subset X\) be nonempty. For \(\varepsilon>0\), define \[N_\varepsilon(x,A):=\{t\in[0,\infty):d(x(t),A)<\varepsilon\},\qquad d(z,A):=\inf_{a\in A}d(z,a).\] Then \(x\) is recurrent at \(x(0)\) exactly when \(N_\varepsilon(x,\{x(0)\})\) is unbounded for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return-time sets record when a trajectory enters a neighborhood of a nonempty target set. Recurrence means that return times to every neighborhood of the initial state are unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\), and \(A\subset X\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), the return-time set is \(N_\varepsilon(x,A)=\{t\in[0,\infty):d(x(t),A)<\varepsilon\}\). Recurrence at \(x(0)\) is equivalent to \(N_\varepsilon(x,\{x(0)\})\) being unbounded for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a nonempty set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: return-time sets give the standard neighborhood formulation of recurrence

children.title: Set-Valued Periodic Orbits
children.top_down_role: Periodic behavior interpreted across branching trajectory families.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Periodic Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed points of the reachable multifunction characterize existence of periodic selections, not universal periodicity from the same state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T>0\) and let \(\mathcal{R}_T(x_0)\) be the set of values \(x(T)\) attained by solution segments of the autonomous inclusion satisfying \(x(0)=x_0\). Define \[P_T:=\{x_0\in X:x_0\in\mathcal{R}_T(x_0)\}.\] If \(x_0\in P_T\), a witnessing solution segment returns to \(x_0\) at time \(T\) and can be repeated to form a \(T\)-periodic solution. Conversely, every \(T\)-periodic solution based at \(x_0\) shows that \(x_0\in\mathcal{R}_T(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state admits a T-periodic trajectory exactly when it is a fixed point of the time-T reachable multifunction; other trajectories from that state may be nonperiodic.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\) defines an autonomous differential inclusion and admits solution segments on \([0,T]\).
\(\mathcal{R}_T(x_0)\) is the set of endpoints at time \(T\) of solution segments starting from \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set of initial states supporting a \(T\)-periodic selection is \(P_T=\{x_0\in X:x_0\in\mathcal{R}_T(x_0)\}\). Membership is witnessed by at least one returning solution segment, which can be extended periodically by repetition.

children.title: Recurrence-Loss Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamical regimes where repeated return behavior breaks down.

knowledge_statements.title: Recurrence-Loss Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete escape-to-infinity mechanism showing that existence and uniqueness do not imply recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Recurrence can fail solely because trajectories escape. For \(X=\mathbb{R}\) and \(F(x)=\{1\}\), the unique solution from \(x_0\) is \(x(t)=x_0+t\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[N_\varepsilon(x,\{x_0\})=\{t\in[0,\infty):|x(t)-x_0|<\varepsilon\}=[0,\varepsilon),\] which is bounded. Thus the trajectory is neither recurrent nor periodic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant drift gives a smooth, unique trajectory that escapes to infinity. Its returns near the initial state occur only for bounded times, so recurrence and periodicity fail.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}\) and the autonomous inclusion is \(\dot x(t)\in\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every solution has the form \(x(t)=x_0+t\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), \(N_\varepsilon(x,\{x_0\})=[0,\varepsilon)\), which is bounded. Hence no trajectory is recurrent or periodic.

children.title: Attractors and Limit Sets
children.top_down_role: Limit sets and attraction for multivalued evolution.

children.title: Global Attractors
children.top_down_role: Compact attracting structures governing long-time multivalued evolution.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space.
\(S:[0,\infty)\times X\rightrightarrows X\) is a multivalued semiflow with nonempty values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a global attractor precisely when it is compact, invariant, and attracts every bounded subset of \(X\).

notation.meaning: One-sided Hausdorff excess from one set to another.
Image of a set under the multivalued semiflow.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global attraction is formulated using the strong, one-sided Hausdorff excess for a multivalued semiflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(\mathcal A\subset X\) is a global attractor for \(S\) if \(\mathcal A\) is nonempty and compact, is strictly invariant in the sense that \(S(t,\mathcal A)=\mathcal A\) for every \(t\geq0\), and attracts every bounded set: for each bounded \(B\subset X\), \[\lim_{t\to\infty}e(S(t,B),\mathcal A)=0.\] If only positive invariance is intended, the equality is replaced by \(S(t,\mathcal A)\subseteq\mathcal A\); this weaker convention must be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global attractor is a compact invariant set approached uniformly by every state reachable at large times from any bounded initial set.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Attractors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the global-attractor leaf, but no citation supports the selected strict-invariance convention for multivalued semiflows.

children.title: Local Attractors
children.top_down_role: Attracting structures associated with restricted neighborhoods or basins.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\(S:[0,\infty)\times X\rightrightarrows X\) is a multivalued semiflow with nonempty values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is a local attractor when it attracts all reachable states from some neighborhood while remaining compact and invariant.

notation.meaning: Open metric neighborhood of a set.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local attraction uses uniform strong attraction on one neighborhood of the invariant set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty compact set \(A\subset X\) is a local attractor for \(S\) if it is strictly invariant, \(S(t,A)=A\) for every \(t\geq0\), and there exists \(r>0\) such that \[\lim_{t\to\infty}e(S(t,N_r(A)),A)=0.\] The basin of strong attraction is the union of all sets \(B\subset X\) satisfying \(e(S(t,B),A)\to0\). Requiring the displayed limit only for individual initial points gives pointwise local attraction and is strictly weaker than uniform attraction of a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local attractor is a compact invariant set that uniformly attracts every reachable state starting in some neighborhood of it.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Attractors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood-attraction definition fits the leaf, but the strict-invariance and basin conventions require a specific source; the union-of-uniformly-attracted-sets formulation also needs support.

children.title: Omega-Limit Sets
children.top_down_role: Accumulation sets generated by long-time trajectory behavior.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\(S:[0,\infty)\times X\rightrightarrows X\) is a multivalued semiflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(B)\) consists exactly of limits of reachable states along times tending to infinity.

notation.meaning: States reachable at time t from initial set B.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition applies to sets of initial states and multivalued reachable-state maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B\subset X\), its omega-limit set under \(S\) is \[\omega(B):=\bigcap_{T\geq0}\overline{\bigcup_{t\geq T}S(t,B)}.\] Equivalently, \(z\in\omega(B)\) if and only if there exist times \(t_n\to\infty\), points \(x_n\in B\), and reachable states \(z_n\in S(t_n,x_n)\) such that \(z_n\to z\). The set may be empty unless an appropriate precompactness or asymptotic compactness hypothesis is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The omega-limit set contains precisely the limits of states reachable from the initial set along sequences of times tending to infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Omega-Limit Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The omega-limit definition, sequential characterization, and content kind are mathematically coherent for a metric-space multivalued semiflow, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Weak Attraction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Attraction based on selected trajectories or nonuniform approach.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\(S:[0,\infty)\times X\rightrightarrows X\) has nonempty reachable sets.
\(A\subset X\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak attraction requires at least one reachable state to approach \(A\), rather than all reachable states.

notation.meaning: Minimum distance between two nonempty sets.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: existential attraction convention for multivalued dynamics
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak attraction is fixed here as existential attraction among the reachable states of a multivalued evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(A\) weakly attracts an initial state \(x\in X\) if \[\lim_{t\to\infty}d_-(S(t,x),A)=0.\] It weakly attracts a set \(B\subset X\) uniformly if \[\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{x\in B}d_-(S(t,x),A)=0.\] Thus, at every sufficiently large time, at least one state reachable from each initial point lies close to \(A\). This condition does not control other reachable branches and therefore does not imply strong attraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak attraction says that each initial point has some reachable branch approaching the target, while other branches may remain far away.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Attraction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas describe existential proximity among reachable states, but terminology varies by source. They do not establish a single coherent reachable branch approaching the target, as asserted in the plain statement, so an authoritative convention and corrected interpretation are required.

children.title: Strong Attraction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Attraction required uniformly across admissible trajectory branches.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\(S:[0,\infty)\times X\rightrightarrows X\) has nonempty reachable sets.
\(A\subset X\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong attraction controls every state reachable at large times and therefore implies weak attraction.

notation.meaning: One-sided Hausdorff excess from D to A.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: universal attraction convention for multivalued dynamics
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong attraction is universal over all branches of the multivalued evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(A\) strongly attracts an initial state \(x\in X\) if \[\lim_{t\to\infty}e(S(t,x),A)=0.\] It strongly attracts \(B\subset X\) uniformly if \[\lim_{t\to\infty}e(S(t,B),A)=0.\] Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(T\geq0\) such that \(S(t,B)\subset N_\varepsilon(A)\) whenever \(t\geq T\). Since the infimum distance does not exceed the excess, strong attraction implies the corresponding weak attraction condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong attraction requires every state reachable from the initial set at sufficiently large times to lie close to the target.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Attraction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The excess-based universal attraction condition is coherent and implies the corresponding infimum-distance condition, but the strong-attraction terminology and convention lack a specific source.

children.title: Asymptotic Compactness Failure
children.top_down_role: Long-time regimes where compact attracting structures cannot be recovered.

assumptions_latex: \((T(t))_{t\geq0}\) is the right-translation semigroup defined below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit of a compactly supported unit vector has no convergent time subsequence, so asymptotic compactness fails.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The translation semigroup exhibits escape without convergent subsequences in an infinite-dimensional phase space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(f\in L^2(0,1)\) with \(\lVert f\rVert_2=1\), extended by zero to \((0,\infty)\), and let \(t_n=2n\). The supports of \(T(t_n)f\) are pairwise disjoint, hence \[\lVert T(t_n)f-T(t_m)f\rVert_2=\sqrt2\qquad(n\neq m).\] Therefore the bounded sequence of initial data \(f_n=f\), together with \(t_n\to\infty\), produces terminal states \(T(t_n)f_n\) having no convergent subsequence. The semigroup is not asymptotically compact, and \(\omega(\{f\})=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Right translations of one compactly supported unit function remain mutually separated, so their large-time orbit has no convergent subsequence or omega-limit point.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Compactness Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translation-semigroup counterexample is mathematically coherent and the counterexample content kind exactly fits the failure leaf, but no inspectable source is provided.

children.title: Contingent-Tangency Conditions
children.top_down_role: Instantaneous compatibility between admissible velocities and constraint geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed subset of \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(F:C\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is the admissible-velocity multifunction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The existential contingent-tangency condition is \(F(x)\cap T_C(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in C\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand contingent cone to C at x.
Distance from a point to C.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record states existential instantaneous compatibility, the quantifier appropriate to viability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), the contingent cone is \[T_C(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{d(x+hv,C)}{h}=0\right\}.\] The existential contingent-tangency condition for the differential inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) is \[F(x)\cap T_C(x)\neq\varnothing\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] It asserts that at each constrained state at least one admissible instantaneous velocity agrees to first order with sequences remaining in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every constrained state, viability requires at least one admissible velocity to lie in the Bouligand contingent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Contingent-Tangency Conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The contingent-cone formula and existential tangency condition fit the terminal condition container, but they have no supporting citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Nagumo Tangency-Preservation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Classical tangency-based viability and invariance result families.

children.title: Nagumo Viability Families
children.top_down_role: Classical tangency-based result families for existence of constraint-preserving trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed.
\(F\) is upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact convex values and has at most linear growth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(F(x)\cap T_C(x)\neq\varnothing\) for all \(x\in C\) yields a viable solution from every initial point in \(C\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand contingent cone to C at x.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional existential Nagumo theorem for upper-semicontinuous compact-convex velocity fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that \[F(x)\cap T_C(x)\neq\varnothing\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Then, for every \(x_0\in C\), there exist \(\tau>0\) and an absolutely continuous curve \(x:[0,\tau]\to C\) such that \(x(0)=x_0\) and \[\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,\tau].\] Under the stated linear-growth assumption, solutions can be continued while finite and hence give the corresponding global viability assertion on every bounded time interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every constrained state admits a contingent velocity, then each initial point has at least one solution that remains in the closed constraint set.
knowledge_statements.title: Nagumo Viability Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the Nagumo viability leaf, but the exact sufficiency and global-continuation hypotheses must be checked against an authoritative theorem statement.

children.title: Nagumo Invariance Families
children.top_down_role: Classical tangency-based result families for universal preservation of constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed.
\(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) has nonempty compact values and is locally Lipschitz in Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The universal condition \(F(x)\subseteq T_C(x)\) yields strong invariance of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand contingent cone to C at x.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-dimensional sufficient strong-invariance form with a universal velocity quantifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that \[F(x)\subseteq T_C(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Then \(C\) is strongly invariant for \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\): every absolutely continuous solution \(x:[0,\tau]\to\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(x(0)\in C\) and \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) for almost every \(t\) obeys \[x(t)\in C\qquad\text{for all }t\in[0,\tau].\] The regularity of \(F\) is essential because pointwise universal tangency alone need not control all solutions for arbitrary multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every admissible velocity is contingent and the multifunction is suitably regular, every solution starting in the constraint set remains there.
knowledge_statements.title: Nagumo Invariance Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The universal-tangency strong-invariance theorem fits the leaf, but the precise regularity assumptions under which contingent-cone inclusion controls every solution require an authoritative source.

children.title: Tangency–Preservation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between boundary velocity geometry and constraint-preserving motion.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed.
\(F\) satisfies the existence hypotheses of the finite-dimensional Nagumo viability theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Viability of \(C\) is equivalent to the existential tangency condition \(F(x)\cap T_C(x)\neq\varnothing\) on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand contingent cone to C at x.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential tangency corresponds to weak preservation, meaning existence of at least one constrained solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed set \(C\) is viable for \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\), meaning that every \(x_0\in C\) initiates at least one local solution remaining in \(C\), if and only if \[F(x)\cap T_C(x)\neq\varnothing\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Necessity follows at the level of right-hand contingent velocities of constrained solutions; sufficiency requires the stated compactness, semicontinuity, convexity, and growth hypotheses. Replacing the existential intersection by \(F(x)\subseteq T_C(x)\) changes the preservation quantifier from some solution to every solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard existence hypotheses, a closed set admits a constrained solution from every point exactly when each point admits a contingent velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangency–Preservation Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed viability–tangency correspondence requires an exact theorem variant. Referring only to unspecified “existence hypotheses” is insufficient, and the generic duality kind is less exact than a theorem or property for this equivalence.

children.title: Regular-Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nagumo-type families organized by regular geometric boundary structure.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), with each \(g_i\) continuously differentiable near \(C\).
The active gradients \(\{\nabla g_i(x):g_i(x)=0\}\) are linearly independent at the point \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(x)=\{v:\langle\nabla g_i(x),v\rangle\leq0\text{ for every active }i\}\).

notation.meaning: Indices of active inequality constraints at x.
Bouligand contingent cone to C at x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: smooth-inequality tangent-cone formula under LICQ
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional inequality constraints under the linear-independence constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every \(x\in C\) satisfying the stated constraint qualification, the contingent cone has the linearized representation \[T_C(x)=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle\nabla g_i(x),v\rangle\leq0\ \text{for all }i\in I(x)\right\}.\] Consequently, the viability tangency test becomes the existence of \(v\in F(x)\) satisfying all active inequalities, whereas the strong-invariance test requires every \(v\in F(x)\) to satisfy them. At interior points, \(I(x)=\varnothing\) and \(T_C(x)=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular smooth boundary, the contingent cone is exactly the set of velocities satisfying every active linearized inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Boundary Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The LICQ tangent-cone representation is standard, precise, and appropriately classified as a representation, but no inspectable citation supports it.

children.title: Irregular-Boundary Extensions
children.top_down_role: Tangency-based preservation results adapted to nonsmooth or nonregular constraint sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed, with no smoothness or constraint qualification imposed.
\(F:C\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is an admissible-velocity multifunction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At irregular boundaries, viability must be tested against the intrinsic contingent cone rather than an unjustified linearized cone.

notation.meaning: Bouligand contingent cone to C at x.
Linearized cone for a chosen inequality description of C.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: intrinsic tangent cones extend tangency tests beyond regular boundaries
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic contingent geometry replaces smooth active-gradient formulas at cusps, corners, and degenerate constraint representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an irregular boundary point \(x\in C\), the intrinsic viability predicate remains \[F(x)\cap T_C(x)\neq\varnothing.\] If \(C\) is represented by differentiable inequalities but a constraint qualification fails, the linearized cone \(L_C(x)\) may strictly contain \(T_C(x)\). Hence the relaxed test \(F(x)\cap L_C(x)\neq\varnothing\) is generally insufficient for viability. Valid extensions must retain \(T_C(x)\), or replace it by another intrinsic tangent construction together with hypotheses appropriate to the desired existential or universal preservation quantifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an irregular boundary, linearized inequalities can admit false tangent directions; intrinsic contingent geometry is required for a valid viability test.
knowledge_statements.title: Irregular-Boundary Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly warns that a linearized cone can overestimate the contingent cone without a constraint qualification, but the claimed extension boundary and alternative tangent constructions need specific sourced hypotheses.

children.title: Constraint-Preservation Quantifier Duality
children.top_down_role: Existential and universal forms of constraint preservation.

children.title: Weak Viability
children.top_down_role: Constraint preservation through at least one admissible forward trajectory.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed.
\(F:K\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) defines the differential inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is weakly viable precisely when the applicable existential trajectory condition holds.

notation.meaning: set of absolutely continuous solutions starting from x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon and forward-time weak viability for an autonomous differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(T>0\), the closed set \(K\) is weakly viable on \([0,T]\) for \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) if
\[
\forall x_0\in K\;\exists x\in\mathcal S_F(x_0)\quad\forall t\in[0,T],\qquad x(t)\in K.
\]
It is weakly viable for all forward time if
\[
\forall x_0\in K\;\exists x\in\mathcal S_F(x_0)\quad\forall t\geq 0,\qquad x(t)\in K,
\]
where the selected solution is defined on \([0,\infty)\). The defining trajectory quantifier is existential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every initial state in the constraint set admits at least one trajectory that remains feasible throughout the specified horizon; forward-time viability requires one such trajectory defined for all nonnegative times.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Viability

children.title: Strong Invariance
children.top_down_role: Constraint preservation across every admissible forward trajectory.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed.
\(F\) defines forward solutions of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong invariance requires preservation by every admissible solution, not merely by one selection.

notation.meaning: set of forward solutions starting from x
maximal existence interval of a solution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong forward invariance under all solutions of a differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed set \(K\) is strongly invariant for \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) if
\[
\forall x_0\in K\;\forall x\in\mathcal S_F(x_0)\;\forall t\in I_x\cap[0,\infty),
\qquad x(t)\in K.
\]
Thus no admissible velocity selection, nonunique solution branch, or switching behavior may drive a solution starting in \(K\) outside \(K\) during its forward existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every admissible trajectory starting in the constraint set must remain there for its entire forward lifetime.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Invariance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The universal-solution definition matches strong forward invariance and the content kind fits the leaf. No cited source is provided, so the precise convention and treatment of maximal solution intervals remain unsupported.

children.title: Existential Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings organized around the availability of a preserving trajectory choice.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and \(T_K(x)\) is its contingent tangent cone.
\(F(x)=\{f(x,u):u\in U(x)\}\) is the velocity set of a controlled system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existential local preservation is expressed by \(F(x)\cap T_K(x)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: contingent tangent cone to K at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise existential tangency regime for controlled constraint preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a state \(x\in K\), the existential preservation condition is
\[
\exists u\in U(x)
\quad\text{such that}\quad
f(x,u)\in T_K(x),
\]
equivalently \(F(x)\cap T_K(x)\neq\varnothing\). Imposing this predicate at every \(x\in K\) is the local tangency condition associated with weak viability: the control or velocity may depend on the current state, and only one feasible choice is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each feasible state, at least one admissible control must generate a tangent velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Existential Preservation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existential tangency condition is mathematically standard and is correctly classified as a condition, but its association with weak viability depends on hypotheses not supplied or cited. A controlled-viability source with a theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Universal Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings organized around preservation for all admissible trajectory choices.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and \(T_K(x)\) is its contingent tangent cone.
\(F(x)=\{f(x,u):u\in U(x)\}\) is the admissible velocity set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universal local preservation is expressed by \(F(x)\subseteq T_K(x)\).

notation.meaning: contingent tangent cone to K at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise universal tangency regime associated with strong invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a state \(x\in K\), the universal preservation condition is
\[
\forall u\in U(x),
\qquad f(x,u)\in T_K(x),
\]
equivalently \(F(x)\subseteq T_K(x)\). Unlike existential preservation, this predicate permits no outward admissible velocity. Under the regularity hypotheses of an appropriate strong-invariance theorem, imposing it for every \(x\in K\) prevents every admissible solution branch from leaving \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each feasible state, every admissible control must generate a tangent velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Universal Preservation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The universal pointwise condition is clearly stated and the record appropriately limits the invariance implication to an appropriate theorem. The necessary regularity theorem and tangent-cone convention nevertheless require a specific source.

children.title: Viability–Invariance Gap
children.top_down_role: Structures permitting viable selections while other trajectory branches escape.

assumptions_latex: \(K=[-1,1]\subset\mathbb{R}\).
The dynamics are \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) with \(F(x)=\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is weakly viable but is not strongly invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary differential-inclusion example separating existential and universal preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x_0\in K\), a solution can choose velocity \(1\) until reaching an interior target and then switch between the velocities \(-1\) and \(1\) so as to remain in \(K\); hence an admissible viable solution exists. However, from \(x_0=1\), the admissible solution \(x(t)=1+t\) satisfies \(\dot x(t)=1\in F(x(t))\) and leaves \(K\) immediately. Therefore weak viability does not imply strong invariance when admissible velocities are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A velocity choice can preserve the interval, while another admissible choice exits it; viability therefore need not imply invariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Viability–Invariance Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly separates existential viability from universal invariance, and counterexample is the correct content kind for this leaf. No inspectable citation supports the example or the adopted solution convention.

children.title: Tangency-Escape Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of feasible forward motion at irregular or incompatible boundaries.

children.title: Tangency Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of admissible forward velocities compatible with the constraint geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(K=\{x:g(x)\leq0\}\), where \(g\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in\partial K\).
For some neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\alpha>0\), every \(y\in V\cap K\) and \(v\in F(y)\) satisfy \(\langle\nabla g(y),v\rangle\geq\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No solution starting at \(\bar x\) can remain in \(K\) throughout any positive initial interval.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform strict failure of tangency at a smooth boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x(0)=\bar x\) and let \(x\) be an absolutely continuous solution of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\). Under the stated uniform strict outward-rate condition, there is no \(\varepsilon>0\) for which
\[
x(t)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,\varepsilon].
\]
Thus the positive margin \(\alpha\) is a local tangency-failure certificate at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform positive outward derivative near the boundary prevents any trajectory starting there from remaining feasible throughout a positive initial interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangency Failure

children.title: Boundary Escape
children.top_down_role: Trajectory departure from a constraint set through its boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(K=(-\infty,0]\subset\mathbb{R}\).
The dynamics are the ordinary differential equation \(\dot x(t)=1\) with \(x(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique solution exits \(K\) at every time \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional immediate escape caused by a strictly outward velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unique solution is \(x(t)=t\). Hence
\[
x(t)>0\quad\text{for every }t>0,
\]
so \(x(t)\notin K\) immediately after the initial time. At the boundary, the contingent tangent cone is \(T_K(0)=(-\infty,0]\), whereas the velocity \(1\notin T_K(0)\). Thus the example realizes boundary escape through explicit failure of the tangency condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting at the endpoint of a half-line, a strictly outward constant velocity leaves the set immediately.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Escape

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-dimensional escape example, tangent cone, and conclusion are correct, and counterexample is an appropriate role for this terminal container. It has no source reference with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Outward-Velocity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundary configurations dominated by velocities directed outside the feasible region.

assumptions_latex: \(K=\{x:g(x)\leq0\}\), where \(g\) is continuously differentiable and \(\nabla g(x)\neq0\) on \(\partial K\).
\(F(x)\) is a nonempty compact velocity set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signs of \(m(x)\) and \(M(x)\) distinguish existential, universal, mixed, and forced-outward regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-velocity classification at a smooth inequality boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\partial K\), the smooth tangent half-space is \(T_K(x)=\{v:\langle\nabla g(x),v\rangle\leq0\}\). Therefore \(m(x)\leq0\) means that some admissible velocity is tangent or inward, while \(M(x)\leq0\) means that every admissible velocity is tangent or inward. The regime \(m(x)\leq0<M(x)\) permits both preserving and escaping selections, whereas \(m(x)>0\) makes every admissible velocity strictly outward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum and maximum normal velocities classify whether some, all, or no admissible directions preserve a smooth constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Outward-Velocity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a regular smooth inequality boundary, the minimum and maximum normal velocities give the stated four-way classification. The property fits the leaf, but the smooth-boundary tangent-cone identity and classification have no cited source.

children.title: Irregular-Boundary Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Constraint-preservation failures associated with nonsmooth or unstable tangent geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(K=(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{R}^2\).
The dynamics are \(\dot x(t)=(1,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clarke-cone tangency fails at the origin although a viable trajectory exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonregular crossing where contingent and Clarke tangent cones differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At the origin,
\[
T_K(0)=K,
\qquad
T_K^{\mathrm C}(0)=\{0\}.
\]
The velocity \((1,0)\) belongs to \(T_K(0)\) but not to \(T_K^{\mathrm C}(0)\). Nevertheless, the solution \(x(t)=(t,0)\) remains in \(K\) for all \(t\geq0\). Thus replacing the contingent cone by the smaller Clarke cone can create a false obstruction to viability at an irregular boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a crossing, Clarke tangency can fail even though a trajectory follows one branch and remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Irregular-Boundary Obstructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crossing example correctly distinguishes the contingent cone from the Clarke tangent cone and exhibits a viable branch. The counterexample fits the irregular-boundary leaf, but no source supports the cone computations or convention.

children.title: Tangency-Recovery Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Transitions at which feasible forward motion reappears or disappears.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and closed.
\(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact convex values.
There is \(c>0\) such that \(\sup_{v\in F(x)}\|v\|\leq c(1+\|x\|)\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(F(x)\cap T_K(x)\neq\varnothing\) for all \(x\in K\) guarantees weak viability of \(K\).

notation.meaning: contingent tangent cone to K at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional contingent-cone viability theorem for a Marchaud-type multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume that
\[
F(x)\cap T_K(x)\neq\varnothing
\qquad\text{for every }x\in K.
\]
Then, for every \(x_0\in K\), there exists an absolutely continuous function \(x:[0,\infty)\to K\) such that \(x(0)=x_0\) and \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) for almost every \(t\geq0\). Thus closedness, compact-convex upper semicontinuous dynamics, linear growth, and contingent tangency form a threshold at which local feasible directions recover global weak viability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For regular compact-convex dynamics, contingent tangency at every feasible state guarantees a globally viable solution from each initial state.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangency-Recovery Thresholds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated finite-dimensional viability theorem is plausible under the listed Marchaud-type assumptions, and theorem is the correct content kind for the recovery threshold. Because the exact global conclusion depends on the full existence theorem, an authoritative theorem-level citation is required.

children.title: Viability State Regions
children.top_down_role: State-set constructions classifying sustainable, connecting, and target-reaching initial conditions.
