children.title: Constraint-Preservation Kernel Pair
children.top_down_role: Maximal sustainable and invariant state regions.

children.title: Viability Kernels
children.top_down_role: Maximal initial-state regions supporting at least one constraint-preserving trajectory.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), \(T\in(0,\infty]\), and \(F\) defines admissible solutions.
Solutions are considered on \([0,T]\) when \(T<\infty\), and on every finite subinterval when \(T=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Viab}_F^T(K)\) is the set of initial states in \(K\) from which at least one trajectory remains in \(K\) through horizon \(T\).

notation.meaning: solutions of the inclusion starting at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite- and infinite-horizon viability kernels under existential trajectory quantification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(T<\infty\), the horizon-\(T\) viability kernel of \(K\) is
\[
\operatorname{Viab}_F^T(K)
=
\left\{x_0\in K:
\exists x\in\mathcal S_F(x_0),
\ \forall t\in[0,T],
\ x(t)\in K
\right\}.
\]
For \(T=\infty\), membership requires a forward solution defined on \([0,\infty)\) that stays in \(K\) for every \(t\geq0\). It is the initial-state region in \(K\) enjoying existential constraint preservation over the selected horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The viability kernel contains exactly the initial states admitting at least one constraint-preserving trajectory over the chosen horizon.
knowledge_statements.title: Viability Kernels

children.title: Invariance Kernels
children.top_down_role: Maximal regions preserved across the relevant admissible dynamics.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), \(T\in(0,\infty]\), and \(F\) defines admissible solutions.
The universal convention counts every solution over its forward existence within the selected horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Inv}_F^T(K)\) is the set of initial states in \(K\) preserved by every admissible trajectory through horizon \(T\), under the stated universal-solution convention.

notation.meaning: solutions of the inclusion starting at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal-solution invariance kernel; terminology varies in controlled-dynamics sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the universal-solution convention, the horizon-\(T\) invariance kernel is
\[
\operatorname{Inv}_F^T(K)
=
\left\{x_0\in K:
\forall x\in\mathcal S_F(x_0),
\ \forall t\in I_x\cap[0,T],
\ x(t)\in K
\right\}.
\]
For \(T=\infty\), every forward solution must remain in \(K\) throughout its existence. This definition uses universal trajectory quantification and is distinct from controlled-invariance conventions that quantify existentially over controls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the universal-solution convention, the invariance kernel contains exactly those initial states from which every admissible trajectory remains feasible over the chosen horizon.
knowledge_statements.title: Invariance Kernels

children.title: Kernel Inclusion Relations
children.top_down_role: Set-theoretic relationships between viability and invariance regions.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(C\subset X\) is closed, and trajectories are absolutely continuous solutions of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
Solutions under consideration exist on every stated finite horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Inv}_T(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Viab}_T(C),\qquad \operatorname{Inv}_\infty(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Viab}_\infty(C),\qquad \operatorname{Viab}_\infty(C)=\bigcap_{T>0}\operatorname{Viab}_T(C).\]

notation.meaning: finite-horizon viability and invariance kernels of the constraint set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic differential-inclusion kernels, with invariance quantified over all solutions and viability over at least one solution.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T>0\), universal preservation implies existential preservation, hence \(\operatorname{Inv}_T(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Viab}_T(C)\). The same implication holds on the infinite horizon. Finite-horizon viability is monotone in the horizon: if \(0<S\leq T\), then \(\operatorname{Viab}_T(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Viab}_S(C)\). Moreover, an initial state is infinitely viable exactly when it is viable on every finite horizon, so \(\operatorname{Viab}_\infty(C)=\bigcap_{T>0}\operatorname{Viab}_T(C)\). Likewise, whenever finite-horizon invariance requires every solution to exist through the horizon, \(\operatorname{Inv}_\infty(C)=\bigcap_{T>0}\operatorname{Inv}_T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invariance kernels lie inside viability kernels, longer horizons produce smaller kernels, and the infinite-horizon kernel is the intersection of all finite-horizon kernels.
knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Inclusion Relations

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusions and horizon monotonicity are standard, but finite-horizon existence alone does not imply that trajectories chosen separately for every horizon admit one infinite viable continuation. The cited optimal-control section has not been inspected for the kernel definitions or the required compactness/extension theorem.

children.title: Finite-Horizon Kernels
children.top_down_role: Sustainable or invariant regions defined over bounded time horizons.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(C\subset X\) is closed, \(T>0\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\) specifies an autonomous differential inclusion.
A trajectory is an absolutely continuous map satisfying \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) for almost every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Viab}_T(C)=\{x_0\in C:\exists x(\cdot),\ x(0)=x_0,\ \dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\ \text{a.e.},\ x(t)\in C\ \forall t\in[0,T]\}.\]

notation.meaning: finite-horizon viability kernel of the constraint set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential finite-horizon viability for an autonomous differential inclusion.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-horizon viability kernel of \(C\) over \([0,T]\) is \[\operatorname{Viab}_T(C):=\left\{x_0\in C:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exists an absolutely continuous }x:[0,T]\to X,\ x(0)=x_0,\\ \dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\text{ for almost every }t\in[0,T],\text{ and }x(t)\in C\text{ for all }t\in[0,T]\end{array}\right\}.\] Thus membership requires one admissible trajectory that respects the constraint throughout the prescribed horizon, including both endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-horizon viability kernel contains exactly the initial states admitting at least one trajectory that remains in the constraint set through time T.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Kernels

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

children.title: Infinite-Horizon Kernels
children.top_down_role: Sustainable or invariant regions associated with indefinite constraint preservation.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(C\subset X\) is closed, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows X\) defines an autonomous differential inclusion.
Every finite-horizon viable trajectory can be extended consistently whenever the stated intersection characterization is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Viab}_\infty(C)=\{x_0\in C:\exists x:[0,\infty)\to X,\ \dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\ \text{a.e.},\ x(t)\in C\ \forall t\geq0\}=\bigcap_{T>0}\operatorname{Viab}_T(C).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-horizon viability, with the finite-horizon intersection formula stated under a compatible-extension hypothesis.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infinite-horizon viability kernel is \[\operatorname{Viab}_\infty(C):=\left\{x_0\in C:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exists an absolutely continuous }x:[0,\infty)\to X,\ x(0)=x_0,\\ \dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\text{ for almost every }t\geq0,\text{ and }x(t)\in C\text{ for every }t\geq0\end{array}\right\}.\] Under a compatible-extension or compactness hypothesis ensuring that finite viable arcs possess a common infinite continuation, \(\operatorname{Viab}_\infty(C)=\bigcap_{T>0}\operatorname{Viab}_T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infinite-horizon kernel consists of states admitting a constraint-preserving trajectory for all future time; under extension compactness it intersects all finite-horizon kernels.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Horizon Kernels

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The infinite-horizon kernel definition is precise, but the intersection equality is not definitional and the stated 'compatible-extension or compactness hypothesis' is not a checkable mathematical hypothesis. A source must establish concrete conditions under which finite viable arcs yield a common infinite trajectory.

children.title: Target-Reachability Basin Pair
children.top_down_role: Initial states supporting target capture or viable connection.

children.title: Capture Basins
children.top_down_role: Initial states from which a prescribed target can be reached under admissible evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K\subset X\) is a closed constraint set, and \(D\subset K\) is a target.
Admissible trajectories are absolutely continuous solutions of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Capt}_F(K,D)=\{x_0\in K:\exists\tau\geq0,\exists x(\cdot),\ x(0)=x_0,\ x([0,\tau])\subset K,\ x(\tau)\in D\}.\]

notation.meaning: capture basin of the target within the constraint set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-time existential capture while satisfying the state constraint until the target is reached.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The capture basin of \(D\) viable in \(K\) is \[\operatorname{Capt}_F(K,D):=\left\{x_0\in K:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }\tau\in[0,\infty)\text{ and an absolutely continuous }x:[0,\tau]\to X,\\ x(0)=x_0,\ \dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\text{ for almost every }t,\ x(t)\in K\text{ for all }t\in[0,\tau],\\ \text{and }x(\tau)\in D\end{array}\right\}.\] The convention \(\tau=0\) implies \(D\subseteq\operatorname{Capt}_F(K,D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capture basin contains states from which some admissible trajectory stays in the constraint set and reaches the target in finite time.
knowledge_statements.title: Capture Basins

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-time constrained reachability set is mathematically precise, but the cited general evolution-inclusion section has not been shown to support this exact capture-basin convention, including allowance of time zero and viability in K.

children.title: Connection Basins
children.top_down_role: Initial states supporting viable transitions between prescribed state regions.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K\subset X\) is closed, and \(D\subset K\) is closed.
Admissible trajectories are complete absolutely continuous solutions of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Conn}_F(K,D)=\{x_0\in K:\exists x(\cdot),\ x(0)=x_0,\ x(t)\in K\ \forall t\geq0,\ \operatorname{dist}(x(t),D)\to0\}.\]

notation.meaning: viable connection basin approaching the target
distance from a point to the target set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic viable connection; literature conventions may instead include finite-time arrival.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic connection basin of \(D\) within \(K\) is \[\operatorname{Conn}_F(K,D):=\left\{x_0\in K:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exists an absolutely continuous }x:[0,\infty)\to X\text{ with }x(0)=x_0,\\ \dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\text{ for almost every }t\geq0,\ x(t)\in K\text{ for every }t\geq0,\\ \text{and }\lim_{t\to\infty}\operatorname{dist}(x(t),D)=0\end{array}\right\}.\] This convention distinguishes asymptotic connection from finite-time capture.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connection basin contains states admitting a complete constraint-respecting trajectory whose distance to the target tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Connection Basins

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports identifying a connection basin specifically with asymptotic approach to the target. In viability literature the term may use finite-time reachability or another connection convention, so the intended mathematical object cannot be confirmed.

children.title: Finite-Time Capture Regions
children.top_down_role: Capture basins organized by bounded target-reaching horizons.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K\subset X\) is closed, \(D\subset K\), and \(T\geq0\).
Admissible trajectories solve \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Capt}_{F,T}(K,D)=\{x_0\in K:\exists\tau\in[0,T],\exists x(\cdot),\ x([0,\tau])\subset K,\ x(\tau)\in D\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capture by a deadline, allowing arrival at any time not exceeding the horizon.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a deadline \(T\geq0\), the finite-time capture region is \[\operatorname{Capt}_{F,T}(K,D):=\left\{x_0\in K:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }\tau\in[0,T]\text{ and an absolutely continuous }x:[0,\tau]\to X,\\ x(0)=x_0,\ \dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\text{ for almost every }t,\ x(t)\in K\text{ for every }t\in[0,\tau],\\ \text{and }x(\tau)\in D\end{array}\right\}.\] Consequently, \(S\leq T\) implies \(\operatorname{Capt}_{F,S}(K,D)\subseteq\operatorname{Capt}_{F,T}(K,D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-time capture region consists of states from which the target can be reached without violating constraints and no later than the deadline.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Time Capture Regions

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deadline-bounded reachability formula and its monotonicity are internally correct, but the supplied source has not been shown to define this object as a finite-time capture region or to support the exact endpoint and time-zero conventions.

children.title: Viable Connection Corridors
children.top_down_role: State-space regions supporting constraint-compatible transitions toward a target.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K\subset X\) is closed, and \(A,B\subset K\) are endpoint sets.
Admissible arcs are absolutely continuous solutions of \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Cor}_F(K;A,B)=\{x(t):\exists\tau\geq0,\exists x(\cdot),\ x(0)\in A,\ x(\tau)\in B,\ x([0,\tau])\subset K,\ t\in[0,\tau]\}.\]

notation.meaning: union of states traversed by viable connecting arcs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space corridor formed by the union of all finite viable arcs connecting two endpoint sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The viable connection corridor from \(A\) to \(B\) inside \(K\) is \[\operatorname{Cor}_F(K;A,B):=\left\{y\in K:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }\tau\geq0,\ t\in[0,\tau],\text{ and an absolutely continuous }x:[0,\tau]\to X,\\ x(0)\in A,\ x(\tau)\in B,\ \dot x(s)\in F(x(s))\text{ for almost every }s,\\ x(s)\in K\text{ for every }s\in[0,\tau],\text{ and }y=x(t)\end{array}\right\}.\] It is the union of the traces of all constraint-respecting connecting arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A viable connection corridor is the union of states traversed by admissible, constraint-respecting trajectories connecting a source set to a destination set.
knowledge_statements.title: Viable Connection Corridors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed union of trajectory traces is coherent, but no source establishes that this is the intended viable connection corridor rather than a state-time corridor, a set of connecting initial states, or another viability object.

children.title: Capture Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Geometric or dynamical structures preventing target attainment.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K\subset X\) is a constraint set, and \(D\subset K\) is a target.
Capture is defined by existence of a finite admissible arc that remains in \(K\) until reaching \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Obs}_F(K,D)=K\setminus\operatorname{Capt}_F(K,D).\]

notation.meaning: capture basin of the target within the constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic obstruction region relative to finite-time viable capture.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The capture-obstruction region is the relative complement of the capture basin in the admissible constraint set: \[\operatorname{Obs}_F(K,D):=K\setminus\operatorname{Capt}_F(K,D).\] Equivalently, \(x_0\in\operatorname{Obs}_F(K,D)\) precisely when no finite time \(\tau\geq0\) and no absolutely continuous trajectory \(x:[0,\tau]\to X\) satisfy simultaneously \(x(0)=x_0\), \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t))\) almost everywhere, \(x(t)\in K\) throughout \([0,\tau]\), and \(x(\tau)\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capture obstructions are the constrained initial states from which no admissible trajectory can reach the target in finite time while remaining feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Capture Obstructions

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complement identity is correct once adopted as a definition, but the citation has not been shown to support calling this complement the capture-obstruction region. The leaf may instead require a failure-boundary or obstruction-certificate statement, so both terminology and mathematical role need authoritative support.

children.title: Uncertainty-Resilient Kernel Family
children.top_down_role: Sustainable regions under disturbances or adversarial choices.

children.title: Discriminating Kernels
children.top_down_role: Sustainable state regions organized around opposing control and disturbance choices.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, \(U\) and \(W\) are control and disturbance sets, and \(f\) defines \(\dot x=f(x,u,w)\).
\(\mathfrak{S}\) is a specified class of nonanticipative control strategies mapping disturbance signals to control signals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Disc}(K)=\{x_0\in K:\exists\alpha\in\mathfrak{S},\ \forall w(\cdot),\ x^{\alpha[w],w}_{x_0}(t)\in K\ \forall t\geq0\}.\]

notation.meaning: discriminating kernel of the constraint set
trajectory generated from x0 by control and disturbance signals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-horizon discriminating kernel under nonanticipative feedback against every admissible disturbance signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed information pattern \(\mathfrak{S}\), the discriminating kernel is \[\operatorname{Disc}(K):=\left\{x_0\in K:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exists a nonanticipative strategy }\alpha\in\mathfrak{S}\text{ such that, for every admissible }w(\cdot),\\ \text{the trajectory }x^{\alpha[w],w}_{x_0}(\cdot)\text{ exists and satisfies }x^{\alpha[w],w}_{x_0}(t)\in K\text{ for all }t\geq0\end{array}\right\}.\] Nonanticipativity means that disturbances agreeing almost everywhere up to time \(t\) induce controls agreeing almost everywhere up to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The discriminating kernel contains states from which a nonanticipative control strategy preserves constraints against every admissible disturbance signal.
knowledge_statements.title: Discriminating Kernels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantifier order is coherent for one differential-game convention, but discriminating kernels depend essentially on which player uses nonanticipative strategies, the admissible signal classes, and the solution convention. No source is supplied to validate this information pattern.

children.title: Robust Viability Kernels
children.top_down_role: State regions preserving viability across a specified uncertainty family.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, and trajectories satisfy \(\dot x(t)=f(x(t),u(t),w(t))\).
Controls lie in an admissible class \(\mathcal U\), while disturbances range over an admissible class \(\mathcal W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{RViab}(K)=\{x_0\in K:\exists u\in\mathcal U,\ \forall w\in\mathcal W,\ x^{u,w}_{x_0}(t)\in K\ \forall t\geq0\}.\]

notation.meaning: admissible control and disturbance signal classes
trajectory under control u and disturbance w from x0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-loop robust viability with one control signal required to withstand every admissible disturbance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The open-loop robust viability kernel is \[\operatorname{RViab}(K):=\left\{x_0\in K:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exists one admissible control }u(\cdot)\in\mathcal U\text{ such that, for every }w(\cdot)\in\mathcal W,\\ \text{the corresponding trajectory }x^{u,w}_{x_0}(\cdot)\text{ exists and satisfies }x^{u,w}_{x_0}(t)\in K\text{ for all }t\geq0\end{array}\right\}.\] The control is selected before the disturbance realization; replacing it by a nonanticipative strategy yields the information-adaptive discriminating-kernel convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust viability kernel contains states for which one admissible control keeps every allowed disturbance realization inside the constraint set forever.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Viability Kernels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula precisely defines an open-loop maximin safety set, but no source supports identifying it with the robust viability kernel. Standard robust-viability conventions may permit feedback or nonanticipative strategies and therefore produce a different set.

children.title: Adversarial Disturbance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Kernel constructions governed by strategic worst-case disturbances.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(W\) are measurable control and disturbance value sets, and \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\times U\times W\to\mathbb{R}^n\) defines the dynamics.
Disturbance signals belong to a prescribed measurable class \(\mathcal W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\alpha\in\mathfrak S\ \forall w\in\mathcal W\quad \dot x(t)=f(x(t),\alpha[w](t),w(t)),\qquad x(t)\in K\ \forall t\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case measurable disturbances with a nonanticipative controller information pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adversarial disturbance regime is specified by the ordered quantifiers \(\exists\alpha\in\mathfrak S\,\forall w\in\mathcal W\), where \(\alpha:\mathcal W\to\mathcal U\) is nonanticipative: for every \(t\geq0\), if \(w_1=w_2\) almost everywhere on \([0,t]\), then \(\alpha[w_1]=\alpha[w_2]\) almost everywhere on \([0,t]\). Constraint preservation from \(x_0\in K\) requires that every closed-loop trajectory satisfying \(\dot x(t)=f(x(t),\alpha[w](t),w(t))\) remain in \(K\) for all \(t\geq0\) and every \(w\in\mathcal W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adversarial regime quantifies over all disturbance signals while allowing only controls generated by a stated nonanticipative information pattern.
knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Disturbance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonanticipativity condition is stated clearly, but the phrase 'every closed-loop trajectory' introduces an additional universal solution quantifier not reflected in the displayed conclusion and may differ from the intended differential-game convention. An authoritative source is required for the timing, information, and solution quantifiers.

children.title: Set-Valued Uncertainty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Robust kernel constructions based on nonstrategic uncertainty sets.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a control set and \(W(x,u)\) is a nonempty set of admissible uncertainty values at each state-control pair.
\(f(x,u,w)\) is the pointwise velocity under uncertainty value \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(x,u)=\{f(x,u,w):w\in W(x,u)\},\qquad \dot x(t)\in F(x(t),u(t)).\]

notation.meaning: set-valued velocity map induced by uncertainty

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise set-valued representation of parameterized uncertain continuous-time dynamics.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Parameterized uncertainty can be represented by the set-valued velocity map \[F(x,u):=\{f(x,u,w):w\in W(x,u)\}.\] Every trajectory generated by a measurable uncertainty selection \(w(t)\in W(x(t),u(t))\) satisfies the differential inclusion \(\dot x(t)\in F(x(t),u(t))\) almost everywhere. Conversely, any inclusion trajectory admits such a pointwise representation whenever the velocity selection has a measurable parameter lifting through \(f\). Thus the inclusion is exact only under the stated measurable-lifting condition; otherwise it is a pointwise uncertainty envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized uncertainty family induces a set-valued velocity map; the differential inclusion represents all uncertainty selections when measurable parameter liftings exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Uncertainty Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

children.title: Robustness-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Thresholds where disturbance tolerance no longer preserves sustainability.

assumptions_latex: A controlled uncertain system admits trajectories \(x(\cdot;x_0,u,d)\) in a metric state space \(X\).
For each uncertainty radius \(\rho\ge 0\), disturbances belong to a class \(\mathcal D_\rho\), and \(K\subset X\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state-space boundary separates the robust viability kernel from its complement locally in \(X\).

notation.meaning: robust viability kernel at uncertainty radius rho
topological boundary in the state space
admissible disturbances at uncertainty radius rho

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: topological boundary of a parameterized robust viability kernel
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space robustness-loss boundary for a fixed uncertainty radius; no identification with a robustness-margin level set is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\rho\ge 0\), define
\[
V_\rho:=\left\{x_0\in K:\exists u\;\forall d\in\mathcal D_\rho\;\forall t\ge 0,\ x(t;x_0,u,d)\in K\right\}.
\]
The state-space robustness-loss boundary at radius \(\rho\) is
\[
\partial_X V_\rho:=\overline{V_\rho}^{\,X}\cap\overline{X\setminus V_\rho}^{\,X}.
\]
Thus every neighborhood in \(X\) of a point in \(\partial_XV_\rho\) meets both \(V_\rho\) and \(X\setminus V_\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed uncertainty radius, the robustness-loss boundary consists of states whose every state-space neighborhood contains both robustly viable and non-robustly-viable states.
knowledge_statements.title: Robustness-Loss Boundaries

children.title: Post-Violation Recovery Basin Family
children.top_down_role: Regions from which viability can be recovered after constraint violation.

children.title: Restoration Basins
children.top_down_role: Initial states from which admissible evolution can return to a viable region.

assumptions_latex: The controlled system has trajectories \(x(\cdot;x_0,u)\) in a state space \(X\).
The desired viable set \(K\subset X\) and admissible recovery domain \(R\subset X\), with \(K\subset R\), are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every state in the restoration basin admits a control that reaches \(K\) and subsequently keeps the trajectory in \(K\).

notation.meaning: restoration basin of K within R

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: capture basin with post-capture invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled recovery to a target followed by indefinite constraint preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The restoration basin of \(K\) relative to \(R\) is
\[
\mathcal B_{\mathrm{rest}}(K;R):=\left\{x_0\in R:\begin{array}{l}\exists u\in\mathcal U\;\exists\tau<\infty\text{ such that }x(t;x_0,u)\in R\text{ for }0\le t\le\tau,\\ x(\tau;x_0,u)\in K,\text{ and }x(t;x_0,u)\in K\text{ for every }t\ge\tau\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Thus restoration requires both finite-time capture by \(K\) and a continuation of the same admissible control, or an admissible concatenation, that preserves membership in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The restoration basin contains states recoverable to the target through the recovery domain, with the target preserved thereafter.
knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Basins

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits Restoration Basins, but no inspectable citation supports this particular capture-plus-invariant-tail convention. A source is needed because restoration-basin terminology is not fully standardized.

children.title: Resilience Basins
children.top_down_role: Initial states supporting recovery from disruptions while retaining long-term sustainability.

assumptions_latex: A controlled uncertain system has trajectories \(x(\cdot;x_0,u,d)\) in \(X\).
The viable set \(K\) lies in a recovery domain \(R\), and disruptions belong to a specified class \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A state is resilient when every allowed disruption can be countered by recovery control that restores and thereafter preserves \(K\).

notation.meaning: resilience basin of K relative to R

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: robust capture basin under nonanticipative recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case post-disruption recovery under nonanticipative control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Gamma\) be the admissible nonanticipative control strategies. The resilience basin is
\[
\mathcal B_{\mathrm{res}}(K;R,\mathcal D):=\left\{x_0\in R:\exists\gamma\in\Gamma\;\forall d\in\mathcal D\;\exists\tau_d<\infty,\ \begin{array}{l}x(t;x_0,\gamma[d],d)\in R\quad(0\le t\le\tau_d),\\ x(t;x_0,\gamma[d],d)\in K\quad(t\ge\tau_d)
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Nonanticipativity means that disturbances agreeing up to time \(t\) induce controls agreeing up to time \(t\). The recovery time may depend on the realized disturbance unless a uniform bound is imposed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resilience basin contains states recoverable after every allowed disruption by a nonanticipative strategy, while remaining in a recovery domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Resilience Basins

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantified nonanticipative recovery definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but the meaning of resilience basins and the orientation of the disturbance-control strategy vary across frameworks. An authoritative source must establish this exact convention.

children.title: Finite-Time Restoration Regions
children.top_down_role: Recovery regions organized by bounded return horizons.

assumptions_latex: The controlled system has trajectories \(x(\cdot;x_0,u)\) in a state space \(X\) for admissible controls \(u\in\mathcal U\) defined on \([0,\infty)\).
A target \(K\subset R\subset X\) and a deadline \(T>0\) are fixed.
The admissible control class \(\mathcal U\) permits any required admissible concatenation at the restoration time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership certifies restoration no later than \(T\), followed by indefinite preservation of \(K\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: time-bounded capture basin with invariant continuation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restoration basin restricted by a fixed recovery deadline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(T>0\), the finite-time restoration region is
\[
\mathcal R_T(K;R):=\left\{x_0\in R:\begin{array}{l}
\exists u\in\mathcal U\;\exists\tau\in[0,T]\text{ such that }x(t;x_0,u)\in R\text{ for every }t\in[0,\tau],\\
x(\tau;x_0,u)\in K,\text{ and }x(t;x_0,u)\in K\text{ for every }t\ge\tau
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
For fixed \(K\) and \(R\), the family is monotone in the deadline:
\[
0<T_1\le T_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathcal R_{T_1}(K;R)\subseteq\mathcal R_{T_2}(K;R).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-time restoration region contains states that admit an admissible trajectory staying in the recovery domain until it reaches the target by the prescribed deadline and remaining in the target thereafter. These regions expand, or remain unchanged, as the deadline increases.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Time Restoration Regions

children.title: Post-Violation Recovery Paths
children.top_down_role: Admissible trajectory families connecting violated states back to sustainable regions.

assumptions_latex: An admissible controlled trajectory \(x:[0,\infty)\to X\) is absolutely continuous.
The target \(K\subset R\subset X\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A recovery path remains in the recovery domain until first restoration and remains in the target thereafter.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: admissible capture trajectory with invariant tail
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trajectory-level object underlying restoration basins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an admissible trajectory \(x(\cdot)\) with \(x(0)\in R\setminus K\), define
\[
\tau_K(x):=\inf\{t\ge0:x(t)\in K\}.
\]
The trajectory is a post-violation recovery path from \(x(0)\) to \(K\) within \(R\) when \(\tau_K(x)<\infty\), \(x(t)\in R\) for every \(t\in[0,\tau_K(x)]\), and \(x(t)\in K\) for every \(t\ge\tau_K(x)\). If only capture, rather than maintained restoration, is intended, the final condition is replaced by \(x(\tau_K(x))\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recovery path stays in the permitted recovery domain, reaches the target in finite time, and then remains there.
knowledge_statements.title: Post-Violation Recovery Paths

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The trajectory-level definition is internally consistent and fits Post-Violation Recovery Paths, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the maintained-restoration convention or terminology.

children.title: Irrecoverable State Regions
children.top_down_role: States from which viability cannot be restored under the available dynamics.

assumptions_latex: The admissible initial-state domain is \(R\subset X\).
The restoration basin \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{rest}}(K;R)\) uses the fixed dynamics, controls, target \(K\), and recovery constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No state in the irrecoverable region admits a qualifying restoration trajectory to \(K\).

notation.meaning: irrecoverable region relative to K and R

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relative complement of the restoration basin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irrecoverability relative to specified dynamics, controls, target, and recovery domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The irrecoverable state region relative to target \(K\) and admissible domain \(R\) is
\[
\mathcal I(K;R):=R\setminus\mathcal B_{\mathrm{rest}}(K;R).
\]
Equivalently, \(x_0\in\mathcal I(K;R)\) precisely when no admissible control produces a finite time \(\tau\) such that the trajectory remains in \(R\) on \([0,\tau]\), reaches \(K\) at \(\tau\), and admits an admissible continuation remaining in \(K\). Irrecoverability is therefore relative, not intrinsic to the state alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Irrecoverable states are admissible initial states from which no allowed restoration path reaches and subsequently preserves the target.
knowledge_statements.title: Irrecoverable State Regions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative-complement definition is precise given the preceding restoration-basin convention and fits the leaf. Its validity as domain terminology nevertheless depends on the uncited restoration definition, so a supporting source is required.

children.title: Extended Viability Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Viability under control choices, disturbances, moving constraints, and hybrid evolution.

children.title: Controlled Viability
children.top_down_role: Constraint preservation through admissible control selection.

assumptions_latex: The dynamics are \(\dot x(t)=f(x(t),u(t))\) on \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with measurable controls \(u(t)\in U(x(t))\).
For every admissible control and initial state considered, an absolutely continuous solution exists.
The constraint set \(K\subset X\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Controlled viability means that each initial state in \(K\) has at least one admissible control whose trajectory never leaves \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time deterministic controlled viability in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The controlled viability kernel of \(K\) is
\[
\operatorname{Viab}_f(K):=\left\{x_0\in K:\exists u(\cdot)\text{ measurable with }u(t)\in U(x(t))\text{ a.e., and }x(t)\in K\text{ for all }t\ge0\right\},
\]
where \(x(0)=x_0\) and \(\dot x(t)=f(x(t),u(t))\) almost everywhere. The set \(K\) is controlled viable when \(\operatorname{Viab}_f(K)=K\). The existential control may depend on the initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint set is controlled viable when every state in it admits a control that keeps the resulting trajectory inside forever.
knowledge_statements.title: Controlled Viability

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Optimal Control of Discrete-Time and Continuous-time Evolution Inclusions p. 160
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional deterministic definition is standard and fits Controlled Viability, but the cited locator is a broad optimal-control section rather than a specific viability definition or result. Full-text inspection or a viability-specific section, definition, theorem, or page is required.

children.title: Uncertainty-Quantified Viability Duality
children.top_down_role: Constraint preservation under uncertainty and disturbance.

children.title: Robust Viability
children.top_down_role: Constraint preservation across a prescribed family of uncertain dynamics.

assumptions_latex: Trajectories satisfy \(\dot x(t)=f(x(t),u(t),d(t))\), with admissible measurable \(u\in\mathcal U\) and \(d\in\mathcal D\).
The constraint set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed, and solutions exist for all quantified signal pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robust viability requires one admissible control choice to preserve \(K\) against every admissible disturbance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: open-loop robust viability with existential-universal order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-loop robust viability with one control working against all disturbances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The robust viability kernel of \(K\) under the open-loop information convention is
\[
\operatorname{Viab}^{\mathrm{rob}}(K):=\left\{x_0\in K:\exists u\in\mathcal U\;\forall d\in\mathcal D\;\forall t\ge0,\ x(t;x_0,u,d)\in K\right\}.
\]
The set \(K\) is robustly viable when \(\operatorname{Viab}^{\mathrm{rob}}(K)=K\). Because the same \(u\) must work for every \(d\), this definition differs from viability based on a disturbance-responsive, nonanticipative control strategy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust viability uses a single admissible control that keeps constraints satisfied for every disturbance in the prescribed class.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Viability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The open-loop existential-universal predicate is explicit and mathematically coherent, but calling this exact information pattern robust viability is convention-dependent. No authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Discriminating Viability
children.top_down_role: Constraint preservation under strategic interaction between controls and disturbances.

assumptions_latex: The uncertain controlled dynamics generate trajectories \(x(\cdot;x_0,u,d)\) for admissible signals.
Controls are selected by nonanticipative strategies \(\gamma:\mathcal D\to\mathcal U\), and \(K\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Discriminating viability permits causal adaptation to observed disturbance history while forbidding anticipation of its future.

notation.meaning: control induced by strategy gamma against d

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: viability under nonanticipative control strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Causal strategy form of viability against disturbance signals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A strategy \(\gamma:\mathcal D\to\mathcal U\) is nonanticipative when, for every \(t\ge0\), equality \(d_1=d_2\) almost everywhere on \([0,t]\) implies \(\gamma[d_1]=\gamma[d_2]\) almost everywhere on \([0,t]\). The discriminating viability kernel is
\[
\operatorname{Disc}(K):=\left\{x_0\in K:\exists\gamma\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{NA}}\;\forall d\in\mathcal D\;\forall t\ge0,\ x(t;x_0,\gamma[d],d)\in K\right\}.
\]
Thus control may react causally to the disturbance but may not use its future values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discriminating viability allows a causal control strategy to react to disturbance history while preserving the constraint against every disturbance.
knowledge_statements.title: Discriminating Viability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonanticipative-strategy definition is precise and fits the intended causal-response leaf, but discriminating-kernel conventions differ in which player uses a strategy and in the quantifier order. The exact orientation requires an authoritative citation.

children.title: Worst-Case Disturbance Semantics
children.top_down_role: Organization of viability according to worst-case disturbance interpretation.

assumptions_latex: The disturbance class \(\mathcal D\) is fixed independently of the controller.
A feasibility predicate \(P(x_0,u,d)\) means \(x(t;x_0,u,d)\in K\) for every \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Worst-case feasibility requires the stated preservation predicate to hold for every disturbance allowed by the model.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: universal quantification over the uncertainty set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical semantics of worst-case constraint preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(x_0\) and control \(u\), worst-case constraint preservation over \(\mathcal D\) is the condition
\[
\forall d\in\mathcal D,\quad P(x_0,u,d),\qquad P(x_0,u,d):\Longleftrightarrow\forall t\ge0,\ x(t;x_0,u,d)\in K.
\]
Hence one counterexample disturbance \(d\in\mathcal D\) falsifies worst-case feasibility. If the controller observes disturbances, \(u\) must be replaced by a declared causal strategy \(\gamma[d]\); the universal disturbance quantifier remains, but admissibility additionally requires nonanticipativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case semantics treat every modeled disturbance as possible; a single disturbance causing constraint violation disproves feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Disturbance Semantics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The universal-disturbance condition correctly expresses worst-case semantics for a fixed control, and the content kind condition fits the leaf. No source supports the robust-control interpretation or its stated strategy extension.

children.title: Control–Disturbance Quantifier Orders
children.top_down_role: Alternative priority structures governing control and disturbance choices.

assumptions_latex: For each initial state \(x_0\), \(P(x_0,u,d)\) denotes satisfaction of the constraint for the entire horizon.
The admissible control and disturbance classes are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The order \(\exists u\,\forall d\) is at least as demanding as \(\forall d\,\exists u\), and the two need not coincide.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary quantifier implication applied to viability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of uniform and disturbance-dependent control feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
V_{\exists\forall}:=\{x_0:\exists u\in\mathcal U\;\forall d\in\mathcal D,\ P(x_0,u,d)\},\qquad
V_{\forall\exists}:=\{x_0:\forall d\in\mathcal D\;\exists u\in\mathcal U,\ P(x_0,u,d)\}.
\]
Then \(V_{\exists\forall}\subseteq V_{\forall\exists}\). Equality is not guaranteed because the control witnessing the second predicate may depend on the entire disturbance. A nonanticipative-strategy predicate \(\exists\gamma\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{NA}}\;\forall d\in\mathcal D,\ P(x_0,\gamma[d],d)\) lies between these interpretations only under explicitly specified information and admissibility conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A control that works for all disturbances is stronger than choosing a separate control after each disturbance is known.
knowledge_statements.title: Control–Disturbance Quantifier Orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusion follows from elementary quantifier logic and the property content kind fits the leaf. However, the record has no citation for its viability interpretation or for the discussion of nonanticipative strategies, so source support is required under the review contract.

children.title: Robustness Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where nominal or selective preservation fails to imply disturbance-wide viability.

assumptions_latex: The same dynamics, constraint set \(K\), and disturbance class \(\mathcal D\) define both kernels.
Open-loop robust controls are admissible as constant nonanticipative strategies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The robustness gap is the set of states viable by causal disturbance response but not by a single disturbance-independent control.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: set difference induced by alternative information patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap caused by allowing causal adaptation to disturbances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V_{\mathrm{rob}}\) use the predicate \(\exists u\;\forall d\), and let \(V_{\mathrm{disc}}\) use \(\exists\gamma\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{NA}}\;\forall d\). Under the assumption that every open-loop control induces an admissible constant strategy,
\[
V_{\mathrm{rob}}\subseteq V_{\mathrm{disc}},\qquad G:=V_{\mathrm{disc}}\setminus V_{\mathrm{rob}}.
\]
The zero-gap regime is \(G=\varnothing\), equivalently \(V_{\mathrm{rob}}=V_{\mathrm{disc}}\). A strict-gap regime occurs when \(G\ne\varnothing\), so some states require causal disturbance-dependent control and admit no single open-loop control preserving \(K\) against all disturbances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The robustness gap contains states preservable by causal response to disturbances but not by one fixed open-loop control.
knowledge_statements.title: Robustness Gap Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the explicitly stated embedding of disturbance-independent controls into the nonanticipative strategy class, the inclusion and set-difference definition are coherent and fit Robustness Gap Regimes. The terminology and inclusion depend on information-pattern conventions and have no authoritative citation.

children.title: Time-Dependent Viability
children.top_down_role: Viability relative to moving or space-time constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(K:[0,T]\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) has nonempty closed values.
\(F:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is a differential-inclusion velocity map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t)\in K(t)\) for every \(t\in[t_0,T]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strong viability for a moving closed constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((t_0,x_0)\) with \(x_0\in K(t_0)\), the differential inclusion is viable in the moving constraint \(K\) from \((t_0,x_0)\) if there exists an absolutely continuous map \(x:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(x(t_0)=x_0\), \(\dot x(t)\in F(t,x(t))\) for almost every \(t\in[t_0,T]\), and \(x(t)\in K(t)\) for every \(t\in[t_0,T]\). The system is viable in \(K\) if this property holds for every admissible initial pair \((t_0,x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time-dependent viability means that every admissible initial state has a trajectory obeying the differential inclusion while remaining in the moving constraint at all later times.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Viability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and finite-dimensional moving-constraint definition fit the terminal container, and the notation and quantifiers are coherent. However, no source reference or inspectable locator is supplied for this nontrivial viability definition.

children.title: Hybrid Viability
children.top_down_role: Constraint preservation across flows, switching, and jumps.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are respectively the flow and jump constraint sets.
\(F:C\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(G:D\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) specify admissible flows and jumps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t,j)\in C\cup D\) throughout the hybrid time domain, with every jump image in \(C\cup D\).

notation.meaning: hybrid trajectory indexed by continuous and jump time

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential viability for a hybrid inclusion with flow and jump constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hybrid trajectory from \(x_0\in C\cup D\) is viable if, on every flow interval, it is locally absolutely continuous, satisfies \(x(t,j)\in C\) and \(\dot x(t,j)\in F(x(t,j))\) almost everywhere, and, at every jump, satisfies \(x(t,j)\in D\) and \(x(t,j+1)\in G(x(t,j))\cap(C\cup D)\). The hybrid system is viable on \(C\cup D\) if every \(x_0\in C\cup D\) admits a nontrivial maximal hybrid trajectory satisfying these conditions throughout its domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hybrid viability requires an admissible trajectory to respect the flow constraint during continuous evolution and the jump constraint and safe image condition at every discrete transition.
knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Viability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for the Hybrid Viability container, but the requirement of a nontrivial maximal trajectory does not clarify whether finite termination without constraint violation counts as viability. An authoritative hybrid-systems source is needed to settle completeness, maximality, and admissible-domain conventions.

children.title: Viability Computation
children.top_down_role: Set-oriented and dynamic-programming families for approximating viable regions.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Viability Theory: New Directions
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Viability Kernels and numerical examples; viability solutions to Hamilton–Jacobi equations
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Viability Theory: New Directions

children.title: Set-Oriented Viability Methods
children.top_down_role: Grid, subdivision, and set-propagation approximation families.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact and \(F:K\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is the velocity map.
\(X_h\) is a finite grid with cell diameter at most \(h\), and \(\tau>0\) is a time step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stabilized set \(V_{h,\tau}\) consists of grid cells admitting arbitrarily long discrete constraint-preserving successor chains.

notation.meaning: grid cell containing a grid point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic outer set-oriented pruning scheme for an autonomous differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(V^0=X_h\cap K\). For each \(x\in V^k\), construct an outer successor set \(S_{h,\tau}(x)\) containing every grid cell intersecting \(x+\tau F(x)\), including the prescribed consistency inflation. Update \[V^{k+1}=\{x\in V^k:S_{h,\tau}(x)\cap V^k\ne\varnothing\}.\] Stop when \(V^{k+1}=V^k\), or when a chosen set-distance tolerance is met, and output the union of retained cells \(V_{h,\tau}\). Adaptive subdivision repeats the construction after refining cells intersecting the retained-set boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-oriented method repeatedly removes grid cells having no admissible successor among the currently retained cells, optionally refining cells near the resulting boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Oriented Viability Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the set-oriented methods container, and the pruning scheme is plausible. Its consistency inflation, grid-cell representation, stopping rule, and relation to a standard set-oriented viability discretization are not specified or sourced sufficiently to validate the exact algorithm.

children.title: Value-Interface Viability Calculus
children.top_down_role: Implicit-set computation through value functions and reachability interfaces.

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Viability Methods
children.top_down_role: Viability computation organized through value-based temporal decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) is a finite horizon, \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g(x)\le 0\}\), and \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous.
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the admissible-control set \(U(x)\) is nonempty and compact, and \((x,u)\mapsto f(x,u)\) is continuous on the graph of \(U\).
The graph of \(U\) is closed and the hypotheses needed for the stagewise minima below to be attained are satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_k=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V_k(x)\le 0\}\) is the set of states from which an admissible control sequence keeps every stage from \(k\) through \(N\) in \(K\).

notation.meaning: backward value function at stage k
finite-horizon viable set at stage k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic discrete-time finite-horizon backward viability recursion with attained stagewise minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(V_N(x)=g(x)\). For \(k=N-1,\ldots,0\), compute \[V_k(x)=\max\!\left\{g(x),\min_{u\in U(x)}V_{k+1}(f(x,u))\right\}.\] Retain a minimizing control at each state where feedback selection is required, and output \(K_k=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V_k(x)\le 0\}\). Under the stated attainment hypotheses, \(x\in K_k\) exactly when an admissible control keeps \(x\) in \(K\) and sends its successor into \(K_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward dynamic programming takes the larger of current constraint violation and the smallest attainable future violation. With attained stagewise minima, its nonpositive sublevel set is exactly the finite-horizon viable set.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Programming Viability Methods

children.title: Level-Set Viability Methods
children.top_down_role: Implicit-interface computation of viable, reachable, or unsafe state regions.

assumptions_latex: \(T>0\), \(U\) is a nonempty compact control set, and controlled trajectories satisfy \(\dot x(s)=f(x(s),u(s))\) for measurable controls \(u:[t,T]\to U\).
\(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g(x)\le 0\}\), and \(f\) and \(g\) satisfy the regularity and growth hypotheses needed for trajectories, dynamic programming, and viscosity comparison.
\(V\) is the unique viscosity solution of the stated obstacle Hamilton--Jacobi terminal-value problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)\le 0\}\) is the backward viable set at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-horizon level-set representation using the obstacle convention associated with minimal worst constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H(x,p)=\inf_{u\in U}p\cdot f(x,u)\). Represent the minimal worst constraint violation by the viscosity solution of \[\max\!\left\{g(x)-V(t,x),\;\partial_tV(t,x)+H(x,\nabla_xV(t,x))\right\}=0,\qquad V(T,x)=g(x).\] Under the stated dynamic-programming and comparison hypotheses, the backward viable region is \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)\le 0\}\). When zero is a regular level, its interface is represented by \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The viscosity solution of the correctly signed obstacle Hamilton--Jacobi problem represents the minimal worst constraint violation, whose nonpositive sublevel set is the backward viable region.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Viability Methods

children.title: Value-Function Representations
children.top_down_role: Scalar representations encoding viability or reachability information.

assumptions_latex: Controlled trajectories satisfy \(\dot x(s)=f(s,x(s),u(s))\) for measurable admissible controls.
\(g(s,x)\) measures constraint violation, with feasibility equivalent to \(g(s,x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is viable from time \(t\) through \(T\) if and only if \(V(t,x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon deterministic value representation of controlled viability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[V(t,x)=\inf_{u(\cdot)}\;\sup_{s\in[t,T]}g\bigl(s,x^{t,x;u}(s)\bigr),\] where the infimum ranges over admissible controls for which the trajectory exists on \([t,T]\). Then \(V(t,x)\le0\) exactly when there exists a control whose trajectory satisfies \(g(s,x^{t,x;u}(s))\le0\) for every \(s\in[t,T]\). Hence the time-dependent viable set is \(\mathcal V(t)=\{x:V(t,x)\le0\}\), while positive values quantify the smallest attainable worst constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal possible worst constraint violation along a controlled trajectory represents viability: initial states with nonpositive value are exactly those viable through the horizon.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the value-function terminal container, and the displayed infimum-supremum formula has the intended deterministic finite-horizon meaning. A source is required to validate the admissible-control class, trajectory existence assumptions, and exact attainment or epsilon-control interpretation behind the stated equivalence.

children.title: Implicit Boundary Propagation
children.top_down_role: Evolution of set boundaries through implicit geometric representations.

assumptions_latex: \(V:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable near \((t,x)\), \(V(t,x)=0\), and \(\nabla_xV(t,x)\ne 0\).
The zero-level interface obeys \(\partial_tV(t,x)+H(x,\nabla_xV(t,x))=0\).
The unit normal is oriented toward increasing values of \(V\), namely \(n(t,x)=\nabla_xV(t,x)/\|\nabla_xV(t,x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_n(t,x)=H(x,\nabla_xV(t,x))/\|\nabla_xV(t,x)\|\).

notation.meaning: unit normal directed toward increasing V
signed normal interface velocity in the direction n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-velocity property at a regular zero-level point under a fixed Hamilton--Jacobi sign and normal-orientation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At every regular zero-level point \((t,x)\), define the signed normal velocity in the direction \(n(t,x)=
abla_xV(t,x)/\|
abla_xV(t,x)\|\). Under the convention \(\partial_tV+H(x,
abla_xV)=0\), the interface velocity is \[v_n(t,x)=- rac{\partial_tV(t,x)}{\|
abla_xV(t,x)\|}= rac{H(x,
abla_xV(t,x))}{\|
abla_xV(t,x)\|}.\] This property concerns only regular interface points and does not assign a classical normal velocity where \(
abla_xV(t,x)=0\) or \(V\) is nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular zero-level point, the signed normal speed equals the Hamiltonian divided by the spatial-gradient norm when the normal points toward increasing values and the stated Hamilton--Jacobi convention is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Boundary Propagation

children.title: Value–Interface Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between value-based characterizations and propagated set interfaces.

assumptions_latex: For fixed \(t\in[0,T]\), \(V(t,\cdot):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous.
The viable set satisfies \(\mathcal V(t)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)\le 0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathcal V(t)\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)=0\}\), with equality under the stated two-sided sign-change condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous sublevel-set representation and its boundary correspondence, with equality requiring two-sided sign change at every zero-level point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed \(t\in[0,T]\), the value--set correspondence is \[\mathcal V(t)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)\le 0\}.\] Continuity of \(V(t,\cdot)\) implies that \(\mathcal V(t)\) is closed and that \[\partial\mathcal V(t)\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)=0\}.\] If every \(x\) satisfying \(V(t,x)=0\) is approached both by points where \(V(t,\cdot)<0\) and by points where \(V(t,\cdot)>0\), then \[\partial\mathcal V(t)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:V(t,x)=0\}.\] Without this two-sided sign change, the zero level may contain points outside the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous viability value represents the viable set by its nonpositive sublevel set. The viable-set boundary lies in the zero level, and the two sets coincide when the value changes sign on both sides of every zero-level point.
knowledge_statements.title: Value–Interface Correspondence

children.title: Local Tangency Certificates
children.top_down_role: Local geometric tests for candidate viable motion.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) specifies candidate velocities.
\(T_K(x)\) is the contingent tangent cone to \(K\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A verifiable local viability certificate at \(x\in K\) is a velocity \(v\in F(x)\cap T_K(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise contingent-cone certificate, without asserting global sufficiency absent regularity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in K\), define \[T_K(x)=\left\{v:\liminf_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x+hv,K)}{h}=0\right\}.\] A local tangency certificate is a displayed vector \(v\) satisfying \(v\in F(x)\cap T_K(x)\). It is checked by verifying both velocity admissibility and the first-order distance condition. Equivalently, there exist \(h_i\downarrow0\) and \(v_i\to v\) such that \(x+h_iv_i\in K\). The certificate establishes first-order compatibility of the dynamics with the constraint at \(x\); global viable motion requires the usual existence and regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate velocity certifies local constraint compatibility when it is both dynamically admissible and tangent to the constraint in the contingent-cone sense.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Tangency Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind exactly fits the terminal container. The contingent-cone definition, sequential characterization, and distinction between local compatibility and global viability are mathematically coherent, but no authoritative viability-theorem source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Numerical Viability Distortion Boundary
children.top_down_role: Numerical creation or loss of viable state regions.

children.title: Approximation Leakage
children.top_down_role: Numerical loss of states or trajectories that are viable in the underlying dynamics.

assumptions_latex: \(V\subseteq K\) is the exact viable set and \(V_h\) is a numerical approximation.
\(K^{+\varepsilon}=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le\varepsilon\}\) is the inflated constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Leakage occurs when \(V_h\setminus K\ne\varnothing\), and its magnitude is bounded by \(\varepsilon\) if \(V_h\subseteq K^{+\varepsilon}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-approximation escape beyond the original state constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Approximation leakage is present when a computed viable approximation contains states outside the original constraint, namely \(V_h\setminus K\ne\varnothing\). Its one-sided leakage radius is \[\ell_h=\sup_{x\in V_h}\operatorname{dist}(x,K).\] If the numerical transition rule was constructed only for the inflated constraint \(K^{+\varepsilon_h}\), then it can guarantee at most \(V_h\subseteq K^{+\varepsilon_h}\), so \(\ell_h\le\varepsilon_h\), not exact constraint preservation. Leakage vanishes in the limit only if \(\varepsilon_h\to0\) and the outer approximations satisfy the required convergence conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation leakage occurs when a numerical viable set extends outside the true constraint. Inflation controls its distance from the constraint but does not provide exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Leakage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits this numerical-distortion leaf, and the leakage radius bound follows from the stated set inclusion. However, the term, its intended numerical regime, and the claimed convergence qualification have no canonical source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Spurious Viability
children.top_down_role: Numerical creation of apparently viable states unsupported by the underlying dynamics.

assumptions_latex: The exact dynamics are \(\dot x=1\) on \(K=[0,1]\), so no state is viable for all future time.
A discretization uses step \(\tau>0\), grid spacing \(h\ge\tau\), and rounds each successor to any grid point within distance \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The numerical fixed point can contain every grid point although the exact infinite-horizon viability kernel is empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete spurious fixed point caused by an overly permissive successor relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\dot x=1\) on \(K=[0,1]\), every exact trajectory exits \(K\) in finite time, so the infinite-horizon viability kernel is empty. Let \(X_h=\{0,h,2h,\ldots,1\}\) and declare \(y\in S_{h,\tau}(x)\) whenever \(|y-(x+\tau)|\le h\). If \(h\ge\tau\), then \(x\in S_{h,\tau}(x)\) for every grid point \(x\), including \(x=1\). Consequently, the pruning update retains all of \(X_h\). Thus the computed fixed point is nonempty solely because transition inflation permits artificial self-loops.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For constant rightward motion on a bounded interval, coarse successor inflation creates artificial grid self-loops and a nonempty numerical kernel although every exact trajectory exits.
knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Viability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits Spurious Viability, and the artificial self-loop mechanism is internally plausible. A source or independently inspectable validation is required, and the grid definition should specify that the endpoint convention produces a finite grid containing 1, since the displayed set presumes compatibility between h and the interval endpoint.

children.title: Boundary Smearing
children.top_down_role: Distortion of viability boundaries caused by spatial or implicit-set approximation.

assumptions_latex: \(V\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and compact.
\(V_h\) is a nonempty finite union of closed cells, every cell has diameter at most \(h\), every retained cell intersects \(V\), and \(V\subseteq V_h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_H(V_h,V)\le h\), while cell-scale representation need not preserve boundary topology at fixed \(h\).

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance between nonempty compact sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cell-union approximation error and possible loss of fine boundary topology at the spatial discretization scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated cell-intersection, coverage, and diameter assumptions, the cell-union approximation satisfies \[d_H(V_h,V)\le h.\] At a fixed resolution \(h\), replacing pointwise membership by whole-cell membership can represent the interface only within a cell-scale band. Boundary components or viable channels separated by distances comparable to or smaller than the cell scale need not retain their exact topology in \(V_h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering by retained cells of diameter at most h has Hausdorff error at most h, but its cell-scale boundary representation can merge nearby components or obscure narrow viable channels.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Smearing

children.title: Grid-Induced Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Artificial viable connections introduced by state-space discretization.

assumptions_latex: The viability computation uses a uniform one-dimensional grid of closed cells of width \(h>0\).
A cell is retained whenever it intersects the continuous viable set \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The digitized set can be connected even when \(K\) is disconnected.

notation.meaning: Union of all grid cells intersecting the set K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cell-intersection digitization can merge components separated below grid resolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete subgrid-separation mechanism for false connectivity under cell-intersection digitization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\varepsilon<h/2\), let \(K=\{-\varepsilon,\varepsilon\}\subset\mathbb{R}\), and choose a uniform grid having one cell \(Q\) that contains both points. Define \(D_h(K)\) as the union of all grid cells intersecting \(K\), with connectivity inherited from cell adjacency. Although \(K\) has two connected components, both points select the same cell \(Q\), so \(D_h(K)=Q\) is connected. Thus any cell-intersection viability scheme can create grid-induced connectivity whenever distinct viable components occupy one cell or an adjacency chain of retained cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cell-intersection digitization may connect distinct viable components when their separation is below the grid scale or retained cells bridge the gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Grid-Induced Connectivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subgrid example supports the stated failure mechanism, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. However, no inspectable source is supplied, and the final claim about any cell-intersection viability scheme is broader than the constructed one-dimensional digitization model. The statement also includes proof-like reasoning that should be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Conservative Approximation Bias
children.top_down_role: Systematic underestimation of viable regions due to restrictive numerical representation.

assumptions_latex: The numerical viable set is formed by retaining only grid cells wholly contained in the exact viable set \(K\).
The grid has maximal cell diameter \(h>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The approximation is viability-preserving but systematically excludes an unresolved boundary layer.

notation.meaning: Union of grid cells wholly contained in K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: inner cell approximations avoid leakage by discarding boundary-intersecting cells
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner-grid bias caused by requiring whole-cell feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed viable set \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), define \(K_h^-\) as the union of grid cells \(Q\) satisfying \(Q\subset K\). Then \(K_h^-\subset K\), so the construction cannot certify an exterior state as viable. However, every point of \(K\) lying only in cells that meet both \(K\) and its complement is discarded. For \(K=[0,1]\subset\mathbb{R}\), a shifted grid generally removes nonempty intervals adjacent to one or both endpoints, and \(K_h^-\) may be empty when no cell fits inside \(K\). This one-sided loss is conservative approximation bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whole-cell inner approximation prevents exterior leakage but discards viable boundary states and can erase thin viable regions entirely.
knowledge_statements.title: Conservative Approximation Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inner-cell construction correctly exhibits conservative geometric bias, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. No inspectable source is supplied. Moreover, set inclusion K_h^- subset K establishes absence of exterior leakage but does not by itself establish dynamical viability preservation, so the conclusion requires a source and more precise terminology.
