children.title: Maximal-Monotone Hilbert-Space Generators
children.top_down_role: Hilbert-space generator class for nonlinear contraction evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is set-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximal monotonicity makes every resolvent \((I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) single-valued and everywhere defined for \(\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: Graph of the set-valued operator A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space maximal monotonicity and its resolvent characterization.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is monotone if \(\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq0\) whenever \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). It is maximal monotone if no proper enlargement of \(\operatorname{gra}A\) remains monotone. Equivalently, by the Hilbert-space range characterization, \(A\) is maximal monotone precisely when \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H\) for every \(\lambda>0\). Such an operator generates the nonlinear contraction evolution associated with \(\dot{x}(t)+A(x(t))\ni0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal-monotone Hilbert-space operator is monotone with no monotone graph extension; equivalently, each positive resolvent equation is solvable everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal-Monotone Hilbert-Space Generators

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity, maximality, and Hilbert-space range characterization are standard, and definition is a reasonable kind for this generator-class topic. The cited variational-inequality page does not establish on its face the nonlinear contraction-evolution generation claim or its solution regime. An authoritative maximal-monotone evolution or nonlinear-semigroup source with a precise theorem locator is required.

children.title: m-Accretive Banach-Space Generators
children.top_down_role: Banach-space generator class for nonlinear contraction semigroups.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space.
\(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is set-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An \(m\)-accretive operator is the generator class for a nonlinear contraction semigroup on \(\overline{\operatorname{dom}A}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the norm inequality and range condition are the standard Banach-space definition of m-accretivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-based Banach-space definition with the full range condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is accretive if, for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) and every \(\lambda>0\), one has \(\|x-y\|\leq\|x-y+\lambda(u-v)\|\). It is \(m\)-accretive if it is accretive and \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=X\) for every \(\lambda>0\). Consequently, each resolvent \((I+\lambda A)^{-1}:X\to X\) is a contraction, and \(-A\) is the generator of the associated nonlinear contraction semigroup on \(\overline{\operatorname{dom}A}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An m-accretive Banach-space operator satisfies the accretive norm inequality and has an everywhere-solvable resolvent, thereby generating nonlinear contraction evolution.
knowledge_statements.title: m-Accretive Banach-Space Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm inequality and full range condition give the standard m-accretive definition, and the generator-class container is appropriate. The contraction-semigroup generation conclusion is nontrivial and has no cited source; it requires an authoritative nonlinear-semigroup theorem locator.

children.title: Subdifferential Generators
children.top_down_role: Energy-generated specializations of monotone evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(\varphi:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex subdifferential \(\partial\varphi\) is maximal monotone and generates energy-dissipating evolution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex Hilbert-space subdifferentials as maximal-monotone energy generators.

source_refs.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in H\), define \(u\in\partial\varphi(x)\) by \(\varphi(y)\geq\varphi(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in H\). The operator \(\partial\varphi:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone. Hence the inclusion \(\dot{x}(t)+\partial\varphi(x(t))\ni0\) belongs to maximal-monotone evolution theory. Along any sufficiently regular solution and for almost every \(t\), choosing \(-\dot{x}(t)\in\partial\varphi(x(t))\) yields the energy identity \(\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(x(t))=-\|\dot{x}(t)\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex energy is maximal monotone and generates a flow that dissipates that energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Generators

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximal monotonicity of the convex subdifferential is standard, and property fits the terminal container. The energy identity requires an explicit subdifferential chain-rule regime rather than the phrase 'sufficiently regular,' and the sentence deriving it is proof-like. The cited variational-inequality page does not clearly support the evolution and energy-identity claims, so a precise evolution or convex-analysis source is required.

children.title: Resolvent-Regularization Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Regularized generator families used in construction and approximation.

children.title: Operator Resolvents
children.top_down_role: Single-valued implicit representations associated with monotone or accretive generators.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resolvent \(J_\lambda=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is an everywhere-defined firmly nonexpansive map.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A at parameter lambda

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent of a maximal-monotone Hilbert-space operator.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator resolvent at parameter \(\lambda\) is \(J_\lambda=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\). Thus \(z=J_\lambda x\) exactly when \(x-z\in\lambda A z\). Maximal monotonicity makes \(J_\lambda\) single-valued on all of \(H\), and it is firmly nonexpansive: for every \(x,y\in H\), \(\|J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y\|^2\leq\langle J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y,x-y\rangle\). In particular, \(J_\lambda\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent solves an implicit monotone inclusion and is an everywhere-defined firmly nonexpansive mapping.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator Resolvents

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Yosida Approximations
children.top_down_role: Regularized generator families indexed by a smoothing parameter.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Yosida approximation \(A_\lambda\) is single-valued, monotone, and \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space Yosida regularization of a maximal-monotone operator.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Yosida approximation by \(A_\lambda=\lambda^{-1}(I-J_\lambda)\). For every \(x\in H\), it satisfies \(A_\lambda x\in A(J_\lambda x)\) and \(x=J_\lambda x+\lambda A_\lambda x\). The map \(A_\lambda:H\to H\) is single-valued and monotone. Moreover, for all \(x,y\in H\), \(\|A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y\|\leq\lambda^{-1}\|x-y\|\), so the possibly multivalued operator \(A\) is replaced by a globally Lipschitz regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Yosida regularization converts a maximal-monotone operator into a single-valued monotone Lipschitz map while retaining a graph point through its resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Yosida Approximations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Resolvent–Regularization Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural relationship between resolvent maps and regularized generators.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Resolvent and Yosida regularization determine one another by exact algebraic identities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Hilbert-space identities linking implicit resolution and Lipschitz regularization.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), the resolvent and Yosida approximation obey \[J_\lambda x=x-\lambda A_\lambda x,\qquad A_\lambda x\in A(J_\lambda x).\] Conversely, knowledge of \(A_\lambda\) recovers the resolvent through \(J_\lambda=I-\lambda A_\lambda\). Their graphs are linked by \[u=A_\lambda x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x-\lambda u,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A.\] Hence implicit resolvent evaluation and single-valued Yosida regularization encode the same operator graph at scale \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each positive scale, the resolvent and Yosida approximation recover each other and encode the same maximal-monotone graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent–Regularization Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Vanishing-Regularization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior of regularized generator families as smoothing is removed.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(x\in\operatorname{dom}A\), and \(A^0x\) denotes the minimum-norm element of \(Ax\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\lambda\downarrow0\), \(J_\lambda x\to x\) and \(A_\lambda x\to A^0x\) strongly.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pointwise vanishing-Yosida convergence on the operator domain is standard maximal-monotone theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise strong limit on the operator domain, including minimal-section recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}A\), the set \(Ax\) is closed and convex and therefore has a unique minimum-norm element \(A^0x\). As \(\lambda\downarrow0\), the resolvent and Yosida approximation satisfy \[J_\lambda x\longrightarrow x,\qquad A_\lambda x\longrightarrow A^0x\] strongly in \(H\). In addition, \(\|A_\lambda x\|\leq\|A^0x\|\). Thus vanishing regularization recovers the original state and selects the least-norm value of the multivalued operator at that state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the operator domain, vanishing Yosida regularization returns the state and converges to the minimum-norm value of the original operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Regularization Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated pointwise strong limits and minimum-norm selection are standard for maximal-monotone operators at points of their domain, and theorem fits the vanishing-regularization leaf. Because this is a nontrivial convergence theorem and no source is supplied, an exact authoritative theorem locator is required.

children.title: Resolvent Stability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of resolvent representations to operator or parameter perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Resolvent evaluation is firmly nonexpansive and hence nonexpansively stable with respect to perturbations of its input.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A at scale lambda

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input stability of a fixed maximal-monotone resolvent.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,y\in H\), the resolvent \(J_\lambda\) satisfies \[\|J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y\|^2\leq\langle J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y,x-y\rangle.\] Consequently, \[\|J_\lambda x-J_\lambda y\|\leq\|x-y\|.\] Thus perturbations of the input are not amplified by resolvent evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal-monotone resolvent is firmly nonexpansive, so perturbing its input cannot amplify the output error.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Stability

children.title: Strong Solution Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solution families with sufficient temporal regularity and pointwise generator compatibility.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone, and \(T>0\).
\(f\in L^1(0,T;H)\) and \(x_0\in\overline{\operatorname{dom}A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strong solution satisfies the differential inclusion almost everywhere with its initial condition attained strongly.

notation.meaning: Sobolev space of absolutely continuous H-valued trajectories

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: almost-everywhere satisfaction by an absolutely continuous trajectory is the standard strong-solution regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong solutions of forced autonomous maximal-monotone Cauchy problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strong solution of \[\dot{x}(t)+A(x(t))\ni f(t),\\ x(0)=x_0\] is a trajectory \(x\in W^{1,1}(0,T;H)\) such that \(x(t)\in\operatorname{dom}A\) for almost every \(t\), the initial condition holds in \(H\), and there exists \(a\in L^1(0,T;H)\) with \(a(t)\in A(x(t))\) and \(\dot{x}(t)+a(t)=f(t)\) for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong solution is absolutely continuous, lies in the operator domain almost everywhere, and satisfies the inclusion almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Solution Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed absolutely continuous, almost-everywhere formulation is a coherent strong-solution definition, and definition fits the terminal container. No authoritative evolution-inclusion source is cited, so the precise integrability and domain requirements cannot be source-verified.

children.title: Mild Solution Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solution families represented through nonlinear semigroup evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone, and \(T>0\).
\(x_0\in\overline{\operatorname{dom}A}\); the displayed definition concerns the unforced problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A mild solution is the uniform limit of implicit-Euler trajectories generated by the resolvent of \(A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resolvent-product limits give the standard mild solution for autonomous m-accretive evolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous mild solutions defined through implicit-Euler resolvent limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a step size \(h>0\), initialize \(x_0^h=x_0\) and define \(x_k^h=J_hx_{k-1}^h\), equivalently \((x_{k-1}^h-x_k^h)/h\in A(x_k^h)\). Let \(x_h\) be the piecewise-constant interpolation of these values. A continuous trajectory \(x:[0,T]\to\overline{\operatorname{dom}A}\) is a mild solution of \(\dot{x}(t)+A(x(t))\ni0\), \(x(0)=x_0\), when \(x_h\to x\) uniformly on \([0,T]\) as \(h\downarrow0\). Equivalently, \(x(t)=\lim_{n\to\infty}(I+(t/n)A)^{-n}x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mild solution is the uniform limit of implicit-Euler resolvent iterations, equivalently the nonlinear exponential formula generated by the operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Mild Solution Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent-product formulation is mathematically plausible for the autonomous maximal-monotone problem, and definition fits the Mild Solution Regimes leaf. The asserted equivalence between uniform implicit-Euler convergence and the nonlinear exponential formula is nontrivial and has no cited nonlinear-semigroup source or theorem locator.

children.title: Strong-to-Mild Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Regimes in which strong trajectories agree with their mild counterparts.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(u\in AC([0,T];H)\), \(u(0)=u_0\), and \(-u'(t)\in A(u(t))\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u(t)=S(t)u_0\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\).

notation.meaning: Nonlinear contraction semigroup generated by minus the maximal monotone operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous Hilbert-space compatibility via the nonlinear semigroup generated by \(-A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(t)u_0=\lim_{n\to\infty}J_{t/n}^{\,n}u_0\), with convergence in \(H\). If \(u\) is a strong solution of \(u'(t)+A(u(t))\ni0\), then it agrees at every time with this semigroup orbit. Consequently every strong solution is also the unique mild solution associated with the same initial datum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every strong solution of an autonomous maximal-monotone Cauchy problem coincides with the resolvent-limit mild solution having the same initial value.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-to-Mild Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the Strong-to-Mild Compatibility leaf and is mathematically plausible in the autonomous Hilbert-space maximal-monotone setting. However, no citation or inspectable locator supports the exponential-resolvent formula, uniqueness convention, and strong-to-mild identification.

children.title: Regularization into Strong Solutions
children.top_down_role: Settings where initially mild evolution acquires stronger temporal or domain regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(\phi:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(A=\partial\phi\) and \(u_0\in\overline{\operatorname{dom}\phi}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(0<\delta<T\), \(u\in W^{1,2}(\delta,T;H)\) and \(-u'(t)\in\partial\phi(u(t))\) almost everywhere.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive-time regularization for convex subgradient flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-time regularization is asserted for convex subgradient flows, not arbitrary maximal-monotone semigroups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u(t)=S(t)u_0\) be the mild solution generated by \(-\partial\phi\). For every \(0<\delta<T\), the restriction of \(u\) to \([\delta,T]\) is absolutely continuous, belongs to \(W^{1,2}(\delta,T;H)\), and satisfies \(u'(t)+\partial\phi(u(t))\ni0\) for almost every \(t\in(\delta,T)\). Thus the mild trajectory becomes a strong solution away from the initial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subgradient-flow mild solution becomes a strong solution on every interval separated from the initial time.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization into Strong Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and positive-time regularization claim fit the leaf, and the restriction to convex subgradient flows avoids overclaiming for arbitrary maximal-monotone operators. An authoritative locator is required to confirm the stated initial-data class and the precise W^{1,2} regularity on every positive-time interval.

children.title: Strong–Mild Solution Gap
children.top_down_role: Domain or regularity structures separating the two solution notions.

assumptions_latex: \(H=L^2(\mathbb T)\), where \(\mathbb T\) is the one-dimensional torus.
\(A=d/ds\) with periodic domain \(D(A)=H^1(\mathbb T)\).
\(u_0\in L^2(\mathbb T)\setminus H^1(\mathbb T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u(t)=u_0(\,\cdot-t\,)\) is mild for all \(t\ge0\), but \(u(t)\notin D(A)\) and is not strong for any \(t\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Periodic Sobolev domain of the translation generator.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: translation semigroup provides a nonsmoothing maximal-monotone example
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonsmoothing example showing that maximal monotonicity alone does not identify mild and strong regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The periodic derivative \(A\) is skew-adjoint and maximal monotone, while \(-A\) generates the translation group \(S(t)\). Sobolev regularity is invariant under translation. Hence, for \(u_0\notin H^1(\mathbb T)\), the orbit \(u(t)=S(t)u_0\) is the unique mild solution of \(u'(t)+Au(t)=0\), but it never enters \(D(A)\) and therefore is not a strong solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A translation semigroup preserves rough initial data, so its mild solution may never enter the generator domain required of strong solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong–Mild Solution Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate, and the translation-group example expresses the intended persistent strong-mild gap. A source with a specific locator is still required for the generator sign, maximal-monotonicity assertion, domain identification, and nonsmoothing conclusion.

children.title: Forced-Perturbed Monotone Evolution Family
children.top_down_role: Monotone dynamics with external forcing and regular perturbations.

children.title: Externally Forced Monotone Evolution
children.top_down_role: Monotone evolution subject to prescribed time-dependent inputs.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(f\in L^1(0,T;H)\) and \(u_0\in\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forced evolution problem is \(u'(t)+A(u(t))\ni f(t)\), with \(u(0)=u_0\).

notation.meaning: Domain of the maximal monotone operator.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard forced maximal-monotone Cauchy problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive time-dependent forcing independent of the state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An externally forced monotone evolution is the Cauchy problem \(u'(t)+A(u(t))\ni f(t)\) for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), together with \(u(0)=u_0\). A strong solution is absolutely continuous and satisfies the inclusion almost everywhere; a mild solution is obtained as the limit of implicit-resolvent time discretizations with cell averages of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: External forcing adds an integrable time-dependent right-hand side to the maximal-monotone evolution inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Externally Forced Monotone Evolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the externally forced evolution leaf and clearly separates additive forcing from state-dependent perturbation. The strong-solution clause is standard, but the particular mild-solution construction using cell averages and implicit resolvents needs a cited source and locator.

children.title: Perturbed Monotone Evolution
children.top_down_role: Monotone dynamics modified by additional operator terms.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(B:[0,T]\times H\to H\) is a single-valued state-dependent perturbation.
\(f:[0,T]\to H\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed problem is \(u'(t)+A(u(t))+B(t,u(t))\ni f(t)\), with \(u(0)=u_0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional decomposition into monotone principal part and perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-dependent perturbation of a maximal-monotone principal evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A perturbed monotone evolution separates a maximal monotone principal part from a generally nonmonotone lower-order term and requires \(u'(t)+A(u(t))+B(t,u(t))\ni f(t)\) almost everywhere, with prescribed initial value \(u(0)=u_0\). This definition alone imposes no existence or uniqueness claim; such claims require growth, measurability, continuity, or one-sided monotonicity conditions on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The evolution combines a maximal-monotone principal operator with a state-dependent perturbation and an optional external force.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Monotone Evolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and decomposition into a maximal-monotone principal part, state-dependent perturbation, and forcing fit the exact leaf. It makes no unsupported well-posedness claim, but the record has no citation or inspectable locator for this convention.

children.title: Lipschitz Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Evolution under regular state-dependent perturbation fields.

assumptions_latex: \(B:[0,T]\times H\to H\) is measurable in time.
There exists \(L\in L^1(0,T)\) such that \(\|B(t,x)-B(t,y)\|\le L(t)\|x-y\|\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is an integrably Lipschitz perturbation, and solution differences satisfy an exponential Gronwall bound.

notation.meaning: Two solutions with respective forcing terms.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integrable Lipschitz perturbation and Gronwall stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global state-space Lipschitz condition with an integrable time modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For solutions driven by \(f_1\) and \(f_2\), monotonicity of \(A\) and the Lipschitz condition imply
\[\|u_1(t)-u_2(t)\|\le e^{\int_0^tL(r)\,dr}\left(\|u_1(0)-u_2(0)\|+\int_0^t\|f_1(s)-f_2(s)\|\,ds\right).\]
In particular, identical initial data and forcing yield uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable time-dependent Lipschitz modulus controls the perturbation and gives uniqueness and continuous dependence through Gronwall's inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Perturbations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integrable Lipschitz condition fits the leaf, and the displayed coarse Gronwall estimate is plausible. A source is needed for the exact stability statement, including the required ambient Hilbert space, maximal-monotone operator, solution class, and forcing assumptions, which are not fully introduced in this independent record.

children.title: Integrable Forcing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Forced evolution organized by time-integrable input classes.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(u_0\in\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forced problem admits an integral mild-solution formulation, with forcing stability measured in the \(L^1\) norm.

notation.meaning: Mild solutions corresponding to forcing terms.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: L1 forcing is natural for contraction-semigroup integral solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bochner-integrable forcing for autonomous maximal-monotone evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The integrable forcing regime requires only \(\int_0^T\|f(t)\|\,dt<\infty\). Mild solutions are defined by approximation with step forcings and implicit resolvent updates. If \(u_f\) and \(u_g\) have initial values \(x\) and \(y\), respectively, contraction yields
\[\|u_f(t)-u_g(t)\|\le\|x-y\|+\int_0^t\|f(s)-g(s)\|\,ds.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bochner-integrable forcing supports the mild formulation and controls trajectory differences by the accumulated forcing difference.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrable Forcing Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits an integrable-forcing regime, but the record does not explicitly introduce the Hilbert space H and gives no source for existence by step-forcing approximation or for the stated L^1 contraction estimate. These claims require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Monotonicity-Breaking Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Perturbation regimes that compromise the generator's dissipative structure.

assumptions_latex: The initial value is \(u(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\tau\ge0\), \(u_\tau(t)=0\) for \(t\le\tau\) and \(u_\tau(t)=(t-\tau)^2/4\) for \(t>\tau\) is a solution.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar waiting-time family demonstrates nonuniqueness without Lipschitz control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar nonuniqueness when a perturbation destroys monotonicity and lacks Lipschitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equation \(u'(t)+B(u(t))=0\) becomes \(u'(t)=\sqrt{\max\{u(t),0\}}\). Besides the zero solution, every waiting-time trajectory \(u_\tau\) stated above is continuously differentiable and satisfies the equation with the same initial value. Thus maximal monotonicity of the principal part alone does not preserve uniqueness under an arbitrary monotonicity-breaking perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-Lipschitz antimonotone scalar perturbation produces infinitely many solutions from the same initial value.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity-Breaking Perturbations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is correct for this leaf, and the scalar waiting-time family is internally consistent with the displayed non-Lipschitz perturbation. The concrete nonuniqueness example nevertheless has no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Nonautonomous Operator-Domain Coupling
children.top_down_role: Nonautonomous generators and evolving operator domains.

children.title: Time-Dependent Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Nonautonomous generator families varying explicitly with time.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
For almost every \(t\in[0,T]\), \(A(t):H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
The graph dependence on \(t\) is measurable in a specified resolvent or graph sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonautonomous Cauchy problem is \(u'(t)+A(t)u(t)\ni f(t)\), with \(u(0)=u_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a measurable nonautonomous maximal-monotone evolution family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time-dependent monotone operator family assigns to almost every \(t\) a maximal monotone graph \(A(t)\). Its evolution problem seeks \(u\) satisfying \(u'(t)+A(t)u(t)\ni f(t)\) almost everywhere and \(u(0)=u_0\). Measurability may be expressed by requiring \(t\mapsto J_\lambda(t)x\) to be measurable for every \(x\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonautonomous monotone evolution uses a measurable family of maximal-monotone operators in the differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Time-Dependent Monotone Operators and appropriately identifies one resolvent-measurability convention. Because several inequivalent temporal regularity frameworks exist, a specific source is needed to support this convention and delimit the associated solution theory.

children.title: Moving Operator Domains
children.top_down_role: Evolution problems whose admissible operator domains change over time.

assumptions_latex: \(A(t):H\rightrightarrows H\) is defined for \(t\in[0,T]\).
\(D(t)=\{x\in H:A(t)x\ne\varnothing\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strong trajectory must satisfy \(u(t)\in D(t)\) almost everywhere, so admissibility changes with time.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: moving domains are the effective domains of a nonautonomous graph family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective domains vary with time and constrain strong trajectories pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A moving operator domain is the set-valued path \(t\mapsto D(t)=D(A(t))\) associated with a nonautonomous operator family. A strong solution of \(u'(t)+A(t)u(t)\ni f(t)\) must lie in \(D(t)\) for almost every \(t\). Mere measurability of \(A(t)\) does not prescribe how points or graph elements transfer between \(D(s)\) and \(D(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of a time-dependent operator may move, and every strong trajectory must remain admissible in the current domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Moving Operator Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and effective-domain interpretation fit the moving-domain leaf. The pointwise admissibility statement is precise, but the record lacks a citation and locator supporting its nonautonomous strong-solution convention.

children.title: Operator–Domain Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Alignment between temporal generator variation and evolving domain geometry.

assumptions_latex: Each \(A(t):H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
\(\omega:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)\) is nondecreasing with \(\omega(r)\to0\) as \(r\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nearby operator graphs admit controlled transfer of every graph element.

notation.meaning: Graph element at time s and its transferred element at time t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graph-transport bounds are standard nonautonomous compatibility hypotheses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A graph-transport formulation of temporal operator–domain compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The family is graph-compatible with modulus \(\omega\) if, for every \(s,t\in[0,T]\) and every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}A(s)\), there exists \((\tilde x,\tilde y)\in\operatorname{gra}A(t)\) such that
\[\|\tilde x-x\|+\|\tilde y-y\|\le\omega(|t-s|)\bigl(1+\|x\|+\|y\|\bigr).\]
This condition couples temporal graph variation to the motion of the effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatibility requires graph elements at nearby times to transfer with an error controlled by a vanishing time modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator–Domain Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Operator-Domain Compatibility, but the displayed symmetric graph-transport inequality is only one possible and comparatively strong compatibility formulation. A precise authoritative source is necessary before fixing this exact modulus, quantification, and norm dependence in candidate knowledge.

children.title: Common-Domain Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonautonomous evolution with a fixed underlying operator domain.

assumptions_latex: \(A(t):H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone for every \(t\in[0,T]\).
There exists a fixed set \(D\subset H\) such that \(D(A(t))=D\) for all \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Domain admissibility is time-independent, although the values \(A(t)x\) may vary with \(t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed effective domain defines the common-domain regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed effective domain with time-dependent operator values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonautonomous family is in the common-domain regime when a single set \(D\) satisfies \(D(A(t))=D\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\). The constraint \(u(t)\in D\) is then independent of time. This condition removes domain-transition effects but does not itself ensure measurability, temporal continuity, existence, or uniqueness for the associated evolution problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All operators share one effective domain, eliminating moving-domain constraints while leaving their values free to vary in time.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Domain Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind exactly fits the common-domain leaf, and the statement correctly avoids inferring measurability or well-posedness from domain equality alone. It still lacks the required citation and specific locator for the adopted nonautonomous common-domain convention.

children.title: Domain-Transition Singularities
children.top_down_role: Regularity or solvability failures caused by abrupt changes in the operator domain.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A(t):H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone for every \(t\in[0,T]\).
The evolution is governed by \(u'(t)+A(t)u(t)\ni f(t)\) with \(f\in L^1(0,T;H)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A transition time may obstruct strong continuation even though one-sided evolutions remain meaningful.

notation.meaning: effective domain of the time-dependent operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure at a discontinuous transition between time-dependent operator domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau\in(0,T)\). A domain-transition singularity occurs when a solution has a left trace \(u(\tau-)\) but \(u(\tau-)\notin\overline{D(\tau+)}\), or when the graph compatibility required to pass from \(A(\tau-)\) to \(A(\tau+)\) fails. Then no continuous strong solution satisfying \(u(t)\in D(t)\) almost everywhere can continue through \(\tau\) with trace \(u(\tau-)\). One-sided strong solutions or a weaker evolution with a jump, projection, or measure-valued correction may still exist, but these are not strong continuations of the original Cauchy problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sudden domain change can prevent strong continuation when the incoming state is inadmissible for the new operator, although weaker or one-sided evolutions may survive.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Transition Singularities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the asserted transition criterion or the alternatives involving jumps, projections, or measure-valued corrections. The required graph-compatibility condition and the meaning of the right-hand domain trace are not defined precisely enough to validate the conclusion.

children.title: Strong-Solvability Domain Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Initial-domain and regularity failures separating solution regimes.

children.title: Initial-Domain Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Incompatibility between starting data and the effective generator domain.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is \(m\)-accretive.
The initial-value problem is \(u'(t)+Au(t)\ni0\), \(u(0)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Initial data outside \(D(A)\) generally preclude strong solvability at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous accretive evolution with initial data outside the generator domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\setminus D(A)\), the semigroup trajectory \(u(t)=S(t)x\) is a mild solution, but the standard strong-solution conditions cannot hold on \([0,T]\): absolute continuity together with \(u(t)\in D(A)\) almost everywhere and an integrable selection \(a(t)\in Au(t)\) would require a compatible right derivative at the initial time. Thus membership of \(x\) in \(D(A)\), or an equivalent initial graph-compatibility condition, is a boundary condition for strong solvability starting at \(t=0\), not for mild solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data in the closure of the operator domain can generate a mild trajectory, while failure to lie in the domain blocks a strong solution starting at time zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Initial-Domain Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim that a strong solution on [0,T] necessarily requires the initial datum to belong to D(A) is convention- and regularity-dependent; domain membership almost everywhere does not itself impose membership at t=0. An authoritative source defining the strong-solution convention and its initial-trace criterion is required.

children.title: Loss of Strong Solvability
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of solution regularity required for the strong regime.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space, \(A\) is \(m\)-accretive, and \(-A\) generates \(S(t)\).
The initial datum satisfies \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong solvability can fail when the semigroup orbit lacks the required domain membership or time regularity.

notation.meaning: semigroup orbit from the initial state

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes existence of a semigroup orbit from strong differential solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mild orbit \(u(t)=S(t)x\) is not a strong solution on an interval \(I\subset[0,\infty)\) if it fails either \(u\in W^{1,1}(I;X)\), \(u(t)\in D(A)\) for almost every \(t\in I\), or the existence of \(a\in L^1(I;X)\) with \(a(t)\in Au(t)\) and \(u'(t)+a(t)=0\) almost everywhere. Such failure may occur at \(t=0\) for \(x\notin D(A)\), or persist for positive times when the semigroup has no regularizing property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generated orbit loses strong status if it lacks absolute continuity, domain membership, or an integrable operator selection satisfying the differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Strong Solvability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated failure test is largely a definition of strong solvability, but no source establishes that this is the intended convention or supports the claims about failure at zero and persistent absence of regularization.

children.title: Persistent Mild Solvability
children.top_down_role: Continuation of mild evolution despite failure of strong solution regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is \(m\)-accretive.
The initial datum lies in \(\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A unique contraction-semigroup mild solution exists even when strong solvability fails.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous mild solvability on the closure of an accretive operator domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), the limit \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}J_{t/n}^{\,n}x\] exists uniformly for \(t\) in bounded intervals and defines a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on \(\overline{D(A)}\). The trajectory \(u(t)=S(t)x\) is the unique integral, hence mild, solution of \(u'(t)+Au(t)\ni0\), \(u(0)=x\). This conclusion does not require \(x\in D(A)\) and therefore persists when the initial-domain mismatch or insufficient orbit regularity prevents a strong solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximal accretivity still produces a unique mild contraction-semigroup trajectory for every initial state in the domain closure, including states that admit no strong solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Mild Solvability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and terminal placement fit, and the resolvent-limit generation claim is standard. Nevertheless, no source or inspectable locator is supplied for the Crandall–Liggett theorem, uniqueness of integral solutions, or the asserted equivalence with mild solutions.

children.title: Instantaneous Regularization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Thresholds determining whether domain-mismatched data enter the strong regime.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space, \(A\) is \(m\)-accretive, and \(-A\) generates \(S(t)\).
The initial datum satisfies \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximal accretivity alone does not imply instantaneous entry of \(S(t)x\) into \(D(A)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between generation and positive-time regularization for accretive flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Instantaneous regularization means that \(S(t)x\in D(A)\) for every \(t>0\), usually with a bound on \(\lvert AS(t)x\rvert\) or on the right derivative of \(S(t)x\). This property is additional to \(m\)-accretivity: the generation theorem guarantees \(S(t)x\in\overline{D(A)}\), but by itself does not guarantee domain entry, differentiability, or a finite operator norm at positive times. Consequently, any assertion that every mild solution becomes strong on \((0,T]\) requires further structural hypotheses, such as subdifferential, analyticity-type, compactness, or quantitative smoothing assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generation alone keeps trajectories in the domain closure; positive-time entry into the operator domain and derivative bounds require additional regularizing structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Instantaneous Regularization Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary claim requires a cited counterexample or theorem showing that m-accretivity alone does not force positive-time domain entry. The proposed additional hypotheses are only illustrative and are not stated precisely enough to support the conclusion.

children.title: Moving-Domain Compatibility Failure
children.top_down_role: Strong-solvability loss caused by incompatibility with an evolving operator domain.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(A(t):H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone for each \(t\in[0,T]\).
A strong solution is required to satisfy \(u(t)\in D(t):=\operatorname{dom}A(t)\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of temporal graph compatibility can destroy strong solvability despite pointwise maximal monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonautonomous failure caused by incompatible motion of maximal-monotone graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Pointwise maximal monotonicity of \(A(t)\) is insufficient for a strong solution of \(u'(t)+A(t)u(t)\ni f(t)\). Compatibility fails when the domains or resolvents vary so irregularly that no admissible curve can simultaneously satisfy \(u(t)\in D(t)\), absolute continuity, and an integrable selection \(a(t)\in A(t)u(t)\). In particular, if at a transition time \(\tau\) the incoming trace lies outside \(\overline{D(\tau+)}\), continuous strong continuation is impossible. A nonautonomous existence theorem must therefore impose quantitative temporal control of the graphs, resolvents, or domain parametrizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even maximal-monotone operators at every time may admit no strong evolution when their domains or graphs move incompatibly with admissible trajectories.
knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Domain Compatibility Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Pointwise maximal monotonicity alone is plausibly insufficient, but the record gives no precise temporal graph assumptions or source. The notation D(τ+) and the claimed trace obstruction require definitions and an applicable nonautonomous existence or failure theorem.

children.title: Nonlinear Semigroup Generation
children.top_down_role: Generation, resolvent approximation, and convergence of nonlinear contraction semigroups.

children.title: Brézis–Kōmura Generation Family
children.top_down_role: Hilbert-space generation from maximal-monotone operators.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
The Cauchy problem is \(u'(t)+Au(t)\ni0\), \(u(0)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator \(-A\) generates a unique strongly continuous nonlinear contraction semigroup on \(\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space maximal-monotone generation in the autonomous homogeneous case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a unique strongly continuous semigroup \((S(t))_{t\ge0}\) of contractions on \(\overline{D(A)}\) such that, for every \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(I+(t/n)A\bigr)^{-n}x.\] If \(x\in D(A)\), the orbit \(u(t)=S(t)x\) is locally absolutely continuous, satisfies \(u(t)\in D(A)\) for almost every \(t>0\), and obeys \(u'(t)+Au(t)\ni0\) almost everywhere. For general \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), the same orbit is the unique mild solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal-monotone Hilbert-space operator generates a unique nonlinear contraction semigroup; domain data give strong solutions, while closure data give mild solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Brézis–Kōmura Generation Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role matches the Brézis–Kōmura generation-family container and the Hilbert-space statement is standard, but no source or locator supports the generation, exponential formula, and strong-orbit regularity claims.

children.title: Crandall–Liggett Generation Family
children.top_down_role: Banach-space generation from accretive operators.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is \(m\)-accretive.
For every \(\lambda>0\), the resolvent \((I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is defined on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implicit-Euler resolvent limit generates a nonlinear contraction semigroup on \(\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space generation by an autonomous m-accretive operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), the limit \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}J_{t/n}^{\,n}x\] exists uniformly for \(t\) in compact subsets of \([0,\infty)\). The family \((S(t))_{t\ge0}\) satisfies \(S(0)=I\), \(S(t+s)=S(t)S(s)\), and \(\lVert S(t)x-S(t)y\rVert\le\lVert x-y\rVert\). It is the unique nonlinear contraction semigroup whose trajectories are integral solutions of \(u'(t)+Au(t)\ni0\). For \(x\in D(A)\), additional regularity yields the corresponding strong solution under the standard differentiability hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An m-accretive Banach-space operator generates a contraction semigroup as the uniform-on-compact-time limit of repeated implicit resolvent steps.
knowledge_statements.title: Crandall–Liggett Generation Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generation theorem fits the container, but it lacks a cited source. The final strong-solution clause also refers to unspecified 'standard differentiability hypotheses,' so its exact Banach-space scope cannot be verified.

children.title: Nonlinear Semigroup Formula Family
children.top_down_role: Resolvent and composition approximations of nonlinear semigroups.

children.title: Nonlinear Exponential Formulas
children.top_down_role: Resolvent-based approximations representing nonlinear semigroup evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is \(m\)-accretive.
The initial state satisfies \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated semigroup equals the strong limit of backward-Euler resolvent powers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent-power exponential formula for autonomous m-accretive evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t\ge0\) and \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), the nonlinear exponential formula is \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(I+\frac{t}{n}A\right)^{-n}x=\lim_{n\to\infty}J_{t/n}^{\,n}x.\] The convergence is strong in \(X\) and uniform with respect to \(t\) on bounded intervals. Each factor is one backward-Euler step for \(u'(t)+Au(t)\ni0\); hence the formula defines the semigroup without assigning a linear exponential to the nonlinear operator \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonlinear semigroup is represented by the strong limit of repeated backward-Euler resolvent steps, uniformly over bounded time intervals.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Exponential Formulas

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and formula fit the terminal container, but no cited theorem with an inspectable locator supports existence and locally uniform convergence of the nonlinear resolvent-power formula.

children.title: Nonlinear Product Formulas
children.top_down_role: Composition-based approximations for evolution generated by multiple operators.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and each contraction \(F(h):X\to X\) satisfies \(F(0)=I\).
A consistency and stability theorem identifies the closure of the infinitesimal generator of \(F\) with an \(m\)-accretive operator \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stable, consistent discrete products converge to the semigroup generated by \(-A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract stable-product approximation of a nonlinear contraction semigroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the nonlinear Chernoff consistency relation \[\lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{F(h)x-x}{h}=-Ax\] holds on a core for \(A\), in the sense required by the chosen nonlinear generation theorem, and the products \(F(t/n)^n\) satisfy its stability and range hypotheses. Then, for every \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}F(t/n)^n x,\] with strong convergence locally uniform in \(t\ge0\). The consistency condition alone is insufficient; stability and generator identification are essential parts of the product formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated nonlinear one-step maps converge to the generated semigroup when they are stable, consistent on a generator core, and satisfy the required range conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Product Formulas

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement invokes whatever consistency, stability, and range hypotheses are required by an unspecified theorem rather than stating a checkable theorem. A precise nonlinear Chernoff theorem and source are needed to determine the correct domains and convergence conclusion.

children.title: Resolvent Iteration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Semigroup approximation organized through repeated resolvent compositions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is \(m\)-accretive.
A partition \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T\) has steps \(h_k=t_k-t_{k-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vanishing-mesh resolvent iterations converge to the mild solution under bounded total time and consistent initialization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant- and variable-step backward-Euler regimes for m-accretive evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(x_0\in\overline{D(A)}\), define \(x_k=J_{h_k}x_{k-1}\). For uniform steps \(h=t/n\), one has \(x_n=J_{t/n}^{\,n}x_0\to S(t)x_0\). More generally, for partitions whose mesh satisfies \(\lvert\pi\rvert\to0\) while \(\sum_k h_k=t\), the terminal iterates and their standard time interpolants converge strongly to the mild trajectory \(S(\cdot)x_0\), subject to the variable-step consistency hypotheses. Nonexpansiveness of every \(J_{h_k}\) supplies stability against perturbations of the initial data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward-Euler resolvent iterations converge as the time mesh vanishes; nonexpansive resolvents make both uniform and admissible variable-step regimes stable.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Iteration Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-step assertion is standard, but the variable-step and interpolant convergence claims are qualified only by unspecified consistency hypotheses. A source stating the admissible partitions, interpolation scheme, and convergence topology is required.

children.title: Operator-Splitting Products
children.top_down_role: Product representations based on decomposing a generator into constituent operators.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A,B:X\rightrightarrows X\) are \(m\)-accretive.
The closure of \(A+B\) is \(m\)-accretive and the nonlinear product-formula stability and range conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Alternating resolvents converge to the semigroup generated by \(-(A+B)\).

notation.meaning: semigroup generated by minus the closed sum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lie resolvent splitting for a well-posed sum of accretive operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every admissible \(x\in\overline{D(A+B)}\) and \(t\ge0\), the Lie splitting representation is \[S_{A+B}(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(J_{t/n}^{A}J_{t/n}^{B}\right)^n x,\] with strong convergence locally uniform in \(t\), whenever the applicable nonlinear product theorem's stability, consistency, and range hypotheses are satisfied. Reversing the factor order gives an analogous formula when the corresponding hypotheses hold. Maximal accretivity of \(A\) and \(B\) separately does not by itself ensure that their sum generates the target semigroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating implicit steps for two accretive operators approximate the sum flow when the sum is itself well posed and the product stability conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Splitting Products

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits, but separate m-accretivity and an m-accretive closed sum do not by themselves validate the displayed nonlinear Lie product formula. The applicable Brézis–Pazy-type stability, consistency, domain, and range assumptions must be stated and cited precisely.

children.title: Product-Formula Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Domain or compatibility regimes where composition approximations fail to represent the target evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(A=N_{\{0\}}\) and \(B=N_{\{1\}}\) are normal-cone operators on \(H=\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resolvent product converges, but it cannot represent a semigroup generated by \(A+B\), because \(D(A)\cap D(B)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of an operator C at step h.
Normal cone to a closed convex set K.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete obstruction caused by incompatible operator domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(A=N_{\{0\}}\), and \(B=N_{\{1\}}\). For every \(h>0\), the resolvents are the constant projections \(J_h^A x=0\) and \(J_h^B x=1\). Consequently, for every \(t>0\), \(n\geq1\), and \(x\in\mathbb R\), \[(J_{t/n}^A J_{t/n}^B)^n x=0.\] Thus the product has a pointwise limit, but \(D(A+B)=D(A)\cap D(B)=\varnothing\); hence \(A+B\) cannot generate a semigroup on any nonempty closure of its domain. Separate maximal monotonicity therefore does not suffice for a product formula identifying the limit with the flow of \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two individually maximal monotone normal cones can have disjoint domains. Their resolvent products converge, yet the operator sum has no domain and generates no corresponding flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Formula Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent and fits the failure-boundary container, but no inspectable citation supports the precise product-formula interpretation.

children.title: Nonlinear Trotter–Kato Theory
children.top_down_role: Semigroup convergence under approximation of generators.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and each \(A_n\), as well as \(A\), is m-accretive.
For some \(\lambda>0\), \(J_\lambda^{A_n}x\to J_\lambda^A x\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated semigroups satisfy \(S_n(t)x\to S(t)x\) uniformly for \(t\) in bounded intervals.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A at parameter lambda.
Nonlinear contraction semigroups generated by A_n and A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-resolvent nonlinear Trotter–Kato theorem for contraction semigroups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n\) and \(A\) be m-accretive operators on a Banach space \(X\), and let \(S_n\) and \(S\) be their nonlinear contraction semigroups. Suppose that for one \(\lambda>0\), \[J_\lambda^{A_n}x\longrightarrow J_\lambda^A x\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Then the same resolvent convergence holds for every positive parameter, and for every \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\) and \(T>0\), \[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|S_n(t)x-S(t)x\|\longrightarrow0,\] provided the approximating initial data are identified in \(X\). Thus strong resolvent approximation of generators transfers to locally uniform strong approximation of their nonlinear flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convergence of one resolvent of m-accretive generators implies locally uniform convergence of the associated nonlinear contraction semigroups.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Trotter–Kato Theory

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative nonlinear Trotter–Kato theorem locator is required. The formulation must clarify whether initial data lie in each semigroup domain or are approximated by data in the corresponding domain; the phrase about identified initial data is insufficiently precise.

children.title: Doubly Nonlinear Evolution
children.top_down_role: Evolution combining nonlinear dissipation with nonlinear energy response.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Rate-Independent Systems: Theory and Application
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Rate-independent and rate-dependent systems in Banach spaces
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Rate-Independent Systems: Theory and Application

children.title: Convex Dissipation-Potential Evolution
children.top_down_role: Doubly nonlinear systems generated by convex dissipation structures.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a reflexive Banach space.
\(\Psi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\mathcal E:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A trajectory is governed by the doubly nonlinear inclusion \(0\in\partial\Psi(\dot u(t))+\partial\mathcal E(u(t))-f(t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space convex formulation with additive external forcing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(T>0\) and \(f\in L^1(0,T;X^*)\), a convex dissipation-potential evolution is an absolutely continuous curve \(u:[0,T]\to X\) for which there exist measurable \(\xi,\eta:[0,T]\to X^*\) satisfying, for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), \[\xi(t)\in\partial\Psi(\dot u(t)),\qquad \eta(t)\in\partial\mathcal E(u(t)),\qquad \xi(t)+\eta(t)=f(t).\] Equivalently, \(0\in\partial\Psi(\dot u(t))+\partial\mathcal E(u(t))-f(t)\). The nonlinearity may occur both in the velocity law through \(\partial\Psi\) and in the restoring force through \(\partial\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex dissipation-potential evolution balances the subgradient of a velocity-dependent dissipation against the energy subgradient and external forcing.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Dissipation-Potential Evolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the convex dissipation-potential container, but no source is supplied for the precise Banach-space formulation or the required measurability and integrability conditions on the subgradients.

children.title: State-Dependent Dissipation
children.top_down_role: Dissipation geometry varying with the evolving state.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a reflexive Banach space.
For each state \(u\), \(v\mapsto\Psi(u,v)\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and satisfies \(\Psi(u,0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The evolution law is \(0\in\partial_v\Psi(u(t),\dot u(t))+\partial\mathcal E(u(t))-f(t)\).

notation.meaning: State-dependent dissipation potential evaluated at state u and velocity v.
Convex subdifferential with respect to velocity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a state-dependent doubly nonlinear evolution law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be an energy and \(f:(0,T)\to X^*\) a forcing. A state-dependent dissipative evolution is an absolutely continuous curve \(u:[0,T]\to X\) satisfying, for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), \[0\in\partial_v\Psi(u(t),\dot u(t))+\partial\mathcal E(u(t))-f(t).\] Here the convex function \(v\mapsto\Psi(u,v)\) determines the local dissipation geometry at state \(u\). Consequently, two identical velocities may incur different dissipation at different states, and existence or energy-balance results require additional continuity and coercivity assumptions on the dependence \(u\mapsto\Psi(u,\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The velocity dissipation potential varies with the current state, so the local dissipation geometry evolves along the trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: State-Dependent Dissipation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local concept is appropriate, but the record neither assumes convexity of the energy nor identifies a nonconvex subdifferential. A source is needed to determine the intended framework and state-dependence hypotheses.

children.title: Multiscale Dissipation Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Partially coercive and multiple-time-scale dissipative evolution.

children.title: Degenerate Dissipation
children.top_down_role: Dissipative evolution with inactive, singular, or noncoercive directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Dissipation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic Hilbert-space model of dissipation with undamped kernel directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(M:H\to H\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and positive semidefinite. Define \[\Psi_M(v)=\frac12\langle Mv,v\rangle.\] In the kernel-degenerate case \(\ker M\neq\{0\}\), every \(v\in\ker M\) satisfies \(\Psi_M(v)=0\), and consequently no constant \(c>0\) can satisfy \(\Psi_M(v)\geq c\|v\|^2\) for all \(v\in H\). For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex energy \(\mathcal E:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and forcing \(f:(0,T)\to H\), the corresponding formal evolution law is \[M\dot u(t)+\partial\mathcal E(u(t))\ni f(t).\] This law provides no direct dissipative control on velocities in \(\ker M\); control of those directions must come from the energy, coupling, constraints, or additional conservation laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernel-degenerate quadratic dissipation vanishes on a nontrivial velocity subspace, so those directions require control from the energy, coupling, constraints, or other laws.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(M:H\to H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, positive semidefinite, and has nontrivial kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every velocity in \(\ker M\) has zero quadratic dissipation, so the dissipation is not uniformly coercive on \(H\).

children.title: Multirate Dissipation
children.top_down_role: Evolution containing components governed by distinct dissipative time scales.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a product Hilbert space.
Each \(M_i:H_i\to H_i\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and uniformly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct coefficients \(\varepsilon^{\alpha_i}\) assign different dissipative time scales to the components.

notation.meaning: Small scale parameter and component rate exponents.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-product quadratic model with power-law-separated rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in H\), choose \(\varepsilon>0\) and exponents \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb R\). The multirate quadratic dissipation is \[\Psi_\varepsilon(\dot u)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon^{\alpha_i}\langle M_i\dot u_i,\dot u_i\rangle.\] Coupled with an energy \(\mathcal E:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), it yields the componentwise system \[\varepsilon^{\alpha_i}M_i\dot u_i(t)+\partial_{u_i}\mathcal E(u(t))\ni f_i(t),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Unequal exponents encode unequal dissipative response scales; their dynamical interpretation also depends on the chosen observation-time normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multirate model weights component velocities by different powers of a small parameter, producing distinct dissipative response scales within one coupled evolution.
knowledge_statements.title: Multirate Dissipation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the multirate-dissipation container and explicitly notes dependence on time normalization, but the selected power-law convention and its interpretation require an inspectable source.

children.title: Partially Coercive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Systems with coercive dissipation restricted to selected state directions.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_c\oplus H_0\) is an orthogonal decomposition.
\(P_c\) and \(P_0\) are the corresponding orthogonal projections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dissipation is coercive on \(H_c\), while compactness in \(H_0\) must come from the energy or constraints.

notation.meaning: Projection onto the dissipatively controlled subspace.
Projection onto the uncontrolled complementary subspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subspace-based partial coercivity condition for dissipation-energy systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of dissipation potentials \(\Psi_\varepsilon:H\to[0,+\infty]\) is partially coercive relative to \(H=H_c\oplus H_0\) if constants \(c>0\) and \(p>1\), independent of \(\varepsilon\), satisfy \[\Psi_\varepsilon(v)\geq c\|P_c v\|^p\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,\] while no uniform bound of this form is required for \(P_0v\). A usable partially coercive evolution regime additionally requires that energy sublevels, constraints, or coupling control the missing component: bounded energy and bounded \(P_cu\) must imply relative compactness or an appropriate bound for \(P_0u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dissipation uniformly controls only a designated subspace; energy, constraints, or coupling must control the complementary directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Partially Coercive Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partial-coercivity inequality is plausible, but the claimed complementary control is not formulated precisely for sequences or a specified topology. A source is needed to select the appropriate compactness framework.

children.title: Fast–Slow Dissipative Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between components evolving on separated dissipative scales.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_s\times H_f\) is a product Hilbert space.
\(M_s\) and \(M_f\) are bounded, self-adjoint, and uniformly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the fast equation formally becomes the equilibrium constraint \(0\in\partial_y\mathcal E(x,y)-f_f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic fast–slow gradient-system scaling and its formal constraint limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u=(x,y)\in H_s\times H_f\), define \[\Psi_\varepsilon(\dot x,\dot y)=\frac12\langle M_s\dot x,\dot x\rangle+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\langle M_f\dot y,\dot y\rangle.\] The corresponding coupled evolution is \[M_s\dot x+\partial_x\mathcal E(x,y)\ni f_s,\qquad \varepsilon M_f\dot y+\partial_y\mathcal E(x,y)\ni f_f.\] The variable \(y\) relaxes on the fast scale \(t/\varepsilon\). Formally, as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the second relation becomes \(0\in\partial_y\mathcal E(x,y)-f_f\), while \(x\) evolves along the resulting equilibrium set. Rigorous convergence requires compactness and stability of that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small coefficient on fast-variable dissipation produces rapid relaxation toward an energy equilibrium constraint coupled to the slow evolution.
knowledge_statements.title: Fast–Slow Dissipative Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fast–slow representation and formal equilibrium constraint fit the container, but no source supports the scaling or supplies hypotheses for the asserted singular-limit interpretation.

children.title: Rate-Separation Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Transitions where distinct dissipative scales can no longer be treated separately.

knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Separation Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of nominal rate separation when the restoring force degenerates at the same scale as fast dissipation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(T>0\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and initial values \(x_0,y_0\in\mathbb R\). Consider \[\dot x_\varepsilon(t)=-x_\varepsilon(t),\qquad \varepsilon\dot y_\varepsilon(t)=-\varepsilon\bigl(y_\varepsilon(t)-x_\varepsilon(t)\bigr),\qquad x_\varepsilon(0)=x_0,\quad y_\varepsilon(0)=y_0.\] Cancellation of \(\varepsilon\) in the second equation gives dynamics independent of \(\varepsilon\), with \[x_\varepsilon(t)=x_0e^{-t},\qquad y_\varepsilon(t)=e^{-t}(y_0+x_0t).\] Hence \[y_\varepsilon(t)-x_\varepsilon(t)=e^{-t}(y_0-x_0+x_0t),\] which is independent of \(\varepsilon\). If \(y_0\neq x_0\), then \[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}|y_\varepsilon(t)-x_\varepsilon(t)|\geq |y_0-x_0|,\] so the constraint \(y=x\) does not emerge uniformly on \([0,T]\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Thus a nominal fast prefactor does not produce rate separation when the restoring force degenerates at the same scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the restoring force carries the same small factor as the purported fast dissipation, the factors cancel and the initial mismatch remains order one, so no uniform fast-equilibrium constraint emerges.
assumptions_latex: The observation interval is \([0,T]\) with \(T>0\).
The parameter satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\), and the initial data satisfy \(y_0\neq x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mismatch is independent of \(\varepsilon\) and remains nonzero in the uniform norm on \([0,T]\), so the constraint \(y=x\) is not obtained as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: Slow and purportedly fast scalar trajectories.

children.title: Monotone Evolution Stability-Asymptotic Synthesis
children.top_down_role: Contractivity, perturbation stability, equilibrium convergence, and loss of monotone structure.

children.title: Contractive-Comparative Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Stability structures inherited from monotonicity and accretivity.

children.title: Metric Contraction Principles
children.top_down_role: Distance-based stability structures inherited from dissipative generators.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space.
\(S(t):X\to X\) is a semigroup satisfying the stated exponential Lipschitz estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distances between trajectories contract by the factor \(e^{-\lambda t}\), yielding uniqueness and stability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential metric contraction and its immediate stability consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a semigroup \(S(t)\) on \((X,d)\) satisfies \[d(S(t)x,S(t)y)\leq e^{-\lambda t}d(x,y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in X,\ t\geq0,\] with \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\). Then any two trajectories \(u(t)=S(t)x\) and \(v(t)=S(t)y\) obey the same estimate. In particular, identical initial data give identical trajectories. If \(\lambda=0\), the flow is nonexpansive; if \(\lambda>0\), it is strictly contractive and any two complete trajectories converge toward one another at least exponentially whenever they are compared at the same time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semigroup-level distance estimate transfers directly to trajectories, giving uniqueness, continuous dependence, and exponential synchronization when the contraction rate is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Contraction Principles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is mathematically consistent and the principle kind fits the terminal container, but the exponential semigroup estimate and its stated consequences have no cited source.

children.title: Order Comparison Principles
children.top_down_role: Order-preserving relations used to compare trajectories or semigroup orbits.

knowledge_statements.title: Order Comparison Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent-to-semigroup order comparison for an m-accretive generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space ordered by a closed positive cone \(X_+\), and let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) be m-accretive. Suppose that every resolvent \(J_h=(I+hA)^{-1}\), \(h>0\), is order preserving: \[x\leq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_hx\leq J_hy.\] Let \(S(t)\) be the nonlinear contraction semigroup generated by \(-A\), represented on \(\overline{D(A)}\) by \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}J_{t/n}^{\,n}x.\] Then, for all \(x,y\in\overline{D(A)}\) and \(t\geq0\), \[x\leq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S(t)x\leq S(t)y.\] Thus order comparison at every resolvent step transfers to the generated evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every resolvent of an m-accretive operator preserves the closed-cone order, then its generated nonlinear contraction semigroup preserves that order.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space ordered by a closed positive cone \(X_+\).
\(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is m-accretive, and every resolvent \(J_h=(I+hA)^{-1}\), \(h>0\), is order preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonlinear semigroup generated by \(-A\) preserves order on \(\overline{D(A)}\).

notation.meaning: Order induced by the positive cone.

children.title: Nonexpansive Semigroup Regimes
children.top_down_role: Evolution regimes characterized by nonincrease of trajectory separation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space.
\(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is m-accretive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The semigroup generated by \(-A\) is nonexpansive on \(\overline{D(A)}\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A at step h.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonexpansiveness of the semigroup generated by an m-accretive operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be m-accretive on a Banach space \(X\). Then each resolvent \(J_h=(I+hA)^{-1}\) is defined on all of \(X\) and satisfies \[\|J_hx-J_hy\|\leq\|x-y\|.\] The exponential formula \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}J_{t/n}^{\,n}x\] defines a strongly continuous nonlinear semigroup on \(\overline{D(A)}\). For every \(x,y\in\overline{D(A)}\) and \(t\geq0\), \[\|S(t)x-S(t)y\|\leq\|x-y\|.\] Hence the evolution is nonexpansive, solutions are unique for their initial data, and perturbations of initial states are not amplified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An m-accretive operator generates a strongly continuous nonlinear semigroup that does not increase distances between initial states.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexpansive Semigroup Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and its content kind fit the nonexpansive-semigroup container, but an authoritative Crandall–Liggett generation locator is required to support the exact hypotheses, domain, exponential formula, and strong-continuity conclusion.

children.title: Generator-to-Semigroup Transfer
children.top_down_role: Passage of contraction or comparison structure from generators to nonlinear evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
For every \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), define \(S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}(I+(t/n)A)^{-n}x\).
