knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(t)\) is a strongly continuous nonexpansive semigroup generated by \(-A\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the maximal monotone operator

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Crandall–Liggett exponential formula for maximal monotone Hilbert-space generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space maximal-monotone version of generator-to-semigroup transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t\ge 0\) and \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), the limit \[S(t)x=\lim_{n\to\infty}J_{t/n}^{\,n}x\] exists uniformly for \(t\) in bounded intervals. It satisfies \(S(0)=I\), \(S(t+s)=S(t)S(s)\), and \[\|S(t)x-S(t)y\|\le \|x-y\|\] for all \(x,y\in\overline{D(A)}\). Moreover, \(u(t)=S(t)x\) is the mild solution of \(\dot u(t)+A(u(t))\ni0\), so resolvent nonexpansiveness transfers from the generator to the evolution semigroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal monotone operator generates, through implicit resolvent products, a strongly continuous semigroup that preserves the generator’s nonexpansive metric estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator-to-Semigroup Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generator-to-semigroup theorem is standard and fits the leaf, but no citation or inspectable theorem locator supports the exponential formula, compact-time convergence, and mild-solution conclusion.

children.title: Comparison-Order Failure
children.top_down_role: Settings where the required ordering structure is absent or not preserved.

assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R^2\) carries the componentwise order induced by \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The semigroup generated by \(-A\) is isometric but not order preserving.

notation.meaning: Rotation semigroup generated by minus the operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that metric contraction alone does not imply comparison-order preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is maximal monotone because \(\langle Ax-Ay,x-y\rangle=0\), and its semigroup \(S(t)=e^{-tA}\) consists of rotations, hence \(\|S(t)x-S(t)y\|=\|x-y\|\). Nevertheless, with \(x=(0,0)\), \(y=(1,0)\), and \(t=\pi/2\), one has \(x\le_K y\) but \(S(t)y=(0,-1)\notin K\). Thus maximal monotonicity and nonexpansiveness do not certify order comparison unless the cone is invariant under the resolvent or semigroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Planar rotations form a nonexpansive semigroup generated by a maximal monotone operator, yet they fail to preserve the componentwise order.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparison-Order Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rotation counterexample is mathematically consistent and its counterexample kind fits the failure leaf, but it has no cited source or specific locator.

children.title: Perturbation Stability
children.top_down_role: Dependence on initial data, forcing, and generators.

assumptions_latex: \(A_n,A:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximal monotone and \(J_\lambda^{A_n}x\to J_\lambda^A x\) for every \(x\in H\) and some \(\lambda>0\).
\(x_n\to x\) in \(H\), and \(f_n\to f\) in \(L^1(0,T;H)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corresponding solutions satisfy \(u_n\to u\) uniformly on \([0,T]\).

notation.meaning: Solutions driven by the perturbed and limiting data

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonlinear semigroup stability under strong resolvent and data convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon stability for maximal-monotone evolution under data and generator perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_n\) and \(u\) be the mild solutions of \[\dot u_n(t)+A_n(u_n(t))\ni f_n(t),\quad u_n(0)=x_n,\] and \[\dot u(t)+A(u(t))\ni f(t),\quad u(0)=x.\] Then \(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u_n(t)-u(t)\|\to0\). In the unperturbed-generator case \(A_n=A\), the sharper estimate \[\|u_n(t)-u(t)\|\le \|x_n-x\|+\int_0^t\|f_n(s)-f(s)\|\,ds\] holds for every \(t\in[0,T]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong resolvent convergence of generators, together with convergent initial states and forcing, yields uniform finite-time convergence of the generated evolutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This theorem fits perturbation stability, but an exact source is needed to verify that resolvent convergence for one parameter, together with the stated data convergence, suffices for uniform convergence of the forced mild solutions under precisely these hypotheses.

children.title: Long-Time Convergence Regime Pair
children.top_down_role: Long-time convergence and averaging behavior of monotone evolution.

children.title: Equilibrium Convergence
children.top_down_role: Long-time approach to stationary states in monotone evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal and \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for some \(\mu>0\).
The zero set \(A^{-1}(0)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every generated trajectory converges exponentially to the unique equilibrium.

notation.meaning: Unique zero of the strongly monotone operator
Semigroup generated by minus the operator

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exponential decay from strong monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly monotone equilibrium regime with exponential pointwise convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong monotonicity means \[\langle a-b,x-y\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|^2\] whenever \(a\in A(x)\) and \(b\in A(y)\). It implies that the equilibrium \(x_\star\), characterized by \(0\in A(x_\star)\), is unique. For every \(x\in\overline{D(A)}\), the trajectory \(u(t)=S(t)x\) satisfies \[\|u(t)-x_\star\|\le e^{-\mu t}\|x-x_\star\|,\qquad t\ge0.\] Hence \(u(t)\to x_\star\) strongly as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity makes the equilibrium unique and forces every semigroup trajectory to approach it at an exponential rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential equilibrium estimate is standard and the theorem kind fits the leaf, but no authoritative source and locator are supplied.

children.title: Ergodic Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaged trajectory behavior when pointwise convergence is unavailable.

assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and has a minimizer \(x_\star\).
\(u\) solves \(\dot u(t)+\partial f(u(t))\ni0\) with \(u(0)=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Cesàro average has objective gap at most \(\|x_0-x_\star\|^2/(2T)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subgradient-flow energy inequality and Jensen averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value ergodic estimate for convex subgradient flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For almost every \(t>0\), the subgradient inequality and the evolution inclusion give \[f(u(t))-f(x_\star)\le-\langle\dot u(t),u(t)-x_\star\rangle.\] Integration over \([0,T]\), followed by convexity of \(f\), yields \[f(\bar u_T)-f(x_\star)\le\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl(f(u(t))-f(x_\star)\bigr)\,dt\le\frac{\|x_0-x_\star\|^2}{2T}.\] Thus averaging supplies a quantitative equilibrium certificate even when no pointwise convergence rate is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging a convex subgradient-flow trajectory gives an objective gap of order one over time without requiring pointwise convergence rates.
knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Averaging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ergodic estimate is standard and locally appropriate, but the record lacks a cited source and includes derivational proof text ('Integration ... followed by convexity ... yields'), which must be removed from a sourced replacement.

children.title: Pointwise-versus-Ergodic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes distinguishing direct trajectory limits from averaged limits.

assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and attains its minimum.
\(u\) is a subgradient-flow trajectory and \(\bar u_T=T^{-1}\int_0^T u(t)\,dt\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ergodic objective convergence requires weaker structure than quantitative pointwise state convergence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinction between strong-monotonicity pointwise rates and convex ergodic rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates pointwise state convergence from ergodic objective convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under convexity alone, averaging guarantees \(f(\bar u_T)-\min f=O(T^{-1})\), but this estimate does not imply \(\operatorname{dist}(u(T),X_\star)=O(T^{-1})\) or strong convergence of \(u(T)\). If, additionally, \(\partial f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, then \(X_\star=\{x_\star\}\) and \[\|u(T)-x_\star\|\le e^{-\mu T}\|u(0)-x_\star\|.\] Thus pointwise rates demand an error-bound or coercivity mechanism absent from the basic ergodic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity gives a rate for averaged objective values, while pointwise state convergence or rates require additional coercivity such as strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise-versus-Ergodic Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly distinguishes averaged objective rates from pointwise state rates and fits the leaf, but neither component theorem nor the asserted structural comparison has an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Monotone Contractivity Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure boundaries for uniqueness, comparison, and semigroup structure.

children.title: Monotonicity Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Failures of order-based comparison or dissipative structure.

assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R\) and \(A(x)=-x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator is not monotone, and its generated trajectories separate exponentially.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar example showing the dynamical effect of losing monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), \[\bigl(A(x)-A(y)\bigr)(x-y)=-(x-y)^2<0,\] so \(A\) violates monotonicity. The equation \(\dot u(t)+A(u(t))=0\) becomes \(\dot u(t)=u(t)\), with solution \(S(t)x=e^t x\). Consequently, \[|S(t)x-S(t)y|=e^t|x-y|,\] and arbitrarily small perturbations of the initial state are amplified. This demonstrates that the monotonicity inequality is essential for the usual dissipative distance estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The anti-monotone scalar operator minus identity produces exponentially expanding trajectories, so initial perturbations are amplified rather than dissipated.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar counterexample is correct and appropriately classified, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Contractivity Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Loss of distance control or stable dependence between trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is \(\rho\)-hypomonotone with \(\rho>0\).
Solutions \(u,v\) satisfy \(\dot u+A(u)\ni0\) and \(\dot v+A(v)\ni0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only the expansion estimate \(\|u(t)-v(t)\|\le e^{\rho t}\|u(0)-v(0)\|\) is generally available.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Grönwall estimate for hypomonotone evolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp transition from contraction to exponential Lipschitz expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Hypomonotonicity means \[\langle a-b,x-y\rangle\ge-\rho\|x-y\|^2\] for \(a\in A(x)\) and \(b\in A(y)\). Along sufficiently regular solutions this yields \(d(t)^2{}'\le2\rho d(t)^2\), hence \[d(t)\le e^{\rho t}d(0).\] The nonexpansive estimate is recovered only at \(\rho=0\). The boundary is sharp: for \(A=-\rho I\), equality holds, so every positive hypomonotonicity defect can produce exponential separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive hypomonotonicity defect replaces nonexpansiveness by exponential Lipschitz growth, and the linear operator minus rho identity attains the bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractivity Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hypomonotone expansion boundary and sharp linear example fit the leaf, but a source is needed to establish the required solution regularity and the estimate under a precise well-posedness framework.

children.title: Coupled Failure Consequences
children.top_down_role: Uniqueness or semigroup failures arising when both structures deteriorate.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(A(x)=x^3-x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Loss of monotonicity simultaneously permits local expansion and multiple equilibria.

notation.meaning: Flow generated by minus the nonlinear operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Double-well flow exhibiting coupled uniqueness and contractivity failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Since \(A'(0)=-1\), the operator is not monotone. The evolution equation is \[\dot u(t)=u(t)-u(t)^3.\] Its equilibrium set is \(E=\{-1,0,1\}\), so no unique global attractor exists. Moreover, the derivative of the flow at the unstable equilibrium satisfies \[D S(t)(0)=e^t,\] proving local expansion and failure of global nonexpansiveness. Initial states of opposite signs converge to different stable equilibria, so small perturbations near zero can also change the selected long-time limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The double-well flow has three equilibria, expands near the unstable one, and sends nearby states of opposite signs to different limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Failure Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The double-well counterexample is mathematically consistent and fits the coupled-failure leaf, but no source or specific locator is provided.

children.title: Constrained Variational Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Continuous constrained motion represented by projections, normal reactions, and differential variational inequalities.

children.title: Projected Dynamical Systems
children.top_down_role: Feasible dynamics selected through projection onto local constraint geometry.

children.title: Convex Projected Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Projected motion on closed convex feasible regions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space \(H\).
\(F:C\to H\) is continuous, and the projected vector field admits an absolutely continuous solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projected motion is equivalently characterized by tangent projection and a normal-cone complementarity relation.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to the convex set
Metric projection onto a closed convex cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional projected dynamics on a closed convex feasible set.

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex projected trajectory is an absolutely continuous map \(x:[0,T]\to C\) satisfying, for almost every \(t\), \[\dot x(t)=P_{T_C(x(t))}\bigl(-F(x(t))\bigr).\] Equivalently, there exists \(n(t)\in N_C(x(t))\) such that \[-F(x(t))=\dot x(t)+n(t),\qquad \langle\dot x(t),n(t)\rangle=0.\] The tangent component supplies feasible motion, while the normal component is the reaction enforcing \(x(t)\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected dynamics retain the feasible tangent component of the driving field and balance the discarded component with a normal reaction.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Projected Dynamics

source_witnesses.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Active-Stratum Projection Geometry
children.top_down_role: Projected motion across faces and active strata.

children.title: Polyhedral Face Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Projected motion restricted to faces of polyhedral feasible sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Gx\le h\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron and \(F:C\to\mathbb R^d\) is continuous.
A projected trajectory remains in the relative interior of a face \(Q\) on an interval \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On \(I\), the trajectory follows the projection of \(-F\) onto the face tangent space.

notation.meaning: Active constraint indices on the relative interior of the face
Tangent space parallel to the face
Orthogonal projection onto the face tangent space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-face reduction of polyhedral projected dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional reduction while a projected trajectory remains on one polyhedral face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(x(t)\in\operatorname{ri}Q\) throughout \(I\), its velocity satisfies \(\dot x(t)\in L_Q\) for almost every \(t\in I\). If the projected field is tangent to \(Q\) along this segment, equivalently \(P_{T_C(x)}(-F(x))\in L_Q\), then \[\dot x(t)=P_{L_Q}\bigl(-F(x(t))\bigr),\qquad t\in I\ \text{a.e.}\] Thus the active equalities remain fixed and the ambient projected system reduces to a smooth lower-dimensional equation on the affine hull of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: While a trajectory stays on one invariant polyhedral face, its active constraints remain fixed and motion is the field projected onto that face.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Face Dynamics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional fixed-face representation is plausible, but no source verifies it. Moreover, continuity of F only yields a continuous reduced vector field; calling the lower-dimensional equation smooth requires additional regularity.

children.title: Stratified Active-Set Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Projected evolution organized by active geometric strata.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) is partitioned into finitely many smooth strata \(M_\alpha\), each with constant active-constraint type.
\(F:C\to\mathbb R^d\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projected vector field is represented stratumwise and switches when the active stratum changes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: active-stratum decomposition of projected motion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-smooth representation away from cross-stratum transition times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On any open time interval for which \(x(t)\in M_\alpha\) and the projected velocity is tangent to that stratum, the constrained dynamics reduce to \[\dot x(t)=V_\alpha(x(t))=P_{T_{M_\alpha}(x(t))}\bigl(-F(x(t))\bigr).\] The active label \(\alpha\) is constant on such an interval. A transition time is a time \(\tau\) at which \(x(\tau)\in\overline{M_\alpha}\cap\overline{M_\beta}\) for distinct strata and the applicable tangent projection changes. Hence the global trajectory is assembled from stratumwise projected arcs and transition events.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected motion is smooth within a fixed active stratum and changes its tangent projection when the trajectory reaches another stratum.
knowledge_statements.title: Stratified Active-Set Dynamics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional stratumwise formula is plausible, but the assumptions do not justify the global arc-and-transition decomposition or smooth within-stratum motion when F is merely continuous. A source with precise stratification, tangency, and transition hypotheses is required.

children.title: Cross-Stratum Transitions
children.top_down_role: Trajectory behavior near changes of face or stratum.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}M_\alpha\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is partitioned into pairwise disjoint smooth strata.
\(x:[0,T]\to C\) is absolutely continuous and, away from transition times, satisfies \(\dot x(t)=P_{T_{M_{\alpha(t)}}(x(t))}f(t,x(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A time \(\tau\in(0,T)\) is a cross-stratum transition when there exist distinct strata \(M_\alpha\) and \(M_\beta\) and sequences \(t_k\uparrow\tau\), \(s_k\downarrow\tau\) such that \(x(t_k)\in M_\alpha\) and \(x(s_k)\in M_\beta\). At such a time the active tangent space may change from \(T_{M_\alpha}(x(\tau))\) to \(T_{M_\beta}(x(\tau))\), so the one-sided projected velocities need not coincide.

notation.meaning: Smooth strata forming the constraint set.
Orthogonal projection onto a set or subspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a transition through changes of active smooth stratum along a projected trajectory.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}M_\alpha\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a stratified constraint set and let \(x:[0,T]\to C\) be an absolutely continuous projected trajectory. A time \(\tau\in(0,T)\) is a cross-stratum transition if the active stratum differs on sequences approaching \(\tau\) from the left and right. When the corresponding tangent spaces have distinct limits, the projected vector field can have distinct one-sided limits, even if \(f\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-stratum transition occurs when a constrained trajectory moves between distinct smooth strata; changing tangent spaces can produce a jump in its projected velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Stratum Transitions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the cited variational-geometry chapter does not specifically support the proposed stratified-dynamics transition notion. Moreover, the assumption uses an undefined index map \(\alpha(t)\), and the conclusion writes tangent spaces at \(x(\tau)\) although that point need not belong to either adjacent stratum; tangent-space limits would need to be stated instead. A dedicated stratified projected-dynamics source is required before fixing the formulation.

children.title: Prox-Regular Projected Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Localized projected motion on regular nonconvex sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and uniformly \(r\)-prox-regular for some \(r>0\).
\(f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is measurable in time and locally Lipschitz in the state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A prox-regular projected trajectory is an absolutely continuous map \(x:[0,T]\to C\) satisfying, for almost every \(t\), \[\dot x(t)=P_{T_C(x(t))}f(t,x(t)).\] Equivalently, at points where the tangent-normal polarity and projection characterization apply, \[\dot x(t)\in T_C(x(t)),\qquad f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t)),\qquad \langle f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t),\dot x(t)\rangle=0.\] The formulation is local to the prox-regularity neighborhood.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to the constraint set.
Proximal or compatible regular normal cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the finite-dimensional local projected formulation on a uniformly prox-regular set.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a closed uniformly \(r\)-prox-regular set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), a vector field \(f\), and \(x_0\in C\), prox-regular projected dynamics seek an absolutely continuous curve \(x:[0,T]\to C\) with \(x(0)=x_0\) such that \(\dot x(t)=P_{T_C(x(t))}f(t,x(t))\) for almost every \(t\). This equation decomposes the desired velocity into a feasible tangential velocity and a normal reaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regular projected dynamics project the desired vector field onto the tangent cone of a regular nonconvex constraint set, locally in the prox-regularity neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Projected Dynamics

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition role fits the topic, but the cited general variational-geometry chapter does not establish the projected dynamics or the claimed equivalence for uniformly prox-regular sets. The record also alternates between proximal and unspecified compatible regular normals and does not identify the neighborhood in which its local qualification applies. A dedicated prox-regular differential-inclusion or projected-dynamics source is needed.

children.title: Projection Selection Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure of single-valued feasible-velocity selection.

children.title: Projection Discontinuity
children.top_down_role: Discontinuous dependence of projected velocities on state or forcing.

assumptions_latex: \(C=(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{R}^2\).
The desired velocity is the constant vector \(f=(1,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(x=(a,0)\) with \(a\ne0\), \(T_C(x)=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\) and \(P_{T_C(x)}f=(1,0)\). For \(x=(0,b)\) with \(b\ne0\), \(T_C(x)=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\) and \(P_{T_C(x)}f=(0,1)\). At the origin, \(T_C(0)=C\) and \[P_{T_C(0)}f=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}.\] Thus no single-valued selection agreeing with the unique nearby projections is continuous at the origin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A crossing of two lines gives a concrete discontinuous tangent-projection map.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) be the union of the two coordinate axes and let \(f=(1,1)\). Away from the origin, projection of \(f\) onto the tangent cone is uniquely \((1,0)\) on the horizontal axis and uniquely \((0,1)\) on the vertical axis. At the origin both vectors are nearest points of \(T_C(0)\) to \(f\). Consequently the tangent-projection correspondence is not single-valued at the crossing and admits no continuous selection compatible with both axes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the crossing of two coordinate axes, tangent projections approach different values along the two branches and become set-valued at the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Discontinuity

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

children.title: Velocity-Selection Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of feasible projected velocities at a common state.

assumptions_latex: \(C=(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{R}^2\).
The state is \(x=0\) and the desired velocity is \(f=(1,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Because \(T_C(0)=C\), the minimization problem \[\min_{v\in T_C(0)}\|f-v\|\] has the two distinct solutions \(v_1=(1,0)\) and \(v_2=(0,1)\), each at distance \(1\) from \(f\). Hence the projected law \(\dot x\in P_{T_C(x)}f\) permits at least two instantaneous velocities at \(x=0\); a single-valued differential equation is not determined there without an additional selection rule.

notation.meaning: Set of nearest points in the indicated set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demonstrates instantaneous velocity nonuniqueness caused by a nonconvex tangent cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the union \(C\) of the coordinate axes, the Bouligand tangent cone at the origin is the nonconvex set \(T_C(0)=C\). With desired velocity \(f=(1,1)\), both \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) minimize distance to \(f\) over this tangent cone. Therefore the projected velocity correspondence \(P_{T_C(0)}f\) has two elements, and the constraint geometry alone does not select a unique instantaneous velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex tangent cone can have two equally near feasible velocities, so the projected evolution law fails to determine a unique velocity.

children.title: Geometric Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Constraint geometries marking the onset of discontinuity or multiplicity.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and \(x\in C\).
Projected velocity is defined through nearest-point projection of \(f(x)\) onto \(T_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard single-valued projected law reaches a geometric failure boundary whenever \(T_C(x)\) is nonconvex and \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in T_C(x)}\|f(x)-v\|\] contains more than one point, or whenever these minimizers fail to vary continuously with \(x\). Such behavior is possible at branch intersections, inward corners, and other points where prox-regularity or tangent-cone regularity fails. Beyond this boundary, an explicit set-valued inclusion or selection rule is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies loss of unique continuous tangent projection as the operative geometric boundary.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed constraint set \(C\), a projected vector field based on \(P_{T_C(x)}f(x)\) ceases to define a continuous single-valued velocity when the tangent cone has multiple nearest points to \(f(x)\), or when the unique nearest point changes discontinuously with \(x\). Nonconvex tangent geometry and failure of local prox-regularity are sufficient mechanisms for this breakdown, although neither is asserted here as necessary in every formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometric boundary is crossed when tangent projection becomes multivalued or discontinuous, so a projected ordinary differential equation no longer supplies a regular velocity field.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Failure Boundaries

A dedicated source is needed to state the valid sufficient conditions and scope without overclaiming.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(x:[0,T]\to C\) is absolutely continuous and \(f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is given.

children.title: Normal-Cone Inclusion Representation
children.top_down_role: Constrained dynamics expressed through normal-cone reactions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(x:[0,T]\to C\) is absolutely continuous and \(f:[0,T]\times C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normal-cone inclusion representation is \[f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t,\qquad x(0)=x_0\in C.\] Equivalently, \[\dot x(t)+N_C(x(t))\ni f(t,x(t)).\] The vector \(f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\) is the normal reaction that removes the outward component of the desired velocity.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to the constraint set.
Normal reaction exerted by the constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex normal-cone inclusion for an absolutely continuous feasible trajectory.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an absolutely continuous feasible trajectory \(x:[0,T]\to C\) in a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), the normal-cone representation of constrained dynamics is \(f(t,x(t))-\dot x(t)\in N_C(x(t))\) for almost every \(t\). In inclusion notation this is \(\dot x(t)+N_C(x(t))\ni f(t,x(t))\). The difference between desired and actual velocity is therefore a normal reaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal-cone representation writes desired velocity as actual velocity plus a reaction normal to the convex constraint set.

children.title: Degenerate Constraint Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric degeneracy obstructing regular velocity or reaction representations.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, \(x\in C\), and \(f\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a desired velocity.
\(T_C(x)\) is the Bouligand tangent cone and \(N_C(x)\) is a specified normal cone used by the dynamics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The geometry is degenerate for the chosen projected-dynamics model at \(x\) if the tangent projection \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in T_C(x)}\|f-v\|\] is not a singleton, or if the model admits distinct complementary velocity-reaction pairs \((v_1,n_1)\ne(v_2,n_2)\) satisfying, for \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \[f=v_i+n_i,\qquad v_i\in T_C(x),\qquad n_i\in N_C(x),\qquad \langle v_i,n_i\rangle=0.\] Either condition obstructs a unique velocity-reaction representation for that model; equivalence with other projected or variational-inequality formulations requires additional regularity and tangent-normal polarity assumptions.

notation.meaning: The specified normal cone used by the dynamics.
Candidate actual velocity and constraint reaction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks nonuniqueness of tangent projection or of a complementary velocity-reaction decomposition for a specified irregular-constraint model.

Such nonuniqueness prevents that model from determining a unique instantaneous velocity-reaction pair without an additional selection or regularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint geometry is dynamically degenerate for a specified model when one desired velocity has multiple nearest tangent velocities or multiple complementary tangent-plus-normal decompositions.

\(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in F(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\iff \langle F(\bar x),y-\bar x\rangle\ge 0\quad(\forall y\in C).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the projected dynamics \(\dot x=\Pi_{T_C(x)}(-F(x))\), a point \(\bar x\in C\) is a variational rest point when its projected velocity vanishes. Equivalently,
\[
0=\Pi_{T_C(\bar x)}(-F(\bar x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in F(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle F(\bar x),y-\bar x\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible state is a rest point exactly when the driving field is balanced by a normal reaction, equivalently when it solves the associated variational inequality.

children.title: Equilibrium Selection Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Dynamic features that distinguish among multiple variational equilibria.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous and monotone, and its variational-inequality solution set \(S\) is nonempty.
\(\phi:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable and strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_\varepsilon\to\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\phi(x)\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\downarrow0.

notation.meaning: Solution set of the unregularized variational inequality
Unique solution of the regularized variational inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tikhonov selection among multiple monotone variational equilibria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(x_\varepsilon\in C\) solve
\[
\langle F(x_\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\nabla\phi(x_\varepsilon),y-x_\varepsilon\rangle\ge0
\quad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Strong monotonicity of the regularized field makes \(x_\varepsilon\) unique. As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the family converges to the uniquely selected equilibrium
\[
x^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\phi(x),
\qquad
S=\{x\in C: \langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing strongly convex regularization selects the unique equilibrium minimizing the regularizer over the original variational-equilibrium set.
knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Selection Mechanisms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Tikhonov selection result is plausible under the given finite-dimensional monotone-VI hypotheses, but the exact convergence theorem has no authoritative citation. Because the record asserts uniqueness and full-family convergence, its hypotheses and conclusion require a theorem-level source. The exact claim is theorem-like rather than merely a generic principle.

children.title: Selection Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings with ambiguous, unstable, or absent equilibrium selection.

assumptions_latex: \(C=[-1,1]\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(F(x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\).
The regularizer is \(\phi_a(x)=\tfrac12(x-a)^2\), with \(a\in\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=C,\qquad x_{\varepsilon,a}=a,\qquad x_{\varepsilon,1}\ne x_{\varepsilon,-1}.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonuniqueness showing dependence on the selection perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unregularized variational inequality has solution set \(S=C=[-1,1]\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), regularization by \(\varepsilon\phi_a'(x)=\varepsilon(x-a)\) yields the unique condition
\[
\varepsilon(x_{\varepsilon,a}-a)(y-x_{\varepsilon,a})\ge0
\quad\text{for every }y\in[-1,1],
\]
so \(x_{\varepsilon,a}=a\). Hence \(a=1\) selects \(1\), while \(a=-1\) selects \(-1\). Without a prescribed regularizer or an intrinsic uniqueness condition, the dynamics does not determine a unique equilibrium selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every feasible point is an equilibrium, different vanishing regularizers select different limits; equilibrium selection is therefore not intrinsic.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally consistent and fits the failure-boundary leaf: the two strongly convex regularizers select opposite endpoints of the common equilibrium set. Nevertheless, the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale satisfying the evidence contract.

children.title: Complementarity-Dynamics Interface
children.top_down_role: Routing to systems with complementarity reactions and switching constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}_+^m\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuous.
Solutions are interpreted componentwise almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dot x_i=-F_i(x)+r_i,\qquad r_i=\begin{cases}0,&x_i>0,\\ \max\{F_i(x),0\},&x_i=0.\end{cases}

source_refs.locator: 1.4.5 Traffic equilibrium models p. 41
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The projected dynamics on the nonnegative orthant,
\[
\dot x=\Pi_{T_{\mathbb{R}_+^m}(x)}(-F(x)),
\]
has the componentwise reaction representation
\[
\dot x_i=-F_i(x)+r_i,
\qquad
r_i=0\ \text{if }x_i>0,
\qquad
r_i=\max\{F_i(x),0\}\ \text{if }x_i=0.
\]
Thus \(x_i\ge0\), \(r_i\ge0\), and \(x_i r_i=0\); the switching rule additionally makes the reaction minimal and ensures viability at the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthant projection equals free motion plus the minimal nonnegative reaction activated precisely when a component reaches its constraint boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity-Dynamics Interface

children.top_down_role: Routing to contact, impact, and mechanical reaction models.

children.title: Unilateral Contact Models
children.top_down_role: Routing to constrained mechanical evolution with one-sided contact.

assumptions_latex: \(q(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(M(q)\) is symmetric positive definite, and \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is differentiable.
Contact is frictionless and described by \(g(q)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M(q)\ddot q+h(q,\dot q)=f+G(q)^\top\lambda,\qquad 0\le g(q)\perp\lambda\ge0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, frictionless, persistent unilateral contact without impulsive velocity jumps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A frictionless unilateral-contact model consists of the mechanical balance
\[
M(q)\ddot q+h(q,\dot q)=f(t,q,\dot q)+G(q)^\top\lambda
\]
together with the Signorini conditions
\[
g(q)\ge0,
\qquad
\lambda\ge0,
\qquad
\lambda_i g_i(q)=0\quad\text{for }i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
A positive gap therefore carries no contact force, while a positive multiplier can act only at a closed contact. These relations describe sustained contact intervals rather than instantaneous impacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unilateral contact couples mechanical balance to nonnegative gaps and compressive reactions that are complementary at every contact.
knowledge_statements.title: Unilateral Contact Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Signorini representation is standard and appropriately restricted to frictionless sustained contact, with a sign convention consistent with the stated gap orientation. No contact-mechanics source or inspectable locator is supplied, so the precise balance and complementarity convention cannot be accepted as sourced candidate knowledge.

children.title: Impact Models
children.top_down_role: Routing to impulsive mechanical events with velocity changes.

assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite and \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is the active-contact Jacobian.
The impact is instantaneous, frictionless, and has restitution coefficients \(e_i\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^+=v^-+M^{-1}G^\top p,\qquad 0\le p\perp Gv^++EGv^-\ge0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton restitution formulated as a frictionless impact complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At an active impact, momentum balance and Newton restitution are represented by
\[
v^+=v^-+M^{-1}G^\top p,
\qquad
0\le p\perp Gv^++EGv^-\ge0.
\]
Equivalently, \(p\) solves the linear complementarity problem
\[
0\le p\perp GM^{-1}G^\top p+(I+E)Gv^-\ge0.
\]
The output is the post-impact velocity \(v^+\). A contact receives positive impulse only when its restitution residual vanishes; inactive components have zero impulse and nonnegative residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instantaneous frictionless impact updates velocity by a normal impulse determined from momentum balance and a restitution complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Impact Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed impulse update and resulting complementarity problem are algebraically consistent for the stated Newton restitution convention. A source is required because simultaneous-contact restitution laws are model-dependent, and the record does not state conditions under which the complementarity problem has a solution or a uniquely determined post-impact velocity.

children.title: Contact–Impact Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interfaces between sustained reaction phases and impulsive events.

assumptions_latex: Each gap \(g_i(q)\) is differentiable near the active configuration.
The normal velocity is \(\gamma_i=\nabla g_i(q)^\top v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_i>0\Rightarrow\text{free};\quad g_i=0,\gamma_i=0\Rightarrow\text{contact candidate};\quad g_i=0,\gamma_i^-<0\Rightarrow\text{impact}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kinematic classification of free flight, sustained contact, impact, and grazing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For contact \(i\), the local regime is classified by the gap and normal velocity:
\[
g_i(q)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{free flight},
\qquad
g_i(q)=0,\ \gamma_i=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{sustained-contact candidate},
\]
\[
g_i(q)=0,\ \gamma_i^-<0\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{impact requiring an impulsive update}.
\]
The boundary case \(g_i(q)=0\) and \(\gamma_i^-=0\) is grazing. Its continuation cannot be decided kinematically alone; acceleration, reaction admissibility, and the chosen contact law determine detachment or maintained contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gap and normal velocity distinguish free flight, contact, impact, and grazing; grazing requires higher-order dynamics to resolve.
knowledge_statements.title: Contact–Impact Transition Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The kinematic distinctions are reasonable and the statement correctly treats zero normal velocity as insufficient to resolve grazing. The precise regime terminology and transition criteria require a contact-dynamics source with a specific locator.

children.title: Moreau Sweeping Process
children.top_down_role: Canonical moving-set evolution and its reaction and hysteresis representations.

children.title: Moving Constraint Sets
children.top_down_role: Time-indexed feasible sets as drivers of sweeping evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
Each \(C(t)\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
There is \(L\ge0\) such that \(d_H(C(t),C(s))\le L|t-s|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C:[0,T]\rightrightarrows H,\qquad d_H(C(t),C(s))\le L|t-s|.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance between nonempty closed sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz moving convex sets suitable for the classical Moreau sweeping process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Lipschitz moving constraint set is a multifunction \(C:[0,T]\rightrightarrows H\) whose values are nonempty, closed, and convex and for which
\[
d_H(C(t),C(s))\le L|t-s|
\quad\text{for all }s,t\in[0,T].
\]
A swept trajectory is required to satisfy \(x(t)\in C(t)\). The Hausdorff estimate controls the speed of boundary motion and supplies the temporal regularity used in the classical convex sweeping inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moving constraint is a closed convex feasible set varying Lipschitz-continuously in Hausdorff distance over time.
knowledge_statements.title: Moving Constraint Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the moving-constraint leaf and correctly isolates the classical Lipschitz convex setting. No sweeping-process source is cited, and the time-horizon parameter should explicitly be introduced as \(T>0\) when the record is sourced and revised.

children.title: Normal-Cone Reaction Balance
children.top_down_role: Normal reactions encoding constrained swept motion.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) is a Lipschitz family of nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(f\in L^1(0,T;H)\), and \(x\) is absolutely continuous with \(x(t)\in C(t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dot x(t)+r(t)=f(t),\qquad r(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\quad\text{a.e.}

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to the instantaneous constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed convex Moreau sweeping process with an explicit normal reaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The perturbed sweeping inclusion
\[
\dot x(t)+N_{C(t)}(x(t))\ni f(t)
\quad\text{for almost every }t
\]
is equivalent to the existence of a measurable reaction \(r(t)\) satisfying
\[
\dot x(t)+r(t)=f(t),
\qquad
r(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t)).
\]
Consequently, for every \(y\in C(t)\),
\[
\langle f(t)-\dot x(t),y-x(t)\rangle\le0,
\]
which is the instantaneous variational form of the reaction balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applied motion splits into feasible trajectory velocity and a normal reaction enforcing membership in the moving set.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Reaction Balance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-reaction decomposition and its variational inequality have the correct sign for the standard convex normal cone. The representation fits the leaf, but no source is supplied. The record should also state explicitly that both reaction relations and the final variational inequality hold almost everywhere.

children.title: Play-Stop Operator Duality
children.top_down_role: Canonical hysteresis operators represented by sweeping dynamics.

children.title: Play Operators
children.top_down_role: Sweeping representations of play-type hysteresis responses.

assumptions_latex: The initial play value is \(p(0)=u(0)-z_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u-p\in[-r,r],\qquad \dot p\in N_{[-r,r]}(u-p)\quad\text{a.e.}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar rate-independent play operator with threshold radius and prescribed initial displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The scalar play output \(p=\mathcal P_r[u;z_0]\) is the absolutely continuous function determined by
\[
z(t)=u(t)-p(t)\in[-r,r],
\qquad
\dot p(t)\in N_{[-r,r]}(z(t))
\quad\text{for almost every }t,
\]
with \(z(0)=z_0\). Equivalently,
\[
\dot p(t)\bigl(y-z(t)\bigr)\le0
\quad\text{for every }y\in[-r,r]
\]
for almost every \(t\). The output moves only when the elastic displacement lies on the threshold boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The play output keeps input minus output within a threshold interval and changes only under an active boundary reaction.
knowledge_statements.title: Play Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar play inclusion and equivalent variational inequality are internally consistent with the stated outward-normal convention and initialization. A hysteresis reference with a definition or page locator is required because play/stop naming and initialization conventions vary across sources.

children.title: Stop Operators
children.top_down_role: Sweeping representations of stop-type hysteresis responses.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\in[-r,r],\qquad \dot u-\dot z\in N_{[-r,r]}(z)\quad\text{a.e.}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar rate-independent stop operator with threshold radius and prescribed initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The scalar stop output \(z=\mathcal S_r[u;z_0]\) is the absolutely continuous function satisfying
\[
z(t)\in[-r,r],
\qquad
\dot u(t)-\dot z(t)\in N_{[-r,r]}(z(t))
\quad\text{for almost every }t,
\]
with \(z(0)=z_0\). Equivalently,
\[
\bigl(\dot u(t)-\dot z(t)\bigr)(y-z(t))\le0
\quad\text{for every }y\in[-r,r]
\]
for almost every \(t\). Thus the output follows the input until constrained by a threshold endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stop output remains inside the threshold interval and follows the input except for the normal reaction active at saturation.
knowledge_statements.title: Stop Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar stop inclusion is consistent with the complementary play convention used in the shard, and the definition kind fits the leaf. It lacks an authoritative hysteresis source and locator confirming this sign and initialization convention.

children.title: Play–Stop Duality
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences between the two canonical operator families.

assumptions_latex: Play and stop operators use the same threshold and compatible initialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P_r[u;z_0]+\mathcal S_r[u;z_0]=u.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive duality under the scalar play and stop conventions used in this shard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z=\mathcal S_r[u;z_0]\) solve
\[
\dot u-\dot z\in N_{[-r,r]}(z),
\qquad z(0)=z_0,
\]
and define \(p=u-z\). Then \(u-p=z\in[-r,r]\) and
\[
\dot p=\dot u-\dot z\in N_{[-r,r]}(u-p),
\]
so \(p=\mathcal P_r[u;z_0]\). Therefore
\[
\mathcal P_r[u;z_0]+
\mathcal S_r[u;z_0]=u,
\]
or equivalently \(\mathcal P_r=I-\mathcal S_r\) and \(\mathcal S_r=I-\mathcal P_r\) under compatible initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With matching threshold and initialization, play and stop outputs are complementary components whose pointwise sum equals the input.
knowledge_statements.title: Play–Stop Duality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive play-stop identity is consistent with the preceding local definitions and the duality content kind fits the leaf. No source supports the convention-dependent identity, and the statement contains a derivational proof sequence ('Then', 'so', 'Therefore') that must be removed before acceptance.

children.title: Geometric Regimes for Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Constraint geometries controlling projection, normal reactions, and uniqueness.

children.title: Convex Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Classical sweeping over closed convex moving sets.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(I=[0,T]\).
\(C:I\rightrightarrows H\) has nonempty closed convex values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t)\in C(t)\) for every \(t\in I\), and \(-\dot x(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) for almost every \(t\in I\).

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to the current constraint set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical unperturbed Moreau process in a Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex sweeping solution with initial state \(x_0\) is an absolutely continuous map \(x:I\to H\) satisfying \(x(0)=x_0\), \(x(t)\in C(t)\) for all \(t\in I\), and \[ -\dot x(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in I. \] Equivalently, for almost every \(t\), \(\langle\dot x(t),y-x(t)\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(y\in C(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A swept state remains in the moving convex set, while its negative velocity is a normal reaction to that set almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Sweeping

source_witnesses.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard and fits the convex-sweeping container, but the cited projection-characterization section does not establish the moving-set differential inclusion or its solution convention. A sweeping-process source with a specific definition or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Prox-Regular Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex sweeping with controlled local projection geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(I=[0,T]\).
Each \(C(t)\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and uniformly \(r\)-prox-regular for one \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t)\in C(t)\) and \(-\dot x(t)\in N^P_{C(t)}(x(t))\) almost everywhere.

notation.meaning: Metric projection onto a closed set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform prox-regularity is conventionally expressed by local single-valued projection and a proximal-normal inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unperturbed nonconvex process with a uniform projection radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The moving set is uniformly \(r\)-prox-regular when, for every \(t\), \(x
obreak\in C(t)\), and \(v\in N^P_{C(t)}(x)\), \[ \langle v,y-x\rangle\le \frac{\|v\|}{2r}\|y-x\|^2\quad\text{for all }y\in C(t). \] A prox-regular sweeping solution is an absolutely continuous map \(x:I\to H\) with \(x(0)=x_0\), \(x(t)\in C(t)\), and \(-\dot x(t)\in N^P_{C(t)}(x(t))\) almost everywhere. The inequality controls local projection geometry despite nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The process uses proximal normals to uniformly prox-regular moving sets, whose nearby metric projections have controlled local geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Sweeping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The prox-regular inequality and proximal-normal evolution are plausible and fit the container, but no source fixes the prox-regularity and normal-cone conventions or supports the dynamic formulation.

children.title: Generalized-Regularity Sweeping Classes
children.top_down_role: Sweeping under generalized nonconvex regularity.

children.title: Subsmooth Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Sweeping behavior supported by subsmooth constraint geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(C(t)\subset H\) is nonempty and closed for every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed hypomonotonicity predicate defines the subsmooth geometric regime used in the sweeping inclusion.

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the time slice.
Closed unit ball of the Hilbert space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subsmoothness is commonly formulated as local approximate monotonicity of bounded normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local uniform subsmoothness of time slices, followed by the normal-cone evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family is locally uniformly subsmooth if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\bar x\in C(\bar t)\), there are neighborhoods in time and space such that, whenever \(x_i\in C(t)\), \(\xi_i\in N_{C(t)}(x_i)\cap\mathbb B\), and both \(x_i\) are near \(\bar x\), \[ \langle \xi_1-\xi_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-\varepsilon\|x_1-x_2\|. \] Subsmooth sweeping seeks a feasible trajectory \(x\) satisfying \(-\dot x(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) almost everywhere, or the corresponding measure inclusion for bounded-variation motion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subsmooth sweeping replaces a uniform curvature radius by local approximate monotonicity of bounded normal vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Subsmooth Sweeping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-normal hypomonotonicity condition resembles a standard subsmoothness formulation, but the normal cone, uniformity in time, neighborhoods, and BV alternative require an exact source. The interval I is also not introduced in the assumptions.

children.title: Directionally Regular Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Sweeping behavior governed by directional geometric regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(C\subset H\) is closed, \(x\in C\), and \(d\in H\) is an admissible direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed directional projection property supplies the local geometry for sweeping motions approaching \(x\) along \(d\).

notation.meaning: Possibly set-valued metric projection onto the slice.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional local projection regularity; terminology varies across sweeping-process sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time slice is directionally projection-regular at \(x\) along \(d\) if there exist \(r>0\) and neighborhoods of \(x\) and \(d\) such that \(P_C(z+s e)\) is single-valued whenever \(z\in C\) is near \(x\), \(e\) is near \(d\), and \(0<s<r\). Directionally regular sweeping restricts the normal inclusion \(-\dot x(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) to trajectories whose relevant approach or reaction directions satisfy this property. No regularity is asserted in transverse directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection geometry is controlled only near directions actually used by the swept trajectory, not uniformly in every nearby direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Directionally Regular Sweeping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Directional regularity has several inequivalent meanings, and the stated directional single-valued-projection condition is not established as the intended sweeping-process regime. A source defining this exact predicate and its connection to the inclusion is necessary.

children.title: Overlapping Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where subsmoothness and directional regularity provide compatible controls.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) is a family of nonempty closed subsets of a Hilbert space.
The regularity predicates are interpreted with compatible normal-cone conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity implies both uniform prox-regularity and subsmoothness, so these geometric regimes overlap rather than partition sweeping processes.

notation.meaning: Time slice of the moving constraint.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the convex normal inequality has zero quadratic defect and monotone normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records implication and intersection, not a disjoint classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed \(t\), if \(C(t)\) is closed and convex, then \(\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\) for all \(x,y\in C(t)\) and \(v\in N_{C(t)}(x)\). Hence the prox-regular inequality holds for every \(r>0\), and monotonicity of the convex normal cone yields the subsmooth inequality with zero defect. Consequently, convex sweeping lies simultaneously in the prox-regular and subsmooth regimes. Other intersections may occur without either predicate implying the other globally, especially when regularity is imposed only along selected directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sweeping regularity classes are not disjoint: every closed convex slice is both prox-regular and subsmooth, while directional intersections depend on conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Regularity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-to-prox-regular and convex-to-subsmooth implications are standard under compatible conventions and the property fits this container. Nevertheless, the exact definitions and the claims about other directional intersections need a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Irregular Closed-Set Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Projection ambiguity, nonunique reactions, and weakened solution concepts.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is closed but no convexity, prox-regularity, or comparable projection condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric projections and normal reactions may be nonunique, so projection-based updates and classical uniqueness conclusions require additional hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Set of nearest points in the closed constraint.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the two-point example directly exhibits multivalued metric projection
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of projection determinacy outside regular geometric regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(C=\{-1,1\}\), and \(y=0\). Then \[ P_C(y)=\{-1,1\}, \] so a catching-up step based on nearest-point projection has two admissible outputs. More generally, for an arbitrary closed moving set, \(N_{C(t)}(x)\) may be nonconvex or contain several incompatible reactions, and nearby projections need not be single-valued. Thus the inclusion \(-\dot x(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) alone does not supply the projection stability used in classical existence and uniqueness arguments; relaxed, discrete, or measure-valued solution concepts may be necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without geometric regularity, nearest-point updates and normal reactions can be ambiguous, invalidating classical projection-stability and uniqueness arguments.
knowledge_statements.title: Irregular Closed-Set Sweeping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-point example correctly demonstrates multivalued projection and fits a failure-boundary record. The broader conclusions about normal reactions, classical existence and uniqueness, and the necessity of relaxed or measure-valued concepts require a dedicated source.

children.title: Temporal Regimes for Moving Sets
children.top_down_role: Regularity classes of set motion and their associated trajectory concepts.

children.title: Regular Set-Motion Regime Pair
children.top_down_role: Regular set motion supporting continuous swept trajectories.

children.title: Lipschitz Set Motion
children.top_down_role: Moving feasible sets with uniform metric variation control.

assumptions_latex: \((H,\|\cdot\|)\) is a Hilbert space and \(I=[0,T]\).
\(C(t)\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and bounded for every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_H(C(t),C(s))\le L|t-s|\) for all \(s,t\in I\).

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance between nonempty closed bounded sets.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard metric-space definition of a Lipschitz set-valued path
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hausdorff-Lipschitz motion of bounded closed constraint sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set-valued path \(C:I\rightrightarrows H\) has Lipschitz set motion if there exists \(L\ge0\) such that \[ d_H(C(t),C(s))\le L|t-s|\quad\text{for all }s,t\in I, \] where \(d_H(A,B)=\max\{\sup_{a\in A}\operatorname{dist}(a,B),\sup_{b\in B}\operatorname{dist}(b,A)\}\). Equivalently, \(t\mapsto C(t)\) is a Lipschitz curve in the Hausdorff metric space of nonempty closed bounded subsets of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The moving constraint is Lipschitz when its Hausdorff distance between any two times is bounded linearly by elapsed time.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Set Motion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a precise standard definition of Hausdorff-Lipschitz motion for nonempty closed bounded sets and fits the terminal container, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Absolutely Continuous Set Motion
children.top_down_role: Moving feasible sets driven by integrable temporal variation.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) is a nonempty closed bounded subset of a Hilbert space for each \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Hausdorff displacement of \(C\) is dominated by the integral of an \(L^1\) speed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard metric-space characterization of absolute continuity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute continuity in the Hausdorff metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set-valued path \(C:I\rightrightarrows H\) is absolutely continuous in Hausdorff distance if there exists a nonnegative function \(m\in L^1(I)\) such that, for every \(0\le s\le t\le T\), \[ d_H(C(t),C(s))\le\int_s^t m(\tau)\,d\tau. \] Equivalently, \(C\) is an absolutely continuous curve in the Hausdorff metric space. Its metric derivative \(|C'|(t)\) then exists almost everywhere and may be chosen as the least admissible speed bound up to null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hausdorff displacement is controlled by the integral of an integrable speed, making the set path absolutely continuous as a metric-space curve.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolutely Continuous Set Motion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integral characterization is the standard definition of an absolutely continuous metric-valued path and fits the container. A source is still required, particularly for the additional assertion about the metric derivative as the least admissible speed.

children.title: Trajectory Regularity Transfer
children.top_down_role: Continuity properties inherited by swept trajectories from regular set motion.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) has nonempty closed convex values in a Hilbert space.
\(d_H(C(t),C(s))\le\int_s^t m(\tau)\,d\tau\) with \(m\in L^1(I)\).
\(x\) solves the unperturbed convex sweeping process.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in AC(I;H)\) and \(\|\dot x(t)\|\le m(t)\) almost everywhere; Lipschitz set motion transfers Lipschitz regularity to \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex Hilbert-space transfer under Hausdorff absolute continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x(0)\in C(0)\), and let \(x\) satisfy \(-\dot x(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) almost everywhere. If \(d_H(C(t),C(s))\le\int_s^t m(\tau)\,d\tau\), then \(x\) is absolutely continuous and obeys \[ \|x(t)-x(s)\|\le\int_s^t m(\tau)\,d\tau,
obreak\qquad \|\dot x(t)\|\le m(t)\quad\text{almost everywhere}. \] In particular, if the set motion is Hausdorff-Lipschitz with constant \(L\), then the swept trajectory is Lipschitz with constant at most \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex sweeping, an integrable or uniform speed bound on the moving set transfers to the swept trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory Regularity Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits trajectory regularity transfer, but the sharp factor-one estimates and their Hilbert-space generality require a sweeping-process theorem citation. As written, saying that x satisfies an inclusion involving its derivative already presupposes regularity that the conclusion purports to establish.

children.title: Bounded-Variation Set Motion
children.top_down_role: Discontinuous constraints and jump-sensitive swept trajectories.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) is a nonempty closed bounded subset of a Hilbert space for every \(t\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) has bounded variation exactly when its Hausdorff variation over \(I\) is finite.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff variation of the set path.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded variation of a metric-valued path is defined by partition sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric bounded variation of the constraint path, allowing jumps.

source_refs.locator: IV.7 Bounded Variation of \( {Au} \) p. 130
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The moving set has bounded variation in Hausdorff distance if \[ \operatorname{Var}_{d_H}(C;I):=\sup_{0=t_0<\cdots<t_n=T}\sum_{i=1}^n d_H(C(t_i),C(t_{i-1}))<\infty. \] The associated variation function is nondecreasing and may have atoms, which represent jumps of the constraint. For a right-continuous convex sweeping convention, a jump at time \(t\) is commonly resolved by the catching-up update \(x(t)=P_{C(t)}(x(t-))\), provided this projection is well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moving set has bounded variation when all Hausdorff partition sums are uniformly bounded; jumps may induce projection updates of the trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Variation Set Motion

source_witnesses.locator: IV.7 Bounded Variation of \( {Au} \) p. 130
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition-sum definition is standard and fits bounded-variation set motion, but the cited section on bounded variation of Au does not evidently support Hausdorff-BV set paths. children.title: Measure-Driven Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Sweeping evolution represented through measure-valued temporal reactions.

assumptions_latex: \(C:I\rightrightarrows H\) has nonempty closed convex values and bounded Hausdorff variation.
\(x:I\to H\) is right-continuous, has bounded variation, and satisfies \(x(t)\in C(t)\).
\(\mu\) is a positive measure dominating both \(Dx\) and the variation measure of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sweeping dynamics are represented by \(-dDx/d\mu\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(t\).

notation.meaning: Vector measure distributional derivative of the BV trajectory.
Radon–Nikodym density of the trajectory derivative.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex BV sweeping represented as a measure differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A measure-driven convex sweeping solution is represented by the vector measure \(Dx\). Choose a positive measure \(\mu\) such that \(Dx\ll\mu\) and the variation measure controlling \(C\) is also absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\). The dynamics require \[ -\frac{dDx}{d\mu}(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))
obreak\quad\text{for }\mu\text{-almost every }t. \] On the nonatomic part, this reduces to the ordinary differential inclusion. At an atom corresponding to a constraint jump, the inclusion is supplemented by the adopted representative convention, commonly the projection update \(x(t)=P_{C(t)}(x(t-))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-variation swept trajectory has a vector-measure derivative whose negative density is a normal reaction, including atomic jump contributions.
knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Driven Sweeping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A measure representation is the correct content kind, but the normal inclusion at atoms depends on representatives, evaluation of C at jumps, and the adopted jump law. These conventions and the displayed density inclusion require an authoritative source.

children.title: Rough Set Motion
children.top_down_role: Moving-set evolution below standard continuous-variation regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique feasible trajectory is \(x=w\), which has infinite variation; hence continuity of set motion alone does not yield a BV sweeping trajectory.

notation.meaning: Continuous scalar path with infinite variation.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: singleton feasibility forces the trajectory to equal the explicitly given infinite-variation path
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous singleton motion showing failure below bounded variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The path \(w\) is continuous on \(I\) but has infinite total variation because its successive alternating extrema produce a divergent harmonic-type variation sum. Since \(C(t)=\{w(t)\}
obreak\), feasibility forces every swept trajectory to satisfy \(x(t)=w(t)\) for all \(t\). Consequently, no feasible trajectory belongs to \(BV(I;\mathbb R)\), and neither the BV measure formulation nor an absolutely continuous normal-inclusion formulation applies. Thus mere continuity of \(t\mapsto C(t)\) in Hausdorff distance is insufficient for BV trajectory regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous singleton constraint can oscillate with infinite variation, forcing its only feasible trajectory to have infinite variation as well.
knowledge_statements.title: Rough Set Motion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singleton example correctly forces x=w, and t sin(1/t) is continuous with infinite variation, so the failure phenomenon fits the container. No inspectable source is supplied for this nontrivial counterexample and its stated consequences for sweeping solution classes.

children.title: Oscillatory Set Motion
children.top_down_role: Rapidly varying feasible sets with repeated temporal fluctuations.

assumptions_latex: \(T=1\) and the ambient space is \(H=\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{n\ge 1}\sup_{t\in[0,1]}d_H(C_n(t),\{0\})\le 1\), but \(\{C_n\}_{n\ge 1}\) is not relatively compact in the uniform Hausdorff topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete high-frequency singleton motion exhibiting loss of temporal regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_n(t)=\{\sin(2\pi nt)\}\) for \(t\in[0,1]\). Then \(d_H(C_n(t),\{0\})\le 1\) for every \(n\) and \(t\), and each map \(t\mapsto C_n(t)\) is continuous in the Hausdorff metric. Nevertheless, \(\operatorname{Var}_{d_H}(C_n;[0,1])=4n\), and the family is not equicontinuous. Consequently, it has no subsequence converging uniformly in Hausdorff distance. Thus uniform spatial boundedness does not provide temporal compactness for rapidly oscillating moving constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly spatially bounded singleton constraints can oscillate ever faster, causing unbounded temporal variation and destroying compactness in the uniform Hausdorff topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Oscillatory Set Motion

children.title: Effective Limit Regimes
children.top_down_role: Limiting swept behavior produced by unresolved temporal irregularity.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a metric space, \(t\in[0,T]\) is fixed, and \(C_n(t)\subset H\) is nonempty for every \(n\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence \(C_n(t)\) converges to \(C_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)\) in the Kuratowski sense exactly when \(\operatorname*{Li}_{n\to\infty}C_n(t)=\operatorname*{Ls}_{n\to\infty}C_n(t)=C_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Kuratowski condition for identifying an effective moving constraint; no trajectory convergence is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed \(t\in[0,T]\), define \(\operatorname*{Li}_{n\to\infty}C_n(t)\) as the set of all \(x\in H\) for which there are points \(x_n\in C_n(t)\) with \(x_n\to x\). Define \(\operatorname*{Ls}_{n\to\infty}C_n(t)\) as the set of all \(x\in H\) for which there are indices \(n_k\to\infty\) and points \(x_{n_k}\in C_{n_k}(t)\) with \(x_{n_k}\to x\). The effective-limit condition is \[\operatorname*{Li}_{n\to\infty}C_n(t)=\operatorname*{Ls}_{n\to\infty}C_n(t)=C_{\mathrm{eff}}(t).\] This is pointwise Kuratowski convergence of the constraints and, without additional uniform temporal control, does not assert convergence of sweeping trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each fixed time, an effective constraint is identified when the lower and upper Kuratowski limits coincide; this pointwise set convergence alone does not assert trajectory convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Effective Limit Regimes

children.title: Temporal Compactness Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of trajectory compactness under insufficient control of set motion.

assumptions_latex: \(T=1\) and the state space is \(H=\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The associated constrained trajectories are bounded but possess no uniformly convergent subsequence.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of compactness in the uniform trajectory topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(C_n(t)=\{\sin(2\pi nt)\}\) on \([0,1]\). Any trajectory satisfying \(x_n(t)\in C_n(t)\) for every \(t\) must equal \(x_n(t)=\sin(2\pi nt)\). Although \(\|x_n\|_{\infty}=1\), the sequence is not equicontinuous: for \(s_n=0\) and \(t_n=1/(4n)\), one has \(|t_n-s_n|\to0\) while \(|x_n(t_n)-x_n(s_n)|=1\). Hence the Arzelà–Ascoli compactness criterion fails and no uniformly convergent subsequence exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rapidly oscillating singleton constraints force equally oscillatory trajectories, violating equicontinuity and compactness despite uniform boundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Temporal Compactness Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary counterexample and its Arzela-Ascoli conclusion are internally coherent and fit the failure leaf, but the record supplies neither a citation nor an inspectable locator. Source support is required before candidate review.

children.title: Quasivariational Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Sweeping governed by endogenous constraint correspondences.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, and \(K:[0,T]\times H\rightrightarrows H\) has nonempty closed convex values.
\(F:[0,T]\times H\rightrightarrows H\) is a prescribed perturbation mapping, and \(x_0\in K(0,x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A quasivariational sweeping trajectory evolves in the constraint \(K(t,x(t))\) selected by its own current state.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-valued quasivariational feasibility coupled to a perturbed normal-cone evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in K(0,x_0)\), a quasivariational sweeping trajectory is an absolutely continuous map \(x:[0,T]\to H\) such that \(x(0)=x_0\) and \[x(t)\in K(t,x(t)),\qquad -\dot x(t)\in N_{K(t,x(t))}(x(t))+F(t,x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T],\] where \(N_{K(t,x(t))}\) is the convex normal cone. The qualifier quasivariational refers to the dependence of the feasible set on the unknown state. When \(F(t,x)=\{0\}\), the definition gives the corresponding unperturbed quasivariational sweep.
