children.title: Inertial Sweeping
children.top_down_role: Sweeping dynamics shaped by momentum or inertial memory.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(m>0\), \(\gamma\ge0\), and \(C(t)\subset H\) is nonempty and closed.
The position has an absolutely continuous velocity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inertial sweeping adds mass and damping to the normal-cone constrained evolution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Damped second-order normal-cone dynamics with classical acceleration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given feasible initial data, an inertial sweeping trajectory satisfies \[x(t)\in C(t),\qquad -m\ddot x(t)-\gamma\dot x(t)+b(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t.\] The term \(m\ddot x\) stores momentum, while \(\gamma\dot x\) dissipates it. Setting \(m=0\) formally recovers a first-order perturbed sweep, but this singular limit requires separate compactness estimates and is not asserted by the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inertial sweeping combines a position constraint with acceleration, damping, external forcing, and a normal reaction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed damped second-order inclusion is plausible, but inertial-sweeping sign conventions and solution concepts vary. A source must establish the intended normal cone and formulation, as well as the scope of the first-order singular-limit comment.

children.title: Momentum-Induced Regimes
children.top_down_role: Oscillation, overshoot, or impact behavior arising from inertial coupling.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and independent of time.
\(x\) is a sufficiently regular solution of \(-m\ddot x-\gamma\dot x\in N_C(x)\), with \(m>0\) and \(\gamma\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(t)=\frac m2\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) is nonincreasing and satisfies \(\dot E(t)=-\gamma\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) almost everywhere.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energy regime for an unforced inertial sweep over a fixed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an unforced inertial sweep over a fixed convex constraint, feasible velocity is tangent to \(C\) and the normal reaction performs no work almost everywhere. Consequently the kinetic energy \(E(t)=\frac m2\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) obeys \[\dot E(t)=-\gamma\|\dot x(t)\|^2\le0.\] Thus \(\gamma>0\) produces dissipative momentum decay, whereas \(\gamma=0\) yields conservation of kinetic energy between any nonsmooth events excluded by the regularity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed convex constraint, damping dissipates kinetic energy while the ideal normal reaction performs no work.
knowledge_statements.title: Momentum-Induced Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The energy identity is plausible for a sufficiently regular fixed-convex-set evolution, but the phrase sufficiently regular does not state hypotheses ensuring the chain rule and zero work of the normal reaction. A precise sourced formulation is required.

Hausdorff-Lipschitz modulus of the moving set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convex Hilbert-space existence and uniqueness regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T>0\), and let \(C:[0,T]\rightrightarrows H\) have nonempty closed convex values. Suppose that there is \(L\ge 0\) such that \(d_H(C(t),C(s))\le L|t-s|\) for all \(s,t\in[0,T]\). Then, for every \(x_0\in C(0)\), there exists a unique absolutely continuous map \(x:[0,T]\to H\) such that \[x(0)=x_0,\qquad x(t)\in C(t)\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T],\qquad -\dot x(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t\in[0,T].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hausdorff-Lipschitz family of nonempty closed convex sets in a Hilbert space generates a unique absolutely continuous sweeping trajectory from every feasible initial state.
knowledge_statements.title: Sweeping Existence Families

children.title: Sweeping Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes supporting a single swept trajectory.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C:[0,T]\rightrightarrows H\) has nonempty closed convex values and is absolutely continuous in Hausdorff distance.
\(f:[0,T]\times H\to H\) is measurable in time and satisfies \(\|f(t,u)-f(t,v)\|\le L(t)\|u-v\|\) with \(L\in L^1(0,T)\).
\(x,y\in AC([0,T];H)\) solve the same perturbed sweeping inclusion and satisfy \(x(0)=y(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t)=y(t)\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\).

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to the set C at x.
Time-dependent Lipschitz modulus of the perturbation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex Hilbert-space uniqueness for an absolutely continuous moving set and a Lipschitz state perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), suppose \(x(t),y(t)\in C(t)\) and \(-\dot x(t)+f(t,x(t))\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\), \(-\dot y(t)+f(t,y(t))\in N_{C(t)}(y(t))\). Monotonicity of the convex normal cone gives \[\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2\le L(t)\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2\quad\text{a.e.}\] Consequently, \[\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le \exp\!\left(\int_0^tL(s)\,ds\right)\|x(0)-y(0)\|.\] In particular, equality of the initial states implies equality of the trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and an integrable Lipschitz bound on the perturbation, two sweeping trajectories with the same initial state coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Sweeping Uniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits Sweeping Uniqueness and the stated convex Hilbert-space estimate is standard, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the hypotheses and conclusion. The statement also includes derivational proof text, which must be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Contractive Dependence
children.top_down_role: Distance control between swept trajectories under differing data.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a Hilbert space for every \(t\).
\(f\) is one-sided dissipative: \(\langle f(t,u)-f(t,v),u-v\rangle\le-\mu(t)\|u-v\|^2\), where \(\mu\in L^1(0,T)\).
\(x\) and \(y\) solve the same sweeping inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential contraction generated by monotone normal reactions and a dissipative perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in AC([0,T];H)\) satisfy \(-\dot x(t)+f(t,x(t))\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) and \(-\dot y(t)+f(t,y(t))\in N_{C(t)}(y(t))\) almost everywhere. Normal-cone monotonicity and dissipativity yield \[\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2\le-\mu(t)\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2.\] Hence \[\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le e^{-\int_0^t\,mu(s)\,ds}\|x(0)-y(0)\|.\] If \(\mu\ge0\), the solution map is nonexpansive; if \(\int_0^t\,mu(s)\,ds>0\), it is strictly contractive at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-sided dissipative perturbation makes the sweeping solution map nonexpansive or exponentially contractive in its initial state.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Dependence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits Contractive Dependence, but the exponential factor contains the malformed expression \(\,mu\) instead of \(\mu\), so it does not faithfully match the assumptions or plain statement. No source is cited for the dissipative sweeping estimate, and the statement contains proof-style derivation.

children.title: Uniqueness Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Transitions where stable single-valued evolution ceases to hold.

assumptions_latex: The moving-set normal mapping obeys an estimate \(\langle n_x-n_y,x-y\rangle\ge-\alpha(t)\|x-y\|^2\).
The perturbation obeys \(\langle f(t,x)-f(t,y),x-y\rangle\le\beta(t)\|x-y\|^2\).
The positive part of \(\alpha+eta\) is not integrable on the interval under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The usual Gronwall uniqueness argument does not provide \(x=y\) from \(x(0)=y(0)\).

notation.meaning: Hypomonotonicity defect of the normal reaction.
One-sided growth modulus of the perturbation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the standard uniqueness mechanism; failure of the estimate does not itself assert nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two candidate trajectories, the hypomonotonicity and one-sided growth estimates imply only \[\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2\le\bigl(\alpha(t)+\beta(t)\bigr)\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2.\] The standard uniqueness regime requires \((\alpha+eta)_+\in L^1(0,T)\). If this integrability fails—for example because the prox-regularity radius approaches zero so that \(\alpha\) becomes singular—the Gronwall estimate cannot force coincident trajectories from coincident initial data. Additional geometry or a different selection principle is then necessary; actual nonuniqueness requires a separate example.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniqueness leaves its standard regime when the combined normal-cone and perturbation growth modulus is nonintegrable; this marks loss of the Gronwall mechanism.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind and the limited claim about loss of the Gronwall mechanism fit the leaf. However, \(\eta\) is undefined and conflicts with the introduced modulus \(\beta\) in both the assumptions and statement. A source is also required for the hypomonotonicity regime and the asserted prox-regularity-radius example.

children.title: Sweeping Perturbation-Stability Calculus
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity to driving sets, perturbations, and initial states.

children.title: Forcing-Perturbation Stability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of swept trajectories to additive or external perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) has nonempty closed convex values in a Hilbert space.
\(x_i\) solves \(-\dot x_i+f_i\in N_{C(t)}(x_i)\) with \(f_i\in L^1(0,T;H)\), for \(i=1,2\).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to the moving set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive forcing stability for two trajectories constrained by the same convex moving set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x_i(t)\in C(t)\) and \(-\dot x_i(t)+f_i(t)\in N_{C(t)}(x_i(t))\) almost everywhere for \(i=1,2\). Monotonicity gives \[\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|x_1(t)-x_2(t)\|^2\le\langle f_1(t)-f_2(t),x_1(t)-x_2(t)\rangle.\] Therefore, for every \(t\in[0,T]\), \[\|x_1(t)-x_2(t)\|\le\|x_1(0)-x_2(0)\|+\int_0^t\|f_1(s)-f_2(s)\|\,ds.\] Thus the solution map is Lipschitz from accumulated \(L^1\) forcing error to uniform state error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a common convex moving set, trajectory error is bounded by initial error plus accumulated forcing error.
knowledge_statements.title: Forcing-Perturbation Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind and additive forcing estimate match Forcing-Perturbation Stability for a common convex moving set. The record has no supporting citation or locator, and its statement includes derivational proof text rather than only the knowledge statement.

children.title: Moving-Set Stability
children.top_down_role: Dependence of swept evolution on changes in feasible-set motion.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space and \(C_i(t)=K+c_i(t)\).
\(c_i\in AC([0,T];H)\), and both processes have the same state-independent forcing \(f\in L^1(0,T;H)\).
\(x_i\) solves the sweeping inclusion for \(C_i\), for \(i=1,2\).

notation.meaning: State in coordinates fixed to K.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A precise moving-set estimate for translated copies of one fixed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(z_i(t)=x_i(t)-c_i(t)\). Translation invariance of the normal cone converts \(-\dot x_i(t)+f(t)\in N_{K+c_i(t)}(x_i(t))\) into \[-\dot z_i(t)+f(t)-\dot c_i(t)\in N_K(z_i(t)).\] Forcing stability on the fixed set \(K\) yields \[\|z_1(t)-z_2(t)\|\le\|z_1(0)-z_2(0)\|+\int_0^t\|\dot c_1(s)-dot c_2(s)\|\,ds.\] Consequently, \[\|x_1(t)-x_2(t)\|\le\|z_1(0)-z_2(0)\|+\int_0^t\|\dot c_1-dot c_2\|\,ds+\|c_1(t)-c_2(t)\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For translated convex constraints, state error is controlled by initial relative error and the displacement and velocity errors of the moving sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Set Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A restricted translational moving-set stability property fits the leaf, but occurrences of \(dot c_2\) omit the required command and time argument, making the displayed estimate malformed and inconsistent with \(\dot c_i(s)\). No source supports this restricted estimate, and the statement contains proof-style transformation steps.

children.title: Initial-State Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of swept trajectories on their starting configurations.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t)\) has nonempty closed convex values in a Hilbert space.
\(f(t,x)\) has integrable Lipschitz modulus \(L(t)\).
\(x\) and \(y\) solve the same sweeping problem with possibly different initial states.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz sensitivity of a convex sweeping trajectory to its feasible initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x(0),y(0)in C(0)\), and suppose \(-\dot x(t)+f(t,x(t))\in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) and \(-\dot y(t)+f(t,y(t))\in N_{C(t)}(y(t))\) almost everywhere. Then \[\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2\le L(t)\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2.\] Hence, for every \(t\in[0,T]\), \[\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le\exp\!\left(\int_0^tL(s)\,ds\right)\|x(0)-y(0)\|.\] Thus the time-\(t\) solution operator is Lipschitz on the feasible initial states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing only the feasible initial state changes the trajectory by at most the initial error multiplied by the perturbation’s Gronwall factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Initial-State Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind and Gronwall sensitivity estimate fit Initial-State Sensitivity. The expression \(y(0)in C(0)\) is malformed, no source or locator is supplied, and the displayed differential estimate is presented as proof text.

children.title: Constraint-Reaction Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness and blocked motion caused by irregular geometry or incompatible constraints.

children.title: Jamming Regimes
children.top_down_role: Blocked or arrested motion caused by active constraint geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is closed and \(x\in C\).
\(f\in H\) is the imposed free velocity.
Admissible velocities must satisfy both the reaction law and first-order viability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_C(x;f)=\varnothing\) characterizes first-order jamming.

notation.meaning: Chosen normal cone in the reaction law.
Set of viable velocities compatible with the reaction law.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instantaneous geometric jamming condition for a constrained reaction law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the compatible-velocity set by \[V_C(x;f):=T_C(x)\cap\bigl(f-N_C(x)\bigr).\] A state \((x,f)\) is first-order jammed when \(V_C(x;f)=\varnothing\): no velocity is simultaneously tangent-feasible and expressible as the free velocity minus an admissible normal reaction. If an absolutely continuous trajectory satisfies \(\dot x(t)in T_{C(t)}(x(t))\) and \(f(t)-dot x(t)in N_{C(t)}(x(t))\) almost everywhere, it cannot pass through a positive-measure time region on which this compatible-velocity set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jamming occurs when no instantaneous velocity is both tangent-feasible and compatible with the prescribed free velocity and normal reaction law.
knowledge_statements.title: Jamming Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition can fit Jamming Regimes, but the chosen normal-cone variant and set regularity are not fixed, so the compatibility set is not mathematically determinate. In the standard closed-convex setting, tangent-normal decomposition can make the proposed emptiness condition vacuous. The trajectory formulas also contain malformed \(in\) and \(dot x\) text, and no jamming source is cited.

children.title: Reaction Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of admissible constraint reactions for a common motion.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is represented as \(C=\bigcap_{j=1}^m C_j\).
At \(x\in C\), reactions are decomposed as \(r=\sum_{j=1}^m r_j\) with \(r_j\in N_{C_j}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reaction ambiguity occurs exactly when the decomposition map is noninjective on the admissible reaction tuples.

notation.meaning: Normal cone to the j-th constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambiguity of component reactions under a fixed total normal reaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The component reaction is ambiguous at \((x,r)\) if there exist two distinct tuples \((r_1,dots,r_m)\ne(\tilde r_1,dots,\tilde r_m)\) such that \[r_j,tilde r_j\in N_{C_j}(x),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m r_j=sum_{j=1}^m\tilde r_j=r.\] Equivalently, the summation mapping from admissible component normals to the total reaction is not injective. Thus a unique state velocity and a unique total reaction need not determine unique contact forces or multipliers. A constraint qualification or linear independence condition is required to exclude this ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with a unique trajectory and total reaction, individual constraint reactions are ambiguous when the same normal vector has multiple admissible decompositions.
knowledge_statements.title: Reaction Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The noninjectivity condition is locally appropriate for Reaction Ambiguity, but the normal-cone convention and admissible tuple domain require a source-backed specification. The statement has multiple malformed commands or equalities, including \(dots\), \(tilde r_j\), and \(sum\), and the assertion that a constraint qualification or linear independence condition is required overstates conditions that are generally sufficient rather than necessary.

children.title: Constraint-Incompatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Geometric configurations where active constraints obstruct consistent evolution.

assumptions_latex: The simultaneous constraint is \(C(t)=\bigcap_{j=1}^m C_j(t)\).
A candidate state \(x\) and free velocity \(f\) are prescribed at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Incompatibility is detected by \(C(t)=\varnothing\) or by \(T_{C(t)}(x)\cap(f-N_{C(t)}(x))=varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Tangent cone to the simultaneous constraint.
Normal cone used by the reaction law.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global and first-order boundaries at which simultaneous constraints cease to admit a sweeping evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Global incompatibility occurs at time \(t\) when \[C(t)=bigcap_{j=1}^m C_j(t)=\varnothing,\] so no feasible state exists. At a feasible state \(x\in C(t)\), first-order dynamic incompatibility occurs when \[T_{C(t)}(x)\cap\bigl(f-N_{C(t)}(x)\bigr)=\varnothing.\] In the latter case, no instantaneous velocity satisfies both viability and the normal-reaction inclusion. Loss of a normal-cone intersection rule or of a constraint qualification marks an additional boundary: componentwise reactions may then fail to represent the normal cone of the intersection, even though \(C(t)\) itself remains nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraints are incompatible when their intersection is empty or when no tangent-feasible velocity satisfies the combined normal-reaction law.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Incompatibility Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the container, but the first-order condition duplicates the proposed Jamming Regimes criterion and needs a source to distinguish the two local concepts. The normal-cone convention and intersection-rule hypotheses are unspecified, while \(bigcap\) and \(varnothing\) are malformed in the LaTeX fields.

children.title: Catching-Up Methods
children.top_down_role: Projection-based time-discretization families for sweeping processes.

children.title: Classical Catching-Up Schemes
children.top_down_role: Exact-projection approximations of moving-set evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(C(t)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(x_0\in C(0)\).
\(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T\) is a partition and \(f_{k+1}\in H\) approximates the forcing on \((t_k,t_{k+1}]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method outputs the projected states \((x_k)_{k=0}^N\) and a chosen time interpolant.

notation.meaning: Metric projection onto a closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau’s exact-projection catching-up update for a forced convex sweeping process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with \(x_0\in C(t_0)\). For \(k=0,dots,N-1\), form the free Euler predictor \[y_{k+1}=x_k+h_k f_{k+1},\] and restore feasibility by the exact projection \[x_{k+1}=P_{C(t_{k+1})}(y_{k+1}).\] Stop after \(k=N-1\) and output \((x_k)_{k=0}^N\), together with either the right-continuous piecewise-constant interpolant or the piecewise-affine state interpolant. Equivalently, the projection optimality condition is \[y_{k+1}-x_{k+1}in N_{C(t_{k+1})}(x_{k+1}),\] which is the discrete normal-reaction relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each step advances by the forcing and then projects exactly onto the new constraint set; the discrete states or their interpolant form the output.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Catching-Up Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind exactly fits Classical Catching-Up Schemes, and the predictor-projection update is appropriate for the stated sign convention. However, \(dots\) and \(in\) are malformed, the optimality discussion is proof-like, and Moreau's scheme is not supported by any citation or specific locator.

children.title: Inexact Catching-Up Schemes
children.top_down_role: Approximate-projection variants and their convergence regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(C(t_k)\) is nonempty and closed, and approximate projections can be computed.
The projection tolerances satisfy \(\eta_{k+1}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a feasible approximate-projection trajectory and its accumulated error \(E_N=sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\eta_{k+1}\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible additive-error variant of the catching-up projection step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with \(x_0\in C(t_0)\). At step \(k\), compute \(y_{k+1}=x_k+h_k f_{k+1}\) and choose \(x_{k+1}in C(t_{k+1})\) satisfying \[\|y_{k+1}-x_{k+1}\|\le d\bigl(y_{k+1},C(t_{k+1})\bigr)+eta_{k+1}.\] Stop at \(t_N=T\) and output the discrete states, an interpolant, and \[E_N:=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\eta_{k+1}.\] A refinement family lies in the vanishing-error regime when its mesh tends to zero and \(E_N\to0\). Convergence to a sweeping solution additionally requires compactness and regularity assumptions appropriate to the chosen moving-set class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each exact projection by a feasible point within a prescribed additive tolerance; convergence regimes require vanishing accumulated error and suitable compactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Catching-Up Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Inexact Catching-Up Schemes, but \(in\), \(eta_{k+1}\), and \(sum\) are malformed. For an arbitrary closed nonconvex set in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, an exact nearest point need not exist when \(\eta_{k+1}=0\), so the stated step is not always executable. The accumulated-error normalization and convergence regime also require a specific source.

children.title: Jump-Capturing Discretizations
children.top_down_role: Discrete treatment of discontinuous set motion and swept-state jumps.

assumptions_latex: \(C:[0,T]\rightrightarrows H\) has nonempty closed convex values and specified left and right limits at each jump time.
The time grid contains every designated jump time of \(C\).
\(x_0\in C(0)\), and the forcing is integrated between grid points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every captured jump \(\tau\), the discrete transition satisfies \(x(	au)=P_{C(	au)}(x(	au-))\), up to the chosen forcing convention.

notation.meaning: Left limit of the swept state at a jump.
Metric projection onto the post-jump constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grid-aligned projection rule for discontinuous convex set motion without atomic forcing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a partition containing every designated jump time. On an interval ending at a continuity point, use the catching-up update \[x_{k+1}=P_{C(t_{k+1})}\bigl(x_k+F_{k+1}\bigr),\] where \(F_{k+1}\) is the forcing increment. If \(t_{k+1}=tau\) is a set jump and forcing has no atom there, first retain the left state and then apply the post-jump projection \[x(\tau)=P_{C(\tau)}\bigl(x(\tau-)igr).\] Output the resulting right-continuous interpolant. The grid must not step across a designated jump without inserting its projection transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Place every set jump on the grid and project the left state directly onto the post-jump set, producing the prescribed swept-state jump.
knowledge_statements.title: Jump-Capturing Discretizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Jump-Capturing Discretizations, but the jump rule depends on a precise right-continuity and measure-forcing convention that is not sourced. The statement also contains malformed \(tau\) and \(igr\), so the displayed post-jump projection is not valid LaTeX. A source must fix the jump and atomic-forcing conventions before the mathematical record is reliable.

children.title: Catching-Up Feasibility Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Accumulated inexactness, missed jumps, and loss of feasibility.

children.title: Projection Error Accumulation
children.top_down_role: Growth of local projection inaccuracies across discrete updates.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and each \(T_k:H\to H\) is nonexpansive.
\(x_{k+1}=T_kx_k+e_k\), \(\bar x_{k+1}=T_k\bar x_k\), and \(\|e_k\|\leq\varepsilon_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every integer \(n\geq1\), \[\|x_n-\bar x_n\|\leq \|x_0-\bar x_0\|+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k.\] In particular, the condition \(\varepsilon_k\to0\) alone does not ensure that the discrepancy tends to zero.

notation.meaning: Exact nonexpansive catching-up update, typically a convex projection composed with a predictor.
Error in the kth approximate projection.
Nonnegative bound on the kth projection error.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic additive errors in nonexpansive Hilbert-space projection updates. The estimate does not assert that summability alone makes the discrepancy converge to zero.

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space. Suppose that \(\bar x_{k+1}=T_k\bar x_k\) and \(x_{k+1}=T_kx_k+e_k\) for every integer \(k\geq0\), where \(T_k:H\to H\) is nonexpansive and \(\|e_k\|\leq\varepsilon_k\) with \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\). Then \(\|x_{k+1}-\bar x_{k+1}\|\leq\|x_k-\bar x_k\|+\varepsilon_k\), and for every integer \(n\geq1\), \[\|x_n-\bar x_n\|\leq\|x_0-\bar x_0\|+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k.\] Consequently, pointwise decay \(\varepsilon_k\to0\) alone does not provide a vanishing global-error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate projection errors accumulate along nonexpansive catching-up steps. Errors tending individually to zero do not by themselves ensure that the discrepancy from the exact iterates tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Error Accumulation

children.title: Feasibility Drift
children.top_down_role: Progressive departure of discrete states from moving constraints.

assumptions_latex: Each inexact correction permits \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},C_{k+1})\leq\operatorname{dist}(x_k,C_k)+\varepsilon_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The admissible choice \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\varepsilon_k\) yields \(\operatorname{dist}(x_n,C_n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k\), so nonsummable residuals can cause unbounded feasibility drift.

notation.meaning: Fixed feasible set at step k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit scalar construction directly verifies the claimed drift
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar construction separating local feasibility tolerance from global feasibility control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(H=\mathbb R\), \(C_k=\{0\}\), and \(x_0=0\). Suppose an inexact correction is accepted whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},C_{k+1})\leq\operatorname{dist}(x_k,C_k)+\varepsilon_k\), with \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\). The admissible choice \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\varepsilon_k\) gives \[x_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x_n,C_n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_k.\] Consequently, local residual control alone permits persistent or unbounded feasibility drift whenever the accumulated tolerances fail to approach zero or remain bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with a fixed feasible set, locally permitted residual increments can accumulate, producing persistent or unbounded distance from feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Drift

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar counterexample and counterexample kind fit the Feasibility Drift leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied. The final phrase about accumulated tolerances failing to approach zero is also imprecise: for nonnegative tolerances the partial sums are nondecreasing, while unbounded drift follows specifically from divergence of the series.

children.title: Jump-Miss Effects
children.top_down_role: Discretization errors caused by unresolved jumps in set motion.

assumptions_latex: A time grid has \(t_k<\tau<t_{k+1}\), and the interpolant holds \(x(t)=x_k=0\) on \([t_k,t_{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\in[\tau,t_{k+1})\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x(t),C(t))=1\); the jump is missed until the next update.

notation.meaning: Jump time of the moving constraint.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-constant interpolation across an unresolved jump of the moving set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(t)=\{0\}\) for \(t<\tau\) and \(C(t)=\{1\}\) for \(t\geq\tau\). Choose a grid with \(t_k<\tau<t_{k+1}\), set \(x_k=0\), and use the left-continuous catching-up interpolant \(x(t)=x_k\) on \([t_k,t_{k+1})\). Then for every \(t\in[\tau,t_{k+1})\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x(t),C(t))=|0-1|=1.\] Thus a grid that does not resolve the jump produces an order-one feasibility miss, independently of the mesh accuracy away from \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a grid step straddles a constraint jump, a held catching-up iterate can remain order-one infeasible until the next update.
knowledge_statements.title: Jump-Miss Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-dimensional construction correctly exhibits a jump missed by a held interpolant, and counterexample is the correct role for this failure leaf. No source with a specific locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental Properties of an Operator-Induced Hilbert Scale
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects embeddings, operator-power isomorphisms, domain-duality identifications, and interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) satisfy the standing assumptions for generating the Hilbert scale \((\mathcal X_s)_{s\in\mathbb R}\). Then: (i) if \(s<t\), \(\mathcal X_t\hookrightarrow\mathcal X_s\) densely and continuously; (ii) for all \(s,t\in\mathbb R\), \(L^{t-s}\) extends uniquely to an isomorphism \(\mathcal X_t\to\mathcal X_s\), and when \(t>s\) this extension is selfadjoint and strictly positive as a restriction in \(\mathcal X_s\); moreover \(L^{t-s}=L^tL^{-s}\) and \((L^s)^{-1}=L^{-s}\); (iii) for \(s\ge0\), \(\mathcal X_s=\mathcal D(L^s)\) and \(\mathcal X_{-s}=(\mathcal X_s)'\); (iv) if \(q<r<s\) and \(x\in\mathcal X_s\), then \(\|x\|_r\le \|x\|_q^{(s-r)/(s-q)}\|x\|_s^{(r-q)/(s-q)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hilbert scale is nested by dense continuous embeddings; powers of its generating operator identify any two levels; nonnegative levels are power domains and negative levels are their duals; and intermediate norms satisfy the stated interpolation inequality.
assumptions_latex: L\text{ satisfies the preceding standing assumptions for a Hilbert-scale generator}.
(\mathcal X_s)_{s\in\mathbb R}\text{ is the Hilbert scale induced by }L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{gathered}s<t\Rightarrow \mathcal X_t\hookrightarrow\mathcal X_s\text{ densely and continuously},\\L^{t-s}:\mathcal X_t\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal X_s,\quad L^{t-s}=L^tL^{-s},\quad(L^s)^{-1}=L^{-s},\\s\ge0\Rightarrow \mathcal X_s=\mathcal D(L^s),\quad\mathcal X_{-s}=(\mathcal X_s)',\\q<r<s,\ x\in\mathcal X_s\Rightarrow \|x\|_r\le\|x\|_q^{\frac{s-r}{s-q}}\|x\|_s^{\frac{r-q}{s-q}}.\end{gathered}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak convergence from quasi-Fejér tail-hull approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonlinear ergodic weak-convergence criterion for two Hilbert-space sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) and \((y_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) be sequences in \(\mathcal H\), and let \(\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathcal H\). For every \(m\in\mathbb N\), set \(C_m=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\{y_k:k\ge m\}\). If \((y_n)\) is quasi-Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}d_{C_m}(x_n)=0\) for every \(m\in\mathbb N\), and every weak sequential cluster point of \((x_n)\) belongs to \(C\), then there exists \(\bar x\in C\) such that \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let x and y be sequences in a Hilbert space and let C be nonempty. For each m, form the closed convex hull of the tail of y beginning at m. If y is quasi-Fejér monotone with respect to C, x asymptotically approaches every such tail hull, and every weak sequential cluster point of x lies in C, then x converges weakly to a point of C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet derivative of a Hilbert-space mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers pointwise and setwise Fréchet differentiability and the inductive second derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathcal H\), let \(C\) be a neighborhood of \(x\), and let \(T:C\to\mathcal K\). Then \(T\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\) if there exists \(\mathrm DT(x)\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\) such that \(\lim_{0\ne\|y\|\to0}\|T(x+y)-T(x)-\mathrm DT(x)y\|/\|y\|=0\). It is Fréchet differentiable on \(C\) if this holds at every point of \(C\). Higher derivatives are defined inductively; in particular, \(\mathrm D^2T(x)\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K))\) satisfies \(\lim_{0\ne\|y\|\to0}\|\mathrm DT(x+y)-\mathrm DT(x)-\mathrm D^2T(x)y\|/\|y\|=0\), whenever it exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is Fréchet differentiable at a point when its increment admits a bounded linear first-order approximation whose norm error is little-o of the increment norm. Differentiability on a set is pointwise, and higher derivatives are defined by applying the same condition to the derivative map.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathcal H
C\in\mathcal V(x)
T:C\to\mathcal K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Subdifferential of a Convex Integral Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes membership in Gamma-zero and an almost-everywhere pointwise subdifferential formula on a Hilbert-valued L2 space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)\) be a complete \(\sigma\)-finite measure space, let \(\mathrm H\) be a separable real Hilbert space, and let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathrm H)\). Set \(\mathcal H=L^2(\Omega;\mathrm H)\) and assume either \(\mu(\Omega)<+\infty\) or \(\varphi\geq\varphi(0)=0\). Define \[f(x)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_\Omega\varphi(x(\omega))\,d\mu(\omega),&\varphi\circ x\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] Then \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[\partial f(x)=\{u\in\mathcal H\mid u(\omega)\in\partial\varphi(x(\omega))\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under finite measure or nonnegative normalization of the integrand, the integral functional on the Hilbert-valued L2 space is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex. Its subdifferential consists exactly of the L2 selections belonging pointwise almost everywhere to the integrand's subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gâteaux derivative of a Hilbert-space mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes pointwise and setwise differentiability, uniqueness, the two-sided directional-limit form, and the inductive second derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathcal H\) be nonempty, \(T:C\to\mathcal K\), and \(x\in C\) satisfy \((\forall y\in\mathcal H)(\exists\alpha>0)\,[x,x+\alpha y]\subset C\). Then \(T\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(x\) if there exists \(\mathrm DT(x)\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\) such that \((\forall y\in\mathcal H)\;\mathrm DT(x)y=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}[T(x+\alpha y)-T(x)]/\alpha\). This operator is unique and, by linearity, the limit may equivalently be taken over \(0\ne\alpha\to0\). The mapping is Gâteaux differentiable on \(C\) when this holds at every point of \(C\). Higher derivatives are defined inductively; in particular, \(\mathrm D^2T(x)\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K))\) satisfies \((\forall y\in\mathcal H)\;\mathrm D^2T(x)y=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}[\mathrm DT(x+\alpha y)-\mathrm DT(x)]/\alpha\), whenever it exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is Gâteaux differentiable at a point when all directional difference quotients converge to the values of one bounded linear operator. The operator is unique, the directional limits can equivalently be two-sided, differentiability on a set means differentiability at every point, and higher derivatives are obtained by differentiating the derivative map.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathcal H\text{ is nonempty}
T:C\to\mathcal K
x\in C
(\forall y\in\mathcal H)(\exists\alpha>0)\;[x,x+\alpha y]\subset C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable at }x\iff(\exists\mathrm DT(x)\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K))(\forall y\in\mathcal H)\;\mathrm DT(x)y=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{T(x+\alpha y)-T(x)}{\alpha}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A linear gradient is self-adjoint and generates a quadratic function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes every real-valued Gâteaux differentiable function whose gradient mapping is bounded and linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be Gâteaux differentiable and let \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)\) satisfy \(\nabla f=L\), i.e. \(\nabla f(x)=Lx\) for every \(x\in\mathcal H\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(E:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For every \(x_0\in\overline{\operatorname{dom}E}\), there exists a unique continuous trajectory \(x:[0,\infty)\to H\), locally absolutely continuous on \((0,\infty)\), satisfying \[\dot x(t)+\partial E(x(t))\ni0\] for almost every \(t>0\), with \(x(0)=x_0\). children.top_down_role: Transitions where metric variation weakens or destroys gradient-flow structure.

assumptions_latex: \(d\geq1\), \(E\in C^1(\mathbb R^d)\), and \(M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite and singular.
The formal flow equation is \(M\dot x(t)+\nabla E(x(t))=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a state \(x\), solvability requires \(\nabla E(x)\in\operatorname{ran}M=(\ker M)^\perp\); when this condition holds, admissible velocities are nonunique modulo \(\ker M\), and the quadratic dissipation does not control the full velocity norm.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary range-kernel characterization for a symmetric singular matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional loss of solvability, velocity uniqueness, and full-speed coercivity for a singular constant quadratic metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\geq1\), let \(E\in C^1(\mathbb R^d)\), and let \(M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite and singular. At a state \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), the equation \[M\dot x+\nabla E(x)=0\] is solvable only if \(\nabla E(x)\in\operatorname{ran}M=(\ker M)^\perp\). When it is solvable, adding any vector in \(\ker M\) to an admissible velocity leaves the equation unchanged. Hence the quadratic dissipation controls no null-direction velocity and does not ensure velocity uniqueness or coercive control of \(\|\dot x\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a singular quadratic metric, the force must satisfy a range compatibility condition, while null-direction velocities remain uncontrolled and nonunique.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Degeneracy Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\geq1\), let \(E\in C^1(\mathbb R^d)\), and let \(\Psi:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Suppose that an absolutely continuous curve \(x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d\) satisfies \[0\in\partial\Psi(\dot x(t))+\nabla E(x(t))\] for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic metric-space notions and sequential topology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines diameter, distance to a set, metric balls and topology, metrizability, and sequence convergence, including the empty-set convention and sequential topological properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathcal X,d)$ be a metric space and $C\subseteq\mathcal X$. Define $\operatorname{diam}C=\sup_{(x,y)\in C\times C}d(x,y)$ and $d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}d(x,c)$, with $d_\varnothing\equiv+\infty$. For $x\in\mathcal X$ and $\rho>0$, the closed and open balls are $\{y:d(x,y)\leq\rho\}$ and $\{y:d(x,y)<\rho\}$, respectively. The metric topology is generated by all open balls, and a topological space is metrizable when its topology is induced by a metric. A sequence $(x_n)$ converges to $x$ exactly when $d(x_n,x)\to0$. Every metric space is sequential Hausdorff, and closedness, continuity, and lower semicontinuity are equivalent to their sequential formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a metric space, diameter is the supremum of pairwise distances, while distance to a set is the infimum of the distances to its points and is identically infinity for the empty set. Open balls generate the metric topology, and metrizability means that a topology is induced by a metric. Sequence convergence is characterized by distance tending to zero; metric spaces are sequential Hausdorff, and closedness, continuity, and lower semicontinuity admit equivalent sequential tests.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in a metric space $(\mathcal X,d)$ is Cauchy if $d(x_m,x_n)\to0$ as $\min\{m,n\}\to+\infty$. The metric space $\mathcal X$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal X$ converges to a point of $\mathcal X$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ekeland Variational Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative form with prescribed objective tolerance and localization radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a complete metric space, let \(f:\mathcal X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below, and let \(\alpha,\beta>0\). If \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) satisfies \(f(y)\leq \inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)+\alpha\), then there exists \(z\in\mathcal X\) such that \[f(z)+\frac{\alpha}{\beta}d(y,z)\leq f(y),\qquad d(y,z)\leq\beta,\] and \[\forall x\in\mathcal X\setminus\{z\},\qquad f(z)<f(x)+\frac{\alpha}{\beta}d(x,z).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous function bounded below on a complete metric space, every point whose value is within alpha of the infimum admits a point z no farther than beta away. The value at z plus the distance penalty is no greater than the original value, and z is a strict minimizer of the function perturbed by the distance penalty of slope alpha over beta.

\(f:\mathcal X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
\(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta>0\).
\(y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(f(y)\leq\alpha+\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-point convergence under summable Lipschitz moduli of iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-maps whose iterates have a summable sequence of global Lipschitz bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathcal X,d)$ be a complete metric space and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$. Suppose there is a summable sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subset\mathbb R_+$ such that $(\forall u,v\in\mathcal X)(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\ d(T^n u,T^n v)\leq\beta_n d(u,v)$, where $T^0=\operatorname{Id}$. Given $x_0\in\mathcal X$, define $x_{n+1}=Tx_n$ and $\alpha_n=\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\beta_k$. Then $T$ has a unique fixed point $x\in\mathcal X$, $x_n\to x$, and $(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\ d(x_n,x)\leq\alpha_n d(x_0,x_1)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let a self-map of a complete metric space have n-fold iterates whose global Lipschitz constants are bounded by a summable nonnegative sequence beta_n. Then the successive-iteration sequence from any starting point converges to the map's unique fixed point. At every index n, its error is at most the tail sum of the beta sequence from n onward times the initial displacement.
assumptions_latex: $(\mathcal X,d)$ is a complete metric space and $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$.
$(\beta_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subset\mathbb R_+$ is summable and $(\forall u,v\in\mathcal X)(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\ d(T^n u,T^n v)\leq\beta_n d(u,v)$, with $T^0=\operatorname{Id}$.
$x_0\in\mathcal X$, $(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\ x_{n+1}=Tx_n$, and $\alpha_n=\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\beta_k$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $(\exists!x\in\mathcal X)\ Tx=x$, $x_n\to x$, and $(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\ d(x_n,x)\leq\alpha_n d(x_0,x_1)$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Banach–Picard fixed-point theorem with error estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict contractions on arbitrary complete metric spaces, including linear convergence and a priori and a posteriori bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathcal X,d)$ be a complete metric space, let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ satisfy $d(Tu,Tv)\leq\beta d(u,v)$ for all $u,v\in\mathcal X$, where $0\leq\beta<1$, and, for an arbitrary $x_0\in\mathcal X$, define $x_{n+1}=Tx_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Then $T$ has a unique fixed point $x\in\mathcal X$. For every $n\in\mathbb N$, $d(x_{n+1},x)\leq\beta d(x_n,x)$, $d(x_n,x)\leq\beta^n d(x_0,x)$, $d(x_n,x)\leq\frac{\beta^n}{1-\beta}d(x_0,x_1)$, and $d(x_n,x)\leq\frac{1}{1-\beta}d(x_n,x_{n+1})$. Moreover, $\frac{d(x_0,x_1)}{1+\beta}\leq d(x_0,x)\leq\frac{d(x_0,x_1)}{1-\beta}$; in particular, $(x_n)$ converges linearly to $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete metric space, every self-map with Lipschitz constant beta strictly below one has a unique fixed point. From any initial point, successive iteration converges linearly to that fixed point. Each step contracts the distance to the fixed point by at least the factor beta; the error is bounded geometrically using either the initial displacement or the current successive-iterate displacement, and the initial fixed-point distance lies between the stated bounds with denominators 1+beta and 1-beta.
assumptions_latex: $(\mathcal X,d)$ is a complete metric space.
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ and $(\forall u,v\in\mathcal X)\ d(Tu,Tv)\leq\beta d(u,v)$ for some $\beta\in[0,1)$.
$x_0\in\mathcal X$ is arbitrary and $(\forall n\in\mathbb N)\ x_{n+1}=Tx_n$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $(\exists!x\in\mathcal X)\ Tx=x$, and $(\forall n\in\mathbb N)$, $d(x_{n+1},x)\leq\beta d(x_n,x)$, $d(x_n,x)\leq\beta^n d(x_0,x)$, $d(x_n,x)\leq\frac{\beta^n d(x_0,x_1)}{1-\beta}$, and $d(x_n,x)\leq\frac{d(x_n,x_{n+1})}{1-\beta}$; also $\frac{d(x_0,x_1)}{1+\beta}\leq d(x_0,x)\leq\frac{d(x_0,x_1)}{1-\beta}$.

children.title: Metric Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Intrinsic trajectory-speed objects.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\(u:I\to X\) is a curve and \(t\in I\) is an accumulation point of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When the limit exists, \(|u'|(t)\) is the intrinsic instantaneous speed of \(u\) at \(t\).

notation.meaning: metric derivative of the curve at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric derivative for curves in an arbitrary metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The metric derivative of \(u\) at \(t\) is the extended-real limit
\[
|u'|(t):=\lim_{s\to t,\,s\in I,\,s\ne t}\frac{d(u(s),u(t))}{|s-t|},
\]
provided this limit exists. If \(u\) is absolutely continuous, then \(|u'|(t)\) exists for almost every \(t\), belongs to \(L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(I)\), and is the least almost-everywhere function \(m\) satisfying \(d(u(s),u(t))\leq\int_s^t m(r)\,dr\) whenever \(s<t\) in \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric derivative is the limit of distance traveled divided by elapsed time; for absolutely continuous curves it exists almost everywhere and is their minimal integrable speed.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Derivatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and almost-everywhere characterization are standard and fit the Metric Derivatives container, but no inspectable source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is cited.

children.title: Upper Gradients
children.top_down_role: Energy-variation controls along metric curves.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
\(g:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is Borel measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality defines a strong upper gradient controlling energy variation along every absolutely continuous curve.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong upper gradients for extended-real energies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(g\) is a strong upper gradient for \(\phi\) if every absolutely continuous curve \(u:[a,b]\to X\) satisfies
\[
|\phi(u(t))-\phi(u(s))|\leq\int_s^t g(u(r))|u'|(r)\,dr
\]
for all \(a\leq s\leq t\leq b\) whenever both endpoint energies are finite. If the right-hand side is integrable along \(u\), this condition implies that \(\phi\circ u\) has an absolutely continuous representative and
\[
|(cphi\circ u)'(r)|\leq g(u(r))|u'|(r)
\]
for almost every \(r\in(a,b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong upper gradient bounds every energy change along an absolutely continuous metric curve by the integral of gradient magnitude times metric speed.
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Gradients

children.title: Metric-Slope Relaxation Pair
children.top_down_role: Local steepness and lower-semicontinuous slope relaxations.

children.title: Metric Slopes
children.top_down_role: Local steepness quantities for energies on metric spaces.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and \(x\in D(\phi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value \(|\partial\phi|(x)\) measures the maximal infinitesimal rate of energy decrease per unit metric displacement from \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descending local slope of a proper energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The descending metric slope of \(\phi\) at \(x\) is
\[
|\partial\phi|(x):=\limsup_{y\to x,\,y\ne x}\frac{(\phi(x)-\phi(y))^+}{d(x,y)}.
\]
If \(x\notin D(\phi)\), set \(|\partial\phi|(x):=+\infty\). At an isolated point of \(D(\phi)\), the limsup over the empty punctured neighborhood is taken to be zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The descending metric slope is the greatest limiting energy decrease per unit distance from a point.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Slopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The descending metric-slope definition fits the leaf and is mathematically standard, including the isolated-domain-point convention, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Relaxed Slopes
children.top_down_role: Lower-semicontinuous slope envelopes used in limiting regimes.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(|\partial\phi|\) denotes the descending metric slope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed slope is the sequential lower-semicontinuous envelope of \(|\partial\phi|\) under joint convergence of state and energy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong relaxed slope using state-and-energy recovery sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in D(\phi)\), define the relaxed slope by
\[
|\partial^-\phi|(x):=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}|\partial\phi|(x_n):x_n\to x,\ \phi(x_n)\to\phi(x)\right\}.
\]
The infimum is taken in \([0,+\infty]\); if no admissible sequence exists it equals \(+\infty\). Set \(|\partial^-\phi|(x):=+\infty\) for \(x\notin D(\phi)\). Thus relaxation permits nearby, energy-consistent states whose slopes are lower than the unrelaxed slope at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed slope is the lowest limiting metric slope attainable along states converging together with their energies.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Slopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent state-and-energy sequential relaxation and fits the Relaxed Slopes leaf. An authoritative source is required because relaxed-slope conventions differ across the literature and no citation is supplied.

children.title: Slope-Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where direct metric slopes differ from their relaxed counterparts.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(|\partial\phi|\) and \(|\partial^-\phi|\) use the preceding local conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A slope-relaxation gap at \(x\) is the strict inequality \(|\partial^-\phi|(x)<|\partial\phi|(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of slope stability under state-and-energy convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in D(\phi)\), one has
\[
|\partial^-\phi|(x)\leq|\partial\phi|(x).
\]
A slope-relaxation gap occurs at \(x\) when
\[
|\partial^-\phi|(x)<|\partial\phi|(x).
\]
Such a gap means that the state-and-energy sequential lower-semicontinuous envelope of the metric slope is strictly smaller than the unrelaxed slope at \(x\). Sequential lower semicontinuity of \(|\partial\phi|\) along all sequences \(x_n\to x\) satisfying \(\phi(x_n)\to\phi(x)\) is sufficient to exclude a gap at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation never raises the slope. A gap occurs precisely when the relaxed slope is strictly smaller than the metric slope at the same point.
knowledge_statements.title: Slope-Relaxation Gaps

children.title: Curves of Maximal Slope
children.top_down_role: Slope-driven metric evolution.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(g:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is an upper gradient for \(\phi\).
\(u:[0,T]\to D(\phi)\) is locally absolutely continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Such a curve dissipates energy at least at the quadratic rate determined jointly by its speed and \(g\).

notation.meaning: upper gradient evaluated along the curve

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic curves of maximal slope relative to an upper gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curve \(u\) is a curve of maximal slope for \(\phi\) with respect to \(g\) if \(\phi\circ u\) has a nonincreasing absolutely continuous representative and, for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\),
\[
-(\phi\circ u)'(t)\geq\frac12|u'|^2(t)+\frac12g^2(u(t)).
\]
Equivalently, for every \(0\leq s\leq t\leq T\),
\[
\phi(u(t))+\frac12\int_s^t|u'|^2(r)\,dr+\frac12\int_s^t g^2(u(r))\,dr\leq\phi(u(s)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curve of maximal slope loses energy fast enough to pay for both its squared metric speed and squared upper gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Curves of Maximal Slope

children.title: Energy-Dissipation Balance Regime Pair

children.title: Energy-Dissipation Equality Solutions
children.top_down_role: Metric-flow solutions certified by exact energy-dissipation balance.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(g:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is measurable.
\(u:[0,T]\to D(\phi)\) is absolutely continuous with \(|u'|,g\circ u\in L^2(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed identity is the energy-dissipation equality on every subinterval.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic energy-dissipation equality with a prescribed dissipation magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curve \(u\) is an energy-dissipation equality solution for \((\phi,g)\) if \(\phi\circ u\) is absolutely continuous and, for every \(0\leq s\leq t\leq T\),
\[
\phi(u(t))+\frac12\int_s^t|u'|^2(r)\,dr+\frac12\int_s^t g^2(u(r))\,dr=\phi(u(s)).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
-(\phi\circ u)'(t)=\frac12|u'|^2(t)+\frac12g^2(u(t))
\]
for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality solution balances every energy drop exactly with the accumulated kinetic and slope dissipation.
knowledge_statements.title: Energy-Dissipation Equality Solutions

children.title: Energy-Dissipation Inequality Solutions
children.top_down_role: Metric-flow solutions certified by a weak dissipation balance.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(g:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is measurable.
\(u:[0,T]\to D(\phi)\) is absolutely continuous with \(|u'|,g\circ u\in L^2(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality defines an energy-dissipation inequality solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic energy-dissipation inequality with a prescribed dissipation magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curve \(u\) is an energy-dissipation inequality solution for \((\phi,g)\) if, for every \(0\leq s\leq t\leq T\),
\[
\phi(u(t))+\frac12\int_s^t|u'|^2(r)\,dr+\frac12\int_s^t g^2(u(r))\,dr\leq\phi(u(s)).
\]
When \(\phi\circ u\) is absolutely continuous, this is equivalent to
\[
-(\phi\circ u)'(t)\geq\frac12|u'|^2(t)+\frac12g^2(u(t))
\]
for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality solution dissipates at least the sum of its kinetic and slope costs, allowing an apparent excess energy loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Energy-Dissipation Inequality Solutions

children.title: Equality-to-Inequality Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Passage from exact balance concepts to weaker solution classes.

assumptions_latex: \(u\) satisfies the quadratic energy-dissipation inequality for \((\phi,g)\).
\(g\) is a strong upper gradient for \(\phi\).
\(\phi\circ u\) is absolutely continuous and \(|u'|,g\circ u\in L^2(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality becomes equality, and \(|u'|(t)=g(u(t))=-(\phi\circ u)'(t)^{1/2}\) in the corresponding quadratic identity almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality recovery from EDI under the strong upper-gradient chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(0\leq s\leq t\leq T\), the strong upper-gradient estimate and Young's inequality give
\[
\phi(u(s))-phi(u(t))\leq\int_s^t g(u(r))|u'|(r)\,dr\leq\frac12\int_s^t\bigl(g^2(u(r))+|u'|^2(r)\bigr)\,dr.
\]
The energy-dissipation inequality gives the reverse bound. Hence both inequalities are equalities, \(u\) satisfies the energy-dissipation equality, and equality in Young's inequality yields \(|u'|(r)=g(u(r))\) for almost every \(r\in(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a strong upper-gradient chain rule, an energy-dissipation inequality cannot contain excess loss: it becomes equality and speed equals gradient magnitude almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality-to-Inequality Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The terminal title denotes relaxation from equality to inequality, whereas the candidate proves the converse recovery of equality from an EDI under a strong upper-gradient condition. It also contains proof text, omits the backslash in one occurrence of phi, and states an ill-formed square-root identity in the conclusion. These are structural rather than merely typographical defects for this immutable container.

children.title: Evolution Variational Inequality Solutions
children.top_down_role: Comparison-based metric evolution supporting contraction and uniqueness.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\).
\(u:(0,T)\to D(\phi)\) is locally absolutely continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed comparison inequality defines an \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\) solution and compares the evolution with every finite-energy competitor.

notation.meaning: evolution variational inequality with parameter lambda

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard metric \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\) formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curve \(u\) is an \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\) solution for \(\phi\) if, for every \(v\in D(\phi)\), the map \(t\mapsto d^2(u(t),v)\) is locally absolutely continuous and
\[
\frac12\frac{d}{dt}d^2(u(t),v)+\frac{\lambda}{2}d^2(u(t),v)+\phi(u(t))\leq\phi(v)
\]
for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An EVI solution compares the evolution's squared distance and energy with every finite-energy competitor.
knowledge_statements.title: Evolution Variational Inequality Solutions

children.title: Nonequivalence of Metric Solution Concepts
children.top_down_role: Weak slopes, absent chain rules, and nonconvexity separating solution notions.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
\(g\) is only a candidate dissipation magnitude, without an assumed strong upper-gradient property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a chain rule or suitable geodesic convexity, EDI, maximal-slope, and EVI formulations need not be equivalent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of equivalence among standard metric gradient-flow notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The implication from an \(\mathrm{EDI}\) to an exact balance uses the chain-rule estimate
\[
|(phi\circ u)'(t)|\leq g(u(t))|u'|(t).
\]
If \(g\) is not a strong upper gradient, this estimate may fail, so an \(\mathrm{EDI}\) can allow uncompensated energy loss and need not represent a curve of maximal slope in the strong sense. Moreover, deriving \(\mathrm{EVI}_\lambda\) requires additional comparison structure, typically lower semicontinuity and \(\lambda\)-geodesic convexity. Without that structure, maximal-slope or energy-dissipation solutions need not satisfy an EVI, contraction, or uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak slopes can break the chain rule, while nonconvex energies can break EVI comparison; consequently the usual metric solution notions may separate.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonequivalence of Metric Solution Concepts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The broad failure boundary is plausible, but no cited counterexample supports separation of the solution notions. Moreover, under the shard's preceding definition, the quadratic EDI is itself the defining inequality for a curve of maximal slope once the stated energy regularity is imposed, so the asserted nonrepresentation in a 'strong sense' is undefined and potentially inconsistent. The displayed chain rule also contains an invalid phi token. A source and a precisely specified counterexample or convention are required before choosing a reliable correction.

children.title: Implicit Variational Time Discretization
children.top_down_role: Incremental energy minimization as a trajectory construction.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, and \(\tau>0\).
Each incremental minimization problem admits a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The piecewise-constant interpolation of the iterates is the implicit variational time-discrete trajectory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward-Euler minimizing-movement scheme in a metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize with \(x^0\). For each integer \(n\geq1\), choose
\[
x^n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\phi(x)+\frac{1}{2\tau}d^2(x,x^{n-1})\right\}.
\]
Define the piecewise-constant interpolation by \(\bar x_\tau(0):=x^0\) and \(\bar x_\tau(t):=x^n\) for \(t\in((n-1)\tau,n\tau]\). For a prescribed horizon \(T\), stop after \(N=\lceil T/\tau\rceil\) steps and output \(\bar x_\tau|_{[0,T]}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each time step, minimize energy plus squared distance from the previous state divided by twice the step size, then interpolate the iterates in time.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Variational Time Discretization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimizing-movement recursion and piecewise-constant interpolation are precise, and algorithm is the correct content kind for this terminal container. No authoritative metric-gradient-flow source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Generalized Minimizing Movements
children.top_down_role: Limit curves arising from subsequential discrete minimizers.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
For every sufficiently small \(\tau>0\), the incremental minimization problems admit solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is a subsequential vanishing-step limit of exact discrete variational trajectories.

notation.meaning: piecewise-constant interpolation of a discrete trajectory

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential definition using exact implicit variational steps and piecewise-constant interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A curve \(u:[0,+\infty)\to X\) is a generalized minimizing movement for \(\phi\) from \(u_0\in\overline{D(\phi)}\) if there exist \(\tau_j\downarrow0\), initial data \(u_{\tau_j}^0\to u_0\), and sequences \((u_{\tau_j}^n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying \[u_{\tau_j}^n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in X}\left\{\phi(v)+\frac{d^2(v,u_{\tau_j}^{n-1})}{2\tau_j}\right\},\] such that the interpolants defined by \(\bar u_{\tau_j}(0):=u_{\tau_j}^0\) and \(\bar u_{\tau_j}(t):=u_{\tau_j}^n\) for \(t\in((n-1)\tau_j,n\tau_j]\) converge to \(u(t)\) for every \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized minimizing movement is any curve obtained as a pointwise subsequential limit of exact implicit variational time-discretizations whose step sizes vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Minimizing Movements
