children.title: Relaxed Minimizing Movements
children.top_down_role: Incremental descent based on relaxed variational selection.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete, \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
The additive tolerances \(\varepsilon_{\tau,n}\) are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any subsequential limit of these relaxed discrete trajectories is a relaxed minimizing movement.

notation.meaning: incremental objective based at the previous iterate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive-error relaxation of the minimizing-movement scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive objective-error version; literature conventions may normalize the tolerance differently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(F_{\tau,n}(v):=\phi(v)+d^2(v,u_\tau^{n-1})/(2\tau)\). A relaxed discrete trajectory satisfies \[F_{\tau,n}(u_\tau^n)\leq\inf_{v\in X}F_{\tau,n}(v)+\varepsilon_{\tau,n}\qquad(n\ge1).\] A curve \(u:[0,+\infty)\to X\) is a relaxed minimizing movement for the tolerance family \((\varepsilon_{\tau,n})\) if, along some \(\tau_j\downarrow0\), the corresponding piecewise-constant interpolants converge pointwise to \(u\), with initial data converging to \(u(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed minimizing movements are vanishing-step limits of proximal trajectories whose incremental objective values lie within prescribed additive errors of the exact infima.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Minimizing Movements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and additive-error construction fit the relaxed-minimizing-movement container, and the variables are introduced consistently. No citation is supplied, however, and both the term "relaxed minimizing movement" and the scaling imposed on additive objective errors vary across sources; the exact convention cannot be validated from the inventory.

children.title: Inexact Minimizing Movements
children.top_down_role: Incremental descent with controlled minimization error.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
A metric subdifferential notion \(\partial\phi\) and its residual norm are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vanishing-step subsequential limit of residual-controlled iterates is an inexact minimizing movement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual formulation; the precise metric subdifferential must be fixed by the surrounding theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact discrete minimizing-movement trajectory with step \(\tau>0\) is a sequence \((u_\tau^n)_{n\ge0}\) for which there exist residuals \(r_{\tau,n}\ge0\) satisfying \[operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\partial\phi(u_\tau^n)+\frac{1}{\tau}\partial_1\frac{d^2(u_\tau^n,u_\tau^{n-1})}{2}\right)\le r_{\tau,n}.\] A curve \(u\) is an inexact minimizing movement when it is a pointwise subsequential limit, as \(\tau\downarrow0\), of the associated interpolants under a specified vanishing or summable residual regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact minimizing movement is a limit of proximal trajectories whose discrete optimality conditions hold only up to controlled residuals.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Minimizing Movements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual formula begins with malformed `operatorname` syntax and, more importantly, uses addition, distance from zero, and a first-variable subdifferential of squared distance without specifying a linear or cotangent structure in which these objects coexist. A cited, precisely defined inexact proximal framework is needed before a reliable replacement can be stated.

children.title: Approximation-Tolerance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Qualitative behavior under differing levels of incremental approximation.

assumptions_latex: For each \(\tau>0\), additive step errors \(\varepsilon_{\tau,n}\ge0\) are given.
A finite horizon \(T>0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated cumulative regimes distinguish vanishing perturbations from errors that can persist in the continuous-time limit.

notation.meaning: additive objective error at step n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cumulative tolerance controls consistency of approximate incremental minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cumulative additive-error regimes on bounded time intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[E_\tau(T):=\sum_{1\le n\le\lceil T/\tau\rceil}\varepsilon_{\tau,n}.\] The tolerance family is vanishing on bounded intervals if \(E_\tau(T)\to0\) for every \(T>0\), uniformly bounded if \(\sup_{0<\tau<\tau_0}E_\tau(T)<+\infty\), and persistent if \(\limsup_{\tau\downarrow0}E_\tau(T)>0\) for some \(T>0\). For additive objective errors, the vanishing regime is the consistency condition that removes accumulated relaxation from the limiting energy inequality; bounded or persistent regimes may instead produce a defect term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation tolerances are classified by cumulative error on bounded horizons: vanishing errors disappear, while bounded or persistent errors may leave a limiting defect.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Tolerance Regimes

children.title: Discretization-Selection Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dependence of limiting flows on minimizer selection and discretization.

children.title: Discrete Minimizer Selection
children.top_down_role: Dependence of incremental trajectories on the choice of minimizers.

assumptions_latex: The incremental objective has at least one minimizer at every discrete step.
No rule selecting among multiple minimizers is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A discrete trajectory is determined only after choosing one element from each set \(M_{\tau,n}\).

notation.meaning: set of minimizers at step n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: set-valued argmin requires a selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued selection at each implicit variational step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(u_\tau^{n-1}\in X\), define \[M_{\tau,n}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in X}\left\{\phi(v)+\frac{d^2(v,u_\tau^{n-1})}{2\tau}\right\}.\] A discrete minimizer selection is any rule choosing \(u_\tau^n\in M_{\tau,n}\) for every \(n\ge1\). If some \(M_{\tau,n}\) is not a singleton, the incremental variational principle defines a set of admissible trajectories rather than one trajectory; uniqueness requires an additional selection rule or uniqueness of the minimizer at every step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an incremental problem has several minimizers, the scheme becomes set-valued and a selection rule is needed to determine a discrete trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Minimizer Selection

children.title: Nonunique Continuous-Time Limits
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of limiting flows generated by vanishing time steps.

assumptions_latex: The same energy \(\phi\) and initial state \(u_0\) are used.
At least two admissible vanishing-step discrete families possess limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct limiting curves show that the minimizing-movement construction is not uniquely determined by \((\phi,u_0)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subsequential limits need not be unique without an applicable uniqueness mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract criterion for nonuniqueness of vanishing-step limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonunique continuous-time limits occur if there are sequences \(\tau_j\downarrow0\) and \(\sigma_j\downarrow0\), with admissible minimizer selections from the same \((\phi,u_0)\), such that \[\bar u_{\tau_j}^{(1)}(t)\to u^{(1)}(t),\qquad \bar u_{\sigma_j}^{(2)}(t)\to u^{(2)}(t),\] for every \(t\) in a common interval, while \(u^{(1)}(t_*)\ne u^{(2)}(t_*)\) for some \(t_*>0\). Thus existence of generalized minimizing movements alone does not yield a single-valued continuous-time evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuous-time limit is nonunique when two admissible vanishing-step selections from the same data converge to different curves.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Continuous-Time Limits

children.title: Discretization-Dependent Branching
children.top_down_role: Distinct limiting branches produced by different discretization choices.

assumptions_latex: A common energy and initial datum admit more than one admissible discrete approximation family.
The compared interpolants converge along vanishing discretization sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dependence of the limit on partitions or selections constitutes discretization-dependent branching.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: loss of uniqueness permits partition- or selection-dependent subsequential limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching caused by changing partitions, step sequences, or discrete minimizer selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Discretization-dependent branching is present when two partition sequences satisfy \(|\mathcal P_j|\to0\) and \(|\mathcal Q_j|\to0\), but admissible interpolants constructed from the same energy and initial datum obey \[\bar u_{\mathcal P_j}(t)\to u(t),\qquad \bar u_{\mathcal Q_j}(t)\to v(t),\] for every \(t\) in a common interval, with \(u(t_*)\ne v(t_*)\) for some \(t_*>0\). The dependence may arise from the partitions themselves, from different minimizer selections, or from approximation errors coupled to the discretization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching occurs when different vanishing partitions or discrete selections for identical data converge to distinct continuous-time evolutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Discretization-Dependent Branching

children.title: Geodesic EVI Generation Theory
children.top_down_role: Metric convexity structures governing generation, uniqueness, contraction, and stability.

children.title: Geodesically Convex Energies
children.top_down_role: Energy convexity along metric geodesics.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a geodesic metric space.
\(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) and \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed interpolation inequality defines geodesic \(\lambda\)-convexity of \(\phi\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of geodesic lambda-convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geodesic \(\lambda\)-convexity along at least one connecting geodesic for every endpoint pair, with the stronger every-geodesic variant distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(\phi):=\{x\in X:\phi(x)<+\infty\}\). The functional \(\phi\) is geodesically \(\lambda\)-convex if, for every \(x_0,x_1\in D(\phi)\), there exists a constant-speed geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to X\) with \(\gamma_0=x_0\) and \(\gamma_1=x_1\) such that, for every \(s\in[0,1]\), \[\phi(\gamma_s)\le(1-s)\phi(x_0)+s\phi(x_1)-\frac{\lambda}{2}s(1-s)d^2(x_0,x_1).\] If the inequality holds along every connecting geodesic, \(\phi\) is strongly geodesically \(\lambda\)-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An energy is geodesically lambda-convex when its value along a suitable connecting geodesic lies below the lambda-corrected chord between endpoint values; requiring this along every connecting geodesic gives the strong variant.
knowledge_statements.title: Geodesically Convex Energies

children.title: EVI Semigroup Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Contractive comparison and semigroup generation for metric flows.

children.title: EVI Contraction
children.top_down_role: Contractive comparison behavior within the EVI solution framework.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\).
The curves \(u,v:[0,+\infty)\to X\) are \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) solutions for the same energy \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(u_t,v_t)\le e^{-\lambda t}d(u_0,v_0)\) for every \(t\ge0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical contraction estimate for two EVI solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contraction theorem for two solutions of the same metric \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u,v:[0,+\infty)\to X\) be locally absolutely continuous curves satisfying, for every comparison point \(y\in D(\phi)\), \[\frac12\frac{d}{dt}d^2(u_t,y)+\frac{\lambda}{2}d^2(u_t,y)+\phi(u_t)\le\phi(y)\] and the analogous inequality for \(v\), for almost every \(t>0\). Then \[d(u_t,v_t)\le e^{-\lambda t}d(u_0,v_0)\qquad(t\ge0).\] In particular, two \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) solutions with the same initial datum coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two EVI solutions for the same energy contract exponentially at rate lambda; consequently, an EVI evolution from fixed initial data is unique.
knowledge_statements.title: EVI Contraction

children.title: Metric Semigroup Generation
children.top_down_role: Single-valued metric-flow evolution organized as a semigroup.

assumptions_latex: For every \(x\) in an invariant set \(D\subseteq\overline{D(\phi)}\), a unique global \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) solution \(u^x\) exists.
Solutions are continuous at time zero and satisfy \(u_0^x=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maps \(S_t x:=u_t^x\) form a strongly continuous semigroup on \(D\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: autonomous uniqueness and time translation generate a semigroup
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous EVI solutions generate a continuous metric semigroup on their invariant domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S_t:D\to D\) by \(S_t x:=u_t^x\). Then \(S_0=\operatorname{Id}_D\), and autonomy implies that \(t\mapsto u_{t+s}^x\) is an \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) solution starting from \(u_s^x\). Uniqueness therefore gives \[S_{t+s}x=S_t(S_sx)\qquad(s,t\ge0,\ x\in D).\] Moreover, \(d(S_t x,x)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Thus \((S_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a strongly continuous metric semigroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unique global solutions of an autonomous EVI define a strongly continuous semigroup by mapping each initial state to its state at time t.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Semigroup Generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits metric semigroup generation. Under the stated global existence, invariance, autonomy, uniqueness, and continuity-at-zero assumptions, the semigroup and strong-continuity conclusions are appropriately scoped. No relevant source or inspectable theorem locator is supplied, so the claim remains source-dependent.

children.title: Contraction-to-Semigroup Link
children.top_down_role: Structural connection between EVI comparison and metric semigroup behavior.

assumptions_latex: A unique global \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) solution exists from every point of an invariant domain \(D\).
The EVI contraction estimate holds for every pair of solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a semigroup and each \(S_t\) is \(e^{-\lambda t}\)-Lipschitz.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: contraction supplies uniqueness while autonomy supplies composition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How EVI contraction and autonomy yield a contractive evolution semigroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t x\) denote the unique \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) solution at time \(t\) starting from \(x\in D\). Contraction gives \[d(S_t x,S_t y)\le e^{-\lambda t}d(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in D,\ t\ge0),\] hence uniqueness for fixed initial data. Applying uniqueness to the time-translated trajectory and the trajectory initialized at \(S_sx\) yields \(S_{t+s}x=S_t(S_sx)\). Thus the same EVI estimate that makes the evolution single-valued also equips the generated semigroup with its quantitative Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EVI contraction ensures uniqueness, and uniqueness plus autonomy yields the semigroup law; every time-t map has Lipschitz constant at most exp(-lambda t).
knowledge_statements.title: Contraction-to-Semigroup Link

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind accurately captures the link between contraction, uniqueness, autonomy, and the semigroup law, and the quantitative Lipschitz estimate is consistently stated. The record has no source supporting this EVI-semigroup correspondence, and none of the inventoried locators is directly relevant.

children.title: EVI Geometric Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of EVI structure, contraction, or unique flow generation.

children.title: Nongeodesic Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Metric geometries lacking suitable geodesic structure for EVI evolution.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space containing points that cannot be joined by a constant-speed geodesic.
No substitute generalized-geodesic structure is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Standard global geodesic convexity and the EVI generation result based on that hypothesis are unavailable for such endpoint pairs.

notation.meaning: two states lacking a connecting geodesic

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a geodesic convexity condition cannot be evaluated along a connecting geodesic when none exists
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the standard geodesic-convexity route, not impossibility of every EVI on nongeodesic spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If there exist \(x_0,x_1\in X\) for which no constant-speed geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to X\) joins the endpoints, then the geodesic \(\lambda\)-convexity inequality cannot be imposed along a connecting geodesic for that pair. Consequently, an EVI generation theorem whose hypotheses require global geodesic \(\lambda\)-convexity cannot be applied without additional structure. This is a boundary of that generation argument; it does not assert that no particular functional on \(X\) can possess an EVI evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without connecting geodesics, a global geodesic-convexity hypothesis and an EVI generation theorem requiring that hypothesis cannot be applied to all endpoint pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Nongeodesic Failure Regimes

children.title: Nonconvex Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Energy landscapes lacking the convexity needed for contractive metric flows.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete geodesic metric space.
\(E:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without geodesic \(\lambda\)-convexity of \(E\), EVI generation is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: Evolutionary variational inequality with parameter lambda
Metric derivative of the curve u

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the standard geodesic-convex EVI generation mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an absolutely continuous curve \(u:[0,\infty)\to X\), the inequality \[\frac12\frac{d}{dt}d^2(u(t),v)+\frac{\lambda}{2}d^2(u(t),v)+E(u(t))\le E(v)\] for every \(v\in\operatorname{dom}E\) imposes a global comparison property. If \(E\) is not geodesically \(\lambda\)-convex, minimizing movements may still produce curves of maximal slope, but neither existence of an \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) solution nor identification of every such curve with an EVI solution follows in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without geodesic semiconvexity, minimizing movements may exist while the stronger EVI comparison inequality and its generation theory fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the terminal container, and the statement correctly distinguishes loss of an EVI guarantee from automatic nonexistence. However, no inspectable citation supports the precise relationship among geodesic lambda-convexity, minimizing movements, curves of maximal slope, and EVI generation.

children.title: EVI Breakdown Consequences
children.top_down_role: Loss of contraction, uniqueness, or canonical flow generation.

assumptions_latex: \(u\) and \(w\) are candidate flows for the same proper energy on a metric space.
The relevant \(\operatorname{EVI}_\lambda\) comparison inequality is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: EVI-based contraction, uniqueness, and quantitative stability cannot be inferred.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical consequences lost when the EVI estimate cannot be established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The usual estimate \[d(u(t),w(t))\le e^{-\lambda t}d(u(0),w(0))\] is obtained by applying the EVI to each trajectory against the other and adding the inequalities. Consequently, when the EVI comparison principle breaks down, this contraction estimate, uniqueness for fixed initial data, and Lipschitz stability with respect to initial data no longer follow from the energy-dissipation formulation alone. Their failure is not automatic, but each requires an independent hypothesis or argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EVI breakdown removes the standard route to contraction, uniqueness, and stability, although those properties may survive for separate reasons.
knowledge_statements.title: EVI Breakdown Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind and local scope are appropriate. The statement carefully says contraction, uniqueness, and stability no longer follow rather than asserting that they necessarily fail, but the EVI contraction argument and claimed logical boundary require a specific authoritative locator.

children.title: Stability of Metric Gradient Flows
children.top_down_role: Compactness and convergence under variation of energies and ambient metric spaces.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Gradient Flows: In Metric Spaces and in the Space of Probability Measures
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Proofs of convergence theorems; uniqueness, contraction semigroups, and error estimates
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Gradient Flows: In Metric Spaces and in the Space of Probability Measures

children.title: Energy-Perturbation Stability
children.top_down_role: Flow convergence under variational convergence of energies.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete, and \(E_n,E:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower semicontinuous energies.
\(E_n\) Gamma-converges to \(E\), the initial data are well prepared, and relevant sublevels are equicoercive.
The descending slopes satisfy the required liminf inequality along bounded-energy convergent sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Subsequential limits of the flows of \(E_n\) are curves of maximal slope for \(E\).

notation.meaning: Descending metric slope of an energy F
Flow trajectory for the energy E_n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sandier–Serfaty-type stability of curves of maximal slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_n\) satisfy the energy-dissipation inequality for \(E_n\). If \(u_n(t)\to u(t)\) along a subsequence for every \(t\), \(E_n(u_n(0))\to E(u(0))\), and whenever \(x_n\to x\) with bounded energies one has \[E(x)\le\liminf_n E_n(x_n),\qquad |\partial E|(x)\le\liminf_n|\partial E_n|(x_n),\] then lower semicontinuity in the energy-dissipation inequality yields \[E(u(T))+\frac12\int_0^T\bigl(|u'|^2+|\partial E|^2(u)\bigr)\,dt\le E(u(0)).\] Thus \(u\) is a curve of maximal slope for \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gamma convergence, compactness, prepared initial data, and a slope-liminf bound transfer energy-dissipation flows to the limiting energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Energy-Perturbation Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits Energy-Perturbation Stability, but this Sandier-Serfaty-type result needs an exact theorem source. The record does not fully specify the compactness topology, action-liminf mechanism, timewise energy bounds, or the upper-gradient convention needed to conclude that the limiting energy-dissipation inequality defines a curve of maximal slope.

children.title: Metric-Space Perturbation Stability
children.top_down_role: Flow convergence under variation of ambient geometry.

assumptions_latex: \((X_n,d_n)\) and \((X,d)\) are complete metric spaces embedded isometrically into a common metric space \((Z,\delta)\).
Energies and initial data converge variationally in \(Z\), with equicoercive sublevels.
Metric derivatives and slopes satisfy the corresponding liminf inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Embedded subsequential limits of the varying-space flows are limit-energy flows on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Isometric embeddings into the comparison space
Energy on X_n and limiting energy on X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-ambient-space formulation of stability under changing geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\iota_n(u_n(t))\to\iota(u(t))\) in \(Z\) for every \(t\) along a subsequence. If \[E(u(t))\le\liminf_nE_n(u_n(t)),\quad |u'|(t)\\le\liminf_n|u_n'|(t),\quad |\partial E|(u(t))\le\liminf_n|\partial E_n|(u_n(t))\] in the integrated lower-semicontinuity sense, then passage to the limit in the energy-dissipation inequalities shows that \(u\) is a curve of maximal slope for \(E\). Equicoercivity supplies the required subsequential compactness; without it the assertion is only conditional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After embedding changing spaces into one comparison space, compactness and liminf bounds pass gradient flows to the limiting geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Space Perturbation Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the varying-geometry stability container, but an exact varying-space theorem is required to determine the necessary convergence and compactness assumptions. In addition, the displayed metric-derivative inequality contains malformed LaTeX (`\\le` in the decoded mathematical text) and must eventually be repaired to `\le`. Source uncertainty presently prevents a reliable complete replacement.

children.title: Evolutionary Variational Convergence
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between static variational limits and dynamic limits.

assumptions_latex: \(E_n\) converges variationally to \(E\), and \(u_n\) are associated energy-dissipation flows.
The trajectories are compact and their actions and slopes obey liminf inequalities.
Initial energies converge to the limiting initial energy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Static energy convergence is compatible with the dynamic limit precisely when the dissipation structure also passes to the limit.

notation.meaning: Energy-dissipation functional of F on a curve v over [0,T]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility criterion for static variational limits and gradient-flow limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mathcal D_F(v;T):=F(v(T))-F(v(0))+\frac12\int_0^T\bigl(|v'|^2+|\partial F|^2(v)\bigr)\,dt.\] Variational convergence of \(E_n\) to \(E\) is evolutionarily compatible along \(u_n\to u\) when \[\mathcal D_E(u;T)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal D_{E_n}(u_n;T)\] for every \(T>0\), together with convergence of initial energies. Hence \(\mathcal D_{E_n}(u_n;T)\le0\) implies \(\mathcal D_E(u;T)\le0\), so the limiting curve retains the energy-dissipation structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static variational convergence yields dynamic convergence only when metric action, slopes, and endpoint energies possess compatible lower-semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Evolutionary Variational Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind is suitable for this compatibility container. The displayed dissipation-functional liminf condition is sufficient for passing the energy-dissipation inequality, but the conclusion's word "precisely" asserts necessity that is not established by the statement. A specific source is needed to determine whether this is intended as a definition, a sufficient criterion, or an equivalence under additional hypotheses.

children.title: Metric-Flow Limit Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-limit failures despite convergence of energies.

children.title: Slope-Liminf Failures
children.top_down_role: Instability of slope information under energy convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(E_n\) variationally converges to \(E\) on a metric space.
There exist \(x_n\to x\) with bounded energies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of slope lower semicontinuity blocks passage to the limiting energy-dissipation inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure mechanism for the dissipation term in evolutionary convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A slope-liminf failure occurs when there are \(x_n\to x\) such that \[\Delta:=|\partial E|(x)-\liminf_{n\to\infty}|\partial E_n|(x_n)>0.\] Then the approximate dissipation terms do not control the limiting one: Fatou-type passage can yield at most the integral of \(\liminf_n|\partial E_n|^2(x_n)\), which may be strictly smaller than \(|\partial E|^2(x)\). Therefore static variational convergence alone cannot identify a limit trajectory as a curve of maximal slope for \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If limiting slopes exceed the liminf of approximate slopes, approximate dissipation cannot certify the limiting gradient-flow inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Slope-Liminf Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind matches the leaf, and the positive slope defect correctly identifies failure of the usual slope-liminf condition. A source is still needed because the record moves from a pointwise sequence to failure of an integrated trajectory argument without specifying the time-dependent realization or measure-theoretic hypotheses.

children.title: Compactness Failures
children.top_down_role: Insufficient trajectory compactness for extracting dynamic limits.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(E_n:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper energies.
For some \(C\), the union of sublevels \(\bigcup_n\{E_n\le C\}\) is not relatively compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform energy and action bounds need not yield a convergent subsequence of trajectories.

notation.meaning: Sublevel set of E_n at height C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of trajectory compactness despite energetic estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_{n,C}:=\{x\in X:E_n(x)\le C\}\). If \(\bigcup_nS_{n,C}\) is not relatively compact, one may choose \(x_n\in S_{n,C}\) having no convergent subsequence. Constant curves \(u_n(t):=x_n\) then have zero metric action and uniformly bounded energy, yet possess no pointwise convergent subsequence. Thus energy and action estimates alone cannot produce a candidate limiting flow; an equicoercivity or compactness hypothesis is indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noncompact common sublevels allow bounded-energy, zero-action trajectories with no convergent subsequence, preventing extraction of a limiting flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits Compactness Failures, and the constant-curve construction correctly shows that energy and metric-action bounds alone do not force pointwise compactness. No citation with a specific locator is supplied, so the claimed indispensability and its intended relationship to gradient-flow compactness remain unsupported.

children.title: Dynamic-Limit Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Failure of candidate limits to retain the intended gradient-flow behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(E_n\) variationally converges to \(E\), and \(u_n\) satisfy approximate energy-dissipation inequalities.
At least one of trajectory compactness, endpoint-energy convergence, action liminf, or slope liminf fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A limit curve may fail to exist or may not solve the gradient flow of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate failure boundary for passage from static to dynamic limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even when \(E_n\) Gamma-converges to \(E\) and \(\mathcal D_{E_n}(u_n;T)\le0\), dynamic convergence does not follow from the static limit alone. Lack of compactness may prevent any subsequential curve limit. If \(u_n\to u\) but an endpoint, metric-action, or slope liminf inequality fails, one cannot conclude \[\mathcal D_E(u;T)\le\liminf_n\mathcal D_{E_n}(u_n;T)\le0.\] The candidate limit may therefore exhibit a dissipation defect or solve an evolution different from the gradient flow of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static energy convergence can coexist with no trajectory limit or with a limit carrying insufficient dissipation to solve the expected flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Limit Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is appropriate. The statement correctly presents failed compactness or liminf assumptions as preventing the standard conclusion rather than forcing breakdown in every example, but the combined dynamic-limit assertion has no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Nonconvex Descent-Convergence Theory
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex generalized-gradient trajectories, desingularization, convergence, and failure of descent.

children.title: Generalized-Gradient Flow Pair
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex flow families associated with distinct generalized gradients.

children.title: Limiting-Subgradient Flows
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex descent trajectories associated with limiting subgradients.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(x:[0,T]\to H\) is absolutely continuous and \(f(x(\cdot))\) is finite almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A limiting-subgradient flow satisfies \(-\dot x(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differential-inclusion definition using the limiting subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limiting subdifferential is \[\partial f(x):=\left\{v:\exists x_k\to x,\ f(x_k)\to f(x),\ v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\right\}.\] A curve \(x\in AC([0,T];H)\) is a limiting-subgradient flow of \(f\) if there exists a measurable selection \(v(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) such that \[\dot x(t)+v(t)=0\] for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), with the prescribed initial condition \(x(0)=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting-subgradient flow is an absolutely continuous curve whose negative velocity belongs almost everywhere to the Mordukhovich limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting-Subgradient Flows

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Limiting-Subgradient Flows, and the finite-dimensional differential inclusion is mathematically standard. The cited chapter-opening page is not a sufficiently specific definition, theorem, or page locator for both the limiting subdifferential formula and the associated flow notion; a targeted source is required.

children.title: Clarke-Subgradient Flows
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex descent trajectories associated with Clarke subgradients.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz.
\(x:[0,T]\to H\) is absolutely continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A Clarke-subgradient flow satisfies \(-\dot x(t)\in\partial^C f(x(t))\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differential-inclusion definition for locally Lipschitz energies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,h\in H\), define \[f^\circ(x;h):=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\s\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+sh)-f(y)}{s},\qquad \partial^C f(x):=\{v:\langle v,h\rangle\le f^\circ(x;h)\ \forall h\in H\}.\] A curve \(x\in AC([0,T];H)\) is a Clarke-subgradient flow if there exists a measurable selection \(v(t)\in\partial^C f(x(t))\) satisfying \[\dot x(t)+v(t)=0\] for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), together with \(x(0)=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke-subgradient flow follows a differential inclusion whose admissible descent directions form the convex Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Subgradient Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the terminal container, and the finite-dimensional Clarke derivative, Clarke subdifferential, and differential inclusion are internally consistent. The record has no citation, so the exact definitions and measurable-selection formulation require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Generalized-Gradient Comparison
children.top_down_role: Differences in trajectory selection induced by the two subgradient constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz.
The limiting and Clarke subdifferentials are evaluated at the same point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)\subseteq\partial^C f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(x)\), with equality under subdifferential regularity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise comparison for finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz functions.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^m\), \[\partial f(x)\subseteq\partial^C f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(x).\] Hence every limiting-subgradient flow is a Clarke-subgradient flow, but the converse can fail because convexification introduces velocities not generated by individual limiting subgradients. If \(f\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\), then the relevant generalized subdifferentials coincide at \(x\), so the two differential inclusions agree wherever regularity holds along the trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential convexifies the limiting subdifferential; thus limiting flows are Clarke flows, while the converse needs regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Gradient Comparison

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind correctly fits a comparison leaf. In finite dimensions the convexification relation is standard for locally Lipschitz functions, but the generic chapter-opening citation does not specifically support the equality, the regularity qualification, or the resulting inclusion between flow classes.

children.title: Prox-Regular Descent Flows
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex descent under localized regularity and hypomonotonicity.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
On a neighborhood of the trajectory, \(f\) is \(r\)-prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous.
An absolutely continuous solution remains in that neighborhood with bounded subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subgradient inclusion has a hypomonotone stability estimate and dissipates energy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local descent and stability consequences of prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(-\dot x(t)\in\partial f(x(t))\) almost everywhere. Prox-regularity yields the local hypomonotonicity estimate \[\langle v-w,x-y\rangle\ge-r\|x-y\|^2\] for admissible nearby graph points \((x,v)\) and \((y,w)\). Consequently, two bounded solutions satisfy \[\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2\le r\|x(t)-y(t)\|^2\] almost everywhere and hence \(\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le e^{rt}\|x(0)-y(0)\|\). Under the prox-regular chain rule, \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local prox-regularity makes the subdifferential hypomonotone, giving controlled trajectory separation and an energy-descent identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Descent Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is suitable for this topic, but the quantitative hypomonotonicity constant depends on the precise convention for prox-regularity and often on localized bounds. The chain rule and energy identity also require exact hypotheses. Without a specific prox-regular flow source, the displayed constants and conclusion cannot be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz Convergence Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Desingularization-based trajectory convergence and qualitative rate regimes.

children.title: Finite-Length Trajectories
children.top_down_role: KL regimes yielding trajectories with finite total variation.

assumptions_latex: \(u:[0,\infty)\to H\) is locally absolutely continuous in a Hilbert space \(H\).
\(E:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and along \(u\), \(-\frac{d}{dt}E(u(t))=\lVert \dot u(t)\rVert^2=|\partial E|^2(u(t))\) almost everywhere.
Near the omega-limit set, \(E\) satisfies a uniform Kurdyka--Lojasiewicz inequality \(\varphi'(E-E_*)|\partial E|\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int_0^\infty\lVert\dot u(t)\rVert\,dt<\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-length consequence of the uniform Kurdyka--Lojasiewicz inequality and the energy identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous curves of maximal slope in a Hilbert space under a uniform KL inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(E(u(t))\downarrow E_*\), the tail of \(u\) lies in a neighborhood where \(\varphi'(E(u)-E_*)|\partial E|(u)\ge 1\), and the energy identity holds. Then, for almost every sufficiently large \(t\), \[-\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(E(u(t))-E_*)\ge \lVert\dot u(t)\rVert.\] Consequently every tail has finite arc length, \(\int_T^\infty\lVert\dot u(t)\rVert\,dt\le \varphi(E(u(T))-E_*)\), and hence the complete trajectory has finite length whenever its initial finite-time segment does.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform Kurdyka–Lojasiewicz inequality converts energy dissipation into an integrable speed bound, so every bounded maximal-slope trajectory has finite total length.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Length Trajectories

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the finite-length leaf, and the displayed dissipation estimate is standard. However, no inspectable citation is supplied. Source support is needed to verify the precise uniform-KL hypotheses and tail-entry conditions. The plain statement also introduces boundedness, which is not the condition used in the LaTeX statement.

children.title: Equilibrium Convergence
children.top_down_role: KL regimes supporting convergence toward a stationary state.

assumptions_latex: The assumptions of the finite-length trajectory theorem hold.
The trajectory \(u\) has a nonempty omega-limit set.
The limiting subdifferential is closed along convergent energy-compatible sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(u_*\in H\) such that \(u(t)\to u_*\) and \(0\in\partial E(u_*)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite length plus subgradient-flow closedness yields convergence to a critical point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equilibrium convergence of a precompact KL-controlled subgradient trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\int_0^\infty\lVert\dot u(t)\rVert\,dt<\infty\), then \(u\) is Cauchy at infinity and there exists \(u_*\in H\) with \(u(t)\to u_*\). If additionally \(E(u(t))\to E(u_*)\) and the flow inclusion supplies vectors \(v(t)\in\partial E(u(t))\) satisfying \(\lVert v(t)\rVert\to0\), closedness of \(\partial E\) gives \(0\in\partial E(u_*)\). Thus the entire trajectory, rather than merely subsequences, converges to one equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite length forces the whole trajectory to converge, and subdifferential closedness identifies its limit as a critical equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits equilibrium convergence, and finite length does imply convergence in a Hilbert space. No inspectable citation supports the subdifferential closedness step, and the assumptions list does not explicitly include the vanishing-subgradient and energy-compatibility conditions introduced in the statement.

children.title: Qualitative Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior organized by desingularization profiles.

assumptions_latex: \(-e'(t)=\lVert\dot u(t)\rVert^2=|\partial E|^2(u(t))\) almost everywhere, where \(e(t)=E(u(t))-E_*\ge0\).
For small positive \(e\), \(|\partial E|(u)\ge c e^\theta\) with \(c>0\) and \(\theta\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes are finite-time extinction for \(\theta<\frac12\), exponential decay for \(\theta=\frac12\), and algebraic decay for \(\theta>\frac12\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rates follow by integrating the scalar differential inequality for the energy residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type KL rates for continuous maximal-slope dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The slope inequality and energy identity imply \(e'(t)\le-c^2e(t)^{2\theta}\). Hence, after entering the KL neighborhood: if \(0\le\theta<\frac12\), then \(e\) reaches zero in finite time; if \(\theta=\frac12\), then \(e(t)\le Ce^{-c^2t}\); and if \(\frac12<\theta<1\), then \(e(t)=O(t^{-1/(2\theta-1)})\). The finite-length estimate further yields \(\lVert u(t)-u_*\rVert=O(e(t)^{1-\theta})\), giving exponential convergence at \(\theta=\frac12\) and \(O(t^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)})\) for \(\theta>\frac12\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-type KL exponent separates finite-time, exponential, and algebraic convergence regimes for the energy and trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualitative Rate Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is suitable for this qualitative-regime leaf, and the stated finite-time, exponential, and algebraic regimes are consistent with the displayed scalar differential inequality. An inspectable source is still required for the trajectory-rate estimate and its exact KL hypotheses.

children.title: Nonconvex Descent Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Generalized-gradient selections and flat landscapes that obstruct genuine descent or convergence.

children.title: Spurious Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Generalized stationary states that do not represent meaningful descent endpoints.

assumptions_latex: Stationarity is interpreted as \(f'(x)=0\).
No convexity or second-order minimality condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: First-order stationarity alone does not certify local or global minimality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct polynomial counterexample to sufficiency of stationarity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth finite-dimensional counterexample to interpreting stationarity as optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2\). Its derivative is \(f'(x)=4x(x^2-1)\), so \(x=0\) is stationary. Nevertheless, \(f(0)=1\), while \(f(1)=f(-1)=0\), and \(f''(0)=-4<0\). Thus \(x=0\) is a strict local maximum and not a minimizer, although it satisfies the same first-order stationarity equation as the two global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polynomial squared double well has a stationary point at zero that is a strict maximum, showing that stationarity need not imply optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Stationarity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind exactly fits the failure-boundary leaf, and the polynomial calculations are internally correct. No citation with a specific locator is supplied, so the candidate lacks the required source evidence.

children.title: Nonconvergent Descent
children.top_down_role: Descent trajectories lacking convergence to a single limiting state.

assumptions_latex: Descent means only \(f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)\).
No sufficient-decrease, relative-error, compactness, or finite-length condition is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotone objective values do not imply convergence of the iterates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary counterexample isolating the insufficiency of objective descent
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of iterate convergence under bare objective monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f(x)=0\) and let \(x_k=(-1)^k\). Then \(f(x_{k+1})=f(x_k)=0\) for every \(k\), so the objective values are nonincreasing and already converged. Also \(f'(x_k)=0\) for every \(k\). However, \((x_k)\) has the two distinct cluster points \(-1\) and \(1\) and does not converge. Therefore descent of function values, even together with pointwise stationarity, is insufficient for trajectory convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence may have constant, hence nonincreasing, objective values and stationary iterates while oscillating forever between distinct points.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvergent Descent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the leaf and correctly shows that bare objective monotonicity, even with stationary iterates, does not force iterate convergence. A source with an inspectable locator is absent.

children.title: Flat-Landscape Trapping
children.top_down_role: Stagnation or ambiguous motion caused by flat nonconvex energy regions.

assumptions_latex: The dynamics is the gradient flow \(\dot x=-f'(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every trajectory initialized in \([-1,\infty)\) is trapped at a nonoptimal stationary point.

notation.meaning: smooth objective with a suboptimal plateau

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit smooth plateau demonstrates trapping caused by vanishing gradients
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth gradient-flow trapping on a suboptimal flat plateau.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(x)=\frac{\rho(x+2)}{\rho(x+2)+\rho(-x-1)}.\] Then \(f\) is smooth, \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\le-2\), and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\ge-1\). Hence every \(x_0\ge-1\) satisfies \(f'(x_0)=0\), and the gradient-flow solution initialized at \(x_0\) is \(x(t)=x_0\) for all \(t\ge0\). Since \(f(x_0)=1>0=\inf f\), the flat region traps the dynamics at a nonoptimal stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth objective can contain a suboptimal flat plateau on which the gradient vanishes, leaving gradient flow permanently trapped.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Landscape Trapping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits flat-landscape trapping, and the cutoff construction consistently produces a smooth suboptimal stationary plateau. No inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Wasserstein Curves
children.top_down_role: Absolutely continuous trajectory structure in probability-measure spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(\mu_t\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) for \(t\in[0,T]\).
The curve is absolutely continuous with respect to the quadratic Wasserstein distance \(W_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its metric derivative exists almost everywhere and admits a minimal-velocity continuity-equation representation.

notation.meaning: probability measures with finite second moment

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard characterization of absolutely continuous Wasserstein curves by the continuity equation
revised: removed malformed terminal-control artifact from the metric-derivative formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolutely continuous curves in quadratic Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A curve \(t\mapsto\mu_t\) belongs to \(AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))\) precisely when it admits a Borel velocity field \(v_t\in L^2(\mu_t;\mathbb R^d)\) such that \(\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\!\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0\) in distributions and \(\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R^d}|v_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt<\infty\). children.title: Transport Flows
children.top_down_role: Routing to continuity-equation evolution dominated by mass transport.

assumptions_latex: \(b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) is Borel.
\(\mu_t\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) and \(\int_0^T\int|b_t|^2\,d\mu_t\,dt<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pure transport evolves mass by the continuity equation without a diffusive flux.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weak continuity-equation formulation of deterministic transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-valued transport governed by a prescribed velocity field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A transport flow driven by \(b_t\) is a narrowly continuous curve \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}\) satisfying \[\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\!\cdot(b_t\mu_t)=0\] in distributions. Equivalently, for every \(\zeta\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)\), \[\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R^d}\bigl(\partial_t\zeta(t,x)+b_t(x)\cdot\nabla\zeta(t,x)\bigr)\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt=0.\] When a regular flow map \(X_t\) exists, \(\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport flow moves probability mass through a velocity field and satisfies the continuity equation, with no diffusion term.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits transport flows, and the distributional continuity-equation formulation is internally consistent. The conditional pushforward statement requires regularity of the flow map, as acknowledged, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Diffusion Flows
children.top_down_role: Routing to dissipative spreading represented through Wasserstein evolution.

assumptions_latex: The initial datum \(\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) has density \(\rho_0\).
The diffusivity \(\kappa>0\) is constant.
Along the formal calculation, \(\mu_t=\rho_t\,dx\), with \(\rho_t>0\) sufficiently regular that \(\nabla\log\rho_t\), the continuity equation, and the displayed integrations are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The entropy gradient flow in \(W_2\) is the heat flow \(\partial_t\rho_t=\kappa\Deltaho_t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical identification of heat flow as the Wasserstein gradient flow of entropy
revised: removed malformed terminal-control artifact and made the formal regularity scope explicit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal identification of linear diffusion as the Wasserstein gradient flow of entropy for sufficiently regular positive densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For absolutely continuous measures \(\mu=\rho\,dx\), define \(\operatorname{Ent}(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho\log\rho\,dx\). For a sufficiently regular positive density curve, the formal \(W_2\)-gradient flow of \(\kappa\operatorname{Ent}\) has velocity \(v_t=-\kappa\nabla\log\rho_t\). Substitution into \(\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho_tv_t)=0\) gives \[\partial_t\rho_t=\kappa\Delta\rho_t.\] Thus the heat semigroup represents the entropy-driven diffusion flow in quadratic Wasserstein space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For sufficiently regular positive densities, the formal quadratic-Wasserstein gradient flow of Boltzmann entropy is the heat equation, with velocity equal to minus the diffusivity times the logarithmic-density gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Diffusion Flows

children.title: Transport–Diffusion Couplings
children.top_down_role: Flow models combining advective transport with diffusive dissipation.

assumptions_latex: \(V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and \(\nabla V\) has sufficient growth control.
\(\kappa>0\), and \(\mu_t=\rho_t\,dx\) is a sufficiently regular probability curve.
The free energy is finite along the curve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Wasserstein gradient flow of free energy couples drift transport with linear diffusion.

notation.meaning: density of the evolving probability measure

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical free-energy gradient-flow representation of the Fokker--Planck equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fokker–Planck flow as coupled potential transport and entropy diffusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \[\mathcal F(ho)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)ho(x)\,dx+\kappa\int_{\mathbb R^d}ho(x)\logho(x)\,dx.\] Its formal Wasserstein gradient velocity is \(v_t=-
abla(V+\kappa\logho_t)\). The continuity equation therefore becomes \[\partial_tho_t=
abla\!\cdot(ho_t
abla V)+\kappa\Deltaho_t.\] The first term transports mass along the drift \(-
abla V\), while the second diffuses mass; together they form the transport--diffusion, or Fokker--Planck, coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Potential drift and entropy diffusion combine as the Wasserstein free-energy gradient flow, producing the Fokker–Planck equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport–Diffusion Couplings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the transport-diffusion coupling leaf, and the formal first-variation calculation yields the stated Fokker--Planck equation. No inspectable citation is provided to support the precise regularity, growth, and gradient-flow conditions under which the formal representation is valid.

children.title: Transport-Proximal Scheme Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Routing to minimizing movements in probability spaces.

children.title: JKO Schemes
children.top_down_role: Variational time discretization for Wasserstein gradient flows.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2)\) is the quadratic Wasserstein space.
\(\mathcal E:\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and each incremental minimization problem attains a minimizer.
The time step satisfies \(\tau>0\), and \(\rho^0\in D(\mathcal E)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence \((\rho^n)_{n\geq0}\) is the JKO discrete trajectory for \(\mathcal E\) with step \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-Wasserstein minimizing movements with a fixed time step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(\rho^0\), recursively choose, for every integer \(n\geq1\),
\[
\rho^n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)}\left\{\mathcal E(\rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\rho,\rho^{n-1})\right\}.
\]
Define the right-continuous interpolation by \(\bar\rho_\tau(0)=\rho^0\) and \(\bar\rho_\tau(t)=\rho^n\) whenever \(t\in((n-1)\tau,n\tau]\). For a prescribed terminal time \(T\), stop after \(N=\lceil T/\tau\rceil\) steps and output \(\bar\rho_\tau|_{[0,T]}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each time step, minimize the energy plus the squared Wasserstein distance from the previous measure divided by twice the step size.
knowledge_statements.title: JKO Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic content kind and JKO recursion fit the terminal container, and the mathematical statement is standard and internally consistent. However, no source reference or inspectable locator is supplied, so the candidate cannot be source-reviewed.

children.title: Transport-Proximal Schemes
children.top_down_role: Proximal constructions using transport-based discrepancy geometry.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space.
\(\Phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and the displayed minimizers exist.
The step sizes satisfy \(\tau_n>0\), with initial state \(x^0\in D(\Phi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update is a metric proximal step, and its transport specialization is obtained by setting \(d=W_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric proximal updates, including optimal-transport state spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\tau>0\) and \(y\in X\), define the possibly set-valued metric proximal map
\[
J_\tau(y):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\Phi(x)+\frac{d^2(x,y)}{2\tau}\right\}.
\]
Starting from \(x^0\), choose \(x^n\in J_{\tau_n}(x^{n-1})\) recursively. The algorithm stops at a prescribed index \(N\) or terminal discrete time \(\sum_{n=1}^N\tau_n\), and outputs \((x^0,\ldots,x^N)\) together with its piecewise-constant interpolation. A transport-proximal scheme is this construction on a space of measures with a transport metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport-proximal iteration minimizes the energy plus a squared metric displacement penalty from the preceding state at every step.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport-Proximal Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind fits the scheme container, and the metric proximal update is mathematically coherent under the stated minimizer-existence assumption. No cited source or specific locator supports the construction or its transport specialization.

children.title: Scheme Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural overlap between JKO constructions and broader transport-proximal families.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\) and \(d=W_2\).
\(\Phi=\mathcal E\) is proper, and the relevant incremental minimizers exist.
Both schemes use the same initial measure and positive time steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The JKO iterates and the Wasserstein transport-proximal iterates coincide step by step.

notation.meaning: Metric proximal map for the energy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity of JKO and metric proximal updates under the Wasserstein specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\tau>0\) and \(\mu\in D(\mathcal E)\), the transport-proximal map specialized to the quadratic Wasserstein metric is
\[
J_\tau^{\mathcal E}(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\rho\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)}\left\{\mathcal E(\rho)+\frac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\rho,\mu)\right\}.
\]
Consequently, if \(\rho^n\in J_{\tau_n}^{\mathcal E}(\rho^{n-1})\), then the recursion is exactly the JKO recursion. Conversely, every JKO update is a transport-proximal update with \(X=\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\), \(d=W_2\), and \(\Phi=\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The JKO method is precisely the metric proximal-point method when the state space is a Wasserstein space and the metric is quadratic Wasserstein distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Scheme Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind is appropriate for the correspondence leaf, and the claimed identity follows from specializing the metric proximal objective to the quadratic Wasserstein metric. The record nevertheless has no source or inspectable locator for independent verification.
