children.title: Rate-Independent Representations
children.top_down_role: Differential, metric, energetic, and parametrized descriptions of rate-independent evolution.

children.title: Differential Rate-Independent Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Local flow-rule representations of rate-independent evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(\mathcal R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, positive, and positively one-homogeneous.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inclusion is the local differential flow rule for a rate-independent evolution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional energy with convex one-homogeneous dissipation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An absolutely continuous curve \(u:[0,T]\to X\) satisfies the differential rate-independent inclusion if
\[
0\in\partial\mathcal R(\dot u(t))+D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t))
\]
for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\). Equivalently,
\[
-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t))\in\partial\mathcal R(\dot u(t)).
\]
Because \(\partial\mathcal R(\lambda v)=\partial\mathcal R(v)\) for every \(\lambda>0\), an increasing time reparametrization changes the speed but preserves the autonomous form of the flow rule, expressing rate independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differential rate-independent trajectory balances the energy gradient against the subdifferential of a convex one-homogeneous dissipation evaluated at its velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Differential Rate-Independent Inclusions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind and differential inclusion fit the local flow-rule container. The final reparametrization assertion requires a precise class of time changes and treatment of the time-dependent energy; no authoritative source or locator is supplied to resolve those qualifications.

children.title: Dissipation-Distance Formulations
children.top_down_role: Metric descriptions based on accumulated rate-independent cost.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional vector space.
\(\mathcal R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, positive, and positively one-homogeneous.
\(u:[a,b]\to X\) is an arbitrary curve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mathsf D}(u;[a,b])\) is the accumulated rate-independent dissipation of \(u\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation-invariant dissipation distance induced by a one-homogeneous potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the possibly asymmetric dissipation distance by
\[
\mathsf D(x,y):=\mathcal R(y-x),\qquad x,y\in X.
\]
The accumulated dissipation of \(u\) on \([a,b]\) is
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathsf D}(u;[a,b]):=\sup_{a=t_0<\cdots<t_N=b}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathsf D(u(t_{i-1}),u(t_i)).
\]
The supremum ranges over all finite partitions. The curve has bounded dissipation variation precisely when this quantity is finite. If \(u\) is absolutely continuous, then \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mathsf D}(u;[a,b])=\int_a^b\mathcal R(\dot u(t))\,dt\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dissipation distance is the one-homogeneous cost of an increment, and total dissipation is its supremal sum over all time partitions.
knowledge_statements.title: Dissipation-Distance Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the dissipation-distance container. The distance and partition variation are standard, but the integral identity for absolutely continuous curves depends on the relevant metric or norm absolute-continuity framework and coercivity or finiteness assumptions. No source is supplied to verify the exact version.

children.title: Energetic Formulations
children.top_down_role: Global-stability and energy-balance organization of evolution.

assumptions_latex: \((X,\mathsf D)\) is a state space with a possibly asymmetric dissipation distance.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) has a defined time derivative along the candidate curve.
\(u:[0,T]\to X\) has finite \(\mathsf D\)-variation and prescribed initial state \(u(0)=u_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global stability together with the exact energy balance constitutes the energetic formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global energetic representation for rate-independent systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The energetic formulation requires, for every \(t\in[0,T]\), global stability
\[
\mathcal E(t,u(t))\leq\mathcal E(t,z)+\mathsf D(u(t),z)\qquad\text{for all }z\in X,
\]
and the energy balance
\[
\mathcal E(t,u(t))+\operatorname{Var}_{\mathsf D}(u;[0,t])
=
\mathcal E(0,u_0)+\int_0^t\partial_s\mathcal E(s,u(s))\,ds.
\]
The first relation compares the current state with every competitor; the second accounts exactly for stored energy, accumulated rate-independent dissipation, and external power.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The energetic formulation combines stability against every competitor with an exact balance of stored energy, accumulated dissipation, and external work.
knowledge_statements.title: Energetic Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind matches the energetic-formulation container, and the two displayed requirements have the standard form. The assumptions do not precisely guarantee measurability and integrability of the power term, and no authoritative source with a locator is cited.

children.title: Parametrized Formulations
children.top_down_role: Time-rescaled descriptions resolving discontinuous transitions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space, and \(\mathcal R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable.
\(t:[0,S]\to[0,T]\) and \(u:[0,S]\to X\) are absolutely continuous, with \(t\) nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((t,u)\) represents physical evolution with jumps resolved along intervals on which \(t'=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arclength-type parametrization of discontinuous rate-independent evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A parametrized description is an absolutely continuous pair \((t,u):[0,S]\to[0,T]\times X\) satisfying \(t'(s)\geq0\) almost everywhere, the endpoint conditions \(t(0)=0\), \(t(S)=T\), and a nondegeneracy normalization such as
\[
t'(s)+\mathcal R(u'(s))=1
\]
for almost every \(s\). On sets where \(t'(s)>0\), the curve follows the physical-time rate-independent evolution. Intervals where \(t'(s)=0\) encode transitions at a fixed physical time, thereby replacing a jump of the original trajectory by a continuous path in parameter time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondecreasing time change and an absolutely continuous state curve resolve physical jumps as continuous transitions occurring while physical time is frozen.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametrized Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind fits the parametrized-formulation container, but the statement gives only a kinematic parametrization and normalization. It does not state the contact, energy-balance, or differential condition that makes the pair a parametrized rate-independent solution, and the claim that it follows the evolution where physical time advances is unsupported. An authoritative source is needed to select the intended formulation.

children.title: Rate-Independent Solution Concepts
children.top_down_role: Competing notions distinguished by stability locality, jump resolution, and approximation mechanism.

children.title: Energetic Solutions
children.top_down_role: Globally stable rate-independent evolution.

assumptions_latex: \((X,\mathsf D)\) is a state space with a possibly asymmetric dissipation distance.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) admits the power term appearing below.
\(u:[0,T]\to X\) has finite \(\mathsf D\)-variation and \(u(0)=u_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A curve satisfying both displayed requirements is an energetic solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard global-stability definition of an energetic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curve \(u\) is an energetic solution if, for every \(t\in[0,T]\), it satisfies
\[
\mathcal E(t,u(t))\leq\mathcal E(t,z)+\mathsf D(u(t),z)
\quad\text{for every }z\in X,
\]
and
\[
\mathcal E(t,u(t))+\operatorname{Var}_{\mathsf D}(u;[0,t])
=
\mathcal E(0,u_0)+\int_0^t\partial_s\mathcal E(s,u(s))\,ds.
\]
Thus stability is global in the state variable, while the energy identity charges every continuous displacement and jump through the same dissipation distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An energetic solution is globally stable at every time and satisfies an exact energy balance charging all motion and jumps by the dissipation distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Energetic Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind is correct for the energetic-solutions leaf, and global stability plus energy balance is the standard structure. The assumptions leave the power term insufficiently specified, and no source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Local-Differential Solution Pair
children.top_down_role: Locally stable evolution tied to differential flow rules.

children.title: Local Solutions
children.top_down_role: Rate-independent evolution governed by local stability criteria.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(\mathcal R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous, and \(K^*:=\partial\mathcal R(0)\).
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable.
\(u:[0,T]\to X\) has bounded variation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local stability excludes an energetically favorable infinitesimal displacement at every nonjump time.

notation.meaning: Energy gradient in the state variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local stability component of a finite-dimensional rate-independent solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A bounded-variation curve \(u\) satisfies the local-stability requirement if
\[
-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t))\in K^*
\]
for every \(t\in[0,T]\setminus J_u\). Since
\[
K^*=\left\{\xi\in X^*: \langle\xi,v\rangle\leq\mathcal R(v)\text{ for every }v\in X\right\},
\]
this is equivalent to
\[
\langle-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t)),v\rangle\leq\mathcal R(v)
\quad\text{for every }v\in X
\]
at each nonjump time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local solution is stable away from jumps when the negative energy gradient lies in the polar set determined by the dissipation.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is an appropriate content kind, but the statement defines only local stability away from jumps while the title claims to define Local Solutions. Standard local-solution notions generally require additional energy or variation conditions, with conventions varying by source. A precise authoritative source is needed before the mathematical version can be fixed.

children.title: Differential Solutions
children.top_down_role: Rate-independent evolution expressed through differential flow structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
\(\mathcal R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An absolutely continuous curve satisfying the inclusion almost everywhere is a differential solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolutely continuous differential solution in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An absolutely continuous curve \(u:[0,T]\to X\) is a differential solution of the rate-independent system \((X,\mathcal E,\mathcal R)\) if
\[
0
i D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t))+\partial\mathcal R(\dot u(t))
\]
for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\). Equivalently, for almost every \(t\) and every \(v\in X\),
\[
\mathcal R(v)\geq\mathcal R(\dot u(t))+
\langle-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t)),v-\dot u(t)\rangle.
\]
The initial condition is imposed separately as \(u(0)=u_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differential solution is absolutely continuous and obeys the rate-independent subdifferential inclusion almost everywhere, together with its prescribed initial condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Differential Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the differential-solutions leaf, and the inclusion and variational inequality are equivalent under the stated convex subdifferential convention. No source reference or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Local-Stability Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Regimes where local stability aligns with differential evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous, with \(K^*=\partial\mathcal R(0)\).
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable.
\(u:[0,T]\to X\) is absolutely continuous and satisfies the differential inclusion almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every differential solution satisfies local stability almost everywhere; at continuity points it holds wherever the inclusion is valid.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility induced by one-homogeneous dissipation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t))\in\partial\mathcal R(\dot u(t))
\]
for almost every \(t\), then
\[
-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t))\in K^*
\]
for almost every \(t\). Indeed, positive one-homogeneity gives \(\partial\mathcal R(v)\subseteq\partial\mathcal R(0)=K^*\) for every \(v\in X\). Hence the differential flow rule implies the local-stability inequality
\[
\langle-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t)),w\rangle\leq\mathcal R(w)
\quad\text{for every }w\in X
\]
at almost every time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because every velocity subgradient of a one-homogeneous dissipation lies in its polar set, the differential inclusion implies local stability almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Stability Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind correctly fits a compatibility leaf. The implication from the differential inclusion to polar local stability is standard for a convex positively one-homogeneous dissipation, but the record supplies no authoritative source or specific locator.

children.title: Balanced-Viscosity Solutions
children.top_down_role: Jump-sensitive solutions selected by viscous approximation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional with norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and \(\mathcal R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable, and \(K^*=\partial\mathcal R(0)\).
\(u:[0,T]\to X\) has bounded variation and prescribed initial state \(u_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local stability plus the contact-potential energy balance defines a balanced-viscosity solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional balanced-viscosity formulation selected by quadratic vanishing viscosity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set
\[
\mathfrak p(v,\xi):=\mathcal R(v)+\|v\|\operatorname{dist}_*(\xi,K^*).
\]
A bounded-variation curve \(u\) is a balanced-viscosity solution if \(-D_u\mathcal E(t,u(t))\in K^*\) for every \(t\notin J_u\) and
\[
\mathcal E(t,u(t))+\operatorname{Var}_{\mathfrak p,\mathcal E}(u;[0,t])
=
\mathcal E(0,u_0)+\int_0^t\partial_s\mathcal E(s,u(s))\,ds.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mathfrak p,\mathcal E}\) equals the ordinary \(\mathcal R\)-variation on continuous portions and assigns each jump the least \(\mathfrak p\)-action among connecting paths at the frozen jump time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced-viscosity solution is locally stable away from jumps and balances energy using a vanishing-viscosity contact cost that resolves each jump path.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced-Viscosity Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the balanced-viscosity-solutions container. However, the dual distance, the precise contact-potential variation, endpoint and jump contributions, and the connection to the specified quadratic viscous regularization are not fully defined. These choices are formulation-dependent, so an authoritative source with an exact locator is required.

children.title: Approximation-Parametrization Solution Pair
children.top_down_role: Solutions selected through discretization or time rescaling.

children.title: Approximable Solutions
children.top_down_role: Rate-independent solutions selected as limits of approximation procedures.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximable Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional vanishing-viscosity notion of an approximable rate-independent solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A curve \(z:[0,T]\to X\) is an approximable solution if there are \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\) and curves \(z_{\varepsilon_k}\in AC([0,T];X)\) satisfying
\[
0\in\partial\mathcal R(\dot z_{\varepsilon_k}(t))+\varepsilon_kJ\dot z_{\varepsilon_k}(t)+D_z\mathcal E(t,z_{\varepsilon_k}(t))
\]
for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), such that \(z_{\varepsilon_k}(t)\to z(t)\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximable solution is a pointwise limit of viscously regularized rate-independent evolutions as viscosity vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space and \(\mathcal R:X\to[0,\infty)\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable with respect to the state variable.
\(J:X\to X^*\) is a fixed linear coercive viscosity operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) is a pointwise vanishing-viscosity limit of the regularized evolutions.

children.title: Parametrized Solutions
children.top_down_role: Rate-independent evolution represented through an auxiliary time parameter.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(\mathcal R\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous, and \(\Psi(v)=\tfrac12\lVert v\rVert^2\).
\(\mathcal E\) is continuously differentiable in time and state.
The parameter interval \([0,S]\) includes graph completions of all physical-time jumps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameterized curve resolves physical jumps through intervals on which \(t'=0\) and \(z'\neq0\).

notation.meaning: distance from a covector to the stable set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized parameterized balanced-viscosity formulation with quadratic viscous correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A normalized parametrized solution is an absolutely continuous pair \((t,z):[0,S]\to[0,T]\times X\) with \(t'\ge0\), \(t(0)=0\), \(t(S)=T\), and
\[
t'(s)+\lVert z'(s)\rVert=1\quad\text{for a.e. }s.
\]
Writing \(e(s)=\operatorname{dist}_{*}(-D_z\mathcal E(t(s),z(s)),K^*)\), it satisfies local stability \(t'(s)e(s)=0\) and the parameterized energy identity
\[
\mathcal E(t(s),z(s))+\int_0^s\!\bigl(\mathcal R(z')+\lVert z'\rVert e\bigr)\,dr
=
\mathcal E(0,z(0))+\int_0^s\!\partial_t\mathcal E(t,z)t'\,dr.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametrized solution completes jumps by freezing physical time while the state traverses a viscously selected transition.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametrized Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the terminal container, but no cited source supports this particular normalized balanced-viscosity formulation. The dual norm underlying the distance and the precise contact-potential hypotheses also require specification.

children.title: Time-Rescaling Selection
children.top_down_role: Solution selection effects associated with temporal reparametrization.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Rescaling Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arclength rescaling used to expose jump transitions in vanishing-viscosity limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(s_\varepsilon(t)=t+\int_0^t\lVert\dot z_\varepsilon(r)\rVert\,dr\), let \(t_\varepsilon\) be its generalized inverse, and set \(u_\varepsilon(s)=z_\varepsilon(t_\varepsilon(s))\). Then
\[
t_\varepsilon'(s)+\lVert u_\varepsilon'(s)\rVert=1
\]
for almost every \(s\) in the rescaled interval. If a subsequence converges uniformly and weakly-star in \(W^{1,\infty}\) to \((t,u)\), then
\[
t'(s)+\lVert u'(s)\rVert\le 1
\]
for almost every \(s\). Under an additional nondegeneracy condition, or after an admissible arclength reparametrization, equality can be imposed. Intervals on which \(t'=0\) and \(u'\ne0\) represent transition paths collapsed to jumps in physical time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmented-arclength rescaling expands fast viscous transitions into parameter intervals; normalization of the limit may require a nondegeneracy condition or reparametrization.
assumptions_latex: \(z_\varepsilon\in AC([0,T];X)\) solves the viscously regularized rate-independent inclusion.
The augmented arclengths \(s_\varepsilon(T)\) are uniformly bounded.
After extension to a common parameter interval, \((t_{\varepsilon_k},u_{\varepsilon_k})\) converges uniformly and weakly-star in \(W^{1,\infty}\) to \((t,u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rescaled limit records viscous transition paths, while exact unit-speed normalization requires an additional condition or reparametrization.

children.title: Global Incremental Minimization
children.top_down_role: Incremental construction associated with energetic solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T\) is a time partition.
\(\mathcal R:X\to[0,\infty]\) is a rate-independent dissipation and \(\mathcal E(t_n,\cdot)\) admits a global minimizer after adding dissipation.
An initial state \(z_0\in X\) is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the piecewise-constant discrete evolution \(\bar z_\tau(t)=z_n\) for \(t\in(t_{n-1},t_n]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global minimizing-movements construction for energetic rate-independent evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(z_0\), compute successively for \(n=1,\ldots,N\)
\[
z_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in X}\left\{\mathcal E(t_n,z)+\mathcal R(z-z_{n-1})\right\}.
\]
If the minimizer is nonunique, a fixed measurable tie-breaking rule must be specified as part of the algorithm. Stop after \(n=N\) and return either the sequence \((z_n)_{n=0}^N\) or its right-continuous piecewise-constant interpolation \(\bar z_\tau(t)=z_n\) for \(t\in(t_{n-1},t_n]\), with \(\bar z_\tau(0)=z_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each time step, globally minimize current energy plus dissipation from the preceding state, then interpolate the discrete states.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Incremental Minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and content kind fit the container, but no authoritative rate-independent-systems citation is supplied. A measurable tie-breaking selector is additional structure and is not guaranteed by the stated existence assumptions.

children.title: Split Incremental Method Family
children.top_down_role: Incremental selection for local stability and coupled variables.

children.title: Local Incremental Methods
children.top_down_role: Incremental selection based on locally stable state changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Incremental Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood-constrained alternative to global incremental minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize with \(z_0\in X\). Given a radius \(\rho_n>0\), choose at step \(n\)
\[
z_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lVert z-z_{n-1}\rVert\le\rho_n}
\left\{\mathcal E(t_n,z)+\mathcal R(z-z_{n-1})\right\}.
\]
Return the discrete sequence and a specified interpolation. The update minimizes the incremental objective only over the prescribed neighborhood and therefore need not be a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each incremental problem is minimized within a prescribed neighborhood of the preceding state, so the resulting update need not be globally stable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
The incremental objective \(F_n(z)=\mathcal E(t_n,z)+\mathcal R(z-z_{n-1})\) is lower semicontinuous.
The feasible set \(\{z\in X:\lVert z-z_{n-1}\rVert\le\rho_n\}\) has a nonempty compact sublevel set containing a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update minimizes \(F_n\) over the prescribed neighborhood but need not minimize it globally.

children.title: Alternating Incremental Methods
children.top_down_role: Incremental evolution using successive updates of coupled variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Incremental Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-coordinate solution of a coupled incremental rate-independent problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At time step \(n\), initialize \((x^0,y^0)=(x_{n-1},y_{n-1})\) and iterate
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F_n(x,y^k),
\qquad
y^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}F_n(x^{k+1},y).
\]
Stop according to a prescribed residual test or iteration cap and return the last pair. If the exact alternating iteration reaches a fixed point \((x^*,y^*)\), then
\[
F_n(x^*,y^*)\le F_n(x,y^*)\quad\text{for every }x\in X,
\]
and
\[
F_n(x^*,y^*)\le F_n(x^*,y)\quad\text{for every }y\in Y.
\]
Such blockwise minimality does not in general imply joint global minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating minimization solves one state block at a time. An exact fixed point is separately minimizing in each block but need not be a joint global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The state is \(z=(x,y)\in X\times Y\), and \(F_n:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is the incremental objective.
Each block subproblem admits a minimizer.
A residual-based stopping test or a maximum inner-iteration count is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact alternating fixed point is blockwise minimizing, whereas finite stopping alone supplies only the guarantee encoded by the chosen residual test.

notation.meaning: incremental objective at time step n

children.title: Coupled-Variable Splitting
children.top_down_role: Structural decomposition of incremental evolution across interacting state components.

assumptions_latex: The state is \((u,z)\in U\times Z\), with stored energy \(\mathcal E(t,u,z)\).
Dissipation \(\mathcal R:Z\to[0,+\infty]\) acts on the internal variable \(z\).
Both split subproblems admit solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The split update separates instantaneous equilibrium in \(u\) from the dissipative update in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lie-type splitting between equilibrium and dissipative variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \((u_{n-1},z_{n-1})\), perform the ordered split
\[
u_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in U}\mathcal E(t_n,u,z_{n-1}),
\qquad
z_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in Z}\left\{\mathcal E(t_n,u_n,z)+\mathcal R(z-z_{n-1})\right\}.
\]
Return \((u_n,z_n)\) and repeat at the next time node. Reversing the two substeps defines a different splitting. Unless additional separability, convexity, or inner convergence is available, one sweep need not solve the coupled global incremental problem
\[
\min_{u,z}\bigl\{\mathcal E(t_n,u,z)+\mathcal R(z-z_{n-1})\bigr\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method first equilibrates the nondissipative variable, then updates the dissipative variable with an incremental dissipation penalty.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Variable Splitting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the coupled-variable splitting container and appropriately disclaims joint optimality, but the particular Lie ordering and its rate-independent interpretation lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Incremental Limit-Passage Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Structural controls used to pass from discrete states to evolution.

children.title: Incremental Stability Controls
children.top_down_role: Discrete structural controls supporting stable incremental states.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Stability Controls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete global stability inherited from exact incremental minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a time node \(t_n\), the discrete state \(z_n\) has the global-stability certificate
\[
\mathcal E(t_n,z_n)
\le
\mathcal E(t_n,w)+\mathcal R(w-z_n)
\quad\text{for every }w\in\operatorname{dom}\mathcal E(t_n,\cdot).
\]
For an exact global incremental minimizer, this certificate is valid whenever the dissipation is subadditive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact global incremental minimizer satisfies the discrete energetic global-stability inequality when the dissipation is subadditive.
assumptions_latex: \(z_n\) globally minimizes \(z\mapsto\mathcal E(t_n,z)+\mathcal R(z-z_{n-1})\).
\(\mathcal R\) is subadditive.
The competitor \(w\) belongs to \(\operatorname{dom}\mathcal E(t_n,\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E(t_n,z_n)\le\mathcal E(t_n,w)+\mathcal R(w-z_n)\) for every admissible competitor \(w\).

children.title: Discrete Compactness Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Compactness sources for sequences of incremental trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Compactness Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Helly compactness for dissipation-controlled incremental trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each partition, let \(\bar z_\tau\) be the right-continuous interpolation of the discrete states. Suppose
\[
\sup_\tau\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(\bar z_\tau;[0,T])<+\infty
\]
and all ranges are contained in a common compact subset of \(X\). Then there are \(\tau_k\downarrow0\) and \(z\in BV([0,T];X)\) such that
\[
\bar z_{\tau_k}(t)\to z(t)
\quad\text{for every }t\in[0,T],
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(z;[0,T])
\le
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(\bar z_{\tau_k};[0,T]).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform dissipation variation and compact state ranges yield pointwise subsequential convergence to a bounded-variation evolution, with lower semicontinuity of variation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(\mathcal R(v)\ge c\lVert v\rVert\) for some \(c>0\).
The interpolants have uniformly bounded \(\mathcal R\)-variation.
All discrete states lie in a common compact subset of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subsequence converges pointwise at every time to \(z\in BV([0,T];X)\), and the \(\mathcal R\)-variation is lower semicontinuous.

children.title: Evolutionary Limit Passage
children.top_down_role: Transition from compact discrete states to rate-independent evolution.

assumptions_latex: Discrete interpolants converge pointwise to \(z\), and their dissipative variations satisfy the lower bound from compactness.
The energies are lower semicontinuous in state, continuously differentiable in time, and their power terms converge appropriately.
Discrete global stability and the discrete energy inequality hold with errors vanishing as \(\tau\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limit \(z\) satisfies global stability and the energetic energy balance, hence is an energetic solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract limit passage from global incremental minimizers to energetic solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated compactness, stability-recovery, and power-convergence hypotheses, the limit curve satisfies, for every \(t\in[0,T]\) and every competitor \(w\),
\[
\mathcal E(t,z(t))\le\mathcal E(t,w)+\mathcal R(w-z(t)).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\mathcal E(t,z(t))+
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(z;[0,t])
=
\mathcal E(0,z(0))+
\int_0^t\partial_s\mathcal E(s,z(s))\,ds.
\]
Consequently, the pointwise limit of the incremental interpolants is an energetic rate-independent evolution with the prescribed initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness, recoverable stability, and convergent power terms pass discrete minimizers to an energetic rate-independent solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Evolutionary Limit Passage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the limit-passage container, but phrases such as “converge appropriately,” “stability-recovery,” and “errors vanishing” do not state checkable hypotheses. The absent source is essential because the assumptions needed to obtain the reverse energy inequality and hence equality are not specified.

children.title: Incremental Selection-Bias Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dependence of branches and jumps on discretization and minimizer selection.

children.title: Metastable Incremental Branches
children.top_down_role: Locally persistent branches arising in incremental evolution.

assumptions_latex: The scalar energy is \(\mathcal E(t,z)=(z^2-1)^2-tz\) on \(\mathbb R\).
A local incremental method restricts every update to a sufficiently small neighborhood of the preceding state.
The initial state lies near the strict local minimum \(z=-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local incremental updates can remain on the negative metastable branch after the positive well has lower global energy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tilted double well illustrating persistence of a locally stable but globally unfavorable branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Stationary points satisfy
\[
4z(z^2-1)-t=0.
\]
For \(0<t<t_{\mathrm{sp}}=8/(3\sqrt3)\), this equation has a negative strict local minimizer \(z_-(t)\), although the positive well has lower energy because of the term \(-tz\). If the neighborhood radius and time increments are small enough to exclude the competing positive well, neighborhood-constrained incremental minimization initialized near \(-1\) selects successive states near \(z_-(t_n)\). Thus local incremental stability permits a metastable branch that global incremental minimization would reject.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local scheme can track the unfavorable well of a tilted double-well energy until that metastable well disappears.
knowledge_statements.title: Metastable Incremental Branches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spinodal value for the tilted double well is consistent, and failure_boundary fits the container. However, the local incremental objective and its dissipation term are not specified, so the asserted tracking of the stationary energy branch does not follow from the stated assumptions.

children.title: Minimizer Selection Bias
children.top_down_role: Dependence of computed evolution on the choice among competing minimizers.

assumptions_latex: The incremental objective at one step is \(F(z)=(z^2-1)^2+\rho|z|\) with \(0<\rho<1\) and preceding state \(z_0=0\).
The objective is symmetric and possesses paired nonzero global minimizers \(\{-a,a\}\).
A subsequent loading term \(-tz\) breaks the symmetry for \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Different admissible tie-breaking rules select distinct discrete branches from identical data.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric nonunique minimizers expose dependence on an algorithmic tie-breaking rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(F\) is even and \(F(\pm1)=\rho<1=F(0)\), its global minimizers are nonzero and occur as a pair \(\{-a,a\}\). Hence both updates \(z_1=-a\) and \(z_1=a\) solve exactly the same global incremental problem. A deterministic rule such as “choose the largest minimizer” selects \(a\), whereas “choose the smallest minimizer” selects \(-a\). After adding the loading \(-tz\), the two choices initialize different continuation branches. Therefore global minimality alone does not make the discrete evolution selection-independent when incremental minimizers are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonunique symmetric incremental minimizers let tie-breaking rules choose different states and thereby seed different later branches.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimizer Selection Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric objective does have paired nonzero global minimizers for the stated range, and counterexample is an appropriate content kind. An inspectable source is nevertheless absent, and the claimed later continuation into distinct branches requires a specified subsequent incremental problem and selection rule.

children.title: Discretization-Sensitive Jump Selection
children.top_down_role: Variation of selected jumps across temporal discretizations.

assumptions_latex: The state space is finite-dimensional, and each incremental problem admits a minimizer.
The dissipation distance \(\mathsf D\) is rate-independent, and \(\mathcal E(t,\cdot)\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct vanishing partition sequences or admissible tie-breaking rules may select different post-jump states, so the incremental limit is not determined by mesh size alone.

notation.meaning: time partition with maximal step tending to zero

review_flags: Authoritative source for discretization-dependent jump selection is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for nonunique incremental minimizers near a rate-independent jump.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(0=t_0^\tau<\cdots<t_{N_\tau}^\tau=T\), let \(u_n^\tau\in\operatorname*{Argmin}_v\{\mathcal E(t_n^\tau,v)+\mathsf D(u_{n-1}^\tau,v)\}\). Suppose that near a critical time \(t_*\), two separated local branches \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) attain the same incremental minimum, while subsequent minimizers initialized on either branch remain separated. If two partition sequences or tie-breaking rules select different branches at their first step crossing \(t_*\), their interpolants can converge along subsequences to distinct rate-independent evolutions. Thus vanishing mesh size does not remove jump-selection ambiguity without uniqueness or a specified secondary selection criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a tied nonconvex jump, different fine time grids or tie-breaking rules can select distinct persistent branches and hence different limiting evolutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Discretization-Sensitive Jump Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and local topic fit, and the conditional branch-selection mechanism is coherent. However, no citation is supplied for the substantive claim that vanishing partitions or tie-breaking can yield distinct limiting rate-independent evolutions; the provided inventory does not specifically support this phenomenon.

children.title: Selection-Induced Branch Locking
children.top_down_role: Persistence on a branch caused by earlier incremental choices.

assumptions_latex: Incremental minimizers are computed successively from the previously selected state.
Two metastable branches are separated by a positive dissipation barrier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A local branch choice can persist under all later sufficiently small increments, producing selection-induced locking.

notation.meaning: incremental objective at time step n

review_flags: A precise source for branch-locking hypotheses and terminology is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistence property for a metastable branch chosen by incremental minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a branch of local states and let \(u_n\in\operatorname*{Argmin}_v\mathcal I_n(v;u_{n-1})\). Assume there are neighborhoods \(U_n\supset B(t_n)\) and numbers \(\delta_n>0\) such that, whenever \(u_{n-1}\in U_{n-1}\), every competing state \(v\notin U_n\) satisfies \(\mathcal I_n(v;u_{n-1})\geq\inf_{w\in U_n}\mathcal I_n(w;u_{n-1})+\delta_n\). Then selection of \(u_k\in U_k\) implies \(u_n\in U_n\) for every later step on which these inequalities hold. Consequently, an initial selection may lock the discrete evolution onto \(B\), even when another metastable branch exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If leaving a selected metastable branch always costs a positive incremental gap, every later minimization remains on that branch until the gap disappears.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Induced Branch Locking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the branch-locking container, and the positive incremental gap supports persistence by successive minimization. A source is still required for this formulation, its hypotheses, and the use of branch-locking terminology in rate-independent incremental evolution.

children.title: Viscosity-Resolved Jump Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Viscous regularization and time rescaling as mechanisms for resolving discontinuous transitions.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Rate-Independent Systems: Theory and Application
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Beyond rate independence
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Rate-Independent Systems: Theory and Application

children.title: Viscous Regularizations
children.top_down_role: Rate-dependent approximations of rate-independent evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(\mathcal R:X\to[0,\infty)\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous, and \(\mathbb V\) is positive definite.
\(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable in the state variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The added term \(\varepsilon\mathbb V\dot u_\varepsilon\) produces a rate-dependent approximation whose formal limit as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) is rate-independent.
review_flags: Standard formulation, but the supplied locators do not substantiate viscous regularization of rate-independent systems.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-viscosity regularization in a finite-dimensional state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), the viscous regularization of the rate-independent system \((X,\mathcal E,\mathcal R)\) is an absolutely continuous curve \(u_\varepsilon:[0,T]\to X\) satisfying, for almost every \(t\in(0,T)\), \[0\in\partial\mathcal R(\dot u_\varepsilon(t))+\varepsilon\mathbb V\dot u_\varepsilon(t)+D_u\mathcal E(t,u_\varepsilon(t)).\] Equivalently, its dissipation potential is \(\mathcal R_\varepsilon(v)=\mathcal R(v)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\langle\mathbb Vv,v\rangle\). The initial condition \(u_\varepsilon(0)=u_\varepsilon^0\) is prescribed, and the vanishing-viscosity regime is \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A viscous regularization adds a small positive quadratic velocity cost to the one-homogeneous rate-independent dissipation and solves the resulting differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Viscous Regularizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the container, and the finite-dimensional quadratic-viscosity inclusion is standard and internally consistent. No cited source or inspectable locator supports this rate-independent viscous-regularization definition; the listed Mordukhovich sections are not specific enough to substitute for such evidence.

children.title: Balanced-Viscosity Jump Costs
children.top_down_role: Variational accounting of viscously resolved transitions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(\mathbb V\) is positive definite.
\(\mathcal R\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous; \(\mathcal E(t,\cdot)\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The balanced-viscosity cost is the least frozen-time contact action connecting the two jump traces.
review_flags: Exact contact-potential representation requires a specialized balanced-viscosity source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quadratic-viscosity jump cost at frozen physical time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(K^*=\partial\mathcal R(0)\) and \(\mathfrak p(v,\xi)=\mathcal R(v)+\lVert v\rVert_{\mathbb V}\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb V^{-1}}(\xi,K^*)\). For a frozen time \(t\) and states \(u_-,u_+\in X\), the balanced-viscosity jump cost is \[\Delta_{\mathrm{BV}}(t;u_-,u_+)=\inf_{\vartheta}\int_0^1\mathfrak p\bigl(\dot\vartheta(r),-D_u\mathcal E(t,\vartheta(r))\bigr)\,dr,\] where the infimum runs over absolutely continuous paths \(\vartheta:[0,1]\to X\) with \(\vartheta(0)=u_-\) and \(\vartheta(1)=u_+\). It records both rate-independent motion and the viscous cost of crossing unstable regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The jump cost is the minimum contact action over internal paths connecting the two jump states while physical time is frozen.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced-Viscosity Jump Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind exactly fits the jump-cost container, and the displayed frozen-time contact-action formula is plausible for quadratic viscosity. Its precise contact potential, metric conventions, and admissible path class require a specialized Balanced Viscosity citation with a theorem or definition locator.

children.title: Time-Rescaled Jump Paths
children.top_down_role: Extended trajectories exposing internal jump dynamics.

assumptions_latex: \(u_\varepsilon\) are viscously regularized trajectories with uniformly bounded energy and dissipation.
The chosen arc-length functions are strictly increasing after harmless regularization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reparameterized limit resolves each physical-time jump as a nonconstant path traversed while the limiting physical time remains constant.

notation.meaning: augmented arc length and its inverse

review_flags: A source is required for the precise compactness and parameterization framework.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-length reparameterization exposing internal trajectories at macroscopic jumps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a viscous trajectory \(u_\varepsilon\), set \(s_\varepsilon(t)=t+\int_0^t\lVert\dot u_\varepsilon(r)\rVert\,dr\), let \(t_\varepsilon\) be its inverse, and define \(\widetilde u_\varepsilon(s)=u_\varepsilon(t_\varepsilon(s))\). A time-rescaled jump path is a subsequential limit \((t,u)\) of \((t_\varepsilon,\widetilde u_\varepsilon)\) with \(t\) nondecreasing. On any interval \([s_-,s_+]\) where \(t(s)=t_*\) and \(u(s_-)\neq u(s_+)\), the curve \(u|_{[s_-,s_+]}\) represents the internal transition occurring at the single physical time \(t_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc-length reparameterization stretches an instantaneous macroscopic jump into a path evolving through internal time while physical time is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Rescaled Jump Paths

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits time-rescaled jump paths, and the statement consistently describes an arc-length parametrization. The asserted subsequential limit and interpretation of constant-time intervals depend on compactness and parametrized-solution hypotheses that have no supporting citation.

children.title: Multirate Viscosity Limits
children.top_down_role: Jump selection under several vanishing relaxation scales.

assumptions_latex: Two state components have positive-definite quadratic viscosities scaled by \(\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon^\alpha\).
The energy is differentiable and the rate-independent dissipations are convex and positively one-homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exponent \(\alpha\) determines whether the jump dynamics are coupled or hierarchically equilibrated.
review_flags: The regime classification requires confirmation from a multirate vanishing-viscosity source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-component vanishing-viscosity hierarchy with power-law-separated relaxation scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the coupled inclusions \(0\in\partial\mathcal R_u(\dot u_\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\mathbb V_u\dot u_\varepsilon+D_u\mathcal E(t,u_\varepsilon,z_\varepsilon)\) and \(0\in\partial\mathcal R_z(\dot z_\varepsilon)+\varepsilon^\alpha\mathbb V_z\dot z_\varepsilon+D_z\mathcal E(t,u_\varepsilon,z_\varepsilon)\), with \(\alpha>0\). At rescaled jumps, \(\alpha=1\) retains coupled viscous motion. If \(\alpha>1\), the \(z\)-viscosity vanishes faster, so \(z\) relaxes on the faster scale while \(u\) is effectively frozen. If \(0<\alpha<1\), the corresponding roles are reversed. Hence different scale ratios can select different limiting jump paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal viscosity scales give coupled jumps; separated power-law scales produce hierarchical relaxation and can select different limiting transitions.
knowledge_statements.title: Multirate Viscosity Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the multirate-limit container, and the stated scale ordering is formally consistent with the coefficients shown. The coupled-versus-hierarchical regime classification is specialized and can depend on the precise rescaling and contact-set framework, so it cannot be accepted without a matching multirate vanishing-viscosity source.

children.title: Evolutionary Limits for Rate-Independent Systems
children.top_down_role: Dynamic convergence, relaxation, and homogenization of rate-independent evolution.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Rate-Independent Systems: Theory and Application
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Approximation, relaxation, and evolutionary convergence
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Rate-Independent Systems: Theory and Application

children.title: Evolutionary Gamma Convergence
children.top_down_role: Dynamic passage from converging energetic systems to limiting evolution.

assumptions_latex: A sequence of energetic systems has equicoercive energies and dissipations.
Initial data are well prepared, and the required mutual recovery sequences and power-control estimates hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every convergent sequence of energetic solutions has a limiting curve satisfying stability and energy balance for the effective system.
review_flags: A specialized source is required for the exact evolutionary convergence hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energetic-solution form of evolutionary variational convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Evolutionary Gamma convergence of \((\mathcal E_\varepsilon,\mathsf D_\varepsilon)\) to \((\mathcal E_0,\mathsf D_0)\) requires more than pointwise-in-time Gamma convergence: compactness, well-prepared initial data, compatible recovery sequences for stability, and convergence of time-dependent power must permit passage to the energy balance. Under these hypotheses, if \(u_\varepsilon\) satisfies global stability and the energy-dissipation balance for the \(\varepsilon\)-system and \(u_\varepsilon(t)\to u(t)\), then \(u\) satisfies \(\mathcal E_0(t,u(t))\leq\mathcal E_0(t,v)+\mathsf D_0(u(t),v)\) for every admissible \(v\), together with the limiting energy-dissipation balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic Gamma convergence combines compactness, stability recovery, and power convergence so that energetic solutions pass to solutions of the effective system.
knowledge_statements.title: Evolutionary Gamma Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind is suitable for this topic, but phrases such as "required mutual recovery sequences," "power-control estimates," and "converge evolutionarily" do not specify a checkable theorem hypothesis set. No source is cited from which the intended evolutionary Gamma-convergence theorem and its exact assumptions can be recovered.

children.title: Rate-Independent Effective-Evolution Synthesis
children.top_down_role: Effective evolution generated by microstructure and variational relaxation.

children.title: Rate-Independent Variational Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Relaxed energetic structures governing effective rate-independent evolution.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological state space and the incremental functional is bounded below.
Previous states converge to a prescribed state \(u_-\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dynamically relevant relaxed step is governed by the lower-semicontinuous envelope of the combined energy-dissipation functional.
review_flags: The exact relaxation topology and compatibility hypotheses require a dedicated source.
The combined relaxation need not equal separate relaxation of energy and dissipation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation of one rate-independent incremental step in a fixed topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed time \(t\) and previous state \(u_-\), define the incremental functional \(\mathcal I_{t,u_-}(u)=\mathcal E(t,u)+\mathsf D(u_-,u)\). Its rate-independent variational relaxation is \[\overline{\mathcal I}_{t,u_-}(u)=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}\bigl(\mathcal E(t,u_n)+\mathsf D(u_-^n,u_n)\bigr):u_n\to u,\ u_-^n\to u_-\right\}.\] A relaxed incremental state minimizes \(\overline{\mathcal I}_{t,u_-}\). Because recovery sequences for the two terms may be incompatible, \(\overline{\mathcal I}_{t,u_-}\) is generally not determined by separately relaxing \(\mathcal E(t,\cdot)\) and \(\mathsf D(u_-,\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rate-independent relaxation lowers the entire incremental energy-plus-dissipation functional along compatible state sequences, not necessarily its two terms separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Independent Variational Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits variational relaxation, and the record correctly emphasizes relaxation of the combined incremental functional. The topology, treatment of the varying previous state, equicoercivity or existence conditions, and claimed possible incompatibility of separate relaxations require a dedicated source.

children.title: Rate-Independent Homogenized Evolution
children.top_down_role: Macroscopic evolutionary behavior produced by fine-scale heterogeneity.

assumptions_latex: The microscopic systems are equicoercive and admit an evolutionary homogenization limit.
Initial data and external loading are compatible with the effective limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under evolutionary homogenization, limits of microscopic solutions solve the rate-independent evolution determined by the effective energy and dissipation.
review_flags: A source is required to specify admissible microstructures and homogenization hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energetic formulation of a homogenized rate-independent evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal E_\varepsilon,\mathsf D_\varepsilon)\) be microscopic rate-independent systems and let \(u_\varepsilon\) be energetic solutions. If the systems converge evolutionarily to \((\mathcal E_{\mathrm{hom}},\mathsf D_{\mathrm{hom}})\), then every compact subsequence satisfies \(u_\varepsilon(t)\to u(t)\), and the limit obeys \[\mathcal E_{\mathrm{hom}}(t,u(t))\leq\mathcal E_{\mathrm{hom}}(t,v)+\mathsf D_{\mathrm{hom}}(u(t),v)\] for all admissible \(v\), together with the homogenized energy-dissipation balance and the effective initial condition. Static homogenization of \(\mathcal E_\varepsilon\) alone does not imply this conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evolutionary homogenization passes microscopic stable states and energy balances to a rate-independent evolution governed by effective energy and dissipation.
knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Independent Homogenized Evolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits homogenized evolution, but the premise that the systems "converge evolutionarily" largely assumes the passage-to-the-limit property asserted in the conclusion. A sourced homogenization theorem is needed to replace this shorthand with concrete hypotheses on the microscopic systems, topology, stability recovery, and energy balance.

children.title: Relaxation–Homogenization Interactions
children.top_down_role: Structural interplay between variational relaxation and scale elimination.

assumptions_latex: Relaxation and homogenization are defined on the same class of incremental functionals and topology.
Both iterated limits exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two procedures commute exactly when their iterated effective incremental functionals coincide; incompatible recovery sequences can make them differ.
review_flags: A concrete sourced noncommutation example is required for stronger certification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Commutation boundary for relaxation and homogenization of incremental problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathscr R\) denote lower-semicontinuous relaxation and \(\mathscr H\) denote homogenization of the incremental functionals \(\mathcal I_\varepsilon\). Relaxation and homogenization commute precisely when \((\mathscr R\mathscr H\mathcal I)(u)=(\mathscr H\mathscr R\mathcal I)(u)\) for every admissible state \(u\). Equality can fail when sequences producing microscopic homogenization cannot simultaneously realize the oscillations or concentrations required for relaxation, especially when energy and dissipation share internal variables. In that case the effective incremental minimizers, and therefore the synthesized rate-independent evolutions, depend on the order in which the two limits are performed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation and homogenization commute only when compatible recovery sequences realize both limits; coupled microstructure can make the two effective evolutions differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation–Homogenization Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container. The equality of the two iterated operators is only the definition of commutation, while the substantive assertions about incompatible recovery sequences and order-dependent effective evolutions require a concrete framework and a sourced noncommutation result or example.

children.title: Microstructure-Driven Effective Dissipation
children.top_down_role: Dissipative behavior emerging from unresolved microscopic mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: The periodic density \(r(y,v)\) is measurable in \(y\), convex and positively one-homogeneous in \(v\), and coercive.
Microscopic rates may redistribute periodically while preserving their mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cell minimization defines a convex, positively one-homogeneous effective dissipation that may differ from the dissipation evaluated at the mean rate.
review_flags: The cell formula applies to a simplified local periodic model and needs a matching source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cell representation for a local periodic, rate-independent dissipation density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a periodic cell \(Y\) and macroscopic rate \(v\), define \[\mathcal R_{\mathrm{eff}}(v)=\inf\left\{\int_Y r(y,w(y))\,dy:w\in L^1(Y),\ \int_Yw(y)\,dy=v\right\}.\] The constraint preserves the macroscopic rate while permitting microscopic redistribution among phases. The resulting \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous. In a homogenized rate-independent evolution, the dissipation of an absolutely continuous segment is \(\int_0^T\mathcal R_{\mathrm{eff}}(\dot u(t))\,dt\), with the corresponding variation used for trajectories containing jumps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Microscopic phases redistribute a prescribed average rate to minimize cell dissipation, producing an effective one-homogeneous macroscopic dissipation.
knowledge_statements.title: Microstructure-Driven Effective Dissipation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits effective dissipation, but the cell formula silently requires a normalized cell measure; for a general cell the mean constraint and integral require normalization. A matching homogenization source is also needed to justify this simplified redistribution formula and its extension from absolutely continuous rates to jump variation.

children.title: Static–Dynamic Limit Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Failure of static variational convergence to determine the intended dynamic limit.

assumptions_latex: \(W\) is nonconstant, smooth, and periodic; \(\Phi\) is coercive and smooth.
The energies are \(\mathcal E_\varepsilon(t,u)=\Phi(u)-\ell(t)u+\varepsilon W(u/\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Static Gamma convergence to the smooth energy does not determine the dynamic limit because the oscillatory forces remain of order one.
review_flags: A source is required for the precise effective dynamic law of the wiggly-energy example.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wiggly-energy mechanism showing that static convergence can miss effective friction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in\mathbb R\) and \(\mathcal E_\varepsilon(t,u)=\Phi(u)-\ell(t)u+\varepsilon W(u/\varepsilon)\), where \(W\) is nonconstant and periodic. Then \(\mathcal E_\varepsilon(t,\cdot)\) converges uniformly, hence Gamma converges, to \(\mathcal E_0(t,u)=\Phi(u)-\ell(t)u\). Nevertheless, \(D_u\mathcal E_\varepsilon(t,u)=\Phi'(u)-\ell(t)+W'(u/\varepsilon)\) contains order-one oscillatory forces. Rate-independent or viscously regularized evolutions can therefore exhibit pinning, delayed motion, or an effective dissipation absent from the evolution obtained directly from \(\mathcal E_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing-amplitude periodic energy wrinkles disappear statically but retain order-one forces, causing pinning or effective friction in the dynamic limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Static–Dynamic Limit Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the static-dynamic mismatch container, and the uniform static convergence and order-one derivative oscillations are correctly identified. The dynamic conclusion is not tied to a specified rate-independent or viscous evolution law, and the claims of pinning, delay, or effective dissipation require a precise wiggly-energy source and model.

children.title: Rate-Independent Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Characteristic pathologies separating energetic, local, and viscosity-selected evolution.

children.title: Premature Energetic Jumps
children.top_down_role: Global stability selecting transitions earlier than local mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: The state space is a metric space \(X\), the dissipation distance is \(\mathcal D:X\times X\to[0,\infty]\), and \(\mathcal E:[0,T]\times X\to(-\infty,\infty]\).
A continuous branch \(u_{\mathrm{loc}}\) remains locally stable until time \(t_{\mathrm{loc}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A premature energetic jump occurs precisely when \(t_{\mathrm{en}}<t_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

notation.meaning: first failure time of global energetic stability
first loss time of local stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energetic solutions with global stability, contrasted with a locally stable continuation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
t_{\mathrm{en}}:=\inf\bigl\{t\in[0,T]:\exists v\in X,\ \mathcal E(t,u_{\mathrm{loc}}(t))>\mathcal E(t,v)+\mathcal D(u_{\mathrm{loc}}(t),v)\bigr\}.
\]
If \(t_{\mathrm{en}}<t_{\mathrm{loc}}\), global energetic stability forces departure from \(u_{\mathrm{loc}}\) although that branch still satisfies the chosen local stability criterion. Such a transition is called a premature energetic jump. The boundary is specific to global-stability solution concepts and need not occur for locally stable or vanishing-viscosity evolutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global energetic stability can force a jump before the followed branch loses local stability; this strict separation of failure times characterizes a premature energetic jump.
knowledge_statements.title: Premature Energetic Jumps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematical intent fit the terminal container, but the claim depends on a specific energetic-solution framework, a precise local-stability criterion, and conventions for the first failure times. No citation is supplied to validate those choices or the assertion that global stability forces the stated departure.

children.title: History-Dependent Branching Regimes
children.top_down_role: Multiple locally stable paths and history-sensitive selection.

children.title: Metastable Local Branches
children.top_down_role: Competing locally stable evolutionary paths.

assumptions_latex: For each loading value \(\lambda\), the incremental functional is \(\Phi_\lambda(v;u^-):=\mathcal E(\lambda,v)+\mathcal D(u^-,v)\).
The state space \(X\) is metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(u_i(\lambda)\) is locally stable but need not minimize \(\Phi_\lambda(\cdot;u_i^-)\) globally.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local incremental metastability in a nonconvex rate-independent system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A map \(u_i:I_i\to X\) is a metastable local branch if, for every \(\lambda\in I_i\), there exists \(r_i(\lambda)>0\) such that
\[
\Phi_\lambda(u_i(\lambda);u_i^- )\leq \Phi_\lambda(v;u_i^-)
\quad\text{whenever }d(v,u_i(\lambda))<r_i(\lambda),
\]
while for at least one \(\lambda\in I_i\) there exists \(w\in X\) with \(\Phi_\lambda(w;u_i^-)<\Phi_\lambda(u_i(\lambda);u_i^-)\). Thus the branch is locally stable but not globally stable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metastable branch consists of local incremental minimizers that, for some loading values, have competitors with strictly lower global incremental energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Metastable Local Branches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the container, but the predecessor notation \(u_i^-\) is not defined as a function of the loading or history. In addition, the conclusion says each branch need not be globally minimizing, whereas the definition only requires a strict global competitor at at least one loading. A source fixing the intended incremental metastability convention is required before choosing the correct formulation.

children.title: History-Dependent Branch Selection
children.top_down_role: Branch choices determined by prior loading or transition history.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic local evolution rule acts on loading histories \(\lambda:[0,T]\to\Lambda\).
At least two locally stable states coexist at some loading value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branch selection is history-dependent if equal present data can produce unequal selected states.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path dependence among coexisting metastable branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
History-dependent branch selection occurs when there exist two admissible loading histories \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\) and a time \(t_*\) such that
\[
\lambda_1(t_*)=\lambda_2(t_*),
\qquad S[\lambda_1](t_*)\neq S[\lambda_2](t_*),
\]
even though both selected states satisfy the same local stability condition at the common present loading. The differing states must result from distinct earlier loading segments, basin entries, or switching events, rather than from different instantaneous data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selection is history-dependent when two load paths reaching the same current loading leave the system on different locally stable branches.
knowledge_statements.title: History-Dependent Branch Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind and path-dependence idea fit the container. However, equality of the current loading alone does not establish equality of all instantaneous data for a state-dependent evolution, and the admissible histories and selection operator are not specified. A hysteresis or rate-independent evolution source is needed to determine the appropriate criterion.

children.title: Branch Switching Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where local stability no longer preserves the active branch.

assumptions_latex: Two distinct locally stable candidates \(u_i(\lambda)\) and \(u_j(\lambda)\) coexist.
The incremental functional is \(\Phi_\lambda(v;u^-)=\mathcal E(\lambda,v)+\mathcal D(u^-,v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equality-and-selection condition defines the switching boundary \(\Sigma_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: boundary between selection regions for branches i and j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Switching boundary for competing local incremental branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed predecessor \(u^-\), define \(\Sigma_{ij}\) as the set of loadings \(\lambda\) satisfying
\[
\Phi_\lambda(u_i(\lambda);u^-)=\Phi_\lambda(u_j(\lambda);u^-),
\]
for which every neighborhood of \(\lambda\) contains admissible perturbations selecting branch \(i\) and admissible perturbations selecting branch \(j\). Equality alone is insufficient: the second condition requires \(\Sigma_{ij}\) actually to separate the two selection regions. Crossing this set may therefore switch the locally followed branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A switching boundary is an equal-cost locus that locally separates perturbations selecting two different metastable branches.
knowledge_statements.title: Branch Switching Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits a switching-boundary leaf, but an equal incremental-cost locus is not a universal switching boundary for locally stable or hysteretic branch-selection rules. Switching may instead be governed by loss of stability, basin boundaries, or history-dependent thresholds. The selection mechanism must be sourced before this model-specific definition can be accepted.

children.title: Jump-Cost Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Dependence of transition costs on regularization and parametrization.

assumptions_latex: A jump connects \(u_-\) to \(u_+\) in a state space \(X\).
Each regularization \(k\in\{1,2\}\) induces a nonnegative transition density \(p_k(u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Jump cost is nonunique when \(c_1(u_-,u_+)\neq c_2(u_-,u_+)\).

notation.meaning: transition cost induced by regularization k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularization-dependent costs assigned to a rate-independent jump.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(k\in\{1,2\}\), let
\[
c_k(u_-,u_+):=\inf_{\substack{\vartheta\in AC([0,1];X)\\ \vartheta(0)=u_-,\ \vartheta(1)=u_+}}
\int_0^1 p_k(\vartheta(s),\dot\vartheta(s))\,ds.
\]
Jump-cost nonuniqueness occurs if two admissible vanishing-regularization or parametrization procedures yield \(c_1(u_-,u_+)\neq c_2(u_-,u_+)\). Consequently the endpoints and the rate-independent dissipation alone do not determine the transition cost; the selected contact potential or path parametrization remains part of the solution concept.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jump cost is nonunique when admissible regularizations or parametrizations assign different minimum transition actions to the same pair of endpoints.
knowledge_statements.title: Jump-Cost Nonuniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-phenomenon kind matches the container, and differing transition actions from distinct regularizations can express jump-cost nonuniqueness. However, dependence on parametrization is not automatic: actions generated by positively one-homogeneous contact potentials are invariant under admissible increasing reparametrizations. A Balanced-Viscosity or parametrized-solution source is required to fix the admissible densities and the exact nonuniqueness mechanism.

children.title: Loss of Rate Independence
children.top_down_role: Residual viscosity and other mechanisms introducing intrinsic time scales.

assumptions_latex: The evolution contains a positively one-homogeneous dissipation \(\mathcal R\) and a residual viscous coefficient \(\varepsilon>0\).
The trajectory \(u\) is absolutely continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The viscous contribution changes under time reparametrization, so the evolution is not rate-independent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of time-reparametrization invariance caused by residual quadratic viscosity.

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Maximum Principle for Continuous-Time Systems with Smooth Dynamics p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the dissipation functional
\[
\int_0^T\left(\mathcal R(\dot u(t))+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\lVert\dot u(t)\rVert^2\right)dt,
\]
a time rescaling \(u_a(t):=u(at)\) preserves the one-homogeneous contribution after the corresponding interval change, but multiplies the quadratic contribution by \(a\). Hence, when \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\dot u\not\equiv0\), traversing the same state-space curve at different speeds changes its dissipation. Time-reparametrization invariance, and therefore rate independence, is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any nonzero quadratic viscous term makes dissipation depend on traversal speed, introducing an intrinsic time scale and destroying rate independence.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Rate Independence

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Maximum Principle for Continuous-Time Systems with Smooth Dynamics p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and scaling observation are mathematically appropriate, but the cited maximum-principle section does not specifically support residual viscosity or rate independence. The statement also uses a norm without introducing a normed state space and defines \(u_a(t)=u(at)\) without specifying the rescaled time interval. A directly relevant source is required to settle the precise formulation.
